title: As students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed Serbia | Novak Simin | The Guardian
description: After freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning state, says Novak Simin, a member of Serbia’s Student List movement
Author: Novak Simin
Headline: After freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning state, says Novak Simin, a member of Serbia’s Student List movement
Content: Student List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/APView image in fullscreenStudent List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/APOpinionSerbiaAs students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed SerbiaNovak SiminAfter freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning stateMon 26 Oct 2026 15.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.56 EDTShareTwo years ago, I harboured no political ambition whatsoever. I was a student at the faculty of technical sciences in Novi Sad, my home town, pursuing a PhD in human resources and simply living my life. That was until thecanopy collapse at the newly renovated train stationin Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people. I took part in street protests and rallies in response to this shocking event, and like many others, realised that it needed to be a turning point.This was not an unavoidable tragedy. Systemic corruption and a culture of entrenched impunity were obvious factors in the collapse. But instead of ordering a full and impartial investigation and coming clean on official failings, the authorities began pushing back against us for demanding justice. We werevilifiedand attacked in the streets but law enforcement did nothing. So we took refuge in our lecture halls and schools, barricading ourselves inside faculty buildings, ready for a long haul.Democratic principles have long been ignored in Serbia but we made sure we observed them in our gatherings. As our coordination developed, we made sure we had the same clear goal for every demonstration we organised: pressuring a corrupt government to meet our demands. And these were demands that in any free country would have been accepted automatically. We wanted, for example, all the documentation concerning the renovation of Novi Sad railway station to be made public, without redaction, and that everyone responsible for the works be held to account. We demanded that those who assaulted us in the streets be arrested and prosecuted. Instead of agreeing, state officials beganbrandingusfascists and traitors.I was personallytargetedfor speaking out. As I handled media relations and communications, this often meant giving interviews to the country’s few remaining independent outlets. For this, I was accused by the regime’spropaganda machineof money laundering “millions” and conspiring with foreign powers. Others had to leave the country after being accused of high treason; some spent months in detention on manufactured, illegally obtained evidence. Many of us were placed under surveillance, our parents threatened, and many were fired from jobs and dragged through the mud in the pro-government popular press.But none of that intimidation broke us; rather it hardened our resolve. And eventually, when it became clear the regime would never concede, we opted to enter the electoral arena ourselves. That was the genesis of theStudent List. Through open, democratic plenary sessions, we nominated individuals of integrity and competence, people who were committed to justice and freedom for a silenced society.Our aims were clear and never wavered: we wantedSerbiato be governed by the rule of law, independent public institutions, transparency and solidarity in a fractured nation. We marched thousands of kilometres across Serbia, campaigning relentlessly and in doing so helped, I believe, to rekindle hope among the broader public. State propaganda could not hope to drown out that much unfiltered grassroots momentum.Now the regime has fallen, our collective effort to rebuild Serbia begins. True, sceptics may argue that we have filled parliament with political novices. The truth is that we have filled it with people eager to serve and willing to learn. Our newly elected representatives are professors, doctors, lawyers, farmers and scientists, all experts in their fields. Each has an established record of honest work and civic integrity. They may lack traditional political backgrounds, but they have spent the past two years studying the realities of governance and public trust. That very lack of direct political involvement is why the Serbian people have placed their faith in us: they did not vote for slick rhetoric or cynical manoeuvreing. They voted for clean hands.We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory; rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.This mandate must first of all dismantle the culture of impunity. That requires verifiably independent prosecutors, fully transparent public procurement processes, and legal accountability for anyone who treated state resources as private spoils. For too long our teachers, healthcare workers and civil servants have seen their expertise subordinated to party loyalty cards. We want to restore the dignity of these dedicated public servants.We have taken our country back, and are proud to stand as free citizens of Serbia. If this historic turning point proves anything, it is that this country does not belong to an untouchable ruling elite. It belongs to all of us. We have proven that dignity is non-negotiable. Now, the real work begins. This victory marks the end of institutional fear. For the first time in years, we can breathe freely.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNovak Simin is a member of Serbia’s Student List movementDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril  | Jordana Timerman | The Guardian
description: After the rejoicing, it will be vital to learn the lessons. The rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible, but progressives cannot rest for a moment, says commentator Jordana Timerman
Author: Jordana Timerman
Headline: After the rejoicing, it will be vital to learn the lessons. The rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible, but progressives cannot rest for a moment, says commentator Jordana Timerman
Content: Supporters gather to watch Lula speak in São Paulo on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters gather to watch Lula speak in São Paulo on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersOpinionBrazilLula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in perilJordana TimermanAfter the rejoicing, it will be vital to learn the lessons. The rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible, but progressives cannot rest for a momentMon 26 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 20.15 EDTShareThe impossible happened. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silvawon a fourth termin Sunday’s runoff election in Brazil, overturning Flávio Bolsonaro’s first-round lead in a historic comeback. No candidate has ever lost the first round and won the second, until now. Grassroots mobilisation, alongside social welfare policies, helped turn the contest into a referendum on Brazilian democracy, rallying voters against a candidate seeking to restore the legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro,imprisoned for plotting a coupafter his 2022 defeat. Lula’s victory suggests that defending democracy can still be a powerful electoral argument against the ascendant right.Having already consolidated most of the leftwing vote, Lula had limited room to attract supporters of other candidates after his first-round defeat. His best chance lay in mobilising abstainers and reconnecting with working-class voters. The Workers’ party intensified its grassroots and digital campaigns, using social media influencers and messaging networks to reach supporters. Nearly 3 million more Brazilians voted in the runoff, and Lula gained ground across the country, particularly in major cities and his north-eastern strongholds. He also appealed to voters’ immediate economic concerns, drawing on a record of reducing poverty and inequality, andincreasing benefits under Bolsa Família, the landmark welfare programme he launched in 2003. Lula framed the election as a choice between protecting social gains and democratic institutions, or returning to the Bolsonaro family’s attacks on both, warning that his opponent would compromise Brazil’s sovereignty by aligning himself with Donald Trump.The implications extend far beyond Brazil. Lula’s victory interrupts a regional trend: rightwing candidateshave won seven presidential electionsacross Latin America in the past 18 months. Two decades ago, Lula was among the leaders of Latin America’s pink tide, a succession of leftwing governments that reshaped the region’s politics and sought greater autonomy from Washington. Today, he finds himself resisting a new regional wave moving in the opposite direction, without a comparable coalition of allies.Lula’s victory is welcome, but we shouldn’t forget that Flávio Bolsonaro wonmore than 48%of valid votes, demonstrating the enduring strength of a movement with substantial representation in an increasingly rightwing congress. His proposals on security and the economy appealed to voters frustrated by high living costs, including working-class Brazilians who had traditionally supported Lula. This mirrors the success of authoritarian-leaning rightwing candidates across the continent. Frustration with crime, economic insecurity and established political parties has propelled a new right promising tougher security policies and attacking progressive social agendas. From Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, to Javier Milei in Argentina, to the recentelection of Abelardo de la Espriellain Colombia.The emerging rightwing alliance is, in many ways, the mirror image of the pink tide, developing in close alignment with Trump and his ambitions to reassert US dominance over the hemisphere.The relationship is mutually reinforcing: rightwing leaders who gained ground through domestic discontent look to Washington to consolidate their power, while the US relies on those same governments and movements to advance its strategic interests. In his victory speech, Lula said the surge of street support in recent weeks “was a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s back yard”. His declaration directly challenges the so-calledDonroe doctrine, which asserts an expanded US role in policing the region.Since returning to office, Trump has used endorsements, sanctions, tariffs and financial assistance to reward allies and put pressure on opponents. Hebacked rightwing candidatesin Honduras and Colombia. He has turned a blind eye to Salvadoran president Bukele’snegotiations with criminal organisations(Bukele denies having made an informal pact with these organisations). And ahead of Argentina’s 2025 legislative elections,he offered Milei a $20bn financial lifelinewhile warning that US generosity depended on the electoral outcome.Security provides a particularly powerful instrument for this alignment. The Trump administration has invoked the fight against “narcoterrorism” to expand its military role and apply pressure on governments to accept Washington’s priorities. Terrorist designations have helped justify the operation that captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela,threats of unilateral strikesagainst Mexican cartels andjoint military operationsin Ecuador. Washington has also discussed similar operations with Colombia. The designations do not themselves authorise military action, but they strengthen the administration’s justifications to intervene beyond US borders.Brazil demonstrates how this strategy can also serve Washington’s allies outside government. The Bolsonaro family had itselfsought Washington’s interventionagainst the Brazilian judiciary during Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The Trump administration imposed tariffs on Brazil and sanctions againstsupreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes. Following lobbying from the Bolsonaros, Washington also designated Brazil’s two largest criminal organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, reinforcing Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign message that Lula was failing to confront organised crime.The stakes extend beyond the Bolsonaro family’s political fortunes. Washington has pressed Lulafor access to Brazil’s critical mineralsas it seeks to reduce dependence on China. Lula has defended Brazil’s freedom to trade with other partners.Brazil shows that Trump’s interventions can backfire. In 2025,Lula’s approval ratings roseafter Washington threatened punitive tariffs over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The president turned the dispute into a defence of national sovereignty, making resistance to foreign interference a defining theme of his re-election campaign. The electoral effect of Trump’s involvement is difficult to isolate, but the backlash helped Lula mobilise support. Combined with grassroots organising, appeals to democracy and social welfare policies, it offers one possible response to the regional right’s advance.Yet a defining feature of that resistance is that it has remained national. Brazil’s size gives it a capacity to resist Washington that none of its neighbours possess. Lula has also been pragmatic in keeping that resistance national, rather than attempting to forge a regional coalition against Trump’s hemispheric ambitions.He also faces a strengthened right at home. Flávio Bolsonaro hasrefused to concede, seeking to annul the election over a last-minute extension of voting hours that both campaigns had requested. Electoral authorities maintain that the extension did not affect the outcome.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe region’s rightward shift also obscures a fragmented political landscape. Across Latin America, deeply divided electorates have produced closely contested elections, complicating claims that either the left or the right has established a durable political hegemony.Brazilis a case in point: Lula’s victory interrupted the right’s advance, but nearly half of voters backed a candidate who embraced much of Trump’s agenda.Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington. Brazil may have stopped the blue tide at its borders, but it has yet to emerge as a regional bulwark against it.Jordana Timerman is a journalist based in Buenos Aires. She is the managing editor of The Ideas Letter and compiles the Latin America Daily BriefingThe Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions about the election and the future of Brazil from 1500 GMT on Tuesday 27 October as part of ourConversationsseries. title: ‘I laughed so hard my Tampax fell out’: Michael Gambon’s pranks revealed by the stars he cracked up | Stage | The Guardian
description: He made Daniel Radcliffe’s Harry Potter fart, left Judi Dench unable to control herself and told a fry-up fantasy about Helen Mirren. A new biography details the star’s mischief
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: He made Daniel Radcliffe’s Harry Potter fart, left Judi Dench unable to control herself and told a fry-up fantasy about Helen Mirren. A new biography details the star’s mischief
Content: ‘I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby’ … Michael Gambon.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby’ … Michael Gambon.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianStage‘I laughed so hard my Tampax fell out’: Michael Gambon’s pranks revealed by the stars he cracked upHe made Daniel Radcliffe’s Harry Potter fart, left Judi Dench unable to control herself and told a fry-up fantasy about Helen Mirren. A new biography details the star’s mischiefChris WiegandMon 26 Oct 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJasper Rees’s authorised biography ofMichael Gambon, published three years afterthe great actor’s death, has nuanced accounts of his performances in Shakespeare, Beckett and Pinter as well as The Singing Detective and the Harry Potter films. There are even chapters devoted to his hands (“the biggest you’ve ever seen on anybody” – Brian Cox) and similarly enormous feet. But, Gambon being Gambon, there are also dozens of accounts of tomfoolery on and off stage …‘One of the funniest people I’ve ever met’David Hare’s 1995 play Skylight is set in a draughty flat where a dish of spaghetti is cooked up on stage. Those kitchen cupboards proved useful for Lia Williams to hide when Gambon’s goofing got to her at theNational Theatre. Gambon would adopt a different accent or speak in tongues during a scene and “when he made me laugh it was hell on Earth because there was nothing I could do about it” said Williams, who called him “one of the funniest people I’ve ever met”. She continued: “One time I laughed so hard that my Tampax fell out and I had to deal with that for an entire act.”View image in fullscreen‘It was hell on Earth!’ … Michael Gambon and Lia Williams in Skylight at the National Theatre in 1995.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDinner with Judi, Ken and NatashaIbsen’s Ghosts was a hot potato when it was first staged in 1882 thanks to its scandalous plot involving syphilis and incest. Gambon had some fun with the spuds when playing the self-righteous Pastor Manders in an 80s BBC TV version. Director Elijah Moshinsky envisioned a tense, sombre dinner scene and Gambon sat alongside Judi Dench and Kenneth Branagh. The potatoes were duly passed around byNatasha Richardson. “I’ll just have the usual eight,” requested Gambon. His co-stars’ corpsing led them to leave the set. “We couldn’t control ourselves at all,” confessed Dench.Dumbledore unleashes Fartis TemporusNot every actor’s biography includes “fart machines” in the index but toots fake and real are let off in several chapters. When Gambon took over the role of Dumbledore in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, he and Alan Rickman prankedDaniel Radcliffeby triggering a fart machine during a closeup of the young star when he was in a sleeping bag alongside fellow Hogwarts students. “I was initially really annoyed,” said Radcliffe, before concluding that if Rickman and Gambon had engineered it then “that is pretty funny”.A storm and a FoolWhen Gambon played King Lear for the RSC in 1982, Antony Sher sported a red nose as the clownish Fool. The poster presented themas a sort of double actand Sher was widely seen as stealing the limelight. Rees likens it to Gambon taking on what is often referred to as an “actor’s Everest” only to find another climber “clambering frantically up the same rope”. Adrian Noble, who directed the tragedy, said Gambon “joshed [Sher] mercilessly”. During the storm scene he reportedly bellowed: “Come on out, you little red-nosed fucker!”View image in fullscreenMichael Gambon and Robert De Niro in The Good Shepherd in 2006.Photograph: Ronald GrantThe fake De NiroWhen he was appearing on stage in Arthur Miller’s A View from the Bridge, Gambon kept a signed photo ofRobert De Niro– with words of admiration for Gambon’s work – on his dressing room table. The pair would appear together in the film The Good Shepherd in 2006 but had never even met by the time he was doing A View from the Bridge. The fake autograph and note – “I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby” – were apparently written by Gambon himself.The play that changed my life: ‘Michael Gambon’s offstage anarchy as Falstaff made the show better’Read moreWink winkOne festive season in the late 60s, Gambon found himself starring in the Christmas show Hans, the Witch and the Gobbin at Birmingham Rep – much to his annoyance, remembered co-star Anthony Higgins. A prodigious swearer, Gambon decided to add to his stage makeup for a performance. “One night he’d written on one eyelid ‘fuck’ and on the other ‘off’,” said Higgins. Gambon blinked each eye to deliver the message to Higgins. Artistic director Peter Dews had to give him a word of warning.View image in fullscreenSurprise chocolate cake … Michael Gambon and Rupert Graves in The Caretaker at the Comedy theatre, London, in 2000.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian‘Rupert wet himself regularly’When Gambon played the tramp Davies ina 2000 revival of Harold Pinter’s playThe Caretaker, he revelled in repelling theatregoers – as well as the brothers played by Douglas Hodge and Rupert Graves. One night, according to Rees’s book, Gambon had his back to the audience and buried his hand in his trousers, where he had stowed away a serving of chocolate cake. He withdrew his smeared fingers and sniffed them, causing his co-stars to crack up. “Rupert was in terrible trouble,” remembered Hodge. “Rupert wet himself regularly.”A fry-up with CleopatraGambon loved to supply journalists with tall tales and see who believed him. He treated one interviewer to an “insight” into how he andHelen Mirrenprepared while in the wings for their roles as Antony and Cleopatra for the RSC. Mirren, he assured the journalist, got into character by performing a mime in which she prepared a dish of ham and eggs for Antony. “Absolute rubbish,” Mirren told Rees, though added: “It’s a lovely story.”Michael Gambon: The Authorised Biography by Jasper Rees is published by Century (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Sin or virtue? How envy can actually be helpful | Well actually | The Guardian
description: In her new book, Envy, Stacy Kim explains how to understand the feeling, identify your deeper desires and use them to achieve your goals
Author: Adrienne Matei
Headline: In her new book, Envy, Stacy Kim explains how to understand the feeling, identify your deeper desires and use them to achieve your goals
Content: ‘Envy signals to us our goals,’ as we tend to envy people similar to ourselves compared to superstars.Photograph: Shannon Fagan/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Envy signals to us our goals,’ as we tend to envy people similar to ourselves compared to superstars.Photograph: Shannon Fagan/Getty ImagesWell actuallySin or virtue? How envy can actually be helpfulIn her new book, Envy, Stacy Kim explains how to understand the feeling, identify your deeper desires and use them to achieve your goalsAdrienne MateiMon 26 Oct 2026 12.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 21.16 EDTShareIn the 16th-centurypoemThe Faerie Queene, envy is a ghoulish figure riding a ravenous wolf, sad to see the fortune of others and “wonderous glad” of their hardship. It’s not a flattering depiction; better to be thankful for what we have, rather than dwell on such a bitter and self-destructive feeling, right?Maybe not. “I think that when we don’t examine our envy, that’s when it leads us astray,” says Dr Stacy Kim, social scientist, life coach and author of the new bookEnvy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Want. Kim wrote the book after seeing the way envy came up for her coaching clients and reflecting on the role it had in her own life. The book is informed by social science and philosophy research, as well as her personal and professional experiences.To Kim, a lifelong envier who says sibling rivalry propelled her to fast-track a PhD in educational policy and leadership, envy tells you “there’s something important here,” Kim says. “Envy signals to us our goals,” as well as “what is within our reach”, as we tend to envy people similar to ourselves more so than, say, superstars.View image in fullscreenIllustration: Courtesy of BalanceBut how to transform envy from sulky to superpower? Kim gave us some points to consider.What kind of envy are you feeling?Envy is “simply wanting something that someone else has”, Kim says. “Everyone envies – it’s normal.”Yet it comes in different forms. In 2009, Dutch researchersexploredand formalized the concepts of “malicious” and “benign” envy. Malicious envy happens “when you are so focused on the person that has what you want” and you want to “take them down”, like the evil queen who hoped to kill Snow White, explains Kim. Benign envy, however, is more like admiration-meets-motivation: it helps you “focus on what it is that you want”, Kim says, rather than sabotage.Jealousy, meanwhile, is a whole different ballpark. It usually involves three parties and the threat of losing a special status or relationship to another person.How would you feel if you had what you envy?Next comes what Kim calls “probably the most important part of the examination”: looking past the thing you covet to the “intangible desire” buried deep within. It’s often not so much the object you’re craving but “thefeelingyou think you’re going to get” when you acquire or achieve it, she says. Kim’s envy of people with bigger apartments, for instance, “is really not just about the apartment”, but rather a desire for a calm, uncluttered home.Once you’ve named the deeper desire, you can look for alternative routes to fulfill it. For Kim, that might mean spending “more time decluttering”. If you have a goal that is out of reach, be creative; if you have a pang of envy watching a 20-year-old ballet dancer but you’re 42 and have never taken a class, you might be interested in being able to move more confidently in your own body. An adult beginner dance course could help with that. If you envy the young, you can access the feeling of a promising new life experience by getting out of your comfort zone and trying something novel and intimidating, like visiting a new country or pursuing further study.Have you listened to the “SIReNs”?When a pang of envy strikes, Kim’s mnemonic tool for processing it is an acronym: SIReN. Here’s what it stands for:Similar target: “You remind yourself: ‘Hey, the reason why I’m feeling this envy is because what I want is within my reach,’” she says.Intangible desire, as mentioned aboveRelevant comparison: Identify which specific domain – something you care about or already participate in – is relevant to your desiresNegative emotion: How long does it last? How intense is the message it’s sending? This tells us how important the feeling is.Does the desire truly come from you – or someone else?Humans are “social beings”, Kim says, and this means we often mirror what everyone else wants – French academic René Girard called this quality mimetic desire. As a result, it’s easy to fall into the trap of keeping up with the Joneses, says Kim.With envious clients, Kim likes to use a technique from psychologist Robert Leahy that can help identify your priorities: imagine you are nothing, a perfect void. Then, one by one, add one thing back into your life. The things you reach for first signal what you value most. Note what they are – your body, your family, your work, your possessions, or something else – and the order they arise in.In Kim’s experience, the exercise often emphasizes that “deep connections with people you care about”, being of service to others, and meaningful work are what people most need to be happy – not superficial wants like an expensive car or country club membership.Can you become closer to the person you envy?An individual you envy today might become a mentor, friend or role model tomorrow. If you know the person, Kim says, “ask some questions” about how they achieved their goals – “usually people will want to be helpful.”If that feels unsafe or they’re a stranger, Kim advises “researching that person”. If it’s appropriate and you feel comfortable – for instance, they’re an artist with a feedback form on their website – you could send them a compliment or thank you note for the work they’ve done that has affected you without “asking anything in return”.This might feel odd to you, and that’s understandable. In Korea, Kim says, the word 부럽다 (buleobda) essentially means “I envy you,” and is “an acceptable phrase to use” as an everyday conversation starter. But in the US, copping to envy might feel exposing and odd, even if honest vulnerability could spark a connection between you and another person. Try “I admire you” or “I’m really curious about how you did that,” instead.Have you tried to focus on your peers instead of those ‘in front’?Envy can come from focusing on people you perceive as being ahead of you. Kim suggests also checking, “Who’s behind me? Or who’s next to me?”When a goal feels impossible, whether because of structural inequalities or just bad luck, you can “hook arms” with people in a similar situation, and look for ways to help each other make progress, she says. Alternatively, offering to collaborate with, share information with or be a mentor to people who may, in fact, admire and envyyoucan not only boost your self-esteem, but also build useful connections and earn you the respect of your peers. When those around you succeed, “you can own some of that success too,” says Kim. A zero-sum game mentality or scarcity mindset isn’t typically as satisfying or useful for overcoming challenges, she notes. Solidarity can be much better.Becoming more aware of envy doesn’t mean the complicated feeling won’t affect you. It may always be unsettling to feel envious of another person, and even to realize you’re an object of envy to others; as Kim says from experience: “Just because you study envy doesn’t mean that it goes away.” And yet, to an extent, envy is normal and unavoidable. Recognizing why it shows up and how it can be harnessed for good can be a valuable skill.Envy: Why Wanting What They Have is the Key to Getting What You Wantby Stacy S Kim is out now via BalanceExplore more on these topicsWell actuallyHealth, mind and body booksHealth & wellbeingShare

title: The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s 21-year tragic arc | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment
Content: Manchester United’s success has been limited since the Glazers took over the club in 2005.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester United’s success has been limited since the Glazers took over the club in 2005.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonManchester UnitedThe horse that ushered in Manchester United’s 21-year tragic arcThere’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected momentSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 26 Oct 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnd so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester Unitedprepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford.Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roofthat leaks symbolically?It’s worth remembering where all this began. The United story has taken on the aspect of a classical tragedy and, like all good tragedies, it begins with a small, seemingly unconnected moment, amplified by pride, that ends up bringing the whole edifice crashing down.In 1999, Mull of Kintyre, a horse owned by the Irish millionaire John Magnier, won the Gimcrack Stakes at York. Traditionally, the winning owner would give a speech at the Gimcrack Dinner, but Magnier was a shy man who hated public speaking so he asked his friend, the United manager Alex Ferguson, to give the speech on his behalf. The racing establishment, though, refused: it had to be the owner. To spite them, Magnier named Ferguson as the owner of another horse, Juniper. The following year, Juniper was narrowly beaten in the Gimcrack Stakes. Magnier, though, was determined. So the year after that, he made Ferguson the owner of Rock of Gibraltar, which had won its first three races. Rock of Gibraltar won the Gimcrack easily and Magnier, waving a metaphorical two fingers at the racing authorities, watched Ferguson give the speech.Magnier was largely making mischief, but he was also happy to do a favor for a friend, to give Ferguson a better experience of racing, and he benefited from the association of the horse with such a famous name. In addition, Ferguson did not get on well with the United chairman, Martin Edwards, and had a sense that football clubs were becoming good investments. Accordingly Magnier and his associate JP McManus bought shares in United. (The full storyis explored by the journalist David Walsh here).It turned out, though, that Rock of Gibraltar was a much better horse than anybody had realized, winning seven Group One races in a row. The stud fees would be worth tens of millions of pounds. Ferguson believed the verbal deal was that he could choose 50% of the prize money won by Rock of Gibraltar (about £800,000) or 50% of the stud fees, which ended up being worth tens of millions. He went for the latter. Magnier’s recollection was rather different: 5% of the prize money or one stud nomination a year.Ferguson sued and, with his name on the ownership documents, probably would have won had it gone to trial. But then rumors started to spread about some of Ferguson’s financial dealings at United. Paid actors at United’s annual general meeting raised awkward points, then Magnier and McManus sent a list of 99 questions to the United board, which mysteriously found their way into the Daily Mail. United were highly embarrassed. Fans began to demonstrate against Magnier and McManus at race meetings. A settlement was reached, with Ferguson paid £2.5m to drop the action. But the damage was done.Magnier and McManus had decided to sell their shares in United, and another shareholder was ready and waiting: Malcolm Glazer. Ferguson backed Glazer, who launched his leveraged buyout. Magnier and McManus sold up in 2005 for £260m, a profit of a little under £100m. Had they waited for Ratcliffe, who bought a similar stake in 2024, they would have received roughly £1bn more than that. For Ferguson, a threat had been dealt with.The problem was that Glazer and his family would provesome of the worst club ownersin English history. For 20 years, United have been addled by debt and have made consistently terrible footballing decisions. Ferguson’s team was good enough, and his personality big enough, that United won five league titles and a Champions League after the takeover, but once his genius had gone, there was nothing left.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA mismatched squad built up over seven flawed managerial appointments and a multiplicity of conflicting approaches will not readily be sorted out. Carrick is the latest victim of a crisis 21 years in the making. For the want of a horse a club was lost.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedSoccer with Jonathan WilsonMichael CarrickUS sportsHorse racingThe Glazer familyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unfair’ cliff-edge rule that punished carers to be abolished in budget | Carer's allowance | The Guardian
description: Controversial mechanism that hit unpaid carers with huge penalties to be scrapped following Guardian investigation
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Controversial mechanism that hit unpaid carers with huge penalties to be scrapped following Guardian investigation
Content: The new digital taper system will see just £1 of carer’s allowance payments removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit.Photograph: Andrew Bret Wallis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe new digital taper system will see just £1 of carer’s allowance payments removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit.Photograph: Andrew Bret Wallis/Getty ImagesCarer's allowance‘Unfair’ cliff-edge rule that punished carers to be abolished in budgetControversial mechanism that hit unpaid carers with huge penalties to be scrapped following Guardian investigationPatrick ButlerandPippa CrerarMon 26 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe controversial rule that led to unpaid carers being punished with penalties amounting to thousands of pounds is to be abolished, the Guardian can reveal.The chancellor,John Healey, is to announce a new digital taper system for carer’s allowance in Wednesday’s budget, effectively ending what is regarded as one of the UK benefit system’s most feared and unfair administrative practices.The scandal was highlighted in a Guardian investigation that revealed howhundreds of thousands of carershave, through no fault of their own, run up life-changing debts in recent years after overstepping weekly earnings thresholds by just a few pence.Those hefty debts were then ruthlessly chased down by welfare officials who pursued carers using legislation designed to recover funds from drug dealers and organised crime bosses. Some unpaid carers were convicted of fraud as a result.The cliff-edge rule dictates that if a carer earns even a penny more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – they forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, currently £86.45. A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40.Although the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) was aware when carers breached earnings limits, it refused to warn them, insisting the onus was on carers to report any changes.Thousands of carers spent long periods unaware of the breach, in some cases for years, resulting in overpayment debts typically of £2-£5,000 but in some cases as much as £20,000.Under new rules set to be announced in the budget, the introduction of a tapered system instead of a cliff-edge means only £1 of carer’s allowance will be removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit, meaning carers are no longer left financially worse off for working additional hours or receiving a pay rise.The announcement is one of five more “everyday fixes” announced by Healey ahead of his budget on Wednesday. His room for manoeuvre is severely constrained by the tight fiscal backdrop, a result of global events including the conflict in Iran.Treasury insiders have warned that the budget will be low-key, with difficult tax and spend decisions put off until the spending review next year. But there is anxiety among some Labour MPs over the scale of the announcements, after Andy Burnham came to power promising major change.Victims of carer’s allowance crisis ‘need speedier repayments’, say campaignersRead moreAmong the other measures to come is making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent – with the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles locked in, and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles to 35p per mile. The Treasury said the move would benefit about 3 million people – employees and self-employed – who use their own vehicle for work.The chancellor’s intervention on the draconian cliff-edge rule comes after anaward-winningGuardian investigationwhich revealed how the DWP had for years known of theprofound distressit caused carers – including warnings from a DWP whistleblower – but did nothing about it.The Guardian’s reporting triggered a government-commissioned independent review of carer’s allowance overpayments by disability rights expert Liz Sayce,published last year. It found unpaid carers suffered depression and hardship on a huge scale after falling foul of a series of systemic injustices, including the cliff edge.In one case highlighted bythe review, a carer was penalised when the national minimum wage had increased at a faster rate than the earnings limit. This put her 15p a week above the limit, even though her hours had not changed. Months later, she was told she had incurred a £2,000 penalty for above-limit earnings totalling just £5.The review found the outdated design of carer’s allowance, coupled withlongstanding DWP failuresin its administration, meant about 180,000 carers ran up overpayment debts amounting to £300m between 2019 and 2025.Campaigners welcomed the decision, calling it a “long-overdue reform” although there was disappointment the technical demands of building a new digital system to run the taper means it will not be introduced before the end of the decade.Carers UKsaid the cliff-edge plays havoc with carers’ attempts to work part-time around their minimum 35 hours a week of caring duties, with many giving up paid work or refusing promotions, overtime or bonuses because of the risks.John Healey, the chancellor, told the Guardian the carer’s allowance system had worked against carers. “That means doing an extra shift or getting a small pay rise can actually leave someone worse off. That cannot be right.“So at this budget on Wednesday, we’re ending that cliff-edge. Carer’s allowance will instead taper as earnings increase, giving carers the freedom to work a little more and earn a little more without suddenly losing all their support.”As well as unpaid carers, Healey’s budget will benefit an extra 150,000 new parents – including self-employed fathers and partners who have previously missed out – with parental support worth up to £194 a week.Ministers are also removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on paraffin.There will also be hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, to make it more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue.Healey will also reportedly raise the minimum wage by about 4% to about £13.20 an hour. However, in a sign of government concern over rates of youth unemployment, the chancellor is said to be about to raise youth rates by roughly the same amount, rather than the inflation-busting levels seen in previous budgets.Labour came to office in 2024 promising to raise the youth rate, which applies to workers under 21, to the same level as the full rate. But ministers have become concerned in recent months that raising the minimum wage for younger workers could be dissuading companies from taking on young employees.“We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn’t mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren’t fair,” Burnham said.“If you’re a nurse driving to work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket.”Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said: “We have listened to [carers’] concerns about the cliff-edge built into the system which leaves them financially worse off for taking on a few more hours, or getting a modest pay rise, and intend to bring that to an end.”Kirsty McHugh, chief executive ofCarers Trust, said: “It is great news that the government is acting to remove the carer’s allowance cliff-edge. This is an important and long-overdue reform.“We would urge the government to use this change as a springboard for a wider and deeper reform of carer’s allowance – a benefit that remains stuck in the 1970s and must be made fit for the future.”Emily Holzhausen,CarersUK director of policy, said: “We have countless stories from carers who have shared their deep fears of going just a few pence over the earnings limit and losing all of their benefit.“It’s absolutely right that the chancellor is thinking of practical changes that will make their lives easier. A taper on the earnings limit should give families much more choice about working and still caring.”Explore more on these topicsCarer's allowanceBudget 2026CarersJohn HealeySocial careBudgetnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election win | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Leaders and governments worldwide congratulate Lula on dramatic comeback seen as an important signal to rest of Latin America
Author: Tom Phillips
Headline: Leaders and governments worldwide congratulate Lula on dramatic comeback seen as an important signal to rest of Latin America
Content: Lula and his running mate Geraldo Alckmin address supporters after winning the presidential runoff in São Paulo, Brazil.Photograph: Natacha Pisarenko/APView image in fullscreenLula and his running mate Geraldo Alckmin address supporters after winning the presidential runoff in São Paulo, Brazil.Photograph: Natacha Pisarenko/APBrazil‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election winLeaders and governments worldwide congratulate Lula on dramatic comeback seen as an important signal to rest of Latin AmericaLula supporters celebrate election victory – in picturesTom Phillipsin São Paulo andTiago Rogeroin BrasíliaMon 26 Oct 2026 11.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 18.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Brazilian president, has vowed that dictatorship and fascism will never return toBrazilafterwinning a historic fourth termin power by defeating his far-right opponent, Flávio Bolsonaro.“This is God’s work – and it’s thanks to all of you,” Lula told tens of thousands of supporters who had gathered in central São Paulo in the early hours of Monday to celebrate his dramatic election comeback.A few hours earlier, Lula pulled off the most stunning political fightback in modern Brazilian history, bouncing back from afirst-round defeatin early October to trounce Bolsonaro by more than 4m votes in the runoff.Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president in defeat of far-right Flávio BolsonaroRead more“Today is a historic day,” Lula declared, before telling a sea of elated supporters: “Democracy always, dictatorship never again. Democracy always, fascism never again.”Never, since the return of democracy after the 1964-85 military regime, had the first-round loser managed to win the second vote.But Lula did precisely that on Sunday, promptingjoyous scenes on the streets of São Pauloand cities all across Brazil. He won with 64.2m votes to Bolsonaro’s 59.8m, a 51.79% to 48.21% victory. It was at least 10m more votes than Lula secured in the first round.While Bolsonaro initially refused to concede, his party acknowledged the election results on Monday, nearly a full day after Lula’s win.“We recognize the presidential ​election ​results,” Liberal party head Valdemar Costa ​Neto said. “But we ​believe ‌the issues ​raised ​need to be properly clarified.“Chart showing increase in second-round votingLula’s health minister, Alexandre Padilha, told the Guardian shortly after the result was confirmed: “This is a huge victory for the Brazilian people who in the second round had the chance to think about what President Lula means for the environment, for the defence of our national health service and our education system and the Brazilian constitution. And the risks that the extreme right candidate entailed.“It’s a massive victory – not just for Brazil. It’s also an important signal to the rest of Latin America and to the world,” Padilha said at the hotel where the president’s team was following the count in São Paulo.Bolsonaro rejected the result, following in the footsteps of his father, the former presidentJair Bolsonaro, who refused to concede after losing the 2022 election to Lula and was later convicted of plotting a coup. He called Lula’s victory “sacanagem”, a Portuguese word that roughly translates as “bullshit”.1:38Lula re-elected for fourth term as Bolsonaro refuses to accept Brazil election result – videoThe US administration had been rooting for a Bolsonaro victory that would have seen the pro-Donald Trump so-called “orange wave” continue its sweep across the region into Latin America’s largest democracy. Trump took almost 24 hours to comment and, on Monday, appeared to endorse Bolsonaro’s claim when asked about Brazil’s election.“It looked terrible to me. I thought it was a terrible look. I didn’t take sides, but it looked like another rigged election, frankly,” the US president said.How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in BrazilRead moreWhen asked if he intended to do anything in response, Trump said: “Well, I’m not running Brazil. I’m running the USA. And I just thought that the election was – I like Lula. I get along with him very well. I just think it had a very bad look, the election, the way it was tabulated. The extension given was very strange.”Other leaders and governments from across the political spectrum were quicker to recognise Lula’s victory. Mexico’s leftwing president, Claudia Sheinbaum, tweeted: “Long live democracy, the people of Brazil won.” Spain’s prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, wrote: “The global progressive resurgence has just begun.”The UK foreign secretary, Ed Miliband, called Lula’s victory “a historic win for the global progressive movement” and said his government looked forward to continuing to collaborate on “shared values of democracy, social justice and climate action”.Rightwing South American leaders also recognised Lula’s victory, with Chile’s president, José Antonio Kast, calling Lula to offer congratulations and Peru’s president, Keiko Fujimori, saluting “the Brazilian people for this democratic day”.View image in fullscreenLula supporters celebrate in São Paulo.Photograph: Sebastião Moreira/EPAEven Colombia’s far-right president, Abelardo de la Espriella – who had publicly backed Bolsonaro and appeared in a recent live broadcast with him on social media – acknowledged Lula’s win, tweeting: “When the people decide at the ballot box, their will is respected because it is sacred. That’s what democracy is all about!”The European Commission president, Ursula von der Leyen, said: “Democracy and multilateralism have won in Brazil.”A spokesperson for China’s foreign ministry said: “China respects the choice of the Brazilian people.”Besides Trump, one of the few powerful international voices of dissent was Elon Musk, who claimed the “math doesn’t add up” for Lula’s comeback, ignoring the fact that it did because of the historically low level of abstention in the second round.9:21Brazil: how did Lula beat far-right Bolsonaro? | The LatestIn the lead-up to Sunday’s vote, the US had been accused of seeking to influence the result through a campaign of economic and diplomatic pressure. Erika Hilton, a transgender lawmaker who recently became the most voted-for woman in Brazil’s congress, said those efforts had failed. “We have defeated the interference of the US government, which thought it could turn our country into its back yard. Brazil and the Brazilians are too gigantic to be anybody’s back yard,” she said.Lula’s victory will also have profound consequences for the environment and the Amazon rainforest in what is the world’s most biodiverse nation. On the eve of the vote, the former environment minister Marina Silvahad warnedthat Bolsonaro, if elected, would seek to finish the “perverse project” of rainforest destruction started by his father, whose 2019-22 administration coincided with a surge in deforestation.On Sunday night, Silva was in a buoyant mood, telling the Guardian: “My heart is happy and filled with gratitude to God and the Brazilian people.”View image in fullscreenSome suspect Flávio Bolsonaro is now likely to flee to the US when his senate term runs out in February.Photograph: Adriano Machado/ReutersShe said: “The thing I most feared was that our Indigenous territories would be invaded again [under another Bolsonaro government]. Now, I am certain that they will be preserved and that there is no risk of illegal miners returning to destroy these populations.”ForFlávio Bolsonaro, the future looks bleak. As the scale of Lula’s victory became clear on Sunday night, the mood at the Brasília mansion where Bolsonaro was watching the count soured, with what had initially resembled a lively birthday party turning into something closer to a wake. Like football supporters heading for the exits midway through the second half because their team was being thrashed, crestfallen guests began heading home.Map of Brazil election results marked in tints of red and blueOne of them approached the dozens of journalists waiting for Bolsonaro’s speech to shout that it was the “north-east’s fault”, insulting the region where Lula has historically won most of his votes.Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril | Jordana TimmermanRead moreOne photographcirculated by Lula supporters showed a dejected Bolsonaro in tears, although it had been taken on the eve of the vote.Another imageshowed a red-faced Bolsonaro flanked by visibly mortified allies as they came to terms with their defeat. São Paulo’s pro-Bolsonaro governor, Tarcísio de Freitas, sat next to him covering his face with his hand.On Paulista Avenue, where huge crowds had gathered to hear Lula speak, one reveller wore a costume of Flávio Bolsonaro behind bars. Some suspect the senator is likely to flee the country to the US once his term runs out in February and he loses parliamentary immunity. Bolsonaro is facing a series of federal police investigations over suspected misdeeds including money laundering, although he maintains he is innocent.Lula supporters delighted in the idea that the far-right politician may soon join his father, who is serving a 27-year sentence for his coup attempt, in jail.“Oh, how awful! Poor little thing!” João Maluf, a 27-year-old psychologist, shouted sarcastically as he held up his mobile phone to the crowd to show them a photograph of a visibly distraught Bolsonaro. “We want rid of these fucking Bolsonaros,” Maluf said.Explore more on these topicsBrazilLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election | Benjamin Netanyahu | The Guardian
description: Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu tours the Mahane Yehuda market in Jerusalem ahead of the national election.Photograph: Kevin Coombs/ReutersView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu tours the Mahane Yehuda market in Jerusalem ahead of the national election.Photograph: Kevin Coombs/ReutersBenjamin NetanyahuNetanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to electionIsraeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in pollsEmma Graham-HarrisonandJulian Borgerin JerusalemMon 26 Oct 2026 15.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s historyRead moreThe Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in asocial media postabout Iran’s nuclear programme.View image in fullscreenAn AI-generated image of a nuclear strike on Tel Aviv was posted on Netanyahu’s X account on Sunday.Photograph: X/Benjamin NetanyahuIsrael’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration withIranat a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convinceDonald Trumpto launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes haddestroyedIran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, is the most likely challenger to Netanyahu as prime minister.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAMost polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.View image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu has been emphasising in his campaign the support he has from Donald Trump.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APIn the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.Explore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelUS-Israel war on IranIranMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend
Content: Andy Burnham had indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about a closer relationship with the EU.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/Pool AFP/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham had indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about a closer relationship with the EU.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/Pool AFP/APBrexitNo 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movementClarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekendAletha AduPolitical correspondentMon 26 Oct 2026 14.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDowning Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue.Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels.Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue.It forced a Downing Street spokesperson to say the prime minister was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option.“He is saying that it’s time for us to discuss what kind of long-term relationship withEuropeis best for Britain and he is referring to the types of areas that that agreement and long-term future could cover,” she said.“He is crucially not leaning either way, and that will be for the British public to decide. And his focus for now is on next month’s summit and the practical arrangements that we hope to make there, which will add billions to the economy.”She said the government was not yet at the stage of confirming whether the public would decide on proposals for the UK to move closer to the EU.Asked whether Burnham accepted that returning to freedom of movement would mean Britain lost control over legal migration, the spokesperson said: “He’s not setting out a concrete position either way. What he’s saying is that he wants to have a conversation with the British public about what our long-term future with theEuropean Unionlooks like.”In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham indicated thatstaying out of free movement would no longer be a red linein discussions about how the UK can move closer to the EU.On Monday, Burnham ruled out the possibility of rejoining the EU within this parliament and indicated he could fight the next general election on a promise to take the UK back into the EU. He said: “I’m not going to move away from the red lines that were in theLabourmanifesto.”Hours later, Burnham told journalists “no” when asked if he would allow the UK to join the EU freedom of movement scheme without a referendum.When asked whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he said: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”Challenged on how his constituents in Makerfield would feel about his discussions about the EU, given 65% of them voted to leave, Burnham added: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing.“The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation toBrexit.”Burnham even ruled out an early general election on a manifesto change on this issue. He told GMB: “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” However, he left the door open to a future fight on a promise to fully rejoin the EU.Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit on 20 November, as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. He believes the Brexit deal has “weakened our economy [and] weakened our control of immigration” and is not good enough for the country.Explore more on these topicsBrexitAndy BurnhamLabourEuropean UnionEuropeForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and his bad behaviour was normalised, trial told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Brand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant alleges
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Brand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant alleges
Content: Russell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court with his wife, Laura, on Monday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenRussell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court with his wife, Laura, on Monday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAUK newsRussell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and his bad behaviour was normalised, trial toldBrand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant allegesEmine SinmazMon 26 Oct 2026 16.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was “normalised and dismissed” by those around him, his former personal assistant has told a court.Helen Berger alleged she had seen Brand treat women badly and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend walking in on him having sex with someone in his dressing room.She also told the court she had overheard the comedian receiving oral sex in a toilet cubicle and once found a celebrity leaving his bedroom in the morning.Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Wearing a grey suit and white shirt, Brand sat still in the dock as statements from prosecution witnesses were read to Southwark crown court on Monday.Berger worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when he was at the height of his fame. She said the job was one of the hardest she had had because Brand had “non-stop energy”, and she left because she was “sick of him” and burnt out.“Though I’d worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level. I think everyone else normalising and dismissing Russell’s behaviour made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is,” Berger said in a May 2024 witness statement to police.Describing his behaviour, she added: “He was always in his underwear, he loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on. I remember Sadie Frost came over to interview him. He did the whole interview in his underwear and no shirt and an open robe.”At the time, Brand had filming commitments for Channel 4’s Big Brother as well as MTV and the BBC, a radio show, a national comedy tour, a weekly Guardian column, and was writing a book.“In addition to his busy work, he had an insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night. He was very open about what his needs were,” Berger said in the statement, which was read out by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC.“He never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed,” Berger alleged. “There were times when I was at his house and he would be on a deadline … and he would get antsy and joke with me: ‘May I go and have sex now?’”She recalled Brand turning to the website Myspace to find random women to sleep with and how women, including an unnamed celebrity, would often be at his flat in Camden, north London, for sexual liaisons. “He was like a peacock, women always approached him,” she said.When Brand was recording an MTV show, Berger alleged, he told her to ask women for their phone numbers, which she said made her feel uncomfortable.She alleged that on other occasions she had to keep Brand’s mother and girlfriend away from his dressing room because he was having sex, and she overheard him receiving oral sex in a women’s toilet. Berger described overhearing Brand talking and recognising his trademark cowboy boots in the cubicle next door.Berger recalled that when Brand was headlining the Edinburgh festival, he ended his show by asking that anyone with “a vagina and heartbeat” meet him at a pub afterwards. Many women showed up, Berger said, and she later found him having sex in the shower at the apartment he was renting.“I never witnessed Russell doing anything against the law,” she said, before adding: “I did see Russell treat women poorly.”She recalled how he was once “hitting on” a woman who revealed she had a boyfriend, before Brand “turned in a way” that startled his then PA. “He literally just switched off his charm and moved on to the next woman,” Berger said.The court also heard a witness statement from the manager of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Brand when she worked at Channel 4 in 2009. The manager said she recalled the alleged victim telling her that Brand’s associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy had “told her she had to give Mr Brand a massage” or he would not continue with the day’s recording.The manager recalled being told that Bayles and Roy “were both there the whole time and watched and laughed while Mr Brand sexually assaulted her right in front of them”.The sister of a woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted and then orally raped by Brand at a Soho bar in 2004 told the court she was “upset and almost in shock” the next morning.In 2023, the woman called her sister in tears and told the “full story” of what had happened, the court heard.“It sounded like she was struggling to catch her breath,” the witness recalled. “She said his [Brand’s] eyes had gone completely black and he was possessed or had been a completely different person.”The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Harry Kane claims men’s Ballon d’Or to end England’s 25-year wait for winner | Ballon d'Or | The Guardian
description: Harry Kane became first Englishman in 25 years to win men’s Ballon d’Or with Spain’s Alexia Putellas securing the women’s award for a third time
Author: Barney Ronay
Headline: Harry Kane became first Englishman in 25 years to win men’s Ballon d’Or with Spain’s Alexia Putellas securing the women’s award for a third time
Content: Spain’s Alexia Putellas and England’s Harry Kane with their Ballon d’Or trophies, which they won in London.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPAView image in fullscreenSpain’s Alexia Putellas and England’s Harry Kane with their Ballon d’Or trophies, which they won in London.Photograph: Tolga Akmen/EPABallon d'OrHarry Kane claims men’s Ballon d’Or to end England’s 25-year wait for winnerAlexia Putellas picks up women’s award for third timeEngland captain acclaimed in London ceremonyBarney Ronayat the London PalladiumMon 26 Oct 2026 19.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 19.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHarry Kane is the Ballon d’Or winner for 2026, the first Englishman to win football’s most prestigious individual trophy in 25 years.Two hours into a lavishly excitable ceremony at the Palladium Theatre in London, Kane’s name emerged from the final envelope to wild cheers inside the auditorium. The women’s Ballon d’Or, awarded moments earlier, was won by Alexia Putellas of London City Lionesses, a third Ballon, five years on from her first in the colours of Barcelona.In the men’s voting, Kane finished ahead of co-favourites Lamine Yamal of Barcelona andKylian Mbappéof Real Madrid, an outcome that will perhaps cause the familiar consternation among the hierarchy of those clubs, not to mention the vast online fan army attached to the superstar players in Kane’s wake.But Kane is also a fully deserving winner of football’s ultimate gong. The L’Équipe-sponsored trophy is awarded by a vote of journalists and administrators across the footballing super-scape. For Kane, it is reward for a year during which he has won the European Golden Boot, played a major role in Bayern Munich’s Bundesliga title, captained England to a World Cup semi-final, and above all shown himself to be a wonderfully humble superstar player.Quick GuideBallon d'Or: full list of winnersShowBallon d’Or MenHarry Kane(England and Bayern Munich)WomenAlexia Putellas(Spain and London City Lionesses)Kopa Trophy (under-21)MenLamine Yamal(Spain and Barcelona)WomenVicky López(Spain and Barcelona)Yashin Trophy (goalkeeper)MenUnai Simón(Spain and Athletic Bilbao)WomenCata Coll(Spain and Barcelona)Gerd Müller Trophy (striker)MenHarry KaneWomenCharlyn Corral(Mexico and Pachuca)Johan Cruyff Trophy (coach)MenLuis de la Fuente(Spain)WomenPere Romeu(Barcelona)Club of the Year MenParis Saint-GermainWomenBarcelonaSócrates Award (humanitarian)Bukayo Saka(England and Arsenal)Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.“It was really tough this year, the incredible players I was up against,” Kane said as he received the trophy, going on to congratulate everyone else nominated for anything else, and thank pretty much everyone he has ever played with.“I am almost speechless. Being here in London has made it extra special,” he added.View image in fullscreenThe Wembley Stadium arch is lit up gold in honour of Harry Kane’s Ballon d’Or win.Photograph: Harry Murphy/The FA/Getty ImagesAs a pure goalscorer, his numbers are astonishing this year, with 89 goals for club and country since the start of August 2025. At Bayern, Kane has also become a darling of the Bundesliga for his all-round game, creativity, intelligence and professionalism. Bayern paid a record €100m fee up front for Kane three years ago, a transfer that broke the club’s usual recruitment patterns and raised some concerns, given Kane was 30 at the time.It is a measure of his contribution on and off the pitch that this outlay is now seen as entirely vindicated. As a Ballon d’Or winner, Kane now enters rarefied company, heir to a prize that revolved around the Messi-Ronaldo two-hander for so many years, and which promises not just a form of sporting ultimacy but a vast uplift in current and future commercial earnings.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFootball DailyKick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of footballEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMore widely, the award is a coronational moment for Kane himself, 16 years into a professional career that has taken in loan spells at Leyton Orient and Millwall, running himself into the ground to make it in the Premier League, and now, for posterity, into the lineage of elite footballers.Earlier this month,Kane equalled England’s all-time caps record, while nudging his international goal tally on to 91 in 125 appearances. Aged 33, he still has a home Euros two years from now in his sights as England’s captain and a final opportunity for a different kind of footballing immortality.Explore more on these topicsBallon d'OrHarry KaneKylian MbappénewsShareReuse this content
