title: ‘Local services are vital’: Former rough sleepers on what helped them off the streets | Homelessness | The Guardian
description: As Andy Burnham hosts a rough sleeper summit, frustration mounts over ‘ridiculous bureaucracy’ and lack of hostel places
Author: Jessica Murray
Headline: As Andy Burnham hosts a rough sleeper summit, frustration mounts over ‘ridiculous bureaucracy’ and lack of hostel places
Content: Martin Fletcher at the building occupied by the Basis Sunderland housing charity before it closed down in July because of a lack of funds.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianView image in fullscreenMartin Fletcher at the building occupied by the Basis Sunderland housing charity before it closed down in July because of a lack of funds.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianHomelessness‘Local services are vital’: Former rough sleepers on what helped them off the streetsAs Andy Burnham hosts a rough sleeper summit, frustration mounts over ‘ridiculous bureaucracy’ and lack of hostel placesJessica MurraySocial affairs correspondentMon 26 Oct 2026 13.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMartin Fletcher had been homeless for more than 20 years after being made redundant before he finally got accommodation in Sunderland in 2024.What was the one thing that finally ended his rough sleeping and sofa surfing? “My mindset, mainly,” the 61-year-old said. “The realisation that I was getting old and I couldn’t live like this for ever. And also help from a charity who didn’t judge, who didn’t bombard me with forms – they made me a cup of tea and built up a picture of what I needed and helped me get back on track.”That charity was Basis Sunderland’s drop-in service for housing support, which closed its doors in July for lack of funding.Fletcher found this devastating: “How are they going to end rough sleeping when services like this are closing? You’ve got to remember, unless people want to come in off the streets, it won’t happen. They said they did it during Covid but they didn’t – I was still on the streets. And not all homelessness is visible. So these local services are vital.”View image in fullscreenMartin Fletcher, who was homeless for more than 20 years, says not all rough sleeping is visible.Photograph: Mark Pinder/The GuardianAndy Burnham, who had announced plans in July to end rough sleeping and offer everyone in need a bed by Christmas, hosted a summit on the issue on Monday.The prime minister told the Downing Street event this commitment would be backed bya further £432m to sustain the support into next year. A number of charities had raised concerns that people would simply end up back on the streets after Christmas. Burnham said he was “bringing together businesses, charities and local leaders in Downing Street to make sure this is a solution that lasts”.Those who work in the homelessness sector have warned there is no easy solution. The Guardian has spoken to several formerly homeless people to find out what helped them back into housing, sometimes after decades of sleeping on the streets.Amy Bell, 37, was street homeless and struggling with heroin addiction for seven years between 2013 and 2020. She said she hit “rock bottom” when her council said it could offer her only a voucher for a two-man tent, which she “cried herself to sleep in at night”.The next morning, workers employed by the same council put her tent and all her belongings in the bin because it was classed as litter. Borrowing a phone from a Citizens Advice centre, she secured a place at a hostel for a few weeks, which enabled her to reconnect with a local drug treatment service, get a phone with a sim card and start to rebuild.She said being offered a bed in a hostel, even though she was still taking drugs, was the key to getting her off the streets. “The hostel system is broken. You are basically set up to fail,” she added.“They don’t accommodate people with addiction problems, and that’s who it should be for. Eventually you will do something that shows you are still using and they ban you. It doesn’t take long to get kicked out of all of them. And then you’re left with nothing.”View image in fullscreenAmy Bell, who was homeless for seven years, says rough sleepers need help from real people rather than mobile phone appsBell said for Burnham to succeed in abolishing rough sleeping he must get rid of the “ridiculous bureaucracy” that stops people from accessing support.“Everything is done by app now. When you’re homeless, you don’t have that – believe me, if you get a decent phone, you sell it,” she said. “The days of being able to walk into the Citizens Advice bureau or the jobcentre don’t exist any more. Homeless people need a real-life person to help them.”Others the Guardian spoke to said they moved from England to Scotland because it was easier to get help there after it abolished the priority needs test in 2012. According to Crisis, Scotland has some of the most progressive homelessness rights in the world.Tony* became homeless after being released from prison in 2024. He told his probation officer he had nowhere to go but was simply advised to contact a council homelessness team the day of his release.No housing was available and he ended up sleeping in a tent in the woods. “I was a prison leaver, I hadn’t made myself intentionally homeless, but there was nothing. The support was nonexistent,” he said. “I was telling my probation officer where I’m sleeping at our weekly meetings but they didn’t help.”A chance meeting led him to the Salvation Army, where he has been living in supported accommodation for the past two years. With evidence suggesting the amount ofpeople being released from prison into homelessnessis on the rise, Tony said the government must deal with this issue if it wanted to end rough sleeping.“I was in for three years, and they only started talking to me about accommodation 10 days before I was released,” he said. “If I’d been set up with a bedsit or something like that, the government would have paid less in the long run. I would have begrudgingly gone to a hostel but that wasn’t even offered. Something has to change.”* Some names have been changed to protect anonymityExplore more on these topicsHomelessnessAndy BurnhamHousingCommunitiesPovertySocial exclusionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Escaping Idi Amin review – there’s a happy ending to this awful tale … and it should be a lesson to us all | Television | The Guardian
description: Four Britons describe the horrors they witnessed as children as thousands were expelled from Uganda – or killed – by the Ugandan dictator. The new lives they made should teach us something important
Author: Jack Seale
Headline: Four Britons describe the horrors they witnessed as children as thousands were expelled from Uganda – or killed – by the Ugandan dictator. The new lives they made should teach us something important
Content: A reconstruction from episode one of the day Harminder (Harmeet Singh) and his father (Nirmal Singh), who had been interrogated by Idi Amin’s soldiers,  finally escaped to Britain.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Television ProductionsView image in fullscreenA reconstruction from episode one of the day Harminder (Harmeet Singh) and his father (Nirmal Singh), who had been interrogated by Idi Amin’s soldiers,  finally escaped to Britain.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Television ProductionsTV reviewTelevisionReviewEscaping Idi Amin review – there’s a happy ending to this awful tale … and it should be a lesson to us allFour Britons describe the horrors they witnessed as children as thousands were expelled from Uganda – or killed – by the Ugandan dictator. The new lives they made should teach us something importantJack SealeMon 26 Oct 2026 18.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 18.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe contributors to Escaping Idi Amin hardly make any direct comparisons to the present day. They don’t say: look, this part of the story is what Britain is now heading towards. This part is where America is already. These are the same words you can hear across the western world in 2026. They don’t need to. The parallels are obvious and deeply shaming, and, in any case, the story of Uganda viciously expelling its Asian community in 1972 is a humbling terror on its own terms.The star witnesses are four people who would become British citizens, but were Ugandans born and bred when, in 1971, army commander Idi Amin took control of a country that was the only home they had ever known. Bharti, Harminder and Paresh were aged between nine and 11; Maz, who has died since filming his interview for this two-part documentary, was in his early 20s.They remember an idyllic everyday existence that didn’t immediately feel threatened when the sound of distant explosions and popping bullets heralded Amin taking power by force. But soon there was the spectacle of Amin’s political opponents being murdered and, later, mass graves. In August 1972, Amin announced that all Asian Ugandans, about 80,000 people out of a national population of 10 million, were obliged to leave the country within 90 days.View image in fullscreenA dramatic reconstruction of how Paresh (played by Praanshu Naidu) and his siblings would hide under the bed in Uganda.Photograph: BBC/Dragonfly Film and Television ProductionsUganda’s singular social history meant that life was extremely rough as an impoverished African Ugandan in this era. Indian immigrants had become a comfortable middle class of doctors, shopkeepers and white-collar workers; at Ugandan golf clubs, the Asians were members while the Africans carried the bags. Simply driving the blameless Asians out, however, rather than doing the hard work of creating a country where all citizens had a chance to prosper, was inhumane, and Amin did it not to help his people but to shore up his dictatorship by scapegoating a minority.In the UK, toxic debate raged. The economic issues of the time were dominated by unemployment rather than the crisis of inequality and living costs of today but it is embarrassing to see how little has changed. Far-right demagogues, led by Enoch Powell, had convinced a section of the populace that immigrants were the cause of their woes; those people were enraged at the prospect of thousands of Ugandans arriving, and not swayed by the idea that, because the UK had transferred Indians en masse to Uganda when the latter country was a British colonial protectorate, Asian Ugandans were British passport-holders and owed sanctuary. Nor were they convinced of a moral obligation to help fellow human beings, regardless of their links to Britain; or even that a bunch of highly educated professionals and entrepreneurs might be an economic boon. When the government finally agreed to rescue a proportion of the expelled Ugandans, it did so while taking heavy flak.In Uganda, the anatomy of a racist purge was on display. It started with harassment of Asians in the street, then came checkpoints and curfews. Harminder’s father was taken away for questioning by soldiers who came to their family home; he eventually returned, but many who were imprisoned were never seen again. Amin’s secret police became even more lawless and brutal than the regular army.A Ugandan quarry worker carrying rocks on her head: Dan Nelken’s best photographRead moreLong before the 90-day deadline arrived, Asian families realised they were in mortal danger and would have to flee to join the queues of desperate people at the British consulate in the capital, trying to obtain settlement papers and a ticket out. Escaping Idi Amin revolves around two awful reminiscences, by Bharti and Paresh, of what they saw on the road to Kampala when they were stopped by Amin’s soldiers. Both tales involve the children of fleeing families being subjected to barbarity so extreme that it is, on one level, incomprehensible, although on another too easy to comprehend because such cruelty had happened before, has happened since and is happening again. Paresh in particular is visibly broken by the memory of what he saw through the window of the bus taking him to safety, aged nine: “Every time I talk about it, it destroys me a little bit.”There is a happy ending, of sorts. Bharti, Paresh, Harminder and Maz never stopped missing the country they were born in, but they made a new home in Britain, and they made Britain better: it would be hard, for example, to calculate the size of the debt we owe Bharti for her 40 years as a social worker safeguarding children in care. Every minute of Escaping Idi Amin contains an urgent lesson to learn.Escaping Idi Amin aired on BBC Two and is available on iPlayerExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV reviewDocumentaryFactual TVreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My death was reported in Rolling Stone’: how the Zombies made Time of the Season | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘A year after we broke up, we heard that two bands had started touring the US as the Zombies. One group said they were the originals but with a new singer – because I’d been killed in a car crash’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘A year after we broke up, we heard that two bands had started touring the US as the Zombies. One group said they were the originals but with a new singer – because I’d been killed in a car crash’
Content: ‘A DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it’ … the band in 1964.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it’ … the band in 1964.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyHow we madeCulture‘My death was reported in Rolling Stone’: how the Zombies made Time of the Season‘A year after we broke up, we heard that two bands had started touring the US as the Zombies. One group said they were the originals but with a new singer – because I’d been killed in a car crash’Interviews byChris BroughtonMon 26 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRod Argent, writer, Hammond L100 organ and backing vocalsOur first single,She’s Not There, was one of the first songs I wrote, when I was 18. It remained our only hit in the UK by the time we recorded our second album,Odessey and Oracle, in 1967 – this was only three years later but it felt like a lifetime. We’d recently signed to CBS and had been given £1,000, which even then was not a huge amount of money. We recorded pretty quickly in a few sessions spread over six months, producing ourselves for the first time.Time of the Season was the last song I wrote for the album. I was sharing a flat with our bass player Chris White, and we were going to each other’s rooms and playing the different things we had. I said: “I think I’ve just written a song that could be a hit.”The lyrics reflected the mood of the time. In 1967 there were pictures of war on TV, and people were seeing what a devastating thing it was and saying: “I’m not going to be part of this.” The “Who’s your daddy?” line was, in a way, going back to Gershwin’s Summertime, one of the first songs we performed together, but “Is he rich like me?” had kind of a double meaning: “rich” in the sense of understanding how to live.double quotation markIf you’re so bloody good, you come in here and sing itWe recorded at EMI Recording Studios, later known as Abbey Road. The Beatles were in before us making Sgt Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band – we had the benefit of some of the same recording engineers, in particular Geoff Emerick. He found this special way of marrying the bass and the tom-tom sound. I suggested the clap before the beat and a vocal sound after, which became the exhalation.We soon used up our £1,000, but because of the tight timeframe we were working to, there was a spontaneity and freshness that was very valuable. It’s a method I try to preserve. It’s just much more fun.Colin Blunstone, lead and backing vocalsI was learning Time of the Season while we recorded it. Standing where the vocal mic had been set up, I was looking at this big red recording light with a clock underneath it while I tried to get it right. The studio was very strict about sessions finishing on time, and there were these guys with long brown coats moving equipment about. On one occasion, we were standing around a piano working out harmonies and they wheeled it out in the middle of a take.Rod always has an overview of his songs in his head – he can hear the drum track, what the bass should be playing and what the lead vocal should be doing. He’s extremely good at phrasing, so he was in the control room saying: “No, this phrase should be on the beat but the next phrase should be pushed …” Meanwhile, all the time I’m watching the big hand creeping towards five o’clock.Things got a little bit heated. I was saying, “If you’re so bloody good, you come in here and sing it,” and he said, “You’re the bloody lead singer, you stand in there until you get it right!” The language was probably richer than that. It makes me smile now to think I was breaking off from saying the most terrible things to Rod to sing these angelic lines: “It’s the time of the season for loving …”Rod likes to think I disliked Time of the Season, but I just thought there were more commercial songs on the album.Care of Cell 44, to me, sounded like the epitome of a hit single, but obviously I was wrong – it was released ahead of Odessey and Oracle and wasn’t successful. By the time the album came out in Terry Quirk’s misspelled sleeve, the band had split.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve never worked out how it can be both of its time and timeless’ … the Zombies in 1965: (l-r) Hugh Grundy, Colin Blunstone, Chris White, Rod Argent, Paul Atkinson.Photograph: Stanley Bielecki/ASP/Getty ImagesThe following year, Al Kooper left the American band Blood, Sweat & Tears and became a staff producer at CBS. He’d just visited London where he bought about 80 albums that weren’t available in the US, and later said Odessey and Oracle was the one that really stood out. On his first day at CBS he went to see the label’s president, Clive Davis, and said: “Whatever it costs, we have to get this album.” And Davis said: “We already have it. We were going to pass on it – it’s not commercial.”Al fought for it, and CBS released two singles that disappeared without trace. I think Time of the Season was only put out as a favour to Al, but one DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it, and that was where our luck turned. It gradually picked up huge radio interest.By then, it was well over a year since we’d broken up and we were all doing other things, but we soon heard that a couple of other bands had started touring the US as the Zombies – one included two members of ZZ Top. The manager of one of these bands claimed they were the original members with a new singer, because Colin Blunstone had been killed in a car crash. It turned out my death was reported in Rolling Stone.The original Zombies didn’t play together again until 1997, when a box set was launched at the Jazz Cafe in London. I was singing with my solo band, but the other guys came up on stage and let it be known they wanted to play – we hadn’t planned it or rehearsed. We did She’s Not There and Time of the Season and it sounded really good. I thought: “You know what? There really was something special about that band.”Can you say a song’s got legs? Time of the Season wasn’t a success in the UK charts, but people know it. It’s often used in films set in the 1960s but also appears in commercials, where it sounds really current. I’ve never quite worked out how it can be both of its time and timeless.The Zombies release Continue Here, an album of remastered mono B-sides and singles, on 30 October. TheirBegin Here festivalis in St Albans, 30 October to 1 November.Explore more on these topicsCultureHow we madePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The best heated clothes airers in the UK to save time and money when drying your laundry – tested | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Heated airers claim to dry your clothes without costing the earth in energy. We put 19 to the test over two years, from covered options to winged racks
Author: Jane Hoskyn
Headline: Heated airers claim to dry your clothes without costing the earth in energy. We put 19 to the test over two years, from covered options to winged racks
Content: View image in fullscreenGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The FilterLife and styleReviewThe best heated clothes airers in the UK to save time and money when drying your laundry – testedHeated airers claim to dry your clothes without costing the earth in energy. We put 19 to the test over two years, from covered options to winged racksThe best electric heatersJane HoskynUpdatedMon 26 Oct 202611.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRising energy bills and perma-drizzle are conspiring to keep the nation’s laundry damp, not least by making it such a turn-off to turn on the heating. No wonder heated clothes airers are having a moment. These modish appliances sell out within hours of reaching shops and inspire evangelistic fervour among owners, who call them “life-savers” and “gamechangers”.Can a hot clothes horse really change your life, let alone dry your soggy washing as fast as a tumble dryer for a fraction of the cost and, in most cases, with none of the noise? After testing 19 bestsellers over the past two years – during which time I took my tumble dryer to the dump and slashed my dependency on radiators – I can confidently say yes.Not every airer I tested made the final cut. A few, though, impressed me so much I’m now fully converted to the belief that the heated clothes airer is the best thing in laundry since the clothes peg.At a glanceBest heated clothes airer overallLakelandDry:Soon Deluxe 3-tier heated airer and cover£194.98 at LakelandBest budget heated airerBlack+DeckerHeated winged clothes airer£46.99 at AmazonBest heated airer for fast dryingMinkySureDri Heat Pod Pro£59.99 at CurrysWhy you should trust meI’ve spent three decades testing products from Sky boxes to mattress toppers, and it’s made me professionally sceptical of manufacturers’ claims to magically solve domestic problems. I also have a solid background in procrastinating by doing laundry, hanging laundry and folding laundry, so I couldn’t resist the Filter’s offer to pay me to watch clothes dry.How I testedView image in fullscreenWe tested the temperature of the heated clothes airers with an infrared thermometer.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianHeated airers all do much the same thing in much the same way. There are small differences in design – some have triangle frames, some are winged and some have covers – but they’re basically all clothes horses that you plug in. I had to find clear distinctions between them, and this chiefly meant devising fair, quantifiable tests to measure how quickly, evenly and cheaply each airer dried clothes.The key test was a half-hourly laundry weigh-in to measure how quickly each airer dried an identical load. Actually, two identical loads – one small (4kg) and one big (8kg) – 19 times, once for every airer. I removed and weighed the clothes every 30 minutes to see how much moisture had evaporated until the fabric was dry, and this gave me an overall drying time. Room temperature remained at a steady 19-20C throughout. For more behind-the-scenes insights into weighing knickers, check outthe Filter’s newsletter.I took other measurements too, not least to give me something (anything) to do while the laundry dried, such as the dimensions of each airer and the length of its heated bars. I used an infrared thermometer to take the bars’ temperature every 30 seconds to compare heat-up times, and a wattage meter to check power usage. I then used the October 2026 electricity price cap (26.32p a kWh) to work out running costs an hour.After testing, I donated the airers to two organisations that do important work in and around Southampton. The first isScratch, which provides services and furniture for families and individuals experiencing poverty, and the other isYellow Door, a charity offering support for people affected by domestic abuse.Here’s my guide to the 10 best heated clothes airers based on my tests.The best heated clothes airers in2026View image in fullscreen‘The most efficient barred airer I tested’: the Lakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe 3-tier heated airer.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianBest heated clothes airer overall:Lakeland Dry:Soon Deluxe 3-tier heated airer and coverLakelandDry:Soon Deluxe 3-tier heated airer and coverfrom£194.98£194.98 at Lakeland£213.13 at AmazonWhat we loveDries almost as fast as a tumble dryer; has timer and coverWhat we don’t loveIt’s expensive – and we’d like a much longer cableView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£194.98 at Lakeland£213.13 at AmazonThis airer is for anyone who’s fed up with choosing between the expense of a noisy tumble dryer, the mess of clothes on radiators, and the rank stink of laundry slowly drying on a conventional clothes horse. With its ventilated heat-retaining cover in place, it’s the most efficient barred airer I tested.Why we love itLakeland’s Dry:Soon Deluxe three-tier heated airer arrives ready to use. It took me only two minutes to unfold the tiers, position the cover, plug in the cable and switch it on. The airer is a handsome chrome rack on its own, but the light grey embroidered cover makes the whole thing look rather gorgeous.The bars warmed up faster than most of its rivals, reaching 27C within 30 seconds before maxing out at 50C. When I laid a 4kg load of damp T-shirts across them and closed the cover, the lot was dry in two hours. That’s no faster than a tumble dryer, but it’s much more energy-efficient, costing about 8p an hourcompared with 79p for my 3kW tumble dryer.The Dry:Soon Deluxe has some excellent user-friendly details. In particular, a timer lets you set it to switch off in hourly increments up to 12 hours ahead. All Lakeland’s airers come with a three-year warranty compared with the basic statutory guarantees for most heated airers.It’s a shame that …this airer costs almost as much as a tumble dryer. Deluxe by name, deluxe by price. But it’s many times cheaper to run,so it might be worth it to keep your bills down.Suitable for:families who want to give up their expensive tumble dryer habitAvailable drying space:21m (up to 36 hanging T-shirts)Dimensions (open):73 x 75 x 137cm (DWH)Dimensions (folded):10 x 75 x 137cm (DWH)Max capacity:15kgTime to dry small load:2 hoursRunning cost:8p/hourLakelandDry:Soon Deluxe 3-tier heated airer and coverfrom£194.98£194.98 at Lakeland£213.13 at AmazonWhat we loveDries almost as fast as a tumble dryer; has timer and coverWhat we don’t loveIt’s expensive – and we’d like a much longer cableBest budget heated airer:Black+Decker heated winged clothes airerBlack+DeckerHeated winged clothes airerfrom£46.99£49.99 at Currys£46.99 at AmazonWhat we loveCheap to buy and run; light to carry and easy to moveWhat we don’t loveNot big or powerful enough to dry a full loadView image in fullscreen£49.99 at Currys£46.99 at AmazonThe Black+Decker doesn’t get particularly hot, which helps if you have curious toddlers and delicate clothes. It still managed to dry my small load of T-shirts in an afternoon, and at £50 with a 6p-an-hour running cost, it’s a decent budget buy. It’s also one of the easiest airers to fold down and slip under the sofa when not in use.Why we love itThe Black+Decker winged airer has a small footprint, taking up about 50 x 50cm on its beam supports, yet it boasts a capacity of 10kg when unfolded, thanks to its ironing-board-style shape. It warmed up to 33C in its hottest spots and dried my small load of T-shirts in just over four hours, with a little help from me flipping them and moving them around.I also like that the wings fold inwards to double up the heat when drying thicker garments, albeit not very large ones, and the dryer is so light (about 3.5kg) that I could move it around using one hand.It’s a shame that …it warmed up slowly and failed to get hotter than 33C even after three hours. That’s great for delicates and damp towels, but not hot enough to dry thick fabrics.Suitable for:drying light fabrics and warming up towelsAvailable drying space:11.5m (up to 20 hanging T-shirts)Dimensions (open):54 x 148 x 93cm (DWH)Dimensions (folded):approx 54 x 100 x 20cm (DWH)Max capacity:10kgTime to dry small load:4 hours 15 minutesRunning cost:6p/hourBlack+DeckerHeated winged clothes airerfrom£46.99£49.99 at Currys£46.99 at AmazonWhat we loveCheap to buy and run; light to carry and easy to moveWhat we don’t loveNot big or powerful enough to dry a full loadBest heated airer for fast drying:Minky SureDri Heat Pod ProMinkySureDri Heat Pod Profrom£59.99£59.99 at Currys£60 at ArgosWhat we loveWorks with your existing clothes horse to speed up dryingWhat we don’t loveIt’s noisy, and the cover won’t fit all airersView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£59.99 at Currys£60 at ArgosHeat pods turn your old unheated airer into a heated version. This one has a cover that fits a standard three-tier clothes horse, plus an electric heater that sits underneath to fill the space with hot air.Why we love itMinky’s pod system is a damp-blitzing machine. With the fan heater emitting plenty of heat and the cover trapping it, even its lowest setting blasted my laundry dry faster than most of the conventional airers in my test. It’s good value, too, even though you have to provide your own airer (this Minky modelfrom Argos is £35), and the zipped cover is excellent quality and looks smart.The Minky Pro’s lowest, middle and highest settings all have a similar energy consumption according to my readings (between 970W and 1,067W), costing roughly 27p an hour. That’s a significantly higher running cost than a barred heated airer, but only about a third as much as running a 3kW tumble dryer.Given that I dried a large 8kg load in less than three hours using the Minky’s highest setting, albeit with a fair amount of rearranging clothes, this gadget could genuinely replace your tumble dryer.The air inside the cover gets very hot, especially when it’s on the highest setting. That’s great for fast drying, but Minky says you should only use the Heat Pod Pro to dry fabric that can “endure temperatures up to 85C”. Save your delicate smalls for a conventional barred airer.It’s a shame that …the Minky’s fan noise is annoying compared with the blissful silence of a barred airer. At 60dB, it’s significantly quieter than a tumble dryer, but a little too loud to have in the same room while you watch TV. I also found the power button liable to get stuck, but that may be my own heavy-handedness.Suitable for:work clothes and school uniforms that need a fast turnaroundAvailable drying space:about 21m, depending on your clothes horseDimensions (heat pod unit):60 x 68 x 135cm (heat pod unit, DWH)Max capacity:about 10kgTime to dry small load:1 hour 30 minutes (setting 1); 40 minutes (setting 3)Running cost:26-28p an hourMinkySureDri Heat Pod Profrom£59.99£59.99 at Currys£60 at ArgosWhat we loveWorks with your existing clothes horse to speed up dryingWhat we don’t loveIt’s noisy, and the cover won’t fit all airersThe best of the restView image in fullscreenThe Dunelm 3-tier A-frame made light work of drying soggy socks.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianDunelm 3-tier A-frame heated airerDunelm3-tier A-frame heated airer£80£80 at DunelmWhat we loveSmall but sturdy, with clever stands to dry soggy shoesWhat we don’t loveLacks the power to dry thick fabricsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£80 at DunelmBest for:runners and dog walkers who need to dry soggy shoes and socksHeated shoe stands are a simple addition and work well on this airer, drying my thick walking socks faster than if I’d laid them across the bars. The A-frame design also makes this among the sturdiest smaller airers I tested, and it stood firm even when I threw a large load of washing at the top tier.It didn’t make the final cut because …my small 4kg load needed an unusually long five hours, even after I’d moved things around and flipped them over. I also hated risking my fingers in the metal-hinged supports each time I folded and unfolded the airer.Available drying space:17m, including shoe stands;dimensions (open):54 x 91 x 146cm (DWH);dimensions (folded):18 x 91 x 146cm (DWH);max capacity:15kg;time to dry small load:5 hours;running cost:9p/hourDunelm3-tier A-frame heated airer£80£80 at DunelmWhat we loveSmall but sturdy, with clever stands to dry soggy shoesWhat we don’t loveLacks the power to dry thick fabricsArgos Home 3-tier heated airerArgosHome 3-tier heated airer£105£105 at ArgosWhat we loveSurprisingly powerful for one of the smallest airers on testWhat we don’t loveToo dinky for a family load, and a little unsteadyView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£105 at ArgosBest for:solo households and small living spacesArgos’s three-tier airer took several minutes to heat up and maxed out at a reasonable 45C – hot enough to dry my small load in about four and a half hours (after a bit of rearranging). The pivoted frame makes it feel less sturdy than airers with feet at each corner, but it’s a breeze to fold and unfold.It didn’t make the final cut because …the Argos Home airer feels less robust than similarly priced rivals.Available drying space:17m;dimensions (open):73 x 70 x 144cm (DWH);dimensions (folded):13 x 70 x 144cm (DWH);max capacity:15kg;time to dry small load:4 hours 20 minutes;running cost:8p/hourArgosHome 3-tier heated airer£105£105 at ArgosWhat we loveSurprisingly powerful for one of the smallest airers on testWhat we don’t loveToo dinky for a family load, and a little unsteadyVonHaus large heated clothes airer with coverVonHausLarge heated clothes airer with coverfrom£129.99£129.99 at VonHaus£129.99 at DebenhamsWhat we loveHigh weight capacity and heat-trapping coverWhat we don’t loveAwkward to put together and fold downView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£129.99 at VonHaus£129.99 at DebenhamsBest for:heavier items such as towels and jumpersWith 17.2m of drying space and a 298W power rating, the VonHaus isn’t as big as the Lakeland or the Dunelm XL, but it claims it can support a mammoth 30kg of damp washing. That’s also more than three times the maximum capacity of my washing machine, and indeed of my arms.Hyperbolic capacity claims aside, this airer has some clever ways to max out its drying space and efficiency, such as adding an unheated top rack (ideal for delicates) and a cover to trap the hot air. The plasticky cover isn’t a patch on those from Lakeland and Minky for quality or aesthetics, but it gets the job done, helping my small load dry in under three hours.It didn’t make the final cut because …the airer doesn’t look as smart as its similarly sized rivals, not least because of the plastic feet that remained defiantly clumpy when I folded down the frame.Available drying space:17.2m;dimensions (open):69 x 73 x 139cm (DWH);dimensions (folded):15.5 x 73 x 139cm (DWH);max capacity:30kg;time to dry small load:2 hours 45 minutes;running cost:8p/hourVonHausLarge heated clothes airer with coverfrom£129.99£129.99 at VonHaus£129.99 at DebenhamsWhat we loveHigh weight capacity and heat-trapping coverWhat we don’t loveAwkward to put together and fold downDunelm heated extra large ladder airerDunelmHeated extra large ladder airer£56£56 at DunelmWhat we loveLooks chic and takes up very little spaceWhat we don’t loveIts bars don’t get hot enough for a fast dryView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£56 at DunelmBest for:drying all your smalls in one placeThis is the new, “extra large” version of the dinky Dunelm ladder airer I tested in 2025 (see below). Its 133cm height and 12 heated bars (58cm each) add up to a much more generous drying capacity than its mini cousin, but it’s still not very powerful. I measured up to 185W energy consumption and an average 30C bar heat. That’s not exactly hot (for comparison, the bars of the Dunelm XL 3-tier airer reached 55C in places) and not warm enough to dry jeans or a jumper fast enough to avoid that slightly stale smell, but I found that it dried lighter T-shirts, hand towels and undies efficiently. As with the smaller version, I love the look of this airer.It didn’t make the final cut because …this won’t dry a whole load, even a small one, but it’s a great wardrobe assistant that doesn’t hog space.Available drying space:6.96m;dimensions (with feet attached):49.5 x 67.5 x 133cm (DWH);max capacity:10kg;time to dry small load:6 hours (all small items, after swapping some);running cost:5p/hourDunelmHeated extra large ladder airer£56£56 at DunelmWhat we loveLooks chic and takes up very little spaceWhat we don’t loveIts bars don’t get hot enough for a fast dryGlamHaus digital electric clothes airerGlamHausDigital electric clothes airerfrom£119.99£119.99 at Robert Dyas£119.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThis large airer’s open design gives you easy accessWhat we don’t loveTouch display is fiddly, and initial setup could be easierView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£119.99 at Robert Dyas£119.99 at AmazonBest for:sizeable wardrobes that contain delicate fabricsThis is one of the biggest and most feature-rich airers I tested, with a ventilated cover, timer and digital temperature controls that I found fairly easy to use. The top setting reached nowhere near the claimed 70C but did manage 52C in places, and I love having the lower-temperature settings for drying flimsy fabrics on the bars. You can attach peg hangers to dangle your smalls in the heat, but they don’t allow much dangle room. As with all the airers I tested, you get a much quicker dry if you lay items across the bars.It didn’t make the final cut because …it doesn’t dry clothes quite as fast as the Dry:Soon Deluxe, and it’s a right old jigsaw to put together the first time you use it. After that, though, I found it easy to open and close.Available drying space:30m;dimensions (open):73 x 70 x 147cm (DWH);dimensions (folded):15 x 70 x 147cm (DWH);max capacity:16kg;time to dry small load:3 hours 30 minutes;running cost:8p/hourGlamHausDigital electric clothes airerfrom£119.99£119.99 at Robert Dyas£119.99 at AmazonWhat we loveThis large airer’s open design gives you easy accessWhat we don’t loveTouch display is fiddly, and initial setup could be easierBeldray winged heated clothes airerBeldrayWinged heated clothes airerfrom£49.99£49.99 at Beldray£49.99 at AmazonWhat we loveDries all your socks and pants in under fourWhat we don’t loveNot powerful enough to dry large itemsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£49.99 at Beldray£49.99 at AmazonBest for:drying undies and other small itemsBeldray’s winged airer is a good buy at £50, but don’t expect it to dry a week’s worth of laundry. Hanging clothes from its 18 bars doesn’t dry them fast enough to avoid mild stinkiness, and there wasn’t enough room to lay more than four of my T-shirts across the bars. It blazed through underwear, though. The bars get surprisingly warm given the airer’s modest 230W power rating, so it made fast work of my damp socks, knickers and boxer shorts, as long as I gave each item its own spot on the bars. It folds up small for storage, too, although you have to wrestle the heated bars off the X-frame stand – not something I managed without a little light swearing.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s a great helper, but not big or powerful enough to dry a load of clothes.Available drying space:12.4m;dimensions (open):54 x 148 x 91cm (DWH);dimensions (folded):54 x 105 x 7.5cm (DWH);max capacity:15kg;time to dry small load:3 hours 30 minutes (all small items);running cost:6p/hourBeldrayWinged heated clothes airerfrom£49.99£49.99 at Beldray£49.99 at AmazonWhat we loveDries all your socks and pants in under fourWhat we don’t loveNot powerful enough to dry large itemsDunelm heated ladder airerDunelmHeated ladder airer£32£32 at DunelmWhat we loveCheap to run and looks rather handsomeWhat we don’t loveFar too small for a laundry load, or even large itemsView image in fullscreenPhotograph: Jane Hoskyn/The Guardian£32 at DunelmBest for:keeping in the hallway to dry damp socks, shoes and glovesThe smallest airer in my test and by far the cheapest to run, Dunelm’s 90W aluminium ladder uses a mere 2p an hour under the October energy price cap, and takes up very little space. Its plastic feet are a pain to attach and add about half a square metre to its footprint when they’re open, but all in all this is a great little gizmo for taking the soggy edge off hand towels, tea towels or even rained-on hats and gloves.It didn’t make the final cut because …it’s not big or powerful enough to dry a load of washing.Available drying space:3m;dimensions (with feet):53 x 34 x 87cm (DWH);max capacity:5kg;time to dry small load:3 hours 30 minutes;running cost:2p/hourDunelmHeated ladder airer£32£32 at DunelmWhat we loveCheap to run and looks rather handsomeWhat we don’t loveFar too small for a laundry load, or even large itemsWhat you need to knowView image in fullscreenHang out to dry: good ventilation is key to keeping damp at bay when using a heated airer.Photograph: Jane Hoskyn/The GuardianAre heated clothes airers worth the spend?Heated clothes airers are such a simple and smart idea that it’s weird they haven’t been around longer. They’re wildly popular, too: Aldi’s winged heated airer sold out within days of going on sale in 2025, and I’m feverishly awaiting news of this year’s model. But do they deserve the hype – and how can you get the best out of yours?How much do heated airers cost to run?Minimal running cost is the biggest selling point of heated airers. Their packaging bears promises that they’ll dry your clothes for as little as 6p an hour, dramatically undercutting all rival methods other than blazing sunshine. With electricity prices marginally lower than a year ago, while gas prices have risen, heated airers are certainly a more cost-efficient way of drying clothes than using your radiators.Six pence an hour was a little optimistic, though. I found that standard barred airers, running at about 320W, worked out at 7p an hour in September 2024 and 8p an hour now. It’s cheaper than putting on the central heating, but it does add up, because most heated airers take a whole afternoon or more to dry a full load of washing, and those 8p hours will add up. Airers that dry clothes faster, such as the fan-heater-based Minky SureDri Heat Pod Pro, cost more to run. At 1kW, the SureDri costs about 26p an hour, adding up to 78p for three hours of drying.That’s still significantly cheaper than running a tumble dryer or, indeed, a washing machine. Under October 2026 energy prices, a tumble dryer running at 3kW costs 79p an hour to run, and it can cost even more to switch on the central heating.How long do clothes take to dry with a heated airer?A standard T-shirt, laid flat and unfolded across several bars of a 300-320W barred heated airer, should dry in about two hours. If you’re drying a whole load of clothes, though, it’ll take a whole afternoon – or about eight hours if the air feels cold or humid. You will need to flip and rearrange items during this time to give the fabric equal access to the bars.Airers that contain a fan heater dry clothes more quickly. The fastest-drying airer in my test, theMinky SureDri, blew out enough hot air to dry my small load of washing in less than two hours. With a large load, I found it easier to halve it and dry it in batches.How can you make clothes dry faster on a heated airer?There are ways you can speed up the drying process. My best tip is to ignore the marketing photos that show airers draped like Christmas trees, with clothes hung from every bar. As I discovered while running this test, your clothes simply won’t dry that way unless it’s a warm day, which rather defeats the point. Instead, lay individual items across the bars.Covered airers cut drying times by almost half, but I’d recommend removing it as soon as your clothes are dry. Covers are vented to avoid condensation, but I found that some moisture crept back in if I left my clothes inside.However powerful your airer, always spin your clothes to remove as much water as possible before laying them on it. Wet clothes won’t dry, and water and electricity are not a happy combination.On that note, don’t use a heated airer in the bathroom. Electric peril aside, bathroom air is notoriously damp. I had the best results when using my test airers in the bedroom with the window ajar – and the faint fabric softener scent was a sweet bedtime bonus.Do heated airers make your house damp?When you dry clothes on any warm surface, whether it’s a heated airer or a radiator, the moisture rises from the clothes – to where? I asked a range of experts about this, and they broadly agreed that the key is to let the moist air escape from your home.“It’s not the drying method alone but the combination of moisture and lack of ventilation that leads to damp problems,” says Dr Anastasia Mylona, technical director at the Chartered Institution of Building Services Engineers. “You can manage this by ensuring good ventilation when drying clothes indoors; for example, by opening windows or using extractor fans.”Adehumidifiercan help avoid damp, as well as speed up the drying process, says cleaning expert Nancy Emery of bathroom retailerDrench. “If you’re investing in a heated airer, my advice is to invest in a dehumidifier as well, and always run them together.”The best dehumidifiers: 14 favourites to beat damp and cut bills, testedRead moreI’ve found heated airers much less likely than radiators to cause damp walls, and property expert Phil Spencer explains why. “Airflow is key, so if you want to use a heated airer, put it in the middle of the room rather than next to the wall,” says Spencer, who, among other things, founded the property advice websiteMove iQ. “This is why heated airers are preferable to wall-mounted radiators.”However, radiators can heat up the room, and heated airers can’t, at least not significantly. That’s an important factor in the battle against damp, says Emery. “Maintaining your home’s temperature above 18C helps because condensation can’t settle on warmer surfaces.”I put these tips to the test usingan affordable humidity meter. I measured the moisture in my spare room’s air before doing any laundry, and then again at various stages of drying a medium load on a large heated airer – with and without opening the windows and using a dehumidifier.It had rained all week, so perhaps it’s no surprise that my house boasted a base humidity level of 70%, 10 percentage points higher than the recommended UK maximum. Iwassurprised, though, when this only rose to 72% once I’d loaded the airer with damp clothes. Running my dehumidifier brought the room’s humidity down to 70%. When I opened the windows, it dropped to 65% – even before the load was completely dry. I’ve now defaulted to leaving the windows open whenever possible, whether or not I’m drying clothes.“Opening windows regularly is the best way to allow humid air to escape, though it may seem counterintuitive in colder weather,” says Nicholas Donnithorne, UK technical services manager at Rentokil Property Care. “Leave quarterlights ajar or trickle vents open. Dehumidifiers can help, but they require regular emptying and aren’t a substitute for proper ventilation.”For more autumn and winter home essentials, read the Filter’s guides to:The best electric blankets and heated throwsThe best electric heaters, testedJane Hoskyn is afeatures journalist and WFH pioneer with three decadesof experiencein rearranging bookshelves and “testing” coffee machines while deadlines loom. Her work has made her a low-key expert in all manner of consumables, from sports watches to solar panels. She would always rather be in the woodsThis article was originally published on 18 October 2024. After publication, this model was the subject of a safety recall from Dunelm, which has advised purchasers to stop using the product and return it for a full refund.
