title: Airport lounges: how did they get so horribly, competitively decadent? | Luxury travel | The Guardian
description: High-end cocktails, nap pods, waffle stations, tapas attendants, sashimi bars and brutalist art. The airlines’ battle to please the 1% is getting increasingly bizarre
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: High-end cocktails, nap pods, waffle stations, tapas attendants, sashimi bars and brutalist art. The airlines’ battle to please the 1% is getting increasingly bizarre
Content: The sky’s the limit …Photograph: Jan Mika/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe sky’s the limit …Photograph: Jan Mika/AlamyPass notesLuxury travelAirport lounges: how did they get so horribly, competitively decadent?High-end cocktails, nap pods, waffle stations, tapas attendants, sashimi bars and brutalist art. The airlines’ battle to please the 1% is getting increasingly bizarreMon 26 Oct 2026 12.53 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleName:Airport lounge wars.Age:American Airlines opened the first airport loungein 1939.Appearance:Dripping in caviar and cocktails.Airport lounge wars – is this a TV show where teams of would-be hospitality entrepreneurs compete to design and deliver airport lounge experiences for a demanding celebrity jury?No (but I’d absolutely watch that). It’s the arms race to provide increasingly extravagant lounges to persuade customers to shell out for first-class plane tickets or fancy credit cards that grant access, as reported by theWashington Post.Hang on, my credit card gives me lounge access! You queue up in a dingy corridor and eventually, if a scowling woman in a blazer deems you worthy, you get a picked-over buffet of dried-out ham and mini croissants, plus the chance to fight for an uncomfortable chair, still warm from the previous set of buttocks.Yes, that’s the lounge experience for your kind of low-value riff-raff – people are increasinglycomplainingaboutqueues and overcrowding;American Airlinesis expecting 18m lounge visits this year. But at the exclusive end of the market, competition has heated up in the last five years and lounges are getting really decadent.What’s on offer?High-end cocktails, nap pods, waffle stations, a “juice wall”… Capital One offers a “tapas attendant” serving important Spanish produce at Reagan Airport in Virginia, andpick-your-own personalised cheese flightsat JFK; Emirates Dubai has asushi and sashimi bar.Meh, I’m lactose-intolerant, teetotal and allergic to fish.How about the Air France “Première” experience at Charles de Gaulle; with a Sisley spa and theWonder Block?Ooh, what’s that? Some kind of amazing massage chair?No, it’s apile of bricks.Excuse me?Sorry, a “renowned work of art”by Jean-Michel Othoniel “combining monumentality with delicacy”.You’re not convincing me to shell out.As if you could afford it. But how aboutSwiss Air Zurich’sprivate bedrooms, with luxurious double beds and a “panoramic view of the Alps”? Singapore Airlines also has bedrooms in Changi, and what theLounge Guru– a luxury flight and lounge influencer – calls “one of the most luxurious airport shower suites I’ve ever seen”.Phwoar, now we’re talking.And I’ve saved the best till last: some lounges offerseparate security linesandpassport controlso you never have to mix with the grubby proles.Air France in Charles de Gaulleeven transports you planeside by Porsche if you’re travelling first class.That’s what lounges are really about, aren’t they? Getting to feel special.Oh yes, it’s all about having – and showing off – your status. Lounge customers “Don’t have to go out in gen pop,” an American Airlines spokesperson told the WaPo.Isn’t that the phrase they use inprisons? Brrrr.Of course, none of this is exclusive enough for real one-percenters.Because they’re …Yep, flying private.Do say:“Can I top up your blackberry-sage spa water before your facial, madam? Or would you prefer a visit from the caviar cart?”Don’t say:“Real luxury is feeling like you’re better than everyone else.”Explore more on these topicsLuxury travelPass notesFlightsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: LS Lowry review – matchstick men, or the broken denizens of a smog-filled hellscape?  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: With his heaps of mud, decaying sheds and chimney-filled skies, Lowry depicts northern England as a spirit-crushing dystopia
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: With his heaps of mud, decaying sheds and chimney-filled skies, Lowry depicts northern England as a spirit-crushing dystopia
Content: Withdrawn and wretched … Lowry’s Coming from the Mill.Photograph: © The Lowry Collection, SalfordView image in fullscreenWithdrawn and wretched … Lowry’s Coming from the Mill.Photograph: © The Lowry Collection, SalfordArt and designReviewLS Lowry review – matchstick men, or the broken denizens of a smog-filled hellscape?MK Gallery, Milton KeynesWith his heaps of mud, decaying sheds and chimney-filled skies, Lowry depicts northern England as a spirit-crushing dystopiaJonathan JonesMon 26 Oct 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile peoplequeue at the British Museum to see the Battle of Hastings, this excellent survey of LS Lowry at the MK Gallery in Milton Keynes takes you back to another, maybe more decisive part of our past – the age when Britain was the most industrialised society on Earth. Laurence Lowry was born in 1887 and worked for 41 years as a rent collector, a job that took him all over his native Greater Manchester observing its people and places. He had the city’s grime and grind in his soul. The MK wants to show him as a fully rounded artist, to uncover the Lowry with a song in his heart, but it’s the misery of his urban hell that holds and harrows you.In his 1930 painting Coming from the Mill it’s the end of the shift and scores of people emerge from a factory’s bleak yellow gatehouse as if leaving prison. Their daily captivity has left them broken and exhausted and the little abstracted figures hunch forwards as they walk without pausing to laugh or chat, going to their separate homes, each one withdrawn, wretched. They are not the painting’s protagonists – they are passive victims. The architecture of industry dominates the picture as it rules their lives. How can any of these little people, dwarfed by the mill that eats their time and energy, attain individuality? No wonder they all look the same except for minor variations in their drab clothes. They’ve been reduced by the Industrial Revolution tomatchstick people.View image in fullscreenLess well known dimensions to his talent … LS Lowry: The Theatre of Life at MK Gallery.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianLowry is the Franz Kafka of industrial Britain. He is not a naive artist who painted crudely because that’s the best he could do. Nor is he a patient social realist laying bare the injustices of capitalism – althoughFriedrich Engelswould surely have recognised his Manchester. He is a modern expressionist who finds his inner melancholy reflected in the industrial sublime. He drinks in its despair, feasts on its poetry of alienation. As you journey through Lowry’s North, you sink ever further into his personal slough of despond.Slough of Despond would make a good alternative title for his 1924 drawing The River Irwell at the Adelphi. Heaps of mud and ash choke the slow-moving river that runs through Salford, its shores lined with decaying sheds and slums against a smoggy, chimney-lined sky. It’s Lowry at his purest as he depicts the stunning, crushing presence of the city itself. He draws and paints the black, gnarled spires of urban churches with as much relish as those monstrous mills. In the second world war he was a fire-watcher with a privileged view of the blitz: a drawing of freshly bombed buildings in Piccadilly, Manchester shows husks of charred brick still wreathed in smoke.View image in fullscreenEerie … Lowry’s A Landmark.Photograph: © The Lowry Collection, SalfordThis show digs out other, less well known dimensions to his talent. But his paintings of the Lake District are even more chilling than his cities. Lake Landscape, painted in 1950, is a vista of low curving hills divided by silvery still water, receding in abstract, musical pulses of sadness. No people or animals inhabit this eerie world. When he paints people close up it’s even more disturbing: a young man with staring eyes, a father and sons who all seem equally desperate. He lightens up to paint his ideal woman with a simplified doll-like face apparently intended as his tribute to Pre-Raphaelite red-lipped beauties but the result is weirdly robotic. Her face is on the exhibition merchandise, perhaps because Halloween is coming.The most bizarre painting, however, is his 1963 work In a Park. At first glance it’s another city crowd scene until you realise everyone in this fenced enclosure has something different about them. A one-eyed face screams while people walk around the white-earthed, empty space with spinal deformities, facial palsies, amputated limbs. The catalogue gets itself in knots – is Lowry mocking the disabled or questioning how we define disability?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tentRead moreBut this painting is not about disability in a political sense at all. It uses it as an image of humanity in general: all people are broken and alone, misshapen in Lowry’s hopeless universe.Lowry is a tricky customer. If it is pure snobbery to look down on him for being popular it is also patronising to see this troubled artist as a warmly sentimental nostalgist of the north. He is a painter of modern life in the age when that meant huge crowds staggering home in the shadow of smoking chimneys in cities blackened by carbon. At his best, Lowry is a great modern artist. His 1919 painting Pit Tragedy shows working-class people waiting for the worst news. They are statuesque, tragically posed in the grey dusty light. A woman turns towards us, her head veiled. Her pain is lost in the past but lives on here, observed and recorded by Lowry, visionary of the industrial age.LS Lowry: The Theatre of Life is at MK Gallery, Milton Keynes until 28 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designPaintingArtExhibitionsLS LowryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuse | Domestic violence | The Guardian
description: Home Office figures show nearly two-thirds of drug tests carried out on arrested abuse suspects detected use of a drug that ‘boosts confidence but increases paranoia’
Author: Robyn Vinter
Headline: Home Office figures show nearly two-thirds of drug tests carried out on arrested abuse suspects detected use of a drug that ‘boosts confidence but increases paranoia’
Content: Cocaine has featured in a number of domestic murder cases in recent years.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenCocaine has featured in a number of domestic murder cases in recent years.Composite: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesDomestic violence‘He was like 10 men after taking cocaine‘: how Britain’s drug habit is fuelling domestic abuseHome Office figures show nearly two-thirds of drug tests carried out on arrested abuse suspects detected use of a drug that ‘boosts confidence but increases paranoia’Robyn VinterNorth of England correspondentMon 26 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDuring lockdown, Charlotte and her ex-partner would spend evenings cooped up in their flat, listening to music, watching YouTube videos and chatting until the small hours. Those nights would be fuelled by alcohol and lines of cocaine.“I wanted to be loved, and when he told me he loved me like nobody ever would and nobody ever will, I drank the Kool-Aid,” Charlotte says. “I wanted to believe that. And there’s a point when you’re with somebody and you’re drinking, you’re doing coke, where you think you have this bond, you think it’s just you two in the world.”But that emotional high would be fleeting. “Without a doubt, without any exception, it would never end peacefully. My ex-partner would get so ridiculously paranoid once he was using cocaine. It was just crazy,” she says. Charlotte’s partner would accuse her of taking more than him, messaging men and hiding things from him. When she denied it, he would subject her to brutal physical assaults.“And then the next day it was all apologies and it’ll all be fine, it’ll all be different.”Data suggests it is a common scenario.Home Officefigures sent to the Guardian show nearly six in 10 police drug tests carried out on people arrested on suspicion of domestic abuse were positive for cocaine between July 2025 and June this year.It is not possible to see the whole picture, as some of the tests were carried out after the police suspected drug-taking, but it tallies with a 2023 pilot study that found 59% of domestic abuse suspects tested positive for cocaine or opiates.One in 10 adults in England and Wales experienced domestic abuse in last year, ONS findsRead moreA wider Guardian investigation has found that Britain’s record-breaking cocaine habit is also driving crimes from assault to dangerous driving. The stimulant is increasingly ubiquitous, fuelling situations ranging from fights on nights out to violence at football matches.Cocaine has featured in a number of domestic murder cases in recent years. Victoria Thomas, a 45-year-old mother-of-two from Cardiff, was strangled to death by her husband, Alcwyn Thomas,who was “argumentative and moody”, having been filmed on CCTV taking cocaine shortly before he killed her on 19 August 2024.On 13 June last year, 32-year-old Izzy Knight was murdered by her husband, Paul Knight, in the house they shared in Northamptonshire while their two daughters slept upstairs. In a note, he blamed “having an addiction to cocaine and spending money I don’t have”.Both men were sentenced to life in prison.Cat Chappell, a BACP-registered therapist specialising in domestic abuse who previously volunteered on the National Domestic Violence Helpline, says cocaine boosts confidence but increases paranoia, “and so much of abuse is around paranoia”. “It’s taking what’s already there, making it like 10 times worse,” she says.It can also make it more difficult to leave, she says, because perpetrators will often offer to get help with their cocaine problem. “And [for victims], that’s what you want to hear in those moments.”View image in fullscreen‘So much of abuse is around paranoia,’ says BACP-registered therapist Chappell.Photograph: Dumitru Gornet/AlamyCharlotte and her ex-partner got together just before the pandemic and, though it was not the first time she had taken cocaine, it was not something she had done regularly. Her ex, on the other hand, was a habitual user.“My ex was a really small man, and after cocaine use he’d be like 10 men. He was like the Incredible Hulk, it was like there was this beast in him and he would get this strength. And I can’t tell you where it was from. Then he would come at me and he would absolutely beat me to a pulp. It was absolutely terrifying,” she says.He would routinely trap her in the bedroom. “I remember one night he got really paranoid that somebody was in the house and he brought knives upstairs. He would pace about all night. It was really, really horrific.“For somebody who’s already [controlling and abusive] it’s like adding fuel to the fire, it really is, with coke.”He often stole from her to fund his habit, using her phone to take money from her bank account, including times when he had knocked her unconscious.Charlotte remembers police visited their flat about 19 times, as a result of her own calls and those made by neighbours, but she would always cover up her ex’s cocaine use.“I would deny a lot of it because I didn’t want to say, ‘Yes, I’ve been doing it as well’, so you’re in this absolute no-win situation because you’re then sticking up for them all the time.”She began to abuse alcohol to cope with the situation she was in. “I didn’t want to be there,” Charlotte says. “I was just drinking because I didn’t want to feel anything. I’d wake up, drink all day. I just wanted to feel numb, numb, numb, numb, numb.”‘I thought the baby would change him’: the women whose pregnancies are blighted by domestic abuseRead moreShe was finally able to leave on Boxing Day in 2021 when her ex went out to score drugs and she wrote an email to her father asking him to pick her up. She has been free of alcohol and cocaine since.After initially attempting to pursue her ex for knocking her teeth out, police later decided to take no action against Charlotte’s abuser. She fears he will go on to abuse someone else.It was Women’s Aid that helped her get her life back on track and she is now an advocate for the charity in her home city of Leeds. She also works for another charity, Smart Works, which helps women get into employment.Nik Peasgood, the chief executive of Leeds Women’s Aid, says Charlotte’s story is increasingly common. She thinks cocaine is having an effect on the levels of violence perpetrated by abusers and she is calling for more research to help understand the relationship between cocaine, domestic abuse and mental health.View image in fullscreenCocaine can worsen the frequency and severity of domestic violence.Photograph: Dani Rodriguez/Alamy“If they’re already abusive and the relationship’s abusive, [cocaine] might lower their inhibitions, it might make the frequency worse, it might make the severity worse, it might mean that they can’t control how they normally control the relationship and the situation. But it doesn’t make somebody abusive or violent if they’re not already. It’s not an excuse for that violence.”Peasgood says that cocaine, unlike a lot of other drugs, is used by a broad range of people, including middle- and upper-class people and those who are well-respected within society and do not fit the stereotype of what people think domestic abusers looks like.The drug can be a barrier to people seeking help, particularly for victims in professional jobs who feel they have a lot to lose if they are caught using illegal substances.“[Contacting the police] has ramifications away from just the perpetrator when there are drugs involved, and [there is] fear around that,” says Peasgood. “Especially if people have got children, it’s something they wouldn’t necessarily want others to know about.”Through her work, Charlotte has now met many others who faced similar situations. “I’m in recovery now and it’s alarming how many people tell the same tale of drinking, doing coke, and it just becoming an absolute explosion of rows and just horrific violence,” she says.“I think it’s not a problem that’s actually going away. If anything, it’s getting worse. You only have to speak to people in the rehab or recovery world and they’ll tell you this is going nowhere. It’s really scary.”She believes the figures don’t show the true scale of the issue. “I think this is much wider reaching than we realise, due to the stigma of reporting it and the shame of the victim using the drug.”For many people, she says, cocaine use is “very much seen as our weekend thing”. “It’s very much behind closed doors and not spoken about. People would be gobsmacked at how many people actually do it. It’s so widespread, it’s unbelievable.”In the UK, call the nationaldomestic abuse helplineon 0808 2000 247, or visitWomen’s Aid. In the US, thedomestic violence hotlineis 1-800-799-SAFE (7233). In Australia, the nationalfamily violence counselling serviceis on 1800 737 732. Other international helplines may be found viawww.befrienders.org.Explore more on these topicsDomestic violenceDrugsAlcoholViolence against women and girlsHome OfficePoliceCrimefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: We’ll revive the in-person shopping experience with a transformation of the area, inspired by the John Lewis and Selfridges founders who first set up there, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Sadiq Khan
Headline: We’ll revive the in-person shopping experience with a transformation of the area, inspired by the John Lewis and Selfridges founders who first set up there, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Content: An architectural illustration for the transformation of the Oxford Street areas, with pedestrianised zones, grass and trees.Computer-generated: AVR LondonView image in fullscreenAn architectural illustration for the transformation of the Oxford Street areas, with pedestrianised zones, grass and trees.Computer-generated: AVR LondonOpinionLondonWe’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music tooSadiq KhanWe’ll revive the in-person shopping experience with a transformation of the area, inspired by the John Lewis and Selfridges founders who first set up thereSadiq Khan is the mayor of LondonMon 26 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTShareAt around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the start of a momentous new era for our nation’s high street. Today, after decades of discussions and deliberations, the action we’ve taken means almost one kilometre of Oxford Street is now officially traffic-free – just in time for Christmas. But this is only the start of a much bigger transformation, and the first step towards a bright new future for this historic thoroughfare.Walk down Oxford Street, and you’re passing through hundreds of years of British history and culture. In 1864, an ambitious young draper called John Lewis opened his first shop on the street. Forty-five years later, the American entrepreneur Harry Gordon Selfridge arrived with a radical idea: to transform shopping from a mundane necessity into an unforgettable experience. He filled his store with dazzling window displays, world-class entertainment, restaurants and lounges. He even installed women’s toilets – a rarity in Edwardian England – giving women a newfound freedom to make the most of the city. As he opened the doors to his first customers, he told them “everyone is welcome”.That spirit has been at the heart of Oxford Street’s success ever since. We love it because it feels as if it belongs to all of us. It’s where teenagers come for their first shopping trip with friends. Where families marvel at the magic of festive lights and decorations. And where generations of Londoners and visitors have come to discover the latest music, fashion and trends. It’s also the beating heart of British retail – pumping billions into our national economy, with the surrounding area accounting for an incredible1% of the UK’s total economic outputin 2022.But in recent years this iconic streethas started to lose some of its sparkle. Changing consumer habits and the legacy of the pandemic have taken their toll. Footfall has fallen. Some of our best-loved stores have closed their doors, only to be replaced by vape shops and candy stores. And, too often, the experience of visiting a chaotic, congested Oxford Street has felt more like an ordeal to survive than a day out to enjoy.View image in fullscreenOxford Street and South Molton Street, visualised by architects for the transformation of the iconic shopping thoroughfare.Computer-generated: AVR LondonIf we’re to restore this beloved street to its former glory, we must rediscover the pioneering spirit of Harry Gordon Selfridge and create a space for everyone to enjoy, breathing new life into the high street and bringing back big brands. And that’s what our bold plans – backed by the overwhelming majority of Londoners and businesses – are all about. And with household names like Ikea, Puma and Clarks investing in new stores, there’s already excitement for what Oxford Street can become.People need a reason beyond simply buying something to visit their high street. And in an age when almost anything can be delivered right to our door, that principle matters more than ever. Coming to Oxford Street should feel like a positive experience. Somewhere you want to spend time, as well as your hard-earned money. A place where you’re not choked by tailpipe fumes or deafened by the noise of passing motorists. And that starts with reclaiming it for pedestrians, not traffic – rebalancing the relationship between cars and people in the centre of our city.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEveryone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?Read moreThat’s why I’m so delighted that, thanks to our efforts, the road stretching between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is now officially traffic-free. But removing cars is just the beginning. Imagine an Oxford Street where you can stroll at your own pace, take a break from shopping with a coffee under the trees, or stumble across some live music, a fashion show, a sports exhibition or a cultural event. We’re determined to put Oxford Street not just on par with top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla, but make it even better.And while it’s a process – we’re deliberately keeping disruption to a minimum over the busy Christmas period – by next spring, visitors can expect to see new trees, new seats and new public plazas, alongside improved lighting and signage. This ambitious project has been far from straightforward or easy. As usual, we’ve had to overcome opposition from a vocal minority, and 14 years of a previous government that didn’t back the plans. But with seven in 10 Londoners expressing support for our vision, after extensive consultation, I knew we owed it to our city and to our businesses to deliver these improvements, which will help to boost jobs, growth and investment as we build a fairer, safer, greener and more prosperous London for everyone.View image in fullscreenThe first John Lewis shop, which opened in 1864, on Oxford Street.Photograph: John Lewis/PAOf course, we’ll continue to listen to Londoners. Many of the initial changes are temporary, and we’ll use real-time feedback to help refine the final designs in a test and review period throughout 2027. But for centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way. And now it’s in need of its next great transformation. One that honours its extraordinary past while creating new possibilities for the future. A future where new memories are made, new businesses flourish and new chapters of British history are written.Today marks the beginning of that journey – and I encourage everyone to come to explore this newly transformed street, as we work together to ensure its best days are still to come. In the words of Harry Gordon Selfridge – everyone is welcome.Sadiq Khan is the mayor of LondonExplore more on these topicsLondonOpinionSadiq KhanShoppingcommentShareReuse this content

title: What the claw arcade game tells us about the cost of living crisis | Zoe Williams | The Guardian
description: No matter how you crunch the UK data, prices are rising while average wages stagnate. The system is rigged – and it’s time we kicked over the toy dispenser, writes Zoe Williams
Author: Zoe Williams
Headline: No matter how you crunch the UK data, prices are rising while average wages stagnate. The system is rigged – and it’s time we kicked over the toy dispenser, writes Zoe Williams
Content: Surely, after pound #7, it should just give you a toy?Photograph: Vukasin Ljustina/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenSurely, after pound #7, it should just give you a toy?Photograph: Vukasin Ljustina/Getty ImagesOpinionUK cost of living crisisWhat the claw arcade game tells us about the cost of living crisisZoe WilliamsNo matter how you crunch the UK data, prices are rising while average wages stagnate. The system is rigged – and it’s time we kicked over the toy dispenserMon 26 Oct 2026 12.54 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.35 EDTShareAbout a decade ago, the financial crash was almost a decade old. Unrelatedly, my kids were under 10, so I was spending a lot more time in arcades. There’s a particular game involving a metal claw – it goes by the name of claw-game. You put in a pound, and try to manipulate the claw to grab a toy that is worth nothing like a pound. You would take that as the price of a bit of family fun, except the claw never grabbed a toy.The frustration for a six-year-old was immense, every lost pound making the probably flammable stuffed hamster more urgently desirable. But it was way worse for me, because I was clinging on to some residual 80s idea of arcade-honour. Surely, after pound #7, the machine would just give you a sodding toy? That would represent an astronomical return, lessen the possibility of an adult kicking the machine to death and assure a returning market of maybe 10% of the dumbest or most spineless parents. But no, nada. No toys, ever.So it wasn’t a good game, but it was starting to feel like a really good metaphor for the economy. This was in the twilight period between 2015 and Brexit, after which politics stopped troubling itself with day-to-day liveability. Previously, if you studied hard you got a job, then if you worked hard, you could afford to live; and in the fullness of time, if you met another person who worked hard, you could have a family and afford to feed them – this was basically the honour-code of capitalism. But it was breaking down and nobody wanted to admit it.double quotation markWe don’t cast ourselves as agents in the economy. Rather, we’re a bunch of luckless dopes who bad things keep happening toTrade unions noticed: the TUC crunched the numbers in 2014 and found that onlyone in 40 new jobswere full time.The geographer Danny Dorlingnoticed that a fifth of people needed a cash benefit to make rent, and average house prices were nearly nine times average salaries in England and Wales. The NHS noticed, in the same year, inasmuch as the number of children withvitamin D deficiency and ricketshad tripled since 2009. A lot of people privately thought, “This whole thing is rigged,” though, as far as I know, I alone noticed the irresistible likeness to the Ramsgate arcade.Scroll forward a decade and people are much more public about their noticing – but expectations have changed and with them, the language. We talk about a cost of living crisis, but we don’t cast ourselves as agents in the economy, whose wages aren’t keeping pace with prices. Rather, we’re a bunch of luckless dopes to whom bad things keep happening. The New Economics Foundation thinktank, with Best for Britain, has dropped into these new times an “attainability index”. It takes the wage data from the past 20 years and calculates how many hours you would have to work to attain a set of things: a holiday, a night out, an outfit, a car.Burnham approves Jackdaw – and Labour’s unity on climate action is imperilled with the stroke of a pen | Zoe WilliamsRead moreThe figures aren’t at all surprising. Low-paid workers have their wages mostly eaten up by essentials. Social participation is sporadic, holidays out of reach. A secondary school teacher looks as though they are doing OK, because they would only have to work 23 hours to afford a ticket to a festival. But that would assume they are not going to do any other discretionary spending whatsoever.Just about the only things that have gone down in price in real terms, over the past 20 years, are gym memberships, budget clothes and meal deals, which makes sense. In all the crazy supermarket moments of this decade, the remarkable value of a prawn mayo sandwich, as long as you get some crisps and a Red Bull at the same time, has often felt like the only thing standing between us and revolution.The important thing isn’t the numbers (no offence, researchers, your data is beautiful) but the fact that everyone is experiencing the same degradation. The pilot of 2026 is as far removed in his or her housing prospects from the pilot of 2006, as is the chef or the accountant from theirs. So much political rhetoric goes into the creation of rivalrous silos – the woke v the anti-woke, the liberal elite v the left-behind – all of it constructed to mask the fact that everybody’s expectations have been thwarted for two decades straight. Realising this might shunt the discourse out of phase “get mad” into phase “get even”.Zoe Williams is a Guardian columnistOn Tuesday 1 December 2026, join your favourite Guardian writers for an evening of candid conversations, witty remarks and surprises as we look back on the year-defining stories of 2026. title: If the PM reboots the UK for working-class people, unions will be with him. But the time for talking is over | Andrea Egan | The Guardian
description: Andy Burnham has railed against neoliberalism – the historic shift must start with this week’s budget, says Andrea Egan, general secretary of Unison
Author: Andrea Egan
Headline: Andy Burnham has railed against neoliberalism – the historic shift must start with this week’s budget, says Andrea Egan, general secretary of Unison
Content: The chancellor, John Healey, and Andy Burnham at the Labour conference in Liverpool, 28 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianView image in fullscreenThe chancellor, John Healey, and Andy Burnham at the Labour conference in Liverpool, 28 September 2026.Photograph: Christopher Thomond/The GuardianOpinionAndy BurnhamIf the PM reboots the UK for working-class people, unions will be with him. But the time for talking is overAndrea EganAndy Burnham has railed against neoliberalism – the historic shift must start with this week’s budgetAndrea Egan is the general secretary of UnisonMon 26 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.45 EDTShareAfter Keir Starmer, things could only get better inside Labour. But Andy Burnham’s arrival as party leader and prime minister didn’t just clear that low bar. It was a cause for hope, especially for those of us in the trade union movement. That’s less because Burnham is streets ahead of his predecessor as a politician – although he is – and more about just how radically the new prime minister has framed his project for the country.I’ve been active in the labour movement for almost four decades. In that time, I cannot count how many times I’ve heard talk of reversing the devastation wreaked by Margaret Thatcher. For socialists and grassroots trade union activists, this kind of political thinking is bread and butter. But not so much for a Labour prime minister.Tony Blair, between torching the Middle East and taking a hammer to our civil liberties, infamously came to build upon Thatcher’s legacy rather than bury it. Gordon Brown and Starmer were more set against the Thatcherite fracturing of our society than Blair. But they both continued to inhabit the political cage she built: the idea that there is no alternative.Before now, the only major party leader ideologically opposed to neoliberalism in a remotely serious way was Jeremy Corbyn, who drew up a programme that would have started to undo the rule of the market. But it wasn’t to be. So in beginning his premiership by insisting that there is, in fact, an alternative way of organising our economy and society to the neoliberal one, Burnham marked a historic shift.This kind of talkisn’tcheap. How the prime minister has articulated his vision really matters, both because it has challenged the assumptions that have shaped our politics for decades and because the analysis is fundamentally correct. Virtually every aspect of this country’s malaise, as Burnham powerfully explained to Kemi Badenoch, can be traced back to the “wrong turns” taken in the 1980s.But the flip side for Burnham is that his diagnosis doesn’t leave any doubt about what Labour must do in government. To measure up to his own ambitions, the party will have to implement changes to the structure of our economy unseen since the immediate postwar period. At a minimum, that means bringing sectors into public ownershipandinvesting on a huge scale to rebuild a social fabric – our public services, infrastructure and collective life – that has been shredded.View image in fullscreenAndy Burnham plays bingo during a visit to Humphrey Booth resource centre in Salford, 9 October 2026.Photograph: Christopher Furlong/Getty ImagesMany of the Burnham government’s measures so far have been welcome. Banking quick wins that don’t require wrangling with the Treasury but signal you are on the side of the people was a sensible approach for the early days. Labour’s steady improvement in the polls reflects that. But four decades of neoliberalism won’t be ended through Google Maps updates of petrol prices, or even with measures toprovide breathing roomin the face of the cost of living crisis.Following up a bold, historical diagnosis with piecemeal measures just isn’t politically sustainable. From US wars to the climate crisis, the factors making essentials ever more unaffordable are out of control. Without the radical action the prime minister has called for, then, the lives of our people and communities are going to keep getting worse, rapidly. And the stakes remain high: it’s the far right that will benefit if this project fails.So the budget must be the moment that the prime minister’s programme starts to match his rhetoric. Unison is clear about that, and so are my colleagues across the trade union movement. We’re not expecting neoliberalism to have melted away by the timeJohn Healeyfinishes reading out his statement. But we are demanding serious measures that actually begin to improve workers’ lives.We expect a big, multiyear funding plan to restore investment and wages in our public services – alongside kicking profiteering vultures out of the public sector through bringing services back in-house. These measures should be funded by finally making the wealthy few pay their fair share of tax. It’s imperative that the prime minister and chancellor defy pressure from the business lobby and the rightwing media to reject changes such asequalising income and capital gains tax.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe decades-long political settlement the prime minister has rightly defined himself against might have impoverished the vast majority, but there were some winners. And those who have profited handsomely from neoliberalism will fight tooth and nail against any attempt to actually break with it.So, if the prime minister sticks with his historic ambition to remake Britain in the interests of the working class, it won’t be easy. But the trade union movement will be by his side. There’s no dodging a battle with the vested interests committed to keeping things as they are – and the budget is the place to begin.Andrea Egan is the general secretary of UnisonExplore more on these topicsAndy BurnhamOpinionTrade unionsEconomic policyTax and spendingJohn HealeyUK cost of living crisiscommentShareReuse this content

title: Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? | Catherine De Vries | The Guardian
description: Anger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives better, says political scientist Catherine De Vries
Author: Catherine De Vries
Headline: Anger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives better, says political scientist Catherine De Vries
Content: Police officers face protesters near Porte de Vincennes in Paris, 24 October 2026.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice officers face protesters near Porte de Vincennes in Paris, 24 October 2026.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionProtestCould Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU?Catherine De VriesAnger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives betterMon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTShareEurope is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris toMilantoMadridshare is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools.The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap electioncalled after parliament voted down key housing reforms. France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher.At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leavesEuropewith a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad?If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table.But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible.The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick.The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone–as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty–changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit.1:44Police and protesters exchange teargas and fireworks in demonstrations across France – videoBut the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted.Negotiationsover the nextseven-year budget,worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist.Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching,Emmanuel Macron has urgedfellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him.Le Pen no longer talks about takingFranceout of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget.Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions | EditorialRead moreYounger Europeans, in particular, facegrowing uncertaintyabout their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU.Recent pollingsuggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act.This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by.Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid. She is the co-author with Alexandros Kentikelenis ofHow Europe SurvivesExplore more on these topicsProtestOpinionEuropean UnionFranceSpainItalyEmmanuel MacronMarine Le PencommentShareReuse this content

title: Harry Styles says his laptop has been dead for six years. Is he just showing off? | Emma Beddington | The Guardian
description: He is either being insincere – knowing he could buy an entire Apple store if he wanted – or he is genuinely overwhelmed by tech. If it’s the latter, he has my sympathy, writes Emma Beddington
Author: Emma Beddington
Headline: He is either being insincere – knowing he could buy an entire Apple store if he wanted – or he is genuinely overwhelmed by tech. If it’s the latter, he has my sympathy, writes Emma Beddington
Content: Floundering or flexing? … Harry StylesPhotograph: XNY/Star Max/GC ImagesView image in fullscreenFloundering or flexing? … Harry StylesPhotograph: XNY/Star Max/GC ImagesOpinionHarry StylesHarry Styles says his laptop has been dead for six years. Is he just showing off?Emma BeddingtonHe is either being insincere – knowing he could buy an entire Apple store if he wanted – or he is genuinely overwhelmed by tech. If it’s the latter, he has my sympathyMon 26 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.30 EDTShareClips of the “epic conversation” (rambling, blokey chat)Rolling Stone orchestrated between Harry Styles and Thom Yorkekeep appearing online, and none more often than the one in which Styles declared his laptop has been dead for about six years. “I don’t know where the charger is,” Styles laughed, prompting a predictable rash of “his computer is NOT OK” jokes from6 Music dadseverywhere.Is this charmingly relatable, or … not? One personal finance influencerdeclared it“a deeply unlikeable clip”, seeing it as the kind of tech-free flex you can get away with only if you are rich and famous. It’s true that the ability to protect your peace by withdrawing from the brain-liquefying churn of online life is a privilege inaccessible to most people, who need tech to function and earn a living. Opting out means delegating digital drudgery to other people:Christopher Nolan’s determination not to have emailmust be a massive pain for his entourage. I betEd Sheeran not having a smartphoneis extremely inconvenient, too – someone else must always have to put the hotel into Google Maps, arrange the Deliveroo dinner and order the Uber.​I’ve seen what Amazon thinks about me – and it revealed a depressing truth | Emma BeddingtonRead moreThis dead laptop business does feel slightly disingenuous – Styles could have an entire Apple store delivered if he fancies a tech upgrade. But I’m inclined to feel more tolerant. He says he uses his phone to write songs, and maybe there is an element of overwhelm at play? I’m always losing cables and procrastinating over tech issues. “I don’t understand why you’re waiting for it to die when you’ll really be in trouble,” my husband said crossly to me this morning as I fought to turn off my ancient phone, which had decided once again that typing was forbidden. But I’m filled with dread and confusion at the thought of replacing it (what model, how many GBs, must I engage with the Cloud?) and my life isn’t too busy or demanding; I can’t imagine what it’s like when you are a global icon on a world tour.So, in case he is floundering not flexing – Harry, check your sock drawer. That’s where I found my charger last time I lost it.Emma Beddington is a Guardian columnistDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? title: I used to think I had impeccable taste in music. My kids taught me to stop being a snob | Myke Bartlett | The Guardian
description: Music may not define them in the way it defined many of my generation, but my children still know a good tune when they hear one
Author: Myke Bartlett
Headline: Music may not define them in the way it defined many of my generation, but my children still know a good tune when they hear one
Content: ‘I am grateful for the new music and artists our kids have discovered,’ writes Myke Bartlett.Photograph: Maskot/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘I am grateful for the new music and artists our kids have discovered,’ writes Myke Bartlett.Photograph: Maskot/AlamyOpinionParents and parentingI used to think I had impeccable taste in music. My kids taught me to stop being a snobMyke BartlettMusic may not define them in the way it defined many of my generation, but my children still know a good tune when they hear oneMon 26 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.30 EDTShareThere was a moment, some years ago in a St Kilda summer, when our family was driving along a busy street, the car windows down, belting out Eric Carmen’s Make Me Lose Control. I had one of those out-of-body experiences parents sometimes get, where you get a clear view of your younger, cooler self looking on in a state of acute embarrassment and despair.How the hell had this happened?There is no better way to examine your own prejudices than attempting to raise children engaged in cultural things. Taking their lead has led me to strange territories, including ballet, medieval festivals and the Gruffalo stage show. But as we enter the hinterland of adolescence, music continues to be the most revealing and unpredictable of journeys.Full disclosure – I am a recovering music snob. My introduction to journalism was being a “rock journalist” (imagine the thrill of that business card) for Cream magazine in the early noughties. Having misspent much of my youth behind the counter of record stores, I was one of those (mostly) young men who saw High Fidelity as a kind of secondhand memoir. Oh, how we judged you for your love of mainstream pap.And yet. The wonderful thing about kids and music is they like what they like. No child is born with an innate sense of cool or cringe. And, being kids, they tend to like fun things. When ours were of an age to move on from Play School records, we let them roam free at local op-shops and choose CDs for their cheap boombox at home. For $1, we ended up with an eight-disc set of Best of the 80s. This proved to be life-changing.I had no nostalgic love for 80s pop. When I was developing my own music taste, my idea of upbeat pop was Morrissey imagining his girlfriend in a coma. Good times! But suddenly our lives were soundtracked by Tears for Fears, A-ha and Bananarama. I knew it was serious when our eldest chose the Beach Boys’ Kokomo as the soundtrack to her final kindergarten presentation.Adapt or die: the Australian live music lovers trying to reinvent an ‘ancient’ and ‘unviable’ industryRead moreI am grateful for the new music and artists our kids have since discovered. Their ever-changing playlists (a source of much conflict on car journeys) have introduced me to diverse acts from Chappell Roan viaRayeto sea shanties and modern folk. But the greatest gift has been the chance to realise how wrong I was about music I already knew.It turns out Queen isn’t tacky and overblown but joyous and extraordinary. Belinda Carlisle didn’t perform disposable fluff but some of the most perfect pop songs ever written. Likewise,the Bangles. Cyndi Lauper? Genius. Cheap Trick? Actually quite good.And who knew that Bowie’s richest period wasn’t the albums Hunky Dory to Low but the first three tracks of Let’s Dance? (With an honourable mention for his and Jagger’s drunken singalong version of Dancing in the Street.) Who knew? The kids knew.What is interesting about this generation of kids is how omnivorous and eclectic they are when it comes to music. The streaming age means almost all of music history is available to everyone, all of the time.New music no longer dominates the old. It’s no harder to hear Eddie Cochran’s Twenty Flight Rock than the Weeknd’s Blinding Lights.The tastes of their parents no doubt play a part – there’s no getting away from how many 80s-themed parties and discos our kids have attended – but their musical world seems far wider than that of my parents, whose music library fitted neatly on to a single, narrow shelf.The algorithm also plays its part, of course. Given our family shares a streaming library, I am long resigned to my recommended listens and favourites being corrupted by the children’s choices. But I try to remind myself they are not polluting the river so much as widening the banks.Outside the house, I am conscious that other algorithms are influencing their listening habits in the same way radio and television once influenced mine. Our kids aren’t yet on social media, but their current playlists are informed by music heard at various sporting events (the Killers, MGMT and Summer of ’69 tend to be on high rotation).I certainly wasn’t listening to music from 40 years earlier when I was 13. More nostalgically, I miss the musical subcultures that were so important and so rigidly defended when I was coming of age. The contained bubbles of popularity allowed by social media enclaves don’t seem quite the same.But that was my journey, not theirs.Our kids have been able to build musical identities out of the very best pop, rock and, uh, however we’re classifying sea shanties without being pinned to the zeitgeist. Sometimes that involves Olivia Dean, sometimes Eric Carmen, sometimes a forgotten track from The Transformers: The Movie soundtrack.Music may not define them in the way it defined many of my generation, but they still know a good tune when they hear one.So, yes, listening to music through the ears of my kids has taught this old snob to listen without prejudice or embarrassment. Because it turns out that serious and important music doesn’t always last, but the fun stuff goes on for ever.Myke Bartlett is a writer and criticExplore more on these topicsParents and parentingOpinionChildrenFamilyPop and rockcommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to power | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: Two years after the Novi Sad tragedy gave birth to a youthful political movement, Sunday’s remarkable election has taken the country into a new era
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: Two years after the Novi Sad tragedy gave birth to a youthful political movement, Sunday’s remarkable election has taken the country into a new era
Content: Supporters of Student List celebrate in Belgrade on Sunday after Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters of Student List celebrate in Belgrade on Sunday after Aleksandar Vučić conceded defeat.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersOpinionSerbiaThe Guardian view on Serbia’s student revolution: from principled protest to powerEditorialTwo years after the Novi Sad tragedy gave birth to a youthful political movement, Sunday’s remarkable election has taken the country into a new eraMon 26 Oct 2026 14.38 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.48 EDTShareThis weekend it will be two years since the collapse of a shoddily constructed train station canopy in Serbia’s second city, Novi Sad. Thetragedy, killing 16 people, was swiftly attributed to state corruption and failures of regulation, sparking student-ledprotestsacross the country.Some of those demonstrators dared to imagine that they could become the catalyst for a democratic revolution.On Sunday, that is more or less what happened. After sustaining their protests and turning them into a political movement, the students resoundinglydefeatedAleksandar Vučić’s autocratic government in a snap legislative poll called by the president himself. Their victory constitutes one of the most remarkable election outcomes in recent European history.For well over a decade Mr Vučić and his Serbian Progressive party (SNS) have exerted a domineering grip over civil society and the media, ruling through a combination of cronyism, patronage and bullying authoritarianism. As a report by international observersconfirmedon Monday, the government made full, unscrupulous use of such tactics to ensure there was no level playing field for the vote. That it was nevertheless routed by a leaderless movement of 20- and 30-somethings will have been noted across a continent in which youthprotestis challenging political priorities.View image in fullscreenAleksandar Vučić.Photograph: Marko Đoković/EPAAs in Hungary, where a focus on corruption helped the opposition tounseatViktor Orbán after 16 years in office, the students’ campaign for basic democratic renewal struck a deeper chord than perhaps even they thought possible. Posing the choice for voters as “Serbia or mafia?”, they put forward a Student List of civic candidates dominated by academics, but also featuring farmers and well-known athletes. A turnout of almost 70% – the highest in a Serbian election since the breakup of Yugoslavia in 1992 – delivered them a comfortable majority.What comes next will necessarily be an experiment in doing things differently. By standing apart from established structures of politics, the student insurgents embodied a freshness of approach and won the trust of the public – including in rural areas presumed to be bastions of Vučić support. In the immediate future, the new government is likely to function as a kind of constituent assembly, dedicated primarily to cleaning up civil society and rolling back the abuses that saw Serbiaplungetowards the bottom of European corruption rankings.Politically, the priority will be to consolidate this domestic agenda by winning the forthcoming presidential election. which is due by late December. But in the longer term there will be less straightforward debates to be had. Mr Vučić’s defeat is good news for the western Balkans as a whole, where he has been a consistently disruptive presence. But on foreign policy issues such as joining the European Union and relations with Russia, opinion across the student movement is divided.As a new government seeks to re-establish the rule of law and a properly functioning and accountable state, Brussels must do all it can to assist that process while outlining a plausible and attractive path to EU membership. Mr Vučić’sSerbia, like Mr Orbán’s Hungary, became a soft autocracy where power was so entrenched that it was hard to imagine how it could be dislodged. But now there are new and better possibilities. In extraordinary fashion, the students’ inspiring journey from principled protest to power has shown just what the art of politics can deliver.Explore more on these topicsSerbiaOpinionEuropeeditorialsShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Lula’s comeback: a victory for Brazil and the world, as well as a Trump rebuff | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working people
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working people
Content: Lula celebrates with his wife, Rosangela ‘Janja’ da Silva, and vice-president Geraldo Alckmin in São Paulo after winning the election on Sunday.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenLula celebrates with his wife, Rosangela ‘Janja’ da Silva, and vice-president Geraldo Alckmin in São Paulo after winning the election on Sunday.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersOpinionBrazilThe Guardian view on Lula’s comeback: a victory for Brazil and the world, as well as a Trump rebuffEditorialA fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working peopleMon 26 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.48 EDTShareLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win inBrazil’s presidential electionis a triumph for him, his country and the world. The 80-year-old incumbent snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, blocked the rise of the far right and saved the planetary air-conditioning system of theAmazon from irreparable destruction. Known universally as Lula, he made history by becoming the first candidate to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round. In triumphing against Flávio Bolsonaro, the leftist stopped what could have been the most dangerous consolidation of authoritarian rule in Brazil since military rule ended. A Bolsonaro presidency could have used a rightwing Congress toextend presidential termsand pack the supreme court, entrenching power for generations.Lula seemed to have been energised by his first-round defeat by Mr Bolsonaro. The three-time president initially pitted his extraordinary life and record against a 45-year-old senator married tocontroversy. But voters wanted answers to economic insecurity, rising prices and poor public services. Lula reversed course in the second round, offering immediate relief fromeveryday costsand indebtedness – including to the rising number of self-employedvoterswhom his rightwing opponent had been courting. Popular mobilisation transformed the runoff into a race to stop a Bolsonaro restoration withstudent protests, massdemonstrationsand a 10 million-strong “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel. It seemed to work. Nearly 5 million more people voted in the second round of the Brazilian election than the first.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump.Photograph: Yuri Gripas/EPAMr Bolsonaro’s desperate refusal to concede follows his father’s playbook. In 2022 then-president Jair Bolsonaro did the same, claiming fraud. The elder Bolsonaro’s attempted coup saw him jailed for27 years. This time Lula’s margin of victory – 4.4m votes – over the younger Bolsonaro was twice that achieved over the father. His win has also been recognised by rightwing regional leaders, conservative newspapers and even aprominent evangelical ally of the Bolsonaros. It may be significant that defeat denied Mr Bolsonaro a presidential shield from allegations ofcorruption and money laundering. Whether he remains in Brazil after his term as senator expires in February remains to be seen.After the Bolsonaro clan, the next biggest loser from the results of the Brazilian election is Donald Trump. Lula’s win broke a run ofseven rightwing presidential winsacross Latin America, a regional advance for which Mr Trump hadclaimed credit. While rightwing leaders in Chile, Paraguay and Peru congratulated Lula on his victory, the White House remained silent. The US president has only himself to blame: he tried to use tariffs topressureBrazil over the elder Bolsonaro’s prosecution and its courts’ enforcement actions against American tech companies. Mr Trump’s meddling handed Lula a winning argument for Brazil’s sovereignty.Brazil remains divided, with a rightwing Congress ready to obstruct Lula – particularly on the environment. But few are better placed to negotiate than the former trade unionist who founded theWorkers’ party. Lula’s victory provides an elected counterweight and that matters for labour rights, public services, Indigenous communities and global climate policy. The win shows the wider democratic left that a broad coalition can defeat the right. Can governing produce the secure livelihoods, strong state provision and meaningful opportunities that make that coalition durable? The next four years in Brazil may provide an answer.Explore more on these topicsBrazilOpinionLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroAmericaseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: France will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebomb | France | The Guardian
description: Letter: Amid widespread protests, Muriel E Cockcroft has sympathy for French youth but fears how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: Amid widespread protests, Muriel E Cockcroft has sympathy for French youth but fears how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion
Content: A protest against the high cost of living in Strasbourg, France, on 17 Oct 2026.Photograph: Roses Nicolas/ABACA/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenA protest against the high cost of living in Strasbourg, France, on 17 Oct 2026.Photograph: Roses Nicolas/ABACA/ShutterstockFranceLettersFrance will lurch from crisis to crisis until it confronts its retirement timebombAmid widespread protests,Muriel E Cockcrofthas sympathy for French youth but fears how much steam will be let out at the next convulsionMon 26 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShareI’m writing in response to your editorial (The Guardian view on France’s protests: a polarised country is in a perilous political moment, 19 October). While the focus is on Emmanuel Macron, let us not forget the hierarchical structure of French administration, from mayors to MPs to senators to prefects and heads of region. All are part of the government, but few stood up to bring leaky school roofs and missing teachers to national consciousness. I deplore the senseless destruction of shops and state buildings. But I also deplore the fact that students had to protest to be heard. In the many administrative tiers of this highly hierarchical country, no one acted and inertia prevailed.Centrally, the government is financially challenged but refuses to acknowledge that having a huge deficit, an ageing population and a low retirement age are perhaps connected. Modest attempts to increase the retirement age also provoked violent protests. Financial tools for individual retirement remain complex and restricted. Thus, this sclerotic system presses on until the next crisis.Neither side of the populist fringe offers a viable path forward. Marine Le Pen’s National Rally and Jean-Luc Mélenchon’s La France Insoumise actively avoid confronting the retirement timebomb, preferring politically expedient promises over fiscal reality.If a system treats retirement as a sacred cow even when the meaning of work is being redefined at lightning speed by AI, if it’s acceptable to have productivity grind to a halt in August because the wisdom of asking employees to all take four to five weeks off in the same month while we live in a 24/7 world is never questioned, and if that same system lets young people study by rote in leaky classrooms while offering its over-60s free social dinners, let us not be surprised if the pressure valve is showing signs of fatigue. My concern is how much steam will be let out at the next convulsion.Muriel E CockcroftDuclair, Normandy, FranceHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: A referendum is not needed for the UK to reach a Bre-entry deal with Europe | Politics | The Guardian
description: Letters: Readers respond to Polly Toynbee’s article on the possibility of rejoining the EU
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Readers respond to Polly Toynbee’s article on the possibility of rejoining the EU
Content: EU Council staff members remove the United Kingdom's flag from the European Council building in Brussels, 31 January 2020.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEU Council staff members remove the United Kingdom's flag from the European Council building in Brussels, 31 January 2020.Photograph: Olivier Hoslet/AFP/Getty ImagesPoliticsLettersA referendum is not needed for the UK to reach a Bre-entry deal with EuropeReaders respond to Polly Toynbee’s article on the possibility of rejoining the EUMon 26 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShareWith all due respect to Polly Toynbee, why do we assume that we would need another referendum to return to Europe (Shall we have another EU referendum? Maybe – but not yet, 19 October)? The last one didn’t work out too well. Asking the electorate to vote a simple yes or no on such a complex and multifaceted deal was never going to be the right approach; nor will it be to go back in.Call it what you will – Brejoin, Bre-entry, Brehabilitation – it shouldn’t be an all-or-nothing deal. The one thing thatBrexithas given us is the opportunity to cherrypick the elements of a relationship that are of mutual benefit to both parties. How about approaching it on a piecemeal basis, processing it through normal parliamentary procedure? No buses required.Gary JonesWimbledon, LondonPolly Toynbee says support for rejoining the EU “grows by the year, partly as older people drop off their perches”. I am still on my perch, but I want us to to rejoin the EU before I fall from it. Why a referendum? Let us just have a detailed manifesto from a trusted prime minister.Michelle EllisonStourbridge, West MidlandsHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Bigger does not always mean better in hospital care | Hospitals | The Guardian
description: Letter: For some medics, working at a large centre means for the same pay you don’t have to work so hard, writes Dr Paul Godwin
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letter: For some medics, working at a large centre means for the same pay you don’t have to work so hard, writes Dr Paul Godwin
Content: ‘Centralising services on fewer sites is a disaster for local populations.’Photograph: Julian Claxton/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘Centralising services on fewer sites is a disaster for local populations.’Photograph: Julian Claxton/AlamyHospitalsLettersBigger does not always mean better in hospital careFor some medics, working at a large centre means for the same pay you don’t have to work so hard, writesDr Paul GodwinMon 26 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShareThe closure of maternity units is always a temptation when the NHS runs into staffing problems, largely of its own making (Up to 20 maternity units in England may have to shut, NHS leader warns, 19 October).In my area the quality of care has already been called into question at the largest local unit, and directing mothers to chance their luck there seems to be an undeserved reward. Likewise a nearby large trust has had the quality of its neonatal care called into question. Closing small units is unlikely to provide the quality gain that is sought.The problem for theNHSis that there is a freedom of ability to employ consultant staff. If you have the money, get on and advertise. This means that the supposedly better, larger units will be able to hoover up all the people they want. The smaller units don’t get a chance.The reason people want to work at big centres is because for the same pay they don’t have to work so hard, or have the same level of responsibility. Government policy has created specialist units in large centres with the belief, promulgated by the medical profession, that bigger means better.When I was appointed as a consultant in 1988, before trusts were invented, the regional health authority made the appointments and made sure that senior medical staffing was fairly spread. You could not have 20 specialists in one district general hospital (DGH) and none in the next.Centralising services on fewer sites is a disaster for local populations. If a DGH loses its obstetrics department, paediatrics would be immediately under threat. It would mean more children would have to travel. Accident and emergency departments would lose specialist support from paediatricians and gynaecologists. Fine if you have a broken arm, not so fine if you have meningitis etc.So, when reviewing the future of obstetrics and midwifery, how about considering the people who live in the area and not just the needs of professors?How about planning to relatively overstaff small units to make sure that they can provide for the needs of the population they serve, and ensuring that the newly qualified are directed towards these posts? After all, the NHS is paid for by everyone, so everyone should get a decent quality of care, without having to travel 50 miles in the dead of night.Dr Paul GodwinKeighley, West YorkshireHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: The regime change we need for Thames Water | Thames Water | The Guardian
description: Letters: Terry Barker says nationalisation changes who owns the shares, it does not change the rules, while James Wallace says the powers to intervene already exist. Plus a letter from Philip Clayton
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Letters: Terry Barker says nationalisation changes who owns the shares, it does not change the rules, while James Wallace says the powers to intervene already exist. Plus a letter from Philip Clayton
Content: ‘The prime minister’s 10-year plan needs a single environmental regulator.’Photograph: Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreen‘The prime minister’s 10-year plan needs a single environmental regulator.’Photograph: Sopa Images/ShutterstockThames WaterLettersThe regime change we need for Thames WaterTerry Barkersays nationalisation changes who owns the shares, it does not change the rules, whileJames Wallacesays the powers to intervene already exist. Plus a letter fromPhilip ClaytonMon 26 Oct 2026 13.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.41 EDTShareAndy Burnham’s instruction to officials to look at all options for Thames Water and not feel constrained (Burnham urges officials to come up with more radical options for Thames Water, 19 October) is welcome, but the options will fail unless they answer the right question.Thames Water is not ill-regulated. It is extractively regulated. For 30 years the rules have allowed dividends paid from borrowing, debt loaded on to customers and sewage discharged into rivers as the cheaper alternative to investment. The creditors now asking for a further £2.4bn are not an aberration; they are the system working as designed.Nationalisation changes who owns the shares. It does not change the rules. A publicly owned Thames under the present regime would inherit the same debt and the same incentive to defer repair; within a decade “public control” would mean ill-regulation by another name.The Cunliffe review’s single water regulator closes one gap. It leaves the larger one: water is still regulated apart from the air, land and soil it moves through, though sewage in a river is a land, soil and water problem at once.The prime minister’s 10-year plan needs a single environmental regulator, with a duty of candour, for air, water, land and soil, with three plain service duties: the service is delivered to standard, the money raised is spent on the service, and the charge is fair to the household that pays it. That, not ownership alone, is what a well-regulated industry looks like.Terry BarkerHonorary professor of environmental sciences, University of East AngliaYour report thatAndy Burnhamhas instructed his team to explore radical solutions to the Thames Water crisis is welcome. But one solution already exists: the special administration regime (SAR), which could bring the company under temporary public control to stabilise and restructure it in the public interest.The forthcoming clean water bill may revisit legislation enabling greater public ownership, but reform must not delay action under existing powers. The Water Industry Act 1991 provides for special administration where statutory conditions are met. Thames Water’s financial instability, service failures and environmental record provide compelling grounds.We at River Action urge the government and Ofwat to petition the high court to place Thames Water into an SAR. A creditor deal will not address the causes of its decline. An SAR offers restructuring that prioritises customers, communities and the environment over creditors.The government should also commission an independent feasibility study of alternative ownership, governance and financing models, including public, mutual and not-for-profit options.No new legislation is needed: the powers and grounds to intervene in Thames Water already exist. Water is an essential public service. Its future must be secured in the public interest.James WallaceCEO, River ActionIf Thames Water is effectively bankrupt, I can’t see why shareholders should get compensation. Broke is broke. Rather than old-style nationalisation, I would turn it into a social enterprise and put it under the control of its engineers.There would be no shares, no dividends, and all profits would be reinvested in infrastructure, such as pipes and new reservoirs.Philip ClaytonLondonHave an opinion on anything you’ve read in the Guardian today? title: Michael Carrick attends Manchester United training ground as club discuss his fate | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: Michael Carrick was at Manchester United’s training ground on Monday to watch the club’s under-21s
Author: Jamie Jackson
Headline: Michael Carrick was at Manchester United’s training ground on Monday to watch the club’s under-21s
