Literally all of life on Earth evolved based on the rhythm of day and night and there is a ton of data showing that messing with this is not a good idea.”“There needs to be some sort of discussion and analysis before we grant these people the right to fundamentally alter the night sky,” he added. “The proposal for 50,000 of these satellite mirrors is crazy and would really end the night sky as we know it.”Bomb the Arctic, dam the Mediterranean and build a second moon: five outlandish plans to remodel our climateRead moreIn August, four groups represented by Earthjusticeasked the FCC to reconsider its approval, citing concerns that opening up the skies to mirrored satellites, which would ascend to about 400 miles (645km) above the Earth’s surface before reflecting light back, would cause a litany of problems.Animals such as birds, insects and mammals rely on the reliable change between day and night to feed, shelter and mate, with any change to this being potentially disastrous for some species.Astronomers, meanwhile, have complained that this night-time glare would worsen existing light pollution and spur an overall rush to add more satellites to orbit – Elon Musk’s SpaceX plansto place 1 million celestial datacenters around Earth– that will obscure the stars and cause more space debris that could descend as pollution back to our world.There are also concerns that the scrambling of night and day will harm people’shealthby disrupting their circadian rhythms as they sleep. Looking directly at the unusual glaring sunlight at night would also, much like doing so during a solar eclipse, harm people’s eyes.Reflect Orbital has said its technology will actually aid the environment by boosting the energy output of solar panels when sunlight is pointed at them during night-time, thereby reducing reliance on fossil fuels.But some climate scientists have warned against meddling with the amount of sun’s energy reaching Earth. Proposals forsolar geoengineering, in which particles are sprayed into the atmosphere to deflect sunlight away from Earth instead of toward it,have also prompted fierce opposition.“Global warming is happening because the Earth has a radiative imbalance due to the massive amounts of greenhouse gases we’ve dumped into the atmosphere,” said David Ho, a climate scientist at the University of Hawaii.“Some people are promoting the already unhinged idea of installing space mirrors facing away from the Earth to reflect the sun’s energy in order to decrease global warming. Imagine wanting to turn those mirrors around so that the Earth gets hotter.”Reflect Orbital said it has had “substantive discussions” with scientists and astronomers on the use of its technology so that areas such as astronomical sites, national parks and other wildlife-rich areas are avoided.“We welcome oversight and want to play a role in shaping it,” a spokesperson said. “We believe it is our responsibility to work alongside governments, scientists and regulators rather than ahead of them.”Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaSpaceSatellitesThe sunGeoengineeringTrump administrationWest CoastfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Autonomy, not flesh’: RAF chief outlines AI drone-powered future | Royal Air Force | The Guardian
description: Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth says technological advances will reduce need for human involvement in warfare
Author: Dan Sabbagh
Headline: Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth says technological advances will reduce need for human involvement in warfare
Content: Typhoon fighters would be accompanied by four AI-enabled drones to monitor its surroundings.Photograph: Okolo Vision/AlamyView image in fullscreenTyphoon fighters would be accompanied by four AI-enabled drones to monitor its surroundings.Photograph: Okolo Vision/AlamyRoyal Air Force‘Autonomy, not flesh’: RAF chief outlines AI drone-powered futureAir Chief Marshal Harv Smyth says technological advances will reduce need for human involvement in warfareDan SabbaghDefence and security editorMon 26 Oct 2026 15.09 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA futureRoyal Air Forcewill rely on “autonomy not flesh”, its chief said on Monday as he described plans in which Typhoon fighters are accompanied by four AI-enabled drones capable of patrolling hundreds of miles in the distance.The technological shift would revolutionise warfare, limit the role of military personnel “towards the outside” and ease the pressure on recruitment, Air Chief Marshal Harv Smyth said in a speech in London.The senior military officer was setting out a strategy for the RAF, which has been told it must be ready to fight against Russia by 2030, at a time when the use of artificial intelligence by the US, Israel, Russia and Ukraine has made warfare more deadly.“AI will enable warfare that speeds well beyond human comprehension, meaning that our role will shift towards the outside, and it will shift towards controlling the activity and setting the guardrails,” Smyth said.The aim, he added, was to mirror the Anglo-American second world war model of “steel, not flesh” – relying on tanks and combat aircraft rather than infantry – to avoid the bloody trench warfare that had led to millions of deaths in the first world war.View image in fullscreenHarv Smyth said humans’ role in the air force would ‘shift towards the outside’.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News“Given today’s changing character of war, I would argue strongly that the modern paradigm must now become autonomy, not flesh,” the chief of air staff said in a lecture at the Royal United Services Institute.Few examples were given about the future use of AI by the air force, but Smyth did point to the £300m Storm Fighter programme of “loyal wingman” drones announced in July as part ofthe delayed defence investment plan. “Crewed platforms are no longer enough,” Smyth said.Four armed, AI-enabled uncrewed craft would work alongside every RAF Typhoon, with the first tests to be conducted next year. The aim is for the drones to be in service by the end of the decade, in line with a Nato directive for the UK and other alliance members to be ready to fight Russia if necessary by 2030.Over the weekend Wes Streeting, the defence secretary, said the UK had “a little over 1,000 days to complete our mission: to be ready with our allies to fight and win”.The drones would “provide force multiplier function and the affordable mass we so definitely require” and, Smyth added, would be “placing sensors, weapons, and united warfare capabilities well within contested airspace”.One possibility would be to use the drones to track Russian aircraft seeking to cross the Greenland-Ireland-UK gap into the north Atlantic, controlling them from a cockpit of a Typhoon flying over Scotland, several hundred miles away.AI has been used by the Israeli and US military to dramatically increase the pace of target selection in the wars in Gaza and Iran, allowing them to run more bombing missions.The IDF used two databases,Lavenderand Habsora (or the Gospel), to increase the pace at which it could attack people and buildings during the war in Gaza. The US’s Maven Smart System, developed in conjunction with Palantir, was used toidentify and strike 1,000 targets in Iranin the first 24 hours of the war this spring.Russia and Ukraine have begun to use AI to identify and strike targets on the ground, eliminating the need for satellite or radio communication as they descend on their bombing mission. In July,Ukrainian investigators concludedthat a drone that killed a person near a Zaporizhzhia gas station in July was relying on AI for its attack.“Autonomous air systems penetrate Russia’s perceived sense of sanctuary on a routine basis,” Smyth said, describing how Ukrainian drones conduct long-range strikes against targets inside Russia, such as oil refineries.Drones would allow the RAF to increase its ability to strike at a time when recruitment has been challenging. The RAF’s fully trained personnel numbers have fallen from 29,800 in 2020 to 27,850 today, and the total has only begun to increase over the last 18 months.Explore more on these topicsRoyal Air ForceMilitaryAI (artificial intelligence)Drones (military)Weapons technologyDefence policyShareReuse this content

title: Jury selected for trial of four accused of sexually assaulting man’s drugged ex-wife | UK news | The Guardian
description: Mr Justice Saini tells the eight men and six women at Winchester crown court the case is likely to be upsetting
Author: Steven Morris
Headline: Mr Justice Saini tells the eight men and six women at Winchester crown court the case is likely to be upsetting
Content: A court artist’s sketch shows (left to right) Norman Macksoni, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins and Mohammed Hassan, who are charged with sexual offences against Joanne Young, the former spouse of Philip Young.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAView image in fullscreenA court artist’s sketch shows (left to right) Norman Macksoni, Connor Sanderson-Doyle, Richard Wilkins and Mohammed Hassan, who are charged with sexual offences against Joanne Young, the former spouse of Philip Young.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAUK newsJury selected for trial of four accused of sexually assaulting man’s drugged ex-wifeMr Justice Saini tells the eight men and six women at Winchester crown court the case is likely to be upsettingSteven MorrisMon 26 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJurors being selected for the trial of four men accused of sexually assaulting the ex-wife of a former Conservative councillor, who has admitted repeatedly drugging and raping her, have been warned the case is likely to be upsetting.Philip Young, 50, has pleaded guilty to multiple charges of abuse against his former wife, Joanne Young, who has waived her right to anonymity.A jury at Winchester crown court will this week begin hearing the trial of four other men charged with sexually assaulting Joanne Young.The alleged offences carried out by the four – Connor Sanderson-Doyle, 32, Richard Wilkins, 62, Norman Macksoni, 48, and Mohammed Hassan, 38 – are said to have taken place between the summer of 2016 and the winter of 2023.Philip Young is named in each of the counts as having committed the alleged offence with the other men.View image in fullscreenA court artist’s sketch of Philip Young, right, who has pleaded guilty to charges of abuse against his former wife.Photograph: Elizabeth Cook/PAA jury panel-in-waiting of 14 – eight men and six women – was randomly selected on Monday to hear the case. After they were brought into court, they were asked to look at the defendants in the dock to check if they recognised them.Mr Justice Saini told the jury they would have realised from a questionnaire they had been asked to fill in that the case they were to hear might upset them.He told them it would involve evidence and videos involving “graphic and sexually explicit imagery” that some people could find upsetting. “It’s not going to be an easy case to be a juror in,” the judge said.Saini asked the panel to reflect overnight if they had any concerns and to let him know on Tuesday morning.The judge also warned the potential jurors not to do any research about the case or discuss it with anyone else. As the panel left the court, one juror could be seen comforting another.Young, formerly of Swindon, has previously admitted offences including voyeurism, rape and administering a substance with intent. He had pleaded guilty to offences over a 13-year period.Young is to be sentenced at the conclusion of the trial, which is expected to last about four weeks.Born in Enfield in June 1976, Young graduated from the University of Westminster in 1998. He was a Conservative councillor on Swindon borough council from 2007 to 2010.He resigned as the cabinet member for culture, regeneration and economic development in May 2010 to devote more time to his family and run his own business, the Swindon Advertiser reported.On the first day of the trial of the four men, a number of women stood outside the court holding up banners in support of the rights of female victims of sexual crimes.Sarah Jones KC is scheduled to open the case on Tuesday.The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Chris Brown given suspended sentence over bottle attack at London club | Chris Brown | The Guardian
description: R&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: R&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023
Content: A masked Chris Brown leaving Southwark crown court on Monday.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersView image in fullscreenA masked Chris Brown leaving Southwark crown court on Monday.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersChris BrownChris Brown given suspended sentence over bottle attack at London clubR&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023Press AssociationMon 26 Oct 2026 08.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe R&B singerChris Brownhas been given a suspended sentence after striking a man twice in the head with a tequila bottle in a central London club.Brown, 37,admitted affrayearlier this year after attacking a former friend with a “heavy” tequila bottle on the dancefloor at the Tape private members’ club in Mayfair in February 2023.Brown was sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, at Southwark crown court on Monday. His vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu, 40, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, and both men were ordered to pay £1,500 costs.In front of a packed public gallery, the singer sat looking at the floor in the dock for much of the hearing.Judge Baumgartner called the attack “plainly dangerous” and warned that “commercial success does not attract preferential treatment” in court.In sentencing, he said: “The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous. It carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained.”CCTV footage was shown in which Brown was seen striking Abraham Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head and then hitting his shoulder.Heidi Stonecliffe KC, prosecuting, told the court Brown used a “heavy square-shaped tequila bottle” to “hit Mr Diaw twice over the left-hand side of his head”. He rained down “further blows” as Diaw turned away, the court heard.Stonecliffe said Akinlolu then grabbed Diaw in a “bear hug”. She said: “Mr Diaw falls to the ground and Mr Brown is also seen throwing punches.”In another clip, Brown, from California, could be seen being pulled away from the victim. The incident took place at about 3am and lasted about 20 seconds, the court heard.Explore more on these topicsChris BrownCrimeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK looking to give carmakers incentives to turn EVs into ‘power plants on wheels’ | Electric, hybrid and low-emission cars | The Guardian
description: V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demand
Author: Jasper Jolly
Headline: V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demand
Content: V2G technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and thensell some of it back to the gridat times of high demand.Photograph: SouthWorks/AlamyView image in fullscreenV2G technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and thensell some of it back to the gridat times of high demand.Photograph: SouthWorks/AlamyElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsUK looking to give carmakers incentives to turn EVs into ‘power plants on wheels’V2G tech enables drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheaper and then sell some back to the grid at times of high demandJasper JollyMon 26 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleElectric cars that can be used as “power plants on wheels” could be given government backing as part of plans under consideration to help UK manufacturers.Ministers are considering giving manufacturers incentives to add “vehicle to grid” (V2G) technology to cars as part of its review of the zero-emission vehicle (ZEV) mandate.The technology allows drivers to charge automatically when electricity is cheap overnight, and thensell some of it back to the gridat times of high demand.If millions of cars have the ability to send power back – or power the driver’s home (V2H) – it couldhelp to solve one of the big problemsof the transition away from fossil fuels to renewables: how to balance the grid during still, cloudy or dark periods when wind and solar generation is lower than electricity demand.The move could give incentives to help to spread a technology that is not yet widely used, but which could lessen the load on the grid and the need to fire up expensive gas power plants to fill gaps in supply. Home batteriescan do the same job.Smart charging tariffs, which do not need V2G tech, already help with the opposite problem by encouraging electric vehicle (EV) owners to charge up when electricity is overabundant and cheap – reducing the need topay renewable generators to switch off.However, campaign groups said the ZEV incentives could also have the perverse effect of allowing carmakers to sell more polluting petrol models in the next few years.Carmakers could earn a “credit” for selling cars installed with V2G technology, also known asbidirectional charging, according to plans detailed in a government consultation that closed on Friday. That credit would allow the carmakers to sell another petrol car without facing the risk of fines if they miss the ZEV targets.The government is preparing to cut electric vehicle sales targets under the ZEV mandate. Environmental groups are braced for changes that could meanan additional 147m tonnes of carbonemitted into the atmosphere by 2050.Ben Nelmes, the chief executive of New AutoMotive, a thinktank tracking the transition to electric cars, said: “Vehicle to grid is exciting technology that could help balance the grid and cut bills, but carmakers should only be rewarded if it’s actually used, not just for fitting it.“Under these proposals, one or even two extra credits worth around £4,000 each would hand manufacturers thousands per car for kit that costs a few hundred pounds, even though few drivers own the expensive charger needed to use it. Ministers should make sure the people who benefit from V2G are drivers and billpayers, not carmakers’ shareholders.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSome people already sell their electricity back to the grid through companies such as OctopusEnergyin the UK, Renault in France, and BMW in Germany. Octopus Energy has claimed that drivers could save £620 a year with the service.Vicky Edmonds, the chief executive of the Electric Vehicle Association England, which represents drivers, said: “We have millions of EV drivers in the UK, but only a fraction are using vehicle to grid or storage technologies. These technologies have enormous potential but consumers are still getting to grips with more immediate questions around the cost of their car, the cost of charging, and whether an EV meets their day to day needs.“It is far too early to be giving manufacturers a credit that effectively allows them to sell fewer EVs, for a technology that has not even been tried and tested, at scale, by drivers in the real world.”Once the technology takes off, electricity supplied by V2G cars could add up to the equivalent of a power station by 2030, able to provide 1.2 gigawatts of power on demand,according tothe National Energy System Operator, which balances Great Britain’s grid. That could grow to as much as 41 GW by 2050, Neso forecasts, enough to meet more than a quarter of peak energy demand.Explore more on these topicsElectric, hybrid and low-emission carsEnergyAutomotive industryEnergy industryMotoringGreenhouse gas emissionsEnergy storagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Jacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentor | Jacinda Ardern | The Guardian
description: Former New Zealand prime minister will focus on leadership, social cohesion and public health in new role
Author: Josh Taylor
Headline: Former New Zealand prime minister will focus on leadership, social cohesion and public health in new role
Content: Jacinda Ardern, pictured with the vice-chancellor, Mark Scott, says she is ‘delighted’ to be joining the University of Sydney.Photograph: Stefanie Zingsheim/The University of SydneyView image in fullscreenJacinda Ardern, pictured with the vice-chancellor, Mark Scott, says she is ‘delighted’ to be joining the University of Sydney.Photograph: Stefanie Zingsheim/The University of SydneyJacinda ArdernJacinda Ardern joins University of Sydney as lecturer and mentorFormer New Zealand prime minister will focus on leadership, social cohesion and public health in new roleFollow ourAustralian politics live blogfor latest updatesGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh TaylorMon 26 Oct 2026 09.01 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 20.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe former New Zealand prime ministerJacinda Ardernwill lecture and mentor at the University of Sydney after moving to Australia earlier this year.Ardern begins this month and her work will focus on empathetic leadership, social cohesion and civic trust. The University ofSydneysaid Ardern would be based in its school of public health, exploring ways to address global health challenges and focusing on equity, inclusion and wellbeing.The former prime minister will host guest lectures and masterclasses and will engage in mentoring, but the university said it was not a full-time teaching role.“I’m delighted to be joining the University of Sydney,” Ardern said. “I’ve found myself especially focused on the question of leadership since leaving office – and how we can better support and encourage the kind of leadership needed to tackle our many global challenges.”Jacinda Ardern and husband Clarke Gayford buy $5.3m home in Sydney’s northern beachesRead moreThe University of Sydney vice-chancellor, Mark Scott, said he had long admired the courage and humanity Ardern brought to public life.“Dame Jacinda led New Zealand through events of profound consequence and her leadership demonstrated that empathy and resolve do not compete with one another; each can strengthen the other,” he said.“For our students, the opportunity to learn from Dame Jacinda is exceptional. They will meet not only a former prime minister, but a thoughtful teacher with a great deal to share about public leadership and service.”In an ABC Conversations interview in July, Ardern said she believed people were seeking empathetic leadership despite many world leaders embodying a “dominant style” of leadership.“You see people voting for parties [that] are often on the fringes of the mainstream. When you dive into the research, the majority of those who are doing that are often not voting for the ideology – they’re just voting against the status quo because they don’t think it serves them any more.View image in fullscreenJacinda Ardern and University of Sydney master of science-sustainability studies student Ting-Jen Kuo.Photograph: Stefanie Zingsheim/The University of Sydney“So I think all the signs actually point to people wanting something different than what they’re getting now.”Ardern retired from politics in January 2023, after more than five years as prime minister and the leader of the Labour party. She led the country through the Christchurch terrorist attack, the Whakaari volcanic eruption and the Covid pandemic.In 2017, aged 37, Ardern became the world’s youngest-serving female leader, later becoming the second world leader to give birth while in office.Ardern has since held fellowships at Harvard University focused on public leadership and technology governance, and published her memoir, A Different Kind of Power, in 2025.Ardern, her husband, Clarke Gayford, and daughter, Neve, moved to Sydneyearlier this year,buying a property in Sydney’s northern beachesfor $5.3m.Explore more on these topicsJacinda ArdernAustralian universitiesSydneyNew South WalesAustralian educationnewsShareReuse this content

title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’ | Global development | The Guardian
description: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze
Author: Mark Townsend
Headline: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze
Content: Armed defectors from the Rapid Support Forces arrive to surrender to the Sudanese military in Omdurman on 19 August.Photograph: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArmed defectors from the Rapid Support Forces arrive to surrender to the Sudanese military in Omdurman on 19 August.Photograph: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP/Getty ImagesGlobal developmentUK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freezeSupported byAbout this contentMark TownsendMon 26 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of amass atrocitythat saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.A year after thefall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected toa travel ban and an asset freeze.The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – thefastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.The killings came at the end of an 18-monthstarvation siegeby the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous,with testimony indicatingroutine detention, torture and unlawful killings.Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UKwarnings were sidelinedin the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre fromthe Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudansaid: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which hasforced 14 million people to flee their homes– has developed increasingly into a drone war.Thelatest strikessaw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSudanAfricaMiddle East and north AfricaWar crimesRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Walter Koenig, actor best known as Chekov on Star Trek, dies aged 90 | Star Trek | The Guardian
description: The actor appeared in the cult 1960s show as well as many of the films but also worked as a writer
Author: Adrian Horton
Headline: The actor appeared in the cult 1960s show as well as many of the films but also worked as a writer
Content: Walter Koenig in Star Trek.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenWalter Koenig in Star Trek.Photograph: CBS Photo Archive/CBS/Getty ImagesStar TrekWalter Koenig, actor best known as Chekov on Star Trek, dies aged 90The actor appeared in the cult 1960s show as well as many of the films but also worked as a writerAdrian HortonMon 26 Oct 2026 14.42 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.18 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWalter Koenig, the actor known for playing Pavel Chekov throughout the Star Trek franchise, has died, his representative confirmed tothe Hollywood Reporter. He was 90.Koenig died at his home in North Hollywood surrounded by his daughter and niece, according to aFacebook postby Zachery McGinnis, the founder of Galactic Productions, an appearance agency that counted the actor as one of its clients. His death was attributed to “old age”, with no other details provided.“Today we mourn the passing of Walter Koenig, whose talent, warmth, and unforgettable performances left a lasting mark on generations of fans around the world,” McGinnis wrote. “Walter’s legacy extends far beyond the screen. Through countless convention appearances and interactions with fans, he shared his kindness, wit, and appreciation with everyone fortunate enough to meet him. He understood whatStar Trekmeant to people and embraced the community that grew around it.”The post concluded: “Thank you, Walter, for the memories, the inspiration, and for boldly going where few have gone before.”“My heart is heavy,” wrote Koenig’s Star Trek co-star George Takei onFacebookon Monday. Takei first met Koenig in the 1960s, “on the bridge of the Enterprise” and remained friends for six decades; Koenig served as Takei’s best man at his wedding in 2008.“Walter was more than Chekov. He was a writer, a teacher, a thoughtful man, and a loyal friend,” Takei wrote. “To the fans who loved him for so many years, thank you. He loved you too. Rest well, my dear friend. Keep navigating a steady course.”Jesse Thorn, the host of the NPR show Bullseye, also confirmed the news onBluesky, citing his friend Danielle Koenig, the late actor’s daughter. “Something I was struck by knowing Danielle, her husband and her late brother Andrew (and talking with George Takei) was the very sincere love those Star Trek cast members had for each other,” he wrote. “That whole thing was thrust upon them and their obvious deep friendship was so clear. What a gift.”Born in Chicago but raised in Manhattan as the child of Lithuanian immigrants, Koenig began his acting career in 1962, with an uncredited role as a sentry in Combat!. He joined Star Trek for the start of the second season and appeared in 36 of the 50 episodes that aired between 1967 and 1969.He continued his role as the Russian Chekov in the first seven Paramount movies derived from the show, released between 1979 and 1991, as well as in a two-part crowdsourced Renegades series that debuted online in 2017. He most recently appeared in a cameo for a 2023 episode of Star Trek: Picard, voicing Anton Chekov, the son of his original character.Koenig also worked as a writer, penning episodes for such series as The Powers of Matthew Star, Family, Land of the Lost and The Incredible Hulk. He wrote, produced and starred in the 2010 sci-film InAlienable, starring Richard Hatch.Koenig was married to the actor Judy Levitt, with whom he appeared in three Star Trek movies as well as another acclaimed sci-fi series, Babylon 5, which ran from 1994 until 1998. The couple were together from 1965 until her death in December 2022 at the age of 83. Their son Andrew, who played Richard “Boner” Stabone in the ABC sitcom Growing Pains, died in 2010 at age 41.Koenig is survived by his daughter, the actor and screenwriter Danielle Koenig.This article was amended on 26 October, 2026 to correct details on Koenig’s cameo on Star Trek: Picard.Explore more on these topicsStar TrekTelevisionScience fiction TVUS televisionnewsShareReuse this content

title: Visa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over fees | Banking | The Guardian
description: Application made for group claim seeking compensation for companies for alleged overcharging on customer card payments
Author: Kalyeena Makortoff
Headline: Application made for group claim seeking compensation for companies for alleged overcharging on customer card payments
Content: Spokespeople for Visa and Mastercard defended the multilateral interchange fees.Photograph: Thomas Fuller/Sopa Images/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenSpokespeople for Visa and Mastercard defended the multilateral interchange fees.Photograph: Thomas Fuller/Sopa Images/ShutterstockBankingVisa and Mastercard threatened with potential £5bn UK lawsuit over feesApplication made for group claim seeking compensation for companies for alleged overcharging on customer card paymentsKalyeena MakortoffBanking correspondentMon 26 Oct 2026 11.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.49 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleVisa and Mastercard are being threatened with a potential £5bn lawsuit for allegedly stifling competition and charging UK businesses excessive fees.The law firms Harcus Parker and Hausfeld have lodged an application at the Competition Appeal Tribunal in hopes of pursuing a group claim that would compensate companies who, they claim, have been overcharged on customer card payments since October 2020.The claim will centre on multilateral interchange fees, which are set by Visa and Mastercard and then paid by businesses through their banks every time a customer pays by card. The argument is that the lack of competition has left businesses at their mercy – and paying higher fees on debit, credit and prepaid cards – as a result.The case will hope to claw back fees charged over the past six years, as well as interest on those losses. Sources close to the claim estimate that it could be worth about £5bn, based on the number of businesses allegedly overcharged between 2020 and 2026.A spokesperson for Mastercard defended the interchange fees, saying the potential group claim was “speculative” and part of a “growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation”.The case is being funded by Bench Walk Advisors, a London-headquartered firm that launched in 2017 and makes money from backing lawsuits. It is being led by Stephen Allen, a British businessman and former travel sector executive who has been pursuing Visa and Mastercard through a number of group legal actions since 2021.If the application is successful, an estimated 1m UK-based businesses, organisations and charities with less than £100m in revenues will be automatically included for compensation, unless they opt out. Their claims could be worth several thousands of pounds each.Larger businesses would have to actively opt in to be included in the claim, and could be due tens of millions over the claim period.However, it could take years for the case to reach a conclusion. Visa and Mastercard last yearagreed to pay a combined $167.5mto settle a class action lawsuit in the US which accused the two companies of conspiring to keep ATM access fees artificially high. That lawsuit was originally filed in 2011.Commenting on the latest group claim application, a Mastercard spokesperson said: “We strongly disagree with the basis of this claim. Interchange plays a vital role in supporting the UK payments ecosystem, and ensures people and businesses can pay and get paid quickly and securely.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotion“This speculative claim does nothing to support UK businesses or consumers and instead reflects the growing trend of opportunistic funder-backed litigation. It is exactly the type of claim the UK government’s recently announced proposed opt-out class action reforms [put out for consultation this summer] are directed at preventing.”A Visa spokesperson said: “Visa continues to believe that interchange is a critical component to maintaining a secure digital payments ecosystem that benefits all parties, including consumers, merchants and banks.”Explore more on these topicsBankingCredit card feesCredit cardsDebit cardsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industry | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability
Content: Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, in Bengaluru, India, on 16 February 2026.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, in Bengaluru, India, on 16 February 2026.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersAnthropicAnthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industryMarket debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viabilityBlake MontgomeryandJohana BhuiyanMon 26 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropichas publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom.Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT,confidentially filedwith US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.“We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’sinvestor prospectusreads. Anthropic researchers and executives have trumpeted the transformative power of AI while simultaneously warning of its potential to cause human extinction.Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030Read moreA leader in the race to create powerful artificial intelligence models and a bellwether of the American AI boom, Anthropic’s chatbot Claude is its flagship product, which offers text generation features as well as advanced coding and cybersecurity capabilities. CEODario Amodeifounded the company after quitting OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.Anthropic’saudited filingswill offer the first public glimpse of its financial health, which have been the object of intense speculation in recent months as questions of apotential AI bubble swirl.The company detailed rapidly rising revenue in the prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.Despite the increasing revenue,Anthropicdisclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.Anthropic has focused on businesses as its primary paying customers, unlike OpenAI, which has courted everyday consumers for ChatGPT. As of 30 September, Anthropic said it had more than 14,000 enterprise customers – 11,900 of which had $100,000 or more of revenue, more than 1,900 that had $1m or more revenue and about 250 enterprise customers that had $10m or more revenue.“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” Anthropic executives wrote.The filing contains some of the hyperbolic language characteristic of AI companies predicting the miraculous potential of their technology. Describing the potential of AI agents, semi-autonomous chatbots that can carry out tasks on behalf of users, Anthropic executives wrote: “The result is something without historical precedent: what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a datacenter, available to every organization and sector of the economy.”Investing in Anthropic and the development of a model that the company claims could revolutionize knowledge work across industries comes with a great deal of risk. Anthropic listed more than 90 pages of potential to its business. For one, a “substantial portion” of the company’s revenue comes from a limited number of customers, and losing any of them could put a huge dent in their revenue. A quarter of Anthropic’s revenue comes from its top five customers, though no single customer represents more than 10% of its business.The company also has incurred $6.2bn in debt as it built out its infrastructure and spends billions yearly on computing power provided by third parties, according to the filing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI modelsRead moreThe misuse of AI and Claude in particular also poses a considerable risk to Anthropic’s business. When it comes to AI, there are four categories of potential risk, executives wrote: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. Anthropic’s most capable models have “capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote. The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended.”Amodei has called for a slowdown of AI’s development, citing existential risk. Anthropic’s stock market listing may elicit a rush of investment in the company and the AI sector more broadly, which could speed up the pace of the industry further.The company disclosed that in September 2025, staffers documented what they believe was the first large-scale cyber-attack that didn’t rely on significant human intervention. Anthropic “detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”.Donald Trump’s administration may also be a risk to the company. Anthropic has been embroiled in a feud with the Trump administration over the use of the startup’s products in warfare, which culminated in the designation of the company as a supply chain risk, a first for an American company. This prevents any military agency from contracting with Anthropic. The company has challenged the blacklisting.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicStock marketsUS marketsAI (artificial intelligence)Dario AmodeiChatbotsIPOsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cuts | Microsoft | The Guardian
description: Tech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reports
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Tech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reports
Content: The Microsoft campus in Mountain View, California.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Microsoft campus in Mountain View, California.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesMicrosoftMicrosoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cutsTech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reportsGaya GuptaMon 26 Oct 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMicrosoft announced that it would offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of artificial intelligence, according to reports, the latest example of how AI is reshaping tech companies and the greater workforce.This is the latest of several trimmings Microsoft has made to its workforce this year. The company announced in April that it was offering voluntary retirement to about 7% of its US workforce, which consisted of about 125,000 employees at the time. Its global workforce is made up of about 223,000 workers globally.Some of Microsoft’s most recognizable divisions – including Xbox, Windows and Copilot, its AI tool – will be participating in the offer, Bloomberg reported on Monday. Employees in certain divisions, including in cybersecurity, datacenters and marketing, would not be eligible for the offer, it said.“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice-president and chief people officer, said in a statement. The company did not respond to a request for comment on further details about the offer.Multiple tech companies have announced layoffs due to the rise of AI and increased investment in the technology this year. Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, announced plans in April to cut 10% of its personnel, or about 8,000 employees, to boost efficiency. Amazon has madeseveral cuts to its workforce, most recently in its retail division. And in June, Oracle shed its workforce by nearly 13%, cutting 21,000 jobs,as a result of AI.But it’s unclear whether these workforce-reduction measureshave translated yet into greater efficiency,and some companies, including Meta, have scaled back their layoff plans. A top leader of Microsoft, Ryan Roslansky, recently complained about “AI slop” in the workforce on social media.The National Bureau of Economic Research also recently published aworking paperwhich found that among the 9,000 senior executives it surveyed from around the world, 90% said AI had yet to result in greater productivity at their companies.Explore more on these topicsMicrosoftAI (artificial intelligence)Job lossesTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Healey is expected to shield low-income pensioners from income tax – but how will it work? | Pensions | The Guardian
description: Retirees will get a personal allowance aligned with the new state pension, but experts say it could get complicated
Author: Hilary Osborne
Headline: Retirees will get a personal allowance aligned with the new state pension, but experts say it could get complicated
Content: A scheme where only those reliant solely on the state pension get an extra allowance could mean that anyone receiving even a tiny income from elsewhere will pay tax on everything over the standard allowance.Photograph: Geoff Smith/AlamyView image in fullscreenA scheme where only those reliant solely on the state pension get an extra allowance could mean that anyone receiving even a tiny income from elsewhere will pay tax on everything over the standard allowance.Photograph: Geoff Smith/AlamyPensionsExplainerHealey is expected to shield low-income pensioners from income tax – but how will it work?Retirees will get a personal allowance aligned with the new state pension, but experts say it could get complicatedHilary OsborneMon 26 Oct 2026 09.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.31 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRetirees in the UK on low incomes are expected to be given a new personal allowance so that they do not have to hand any of their state pension to HMRC.The full details are due to be revealed by the chancellor, John Healey, in Wednesday’s budget, but here is what we know so far.New state pension is set to overtake personal allowanceThe state pension rises each April.There are two different pensions, the basic state pension which is received by older retirees and the new state pension which is received by anyone who has retired since 6 April 2016.How much the new state pension goes up by is determined bythe triple lock, which promises that it will be the highest of inflation, wage growth or 2.5%.This year, the highest of the three has been wage growth, which for the relevant month was 3.9%. As a result, from April 2027 the full state pension will be worth £13,036 a year. Thanks to a freeze in the personal allowance that applies to everyone, the amount anyone can earn before paying tax hasremained at £12,570 since 2021.This year, the full new state pension was just under that figure, at £12,547.Graph showing the rise in pensions and personal allowances over timeProtection for the poorestLots of pensioners have money from private and workplace pensions which already puts them over the personal allowance, and 9.6 million are already taxpayers.As the prospect of the state pension overtaking the allowance loomed last year, the then chancellor, Rachel Reeves, promised that anyone derivingall of their incomefrom the state pension would not be taxed. This wasconfirmed this year.It had been suggested that this could be done by writing off tax bills below £100, as next year’s numbers would mean people owing about £90 each if they were on only the state pension. However, it is reported that instead pensioners will have a higher personal allowance.New allowance for someA report in the Times suggests Healey will set a personal allowance for low-income pensioners that is exactly aligned with the full new state pension. This means that in the 2027-28 tax year it will be £13,036, and it will rise in subsequent years in line with the pension increases.With the regularpersonal allowance frozen until 2030-31and the triple lock in place until 2030, that means this special allowance is expected to pull away from the one that most taxpayers will have.It could get very complicatedThe former pensions minister Steve Webb says that this way of lifting the pension out of tax could prove “messy and increasingly expensive”.We do not know the details, but a scheme where only those reliant solely on the state pension get an extra allowance could mean that anyone receiving even a tiny income from elsewhere will pay tax on everything over the standard £12,570 allowance.Trying to solve this could mean introducing complicated tapering.Webb says: “The gap between the new state pension and the tax threshold is set to grow every year, which will make the policy hard to switch off. But if it continues, the cost will grow and grow.“And if the extra allowance is available only to those on a low income, there could be a growing ‘cliff-edge’ problem where those with very small amounts of private income lose the whole allowance and end up worse off than those with nothing.”To make things more complicated, it is not clear how pensioners on the old state pension will be given the same protection. Their pension consists of two elements and in some cases people who get only the state pension are already being paid a figure above the personal allowance.Pensioners’ higher allowance has been scrapped beforeUp until the 2013-14 tax year, people aged 65 or older could claim one of two age-related additions to the personal allowance. The year before this was introduced, the personal allowance was £8,105 for under-65s, £10,500 for those aged 65-75, and £10,660 for those aged over 75. The allowance was tapered so pensioners with incomes of just over £30,000 did not get the extra relief.The larger allowance was supposed to help older people retain money to meet higher heating costs and other expenses associated with ageing.The change was made by the then chancellor, George Osborne, to make the system simpler: lots of pensioners did not realise they had to claim it, and the tapering was complicated. He froze the existing allowance for pensioners.He said at the time: “This will protect the existing level of allowance pensioners have while introducing a new single personal allowance for all. It is a major simplification, it saves money, and no pensioner will lose in cash terms.”The change will benefit only pensionersAnother thing that might make the policy unpopular is that it will give pensioners a benefit that is not shared by low-income workers. Some may argue that it would be fairer to increase the personal allowance for everyone. That would, of course, be much more expensive for the government.Explore more on these topicsPensionsOlder peopleBudget 2026BudgetEconomic policyState pensionsTaxexplainersShareReuse this content

title: ‘Nothing worked for me until I was clean and sober’: Ashley Walters on acting, directing – and turning his life around | Movies | The Guardian
description: In Adolescence he proved himself one of the UK’s best actors. Now he has directed his first film, Animol. He reflects on the road from prison and addiction to soaring success
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: In Adolescence he proved himself one of the UK’s best actors. Now he has directed his first film, Animol. He reflects on the road from prison and addiction to soaring success
Content: ‘I’ve got eight kids, three grandkids, I’m paying a mortgage!’ … Ashley Walters.Photograph: Jamie Salmons/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’ve got eight kids, three grandkids, I’m paying a mortgage!’ … Ashley Walters.Photograph: Jamie Salmons/The GuardianThe big interviewMoviesInterview‘Nothing worked for me until I was clean and sober’: Ashley Walters on acting, directing – and turning his life aroundSteve RoseIn Adolescence he proved himself one of the UK’s best actors. Now he has directed his first film, Animol. He reflects on the road from prison and addiction to soaring successMon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAshley Walters seems to have lived his life on fast-forward. Before he turned 21 he had already had a No 1 hit, performed on TV and the West End stage, become a father and served seven months in prison. He has had another lifetime’s worth of incident since – including seven more children – but at the ripe old age of 44, enough water has passed under the bridge for Walters to have some perspective on his youth. Not that all that living appears to have left a mark: when we meet in London, he’s the picture of health, his face unwrinkled, eyes twinkling, hair cut in a crisp lineup.Back in the early 2000s, he fit a certain stereotype of Black British youth as Asher D, the rapper from deprived and supposedly crime-ridden Peckham, who rolled with the street-tough So Solid Crew, got into beefs with east London rivals such as Dizzee Rascal, was demonised by the tabloids andcalled a “boasting macho idiot rapper” by the then culture minister Kim Howells.So Solid Crew were trailblazing in terms of British hip-hop, but Walters’ view of those times is far from rose-tinted. “Everything other than the music, it was bad, it was negative,” he says. “The music was very British, but if you looked at our style, our clothes, the jewellery, the cars, that was all the Americanised stuff that we wanted to bring into it.” That also included guns – even if, in Walters’ case, the firearm was a modified air pistol.Asher D was never really him, he says. “Behind the scenes, in all honesty, I was questioning if I was doing the right thing. Because a lot of our success was underpinned with street stuff: you can’t go to that area because you might get shot; you can’t do this because that person has had beef with this person; and it was, like, all this politics.”He’d got in with the wrong crowd, he suggests, “and it took me down the road of just not giving a shit any more … but the realisation came to me when that door was shut in the prison cell. And I was like: ‘Hold on. How the f– did I get here?’”View image in fullscreen‘I wanted it to feel, look and sound the way it felt, looked and sounded to me’ … Walters on the set of Animol.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/SkyWe’re talking about his prison days because Walters is now revisiting them, from the other side of the door. He has just directed his first film, Animol, which is set in a young offender institution. It is by no means autobiographical (it was written by Nick Love, of Football Factory fame), but he says that a lot of it is based on his own experience and memories of being locked up. “I wanted it to feel, look and sound the way it felt, looked and sounded to me.”This is a genre that comes with certain expectations: brutality, bullying, staff-inmate relations, internal hierarchies. Animol meets many of them.The tension winds up from the first scene, when the story’s 15-year-old protagonist, Troy (Tut Nyuot), is coerced into smuggling in a phone. But the film also defies those expectations in surprising ways, not least with a queer romantic element that’s sensitively and sensuously handled. In that sense, it’s as muchMoonlightas Scum – “slightly elevated,” as Walters puts it. “I didn’t want it to feel grey and gloomy like the other prison-genre films.”Like Walters in his youth, these young men are playing roles, Animol suggests, concealing their authentic selves in order to navigate a landscape of fear, shame, trauma and codes of masculinity that has really changed very little over the years. “Every character in there, no matter how bad they are, no matter how manipulative or violent even at times, all of their actions are born from fear,” he says. “The idea a lot of people grow up with, like I did, of masculinity: being hard, never backing down, stoic, keep your emotions to yourself and never cry in front of other people. I was brought up with those rules and those regulations.”View image in fullscreenMarginalised … Tut Nyuot as Troy in Animol.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/SkyTroubled young men, masculinity, fathers and sons – one way or another, these have become recurring themes in Walters’ career. There’s a continuity, I suggest, between Animol and his recent role in the highly acclaimed Netflix drama Adolescence. He anchored the second episode as the investigating detective visiting the perpetrator’s school, seeking answers. The technical aspect alone was a ballet dance – Walters had to hit multiple marks as the one-take episode roved around a chaotic secondary school – but on top of that, he delivered a soulful, understated performance as a father struggling to connect with his teenage son.It’s not a link he would make himself, Walters says, “but the theme, I guess, that runs through it is uncovering a marginalised group of people. And in the UK one of the biggest marginalised groups is kids.” And especially young men. “Over the years we’ve been pushed into repression and keeping your mouth shut, not questioning things and not having conversations with your friends and your peers about how you feel about life … Men just don’t do that. I think women find that a lot easier. That’s why we find we have a lot higher suicide rates, especially in young men in the UK.”View image in fullscreenFathers and sons … Amari Jayden Bacchus as Adam Bascombe and  Walters as DI Bascombe in Adolescence.Photograph: Ben Blackall/NetflixWalters’ own struggle through this territory would make for a movie in itself. He was mainly raised by his mother, Pamela, who worked in local government. She enrolled him at the Sylvia Young Theatre School aged seven (as a child actor, he performed in the stage version of Oliver!, had a role in Grange Hill and studied ballet and tap).His father was mostly absent, Walters says. “He’d turn up one Sunday and then you wouldn’t see him for four months. And then he’d try and take me out, and then not take me somewhere and get drunk instead, and then I’d have to come home by myself.” He died in 2005, by which time they had made their peace. “He wanted to be a dad; he just didn’t have the tools and the resources. And he didn’t have the best start in his own life.” Born in the UK to Jamaican parents, Walters’ father was put in care, and was in and out of borstal, then prison, his whole life.So when that prison door slammed on Walters in 2002, he felt as if he was repeating the cycle. Except he was a celebrity, so all the other inmates knew who he was. When he arrived that first night, “all hell broke loose”. For hours, people shouted insults, and threatened to kill him in the morning.“It wasn’t a pleasant experience at all,” he says. “I was tried, I was tested, it was pressure, there was loads of fear. But I had no choice. It’s an experience I had to go through, and actually it was one of the best things that happened to me.”How so? “It pushed me to the thoughts I needed to have: who do I want to be? What do I want from life? And then, looking around me and seeing my circle of friends and entrusted loved ones, do they reflect that? And the answer was a big resounding no.”He was in effect starting again. “When I came out of prison, I didn’t know what I was going to do with my life, and a lot of doors were shut.” His music career had ground to a halt; he didn’t have an acting agent; he was not allowed to travel to the US owing to his conviction. Fortunately, the British film-maker Saul Dibb had written a role with him in mind: Bullet Boy, the story of a young ex-con returning to a very familiar set of troubles: guns, local rivalries, council estate life.View image in fullscreenBreakthrough role … Walters, 21, in Bullet Boy.Photograph: AccuSoftThe film, and Walters’ performance, werewidely praisedand his acting career hit its stride: shows such as MTV’s stoner sitcom Top Buzzer; a part in 50 Cent’s biopic Get Rich or Die Tryin’; the adaptation of Andrea Levy’s immigrant drama Small Island. Then in 2011 came the role that pushed him into the mainstream: as Dushane in Channel 4’s Top Boy, chief drug dealer on his Hackney estate, whose quest for bigger and better things takes him on what becomes an epic journey.As with So Solid Crew,Top Boywas accused of glamorising crime and violence, but Walters disagrees. The show went deeper in terms of character, morality and complexity, he argues. Many of the storylines and characters were based on real people and events. “It came from the source, so it felt real and rich,” Walters says. “Our whole thing was, we wanted the drug dealers to like it. If the drug dealers call us and go, ‘Bro, that’s the first time I’ve seen myself portrayed properly,’ then the rest should fall in place.”View image in fullscreenAs Dushane in Top Boy.Photograph: Chris Harris/NetflixIt wasn’t just the drug dealers; Top Boy became a global hit – and people still identify him with the role. “A lot of the time, if I walk down the street, my name’s Dushane. I spend a lot of my time having to tell people that stop me: I’m a 44-year-old man. I’m not even a ‘boy’ any more. I’ve got eight kids, three grandkids, I’m paying a mortgage! Like, I’m really not in that life.”After Top Boy, his next act was something of a breakthrough, albeit a tainted one from today’s perspective. Bulletproof was a buddy cop series that unprecedentedly featured two Black leads: Walters and Noel Clarke. The two of them spent years trying to get the series made, pitching it as a British Bad Boys, and being told it could only work if one of the characters was white. When it came out on Sky in 2018, the show was a success, running for three seasons, but it was cancelled after allegations against Clarke came to light in April 2021.At the time, Walters put out a statement saying his thoughts were with the women who had made the allegations. He and Clarke have not spoken since, he says. “But I don’t want to hate on anyone. Everyone has got their own journey and everyone has their own story to tell, and I think when they are ready to tell it, they will tell it.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s no coincidence that my life’s changed, like, amazingly.’Photograph: Jamie Salmons/The GuardianWalters had been going through his own struggles around that time. He had been an alcoholic and a drug user – predominantly cocaine – for about 15 years, and things had come to a head a few months before, in November 2020.“Maybe in the first year, alcohol and substances were great,” he says. “They helped me perform, they helped me be more lively at parties and network with people that I was shit-scared to talk to before.”Does he mean performing on set? “Performing on set I was freer, maybe wilder – who knows how I looked at that point? I felt I was doing a good job and giving people what they wanted, but the truth is, very, very quickly it stopped working, and started to hold me back.”The breaking point came during lockdown, after an argument with his wife about his drinking and drug use. He had been married to Danielle, the mother of his four youngest children, since 2013 (his eldest child is now 27, his youngest 10).He immediately sought help. “The next morning, my wife dropped me at rehab and I was there for four weeks, came out and I’ve never drunk or drugged since and it’s coming up to six years in November. So, very thankful for that. Sad it took me so long to get there, and there’s a lot of amends to make with family and kids and friends, but one of the best things I’ve ever done.” He also moved out of London in 2021, and now lives on the Kent coast. “In the last six years, it’s no coincidence that my life’s changed, like, amazingly. The truth is, nothing started working for me until I was clean and sober.”View image in fullscreenWalters and Stephen Graham at Netflix’s Golden Globe afterparty in January.Photograph: Gonzalo Marroquin/Getty Images for NetflixThat includes his sensitive turn in Adolescence, and his new career as a director, which began with a short film in 2021, Boys, then episodes on multicultural school drama Ackley Bridge and underrated Victorian crime series A Thousand Blows. The latter came thanks to his old friend Stephen Graham, who starred and co-produced the series – they’ve been mates since the 2004 sitcom Top Buzzer. After that, Graham cast him in Adolescence. Graham now plays the welfare officer in Animol. He gives the young inmates a stirring talk about shame that ends the film on a cathartic, hopeful note.“This is a tender, tactile sort of film where you’re seeing men hold each other – even the ones that are not gay, they’re embracing each other,” Walters says. “There’s love, and I’m like that with my friends. I kiss my friends on the cheek, my stepdad will give me a kiss, I still kiss Mum, I’ll kiss my kids. I wanted to show that on screen, like how boys are with each other, even in the worst environments, even when they’re going through the worst things.”The theme resonates with Walters, of course, but this is also him challenging those codes of masculinity and male relationships that shaped his own life, and his father’s, and many others besides. “I realised that vulnerability is part of a man’s DNA as well,” he says. He’s breaking the cycle.Animol is out on 30 October in the UKDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article? If you would like to submit a response of up to 300 words by email to be considered for publication in ourletterssection, pleaseclick here.Explore more on these topicsFilmThe big interviewGrimeAshley WaltersCrime filmsTop BoyinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: As mega-hit Into the Woods wows the West End, what’s the secret weapon of this Sondheim spectacular? | Theatre | The Guardian
description: With its shimmering forest and its plunge into darkness and destruction, this fairytale romp bagged an Olivier for its lighting – and, reveals designer Aideen Malone, it wasn’t even finished
Author: David Jays
Headline: With its shimmering forest and its plunge into darkness and destruction, this fairytale romp bagged an Olivier for its lighting – and, reveals designer Aideen Malone, it wasn’t even finished
Content: Breathtaking … light breaks through the trees behind Oliver Savile and Rhys Whitfield in Into the Woods.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBreathtaking … light breaks through the trees behind Oliver Savile and Rhys Whitfield in Into the Woods.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreInterviewAs mega-hit Into the Woods wows the West End, what’s the secret weapon of this Sondheim spectacular?David JaysWith its shimmering forest and its plunge into darkness and destruction, this fairytale romp bagged an Olivier for its lighting – and, reveals designer Aideen Malone, it wasn’t even finishedMon 26 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 06.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a minute I worry that Aideen Malone might return her Olivier award. “It’s funny that I won an award for it, because I would say Into the Woods is one of the most unfinished pieces I have ever done,” declares the lighting designer. “There was a lot of detail we never got a chance to finish. We ran out of time – big time!”Luckily, the judges and audiences disagreed. If you want to see enchantment, take yourself toStephen Sondheim’s musical set in the twisted world of fairytale. Cinderella, Red Riding Hood and others bounce into the forest, which shimmers in a weave of powdery, gleaming branches and light angling through all the trees. Now transferred to the West End fromLondon’s Bridge theatre, it’s a breathtaking piece of design for a seriously playful musical.double quotation markInto the Woods offers a series of smoke and mirror surprises for which Malone uncages a misty spectrum of smoke and haze“This is a stunning piece, but it’s a monster,” Malone declares. “There was a lot of problem-solving.” From a lighting point of view, it is “about the passing of time, day and night. The woods are very luscious and inviting initially, and then become darker and more mysterious.” As tales old and new collide, and characters stumble far beyond their happy ever afters, design signposts the journey. After the initial quest into the woods, the characters return to find that arcadia has collapsed into “destruction and wasteland”.View image in fullscreenSending light through wheat fields in the Olivier-winning Fiddler on the Roof in London’s Regent’s Park.Photograph: Marc BrennerRangy and witty, the Irish designer arrives for our interview convinced that I’ll be chatting to all the “absolutely stunning” creatives behind Into the Woods; Jordan Fein (director), Tom Scutt (set) and Roland Horvath (video). “It’s a great team effort,” she insists. She previously sent light through Scutt’s wheat fields in their Olivier-winningFiddler on the Roof. Into the Woods offers a series of smoke and mirror surprises, for which Malone uncages a whole spectrum of smoke and haze: “A fog that’s quite dense but rises, and then a cool fog that stays low on the ground.” Light pierces the layers, especially when characters experience an epiphany (Red Riding Hood plucked from the wolf’s belly, Jack dismounting the beanstalk).What was her own career-setting epiphany? “Was I a little theatre kid?” she considers. “Not really.” A Dublin pantomime at an impressionable age was a turning point, while at her all-girls secondary school, the annual musical cast the tall Malone as swaggering blokes in Oklahoma! and The King and I. Acting beckoned – but her degree at Dublin Trinity and then Goldsmiths in London also covered backstage roles. “I fell upon lighting, and was definitely more comfortable with not being on the stage, collaborating with the whole team. I enjoyed how lighting is very technical and creative at the same time. I haven’t looked back since.”View image in fullscreen‘Devised work is nerve-racking’ …  A Monster Calls at the Old Vic, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHer career in lighting began on the fringe and working on dance shows. She toured with dancer and choreographerAkram Khan, enjoying how dance let her “play with beautiful bodies in space. It’s very sculptural. Often you don’t need to worry about the faces, and you can play with angle.”View image in fullscreen‘A bit of magic’ … Aideen Malone.Photograph: Ian TaitTheatre then became her home turf. Do all directors understand lighting? “Not to name any names,” she grins, “but some are very visual, and some aren’t.” She prefers “somebody with nerves of steel who is prepared to try stuff” – like Sally Cookson, with whom she devised hit shows such asJane EyreandA Monster Calls. “Devised work is nerve-racking,” says Malone, “because you don’t know what you’ve got till the last week of rehearsals. You have to figure it out once you’re in the space.” Their2016 Peter Pan at the Nationalwas touch and go, she admits: “But we always get there for press night.”The pandemic prompted a long-contemplated masters in light and lighting at University College London. “I thought I knew a lot about colour,” Malone says, “but I learned so much about the detail of a light source, which makes a huge difference when you’re lighting skin tones.” This fascination carries back into her stage work. “Two people in daylight might look the same, but put them under theatre light and they’re quite different. One person needs 1% more magenta, and one needs 1% less. It’s a challenge.”View image in fullscreenTouch and go … Peter Pan at the National, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMalone has always been drawn to “the cool and warm natural colours of daylight” – a favourite venue is the Open Air theatre in London’s Regent’s Park, where she and Scutt designedCarouseland Fiddler. She also embraces projects blending architectural and theatrical knowhow, such as Sadler’s Wells East, which opened last year. A neon sign above the entrance proclaims: “You are welcome” – but glowing lighting through the building must sustain that welcome from morning to night.Although she is broadening her work, theatre retains its essential appeal for her. “You have a work light on and the space looks flat – then you put a spotlight on and it’s transformed. It’s a bit of magic.”Into the Woods is at theNoël Coward theatre, London, until 9 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsTheatreStagecraftStephen SondheimWest EndMusicalsOlivier awardsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Never After Dark review – ghostbuster-for-hire meets her match in Japanese exorcism horror | Movies | The Guardian
description: Shogun’s Moeka Hoshi stars as a travelling caster-out of ghosts who confronts a wounded and recalcitrant spirit in this inventive chiller
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Shogun’s Moeka Hoshi stars as a travelling caster-out of ghosts who confronts a wounded and recalcitrant spirit in this inventive chiller
Content: Spontaneity and intelligence … a scene from Never After Dark.Photograph: Blue Finch Film ReleasingView image in fullscreenSpontaneity and intelligence … a scene from Never After Dark.Photograph: Blue Finch Film ReleasingMoviesReviewNever After Dark review – ghostbuster-for-hire meets her match in Japanese exorcism horrorShogun’s Moeka Hoshi stars as a travelling caster-out of ghosts who confronts a wounded and recalcitrant spirit in this inventive chillerLeslie FelperinMon 26 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you watched this Japanese-language ghost-story horror thriller cold, you might be a little surprised that the credits reveal that the director is one Dave Boyle – and not someone fromJapan, so steeped is it in Japanese lore and culture. It turns out that Boyle has been interested in Japan for a long time, and even wrote, directed and starred in the 2006 feature film Big Dreams Little Tokyo, about an American sharing a flat with an aspiring sumo wrestler.More recently, Boyle was a key director-producer for the Netflix series House of Ninjas, and Never After Dark seems to have evolved as a spun-off side hustle between Boyle and Ninjas star Kento Kaku, who produced it and takes a supporting role.That all goes a little way to explain how this ends up feeling like a larky, low-stakes, one-for-funsies exercise – inventive and full of charm even if the scares are sort-of predictable.Shogun’s Moeka Hoshi stars as Airi, a young woman who looks like a hipster with her torn jeans and raggedy haircut and who travels the country in her Volvo as an itinerant ghostbuster for hire. The ghost of Airi’s dead older sister Miku (Kurumi Inagaki) is always by her side but is only visible in mirrors (as per folklore), and is available to give advice about imminent danger and vibes in the spirit world.Airi’s latest gig is to exorcise a spirit haunting what used to be a hotel in the sticks. New proprietor Teiko (Tae Kimura) has been hearing bumps in the night and getting creepy phone calls that are either from spirits or perverts, or possibly both. Teiko’s son Gunji (Kaku) is less convinced there’s a supernatural explanation but he takes a shine to Airi all the same, especially when it is revealed that they share a taste for niche music.Soon Airi works out that the apparition wandering the corridors and scrabbling at the wainscoting is a man with a gruesomely smashed jaw (Mutsuo Yoshioka), and she can interact with him on the astral plane via a ritual involving a candle, burnt offerings of her own hair (thus the shaggy hairstyle), and aphenakistoscope, a 19th-century persistence-of-vision toy, which in this case depicts a spirit rising from a body. But getting the smashed-mouth spirit out of the house proves to be anything but the run-of-the-mill exorcism Airi expected.Boyle and his collaborators deploy charmingly old-school physical effects, the sort of thing actual phenakistoscope users might have been impressed by in films by the likes ofGeorges Méliès. It’s mostly a matter of camera angles capturing faces in mirrors and reflections, wire work and well choreographed use of body doubles. The old school vibe makes this particularly endearing, even if the characterisation isn’t especially complex or nuanced, but Hoshi brings a spontaneity and intelligence to the lead role that is consistently winning.Never After Dark is on digital platforms from 2 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsJapanAsia PacificreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t give a damn what people think any more!’ Jimmy Webb on his wild days – and writing hits for Dolly, Glen and Frank | Music | The Guardian
description: From Wichita Lineman to MacArthur Park, he penned masterpieces. As the great hit-maker resurrects his lost songs, he recalls writing for giants – and the night Richard Harris stripped off and disappeared
Author: Dave Simpson
