Headline: From Wichita Lineman to MacArthur Park, he penned masterpieces. As the great hit-maker resurrects his lost songs, he recalls writing for giants – and the night Richard Harris stripped off and disappeared
Content: ‘When I was 14, I was driving a tractor in a wheat field listening to a young Glen Campbell’ ... Jimmy Webb in 1971.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘When I was 14, I was driving a tractor in a wheat field listening to a young Glen Campbell’ ... Jimmy Webb in 1971.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesMusicInterview‘I don’t give a damn what people think any more!’ Jimmy Webb on his wild days – and writing hits for Dolly, Glen and FrankDave SimpsonFrom Wichita Lineman to MacArthur Park, he penned masterpieces. As the great hit-maker resurrects his lost songs, he recalls writing for giants – and the night Richard Harris stripped off and disappearedMon 26 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Flat for 50 miles,” recalls Jimmy Webb, remembering the desolate stretch of Oklahoma that inspired his classic song, Wichita Lineman. “Nothing out there except endless railroad tracks and telephone poles. Then suddenly there’s a guy at the top of one of the poles. He’s got his phone, he’s talking to somebody and then … whoosh! He goes by. I never saw him again, but I never forgot him.”Webb immortalised the unknown telephone worker’s solitude (and imagined conversation with a distant lover) with a 1968 smash hit forGlen Campbell. “But you wouldn’t believe what some people thought it was about,” chuckles the songwriter, now a chatty, self-effacing 80-year-old, video-calling from his kitchen in Long Island. “One guy who wrote to me thought it was about a football lineman, and a woman thought the young man in the song gets electrocuted because ‘the Wichita lineman is still on the line’.”double quotation markFrank Sinatra took a drag on his Marlboro and said: ‘That song’s not quite baked yet, is it, son?’Webb also wrote By the Time I Get to Phoenix, Galveston and MacArthur Park, all 1960s classics that remain part of the culture. Only this year, Nick Cave and Flea recorded Wichita Lineman, Guns N’ Roses played it live and in February the octogenarian, who has three Grammys, was even involved in the 2026 awards after Kendrick Lamar’s TV Off, which samples a jazz version of MacArthur Park, won best rap song.View image in fullscreen‘I’m at an age where I don’t give a damn what people think’ ... Webb.Photograph: Kitty Williams“Another big moment for me was when Alysa Liu skated to an Olympic gold with MacArthur Park in the background,” smiles Webb. “She sort of took me along on this wonderful skate with her. I’m very fortunate, because I didn’t know I had a future.”He’d been “ready to hang up” his travelling shoes, “just maybe do some teaching or mentoring” when he noticed that his old friend and collaborator Art Garfunkel, 84, was booked to play the Royal Albert Hall in London. “I thought, ‘If Artie can do it …’,” Webb sniggers. So he has carried on touring and has a new, star-studded album, his first in 13 years, after producer Fred Mollin’s gentle reminder of how long it had been “hit me in the face like a cast-iron skillet”.The album, Yours for the Taking: The Found Songs of Jimmy Webb, contains new recordings of previously unheard songs that somehow got left behind when Webb was writing “three or four songs a week, too fast sometimes, but you feel the pressure of the marketplace.” That hustle left behind a trove of lost or unfinished songs that Webb felt could be improved. “Some were turned down by an artist,” he explains. “As a young songwriter, you don’t want to put those songs with your others. You want to take them outside and bury them in the back yard.”One such song, I Miss the Mistakes, was intended for Dolly Parton, while Webb originally penned the beautifully emotive Winter Clothes (sung withGraham Nash) for Frank Sinatra. “But as I was playing it to Mr Sinatra I was thinking, ‘Maybe this could be a little premature,’” the songwriter remembers. “He gently smiled, took a drag on his Marlboro and a shot of Jack Daniel’s and said, ‘Well, that one’s not quite baked yet, is it son?’ So I baked it all these years later.”View image in fullscreen‘That’s the guy I want to sing my songs’ ... Glen Campbell in 1967.Photograph: Donaldson Collection/Getty ImagesWebb, the son of an Oklahoma Baptist preacher, started writing songs for church but he talks about his subsequent celebrated career with a childlike marvel that it happened. “This sounds like something some genius publicist would make up,” he says, “but when I was 14 or 15 I was driving a tractor in a wheat field when Turn Around, Look at Me by a young Glen Campbell came on my transistor radio. There was something plaintive in his voice. I thought ‘That’s the guy I want to sing my songs.’” Six years later, by which time Webb had cut his songwriting teeth at Motown, Campbell’s recording of By the Time I Get to Phoenix sold a million copies.Webb vividly remembers how Campbell asked him for a follow-up. “He said, ‘I’ve got a pile of demos here and they’re all steaming crap,’” he smiles. “‘Could you write me another song about a town?’” Webb didn’t want to be known as “the guy who writes about towns” but wrote Wichita Lineman, which Campbell recorded before it was completed. “I said, ‘But Glen, it isn’t finished.’ He said, ‘It is now.’” Webb’s status as Campbell’s favourite songwriter was cemented by Galveston, an anti-war song penned during the Vietnam conflict. So how does one write a timeless classic?“By listening to other people’s songs and trying to copy them,” Webb shrugs. “Really, I wanted to be a film director, because all I do is watch films. I’ve had the pleasure of meeting guys like Steven Spielberg and Robert Altman and have been really surprised that they were people like me. I always thought they’d have a special aura. I think I could have made films because that’s the way I see things.” Hence his many film scores, but his pop songs haven’t done too badly.“Billy Joel used to take the stuffing out of me at the Songwriters Hall of Fame,” he remembers, and one year Joel deconstructed Wichita Lineman. “He said, ‘And I need you more than want you … that’s divorce, right?’ The audience were roaring. Then he got to ‘and I want you for all time’ and said, ‘Ultimately Wichita Lineman is about an ordinary man thinking extraordinary thoughts.’ And I got tears, you know. Some people think songwriters go around crying all the time, but most of us are lone eagles. We think of ourselves as tough but we’re not immune. Songwriting is like a hospital. We see the patients and the wounds.”View image in fullscreen‘She took me on this wonderful skate’ ... Alysa Liu celebrates winning Olympic gold skating to MacArthur Park.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianSome of his greatest songs were driven by his own hurt. Breaking up with early love Susan Horton (who had already inspired By the Time I Get to Phoenix) fuelled 1967’s extraordinary, seven-minute MacArthur Park, which gave the legendary Irish actor Richard Harris a Top 5 hit (and Donna Summer a disco No 1 in 1978). “Richard and I were a perfect team,” Webb reflects of their two albums together. “He was like my older brother. Oh, the things we did. He showed me around Ireland during the Troubles. In Belfast we played in a club guarded by men with machine guns. I’d never had a drop of hard liquor before I met Richard, but before long I could have been on the Olympic drinking team.”One night, they were in the actor’s flat in Belgravia, central London, where Harris drank so much brandy he started taking off his clothes. “I thought, ‘I’m not staying around for how this ends’, so I went to bed,” Webb grins. Hours later, he was woken up by a cab driver, returning Harris, who was by this point wearing only underpants. “The cab driver said, ‘Excuse me guvnor, I found this gentleman on the King’s Road, where he was singing.’”Webb forged another great boozy friendship with singer Harry Nilsson, the pair even becoming embroiled inJohn Lennon’s infamous “lost weekend” bender. “You’d go out for a drink with Harry not knowing if you’d end up in Scotland,” Webb says, admitting that one of the downsides of reaching a ninth decade is outliving such gigantic figures in his life.View image in fullscreen‘He was like my older brother’ … Webb and Richard Harris in 1968.Photograph: Chris Walter/WireImage“I think about Harry twice a day, and Richard was so beyond the pale, so fearless. Sometimes, I’ll come up with a new song and for a moment I’ll think, ‘I gotta play this for Glen. Or Harry.’ And then it hits me all over again that there’s no Glen, no Harry, no Richard. But to me these people are still alive in one way or another and I think about them every day.”Webb, who has been teetotal since 2002, still likes to smell a Guinness, but concedes that getting old means “I don’t have to agonise about everything. When I was 23 I couldn’t go on stage without a couple of Jack Daniel’s and I didn’t play my first sober show until 24 years ago, but it’s made a big difference. I’m really proud of my voice now, but I used to get a lot of criticism of my singing because I was singing in some rarefied company. I’d pitch to Mr Sinatra or Tony Bennett, then I’d come out with my little midwestern squeaky voice. So I used to imbibe to build up dutch courage. Now I’m at the age where I don’t give a damn what people think about what I’m doing …” He flashes a warm smile. “But people seem to think it’s pretty good.”Today, Webb is one of the survivors of a golden age where hope, playfulness and stellar pop music became entwined. As a grandfather reflecting on decades on the planet, he argues that we have become obsessed with material things. “We’ve devalued some things that are really important and put other things in their place, which is symbolised by the leadership in my country. As an 80-year-old, I want this album to show the world that 80-year-old people can still be human beings. We can still love, can still feel and be sensitive to the plight of future generations, and we can be very active.”True to his word, he’s already written songs for another album. “Turning 80 doesn’t mean we have to sit around like lumps of coal.”Yours for the Taking: The Found Songs of Jimmy Webb is released on 23 October on Sun Records. A star-studded career celebration, Jimmy Webb: American Songwriter, airs on 30 October on PBS. title: Mac DeMarco review – glowing melodies and shirtless antics at Carnegie Hall | Mac DeMarco | The Guardian
description: After winning over gen Z, the cult indie rocker makes the historic venue swoon with introspective anthems and a Michael Jackson cover
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After winning over gen Z, the cult indie rocker makes the historic venue swoon with introspective anthems and a Michael Jackson cover
Content: Mac DeMarco performs at Carnegie Hall.Photograph: Adela LoconteView image in fullscreenMac DeMarco performs at Carnegie Hall.Photograph: Adela LoconteMac DeMarcoReviewMac DeMarco review – glowing melodies and shirtless antics at Carnegie HallCarnegie Hall, New YorkAfter winning over gen Z, the cult indie rocker makes the historic venue swoon with introspective anthems and a Michael Jackson coverLarry FitzmauriceMon 26 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 68 years afterLeonard Bernstein’s first-ever Young People’s Concert, Carnegie Hall was yet again overrun with youthful energy on Sunday night. The occasion was the first of two sold-out performances from gap-toothed indie-pop scionMac DeMarco, whose adoringly parasocial cross-genre fanbase has been one of the few in 2010s indie to continue an increasingly aged-down trajectory. There was many a parental chaperone next to their beaming teens, while a group of bright-eyed and bushy-tailed post-adolescents sitting behind me – having travelled all the way from Wisconsin for the occasion – audibly Googled: “Where to find Mac DeMarco after the concert” and quizzed each other on whether they’d lay a smooch onThe 1975’s devilish frontman Matty Healy if given a chance.Super Graphic Spectacular review – Chappell Roan dazzles at her gloriously gay mini-festivalRead more“I can’t believe how fancy this place is for Mac,” one of them marveled – and it has indeed been a strange trajectory for DeMarco, who emerged from the shores of Vancouver in the early 2010s resembling a party-hardy modern-day Pigpen and with an aural suitcase stuffed with lovely guitar-warbles, stained with nicotine and carrying the faint stink of cheap brew. His early live sets were equally prone to Limp Bizkit covers and spontaneous audience makeout sessions; the 2014 docu-shortPepperoni Playboywas replete with scenes of new-indie-money dirtbag opulence, as DeMarco and his ragtag group drank champagne out of lobster shells and went cliff-diving amid a nonstop tour schedule.But as with many aspects of popular culture, Covid represented a turning point for DeMarco’s career. Afforded with his first real sense of downtime in nine years, he sobered up (yes, cigs included) and receded from the public spotlight for several years, allowing his back catalogue to resonatevirallyand otherwise before returning to proper songcraft with last year’s fine-feathered Guitar. DeMarco’s 2020s output has often taken a prolific and largely subdued turn; his 2023 compilation One Wayne G ran nearly nine hours long, while this year saw the official release offourlargely instrumental albums that radiated a mature, monastic beauty.View image in fullscreenMac DeMarco performs at Carnegie Hall on Sunday.Photograph: Adela LoconteDeMarco has, undoubtedly and somewhat improbably, grown up – and in the moments before he and his band took Carnegie’s tony and iconic stage, it was certainly fair game to question whether he’d clean himself up further for such a serious-seeming venue. Fear not: DeMarco and co’s two-and-a-half-hour set was a spring-loaded outing for indie’s reigning court jester. There were thrills, spills and shirtless reveries in the form of a surprisingly radiant cover of Michael Jackson’s Human Nature (which fellow joking-not-joking provocateur-of-the-moment Nathan Fielderjoined him on stagefor in Los Angeles just several weeks ago). Mac may have settled down in regards to his personal life, but he’s more than happy – knowingly so, even – to continue playing the giddy fool, and the audience eats it up in kind.Ironically, this current tour, an exhaustive and career-spanning showcase that even prompted its star to mock-apologize two-thirds of the way through, makes a very serious case for DeMarco as one of the 21st century’s most impressive and deeply felt pop songwriters. Aside from the ruminative melancholy that runs through even his most energetic tunes, the glowy guitar-and-keys fantasias contained within his catalog remain unmatched despite the legion of imitators, and Carnegie Hall proved the perfect venue for driving home his textural genius. The fat globs of melody that open Passing Out Pieces, from 2014’s breakthroughSalad Days, were practically hair-raising in their pronounced nature; a slowed-down take on the smoke-’em-if-you-got-’em tribute Ode to Viceroy (its tempo set to match the set’s more mellow midsection) was richer than a slice of tres leches with ice-cream on top.With a collection of tunes like DeMarco’s, extended goofs and acrobatic stage antics are rendered unnecessary; nevertheless, during a beefed-up take on One Wayne G’s straight-and-simple love song I Like Her, the man of the hour reassembled a mic stand to function as a track-and-field hurdle, unsuccessfully clearing it and crashing to the ground. Several songs later, he stalked the back of Carnegie’s cavernous stage like an apex predator before returning to his mic-stand foe and, to much applause, clearing the jump with ease.Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’Read moreHis stage banter was frequently delivered in a voice resembling late Hollywood spook-meister Vincent Price, and at one point he gave the microphone to an audience member to ask them how comfortable the seats were. (More comfortable than Radio City Music Hall, in case you were wondering.) Several songs – including the title track of his twilit 2017 masterpieceThis Old Dog– were dedicated to his own canine pal, the improbably named Buck Naked DeMarco; later in the set, DeMarco rhapsodized on visions of “a trough filled with chopped cheese meat” and, strikingly, engaged in some quasi-Oedipal reflection mirroring the plight his millennial cohort perpetually faces: “I wish to be a small crying baby, to crawl back into the mother … to be born, again.”There persists the question as to whether DeMarco’s unabashed onstage silliness has kept him at arm’s length from being taken seriously by more discerning music listeners. But, for now, his fans are still making their voices heard when it comes to what they expect from him, in a very literal sense. “Do a flip!” a male concertgoer in the orchestra seats hollered during a quiet moment; “Do you think I’mableto do a flip?” DeMarco seriously asked, before performing a perfect cartwheel to a rapturous reception. “I want to be your pig,” he gamely grunted after catching his breath. Fair enough.Explore more on these topicsMac DeMarcoPop and rockNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Igor Levit: Resistance album review – essential listening in a time of bullies and despots | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The German pianist performs these works by Beethoven and Schoenberg – linked by Napoleon – with his characteristic exquisite touch, in interpretations full of poetry
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The German pianist performs these works by Beethoven and Schoenberg – linked by Napoleon – with his characteristic exquisite touch, in interpretations full of poetry
Content: Never afraid to stick his head above the parapet: Igor Levit performs at the Southbank Centre in April 2025.View image in fullscreenNever afraid to stick his head above the parapet: Igor Levit performs at the Southbank Centre in April 2025.Classical musicReviewIgor Levit: Resistance album review – essential listening in a time of bullies and despotsLevit/Kammerakademie Potsdam/Manacorda/Lyssewski(No Silence/Sony)The German pianist performs these works by Beethoven and Schoenberg – linked by Napoleon – with his characteristic exquisite touch, in interpretations full of poetryClive PagetMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleResistance is one of the inaugural offerings on Igor Levit’s own label,No Silence Records, released in collaboration with Sony Classical. Never afraid to stick his head above the parapet, the German pianist has chosen two works exploring ideas of human resilience in the face of political power, with Liszt’s transcription of Beethoven’s Symphony No 3, the Eroica, rubbing shoulders with Schoenberg’s Ode to Napoleon. The link, of course, is the French general whose self-proclamation as Emperor caused a disgusted Beethoven to scratch the forrmer’s name from the front page of what was to have been his Buonaparte Symphony.View image in fullscreenIgor Levit: Resistance album cover.Levit rightly sees Liszt’s piano realisation as a masterwork in and of itself and his dramatic interpretation is full of poetry, often surprisingly gentle, and with breathtaking pianissimos. When required, there’s no shortage of firepower, but at its heart is the long, drawn-out funeral march, an aching lament for the passing of a great soul. It’s here that Levit, whose finely balanced touch is exquisite, gets to the beating heart of the matter.The Ode to Napoleon, Schoenberg’s thinly veiled condemnation of Hitler, features a commanding Levit alongside Kammerakademie Potsdam under Antonello Manacorda. Byron’s sardonic text is delivered in lacerating English by German actor Dörte Lyssewski. In a time of bullies and despots, this is essential listening.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: War Is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman review – are we on the brink of world war three?  | Politics books | The Guardian
description: A foreign affairs expert’s bleak assessment of the state of global security
Author: Charlie English
Headline: A foreign affairs expert’s bleak assessment of the state of global security
Content: A tactical military exercise in Tainan, Taiwan, 2026.Photograph: Cheng Chia Huang/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA tactical military exercise in Tainan, Taiwan, 2026.Photograph: Cheng Chia Huang/Getty ImagesPolitics booksReviewWar Is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman review – are we on the brink of world war three?A foreign affairs expert’s bleak assessment of the state of global securityCharlie EnglishMon 26 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAre we on the brink of a new world war? This bleak subject is increasingly invoked by leaders, soldiers and officials, from Donald Trump to Vladimir Putin to the heads of our military and intelligence services. It’s an urgent theme, then, for the FT foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman to explore in his latest survey of global diplomacy. Rachman draws his title from the expression, sometimes attributed to Trotsky: “You may not be interested in war, but war is interested in you” – the idea being that conflict doesn’t much care whether we like to think about it or not: it will come knocking on our doors regardless.Clearly, humanity is in a particularly unsafe spot right now, but seeing our security issues laid out like this, catalogued and mapped and analysed, they seem almost overwhelming. To summarise: the most powerful, nuclear-armed states – the US, China andRussia– are led by unscrupulous, self-dealing “strongmen”, each of whom is playing with the nationalist “Great Again” politics epitomised by Trump. Democracy is being rolled back around the world, and even bastions of liberalism such as the UK, France and Germany seem vulnerable to takeover by the Putin-friendly far right. The so-called rules-based international order and its institutions – the UN, the WTO, Nato – are being deliberately undermined by the aforementioned strongmen, and are as weak now as they have ever been.double quotation markOf all the potential flashpoints, it is Taiwan that may offer the fastest route to a world warPutin has described the new world order with the term “might makes right”, and the result is that conflicts have been breaking out at a rate unprecedented in the postwar era. According to Rachman, there were 61 in 2024 alone, and 11 full-blown wars. This included Gaza as well as some conflicts far less visible in the west, such as the one in Sudan, which by mid-2025 had led to 150,000 battlefield deaths. In 2026 many “state-based conflicts” are ongoing, including the largest land war inEuropesince 1945 (in Ukraine) and the most disruptive in the Middle East for more than 20 years (Iran). Although these are mostly confined to their regions, they have begun to overlap and spread, as Russia deploys North Korean troops and tests Nato’s resolve, Iran throttles global shipping, and Ukraine advises Gulf states on drone use. And even as these grind on, others threaten to explode, including between India and Pakistan, North and South Korea, and China and Taiwan.Of these potential flashpoints, it is Taiwan that may offer the fastest route to a world war, since it could bring China and the US into direct conflict. For decades, Taiwan’s security was guaranteed by US naval superiority; now Beijing, after a massive military buildup, has more warships than Washington. It’s said that the single Chinese shipyard on Changxing Island has more capacity than all US yards combined. Still, Xi Jinping knows that if the US comes to Taiwan’s aid, the result would be a bloodbath, which is why US presidents have mostly been keen to emphasise the US’s commitment to Taiwan. But Trump has been far more ambivalent – declaring in May this year, for instance, that “I think the last thing we need right now is a war that’s 9,500 miles away” – which only increases the risk of China attempting an assault.It’s here, in the shifting power balance between China and the US, that the root of the new global insecurity lies. Whatever you think of American hegemony, the US maintained a sort of stability, after the cold war, in which victims could plausibly appeal to international law. The 2003 invasion of Iraq destroyed that system, and US failure there and in Afghanistan persuaded future presidents against intervention. Three times, between 2012 and 2015, Obama chose not to step in to address illegal acts by the Assad regime, Russia and China, which signalled an American retrenchment. The Trump administration has taken this further, reverting to the kind of isolationist, tariff-based protectionism that postwar institutions such as the UN security council and WTO were built to avoid. It’s hard not to spot echoes here of the 1930s – the time, incidentally, when the slogan “America first” was popularised.How to offset these risks? Rachman surveys a handful of mechanisms that have helped maintain the peace, and finds them wanting. The rules-based international order, for instance, barely functioned in its heyday; now, as Mark Carney put it plainly, it “no longer works”: we are living through a “rupture”. What about spreading democracy and economic stability as a path to peace – a principle exemplified by the “Golden Arches” theory, which states that no two nations with McDonald’s will wage war on each other? There’s no comfort here either, as that was proved wrong in the 1990s, and the number of democracies has been declining steadily since 2006. Then there’s deterrence, which still by and large keeps us safe. But it hasn’t stopped fighting between nuclear-armed India and Pakistan, and China and North Korea are rapidly expanding their atomic arsenals.What we’re left with, then, as American primacy declines, is a global version of Trump’s “Donroe doctrine”, in which each major power gets a “sphere of influence” where they call the shots. In this scenario, Washington rules over the Americas, Beijing over east Asia, and Moscow the old Soviet zone. Clashes are sorted out by one-to-one conversations between authoritarian leaders. But what if these rulers fall out? And anyway, who wants to live in the shadow of an overbearing neighbour?While the outlook of War Is Interested in You is undoubtedly gloomy, Rachman’s book is not. His writing is engaging and anecdotal, and he brings vast experience to bear on a vital subject. He won’t go so far as to say a new world war is inevitable, but the threat is becoming impossible to ignore.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li review – a virtuosic interrogation of the power of art | Books | The Guardian
description: What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality? Li examines the gulf between talent and genius through the marriage of two real-life musicians
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality? Li examines the gulf between talent and genius through the marriage of two real-life musicians
Content: Pure readerly pleasure … Yiyun Li.Photograph: Maria SpannView image in fullscreenPure readerly pleasure … Yiyun Li.Photograph: Maria SpannBook of the dayBooksReviewMusic Against the Night by Yiyun Li review – a virtuosic interrogation of the power of artWhat does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality? Li examines the gulf between talent and genius through the marriage of two real-life musiciansKevin PowerMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his recently publishedA History of the Novel in Britain, Philip Hensher makes a bold claim. Historical novels, he tells us, don’t last. However popular and prestigious a historical novel might be in its day, it will almost always get thrown overboard as the ship of literary culture sails on, piled high with novels of contemporary life. He might be on to something. Who now prefers Walter Scott to Jane Austen? The historical novel risks a double obsolescence, courting a future in which it has become an old-fashioned vision of an old-fashioned time.However much this news might dismay writers of historical novels, Hensher is untroubled: “As readers enjoying our contemporaries, we should not let our readerly pleasures be affected by the probability of ultimate oblivion.” Will the future, what there is of it, rate Wolf Hall as highly as we do? It doesn’t matter. Posterity, as Gore Vidal once wrote, is “a permanent darkness where no whistle sounds”. What matters is us, now, what we make of history and of our lives – in our novels and elsewhere.Posterity and its ironies form a central theme of Yiyun Li’s new historical novel. In several senses Music Against the Night isn’t, in fact, “a historical novel” – certainly not in the supermarket-own-brand sense of a cosplay adventure in which affable protagonists find themselves chatting with Byron or whoever. Readers of Li will already know that she soars far above the well-meant strivings of lesser writers, occupying a luminous realm of her own. She has the craft that makes craft invisible, and the art that makes art itself her obsessive subject. In Music Against the Night the art is music, as perceived through the lives, and the real and hoped-for afterlives, of two musicians.Real musicians, as it happens: a married couple, bound by a “contrapuntal fate”. The pianist and composer John Field, born in Dublin in 1782, is now remembered as the inventor of the nocturne, the form perfected by Chopin. There is a room in the National Concert Hall in Dublin called The Field Room. But to listen to Field’s nocturnes when you know Chopin’s is to ponder the gulf between talent and genius. In Li’s telling, Field himself compulsively ponders this gulf, as he becomes “a footnote in the life of Frédéric Chopin”. Li knows that footnote status is the fate of most artists. What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality?In 1807 Field, by then living in Moscow, took on a student named Adelaide Percheron, an orphan raised by her grandmother in Pondicherry, French India. Adelaide too was a gifted musician, but her ambition was thwarted by the patriarchal strictures of the society into which she was born. John and Adelaide (she was known as “Percherette”), separately wrestling with the enemies of promise, married in 1810. It was not an auspicious union.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markLi has the craft that makes craft invisible, and the art that makes art itself her obsessive subjectThe ordinary historical novelist starts there, and labours through the tempestuous marriage: Field’s drinking, his affairs, Percherette’s despair. But Li’s subject isn’t marriage. Music Against the Night is about the relationship between life and art; about what it means to sacrifice a life to art; and about what exactly is sacrificed, when such a sacrifice is made. Field and Percherette’s marriage is given to us in brief Muriel Spark-like flash-forwards. Long sections, split between Dublin and Pondicherry, follow Field and Percherette closely through late childhood and early adolescence; this is the bulk of the book. Childhood, for both, is short. Both are prodigies: Field on the pianoforte, Percherette as a kind of psychologist, perceiving the hidden truths of human behaviour. What they share is a “willingness to be rescued from an ordinary childhood”.Li’s narration is unapologetically omniscient, but she has no use for pastiche: she acknowledges she is writing in the 2020s, and yet there’s no historical-novel clutter about horses or furniture. Only that which impinges on her characters, or her theme, is noted. Her narrator is insistently aphoristic: “To be known is the desire that drives much of the world’s progress, also much of its destruction. History is a discourse against obscurity.” Not all the aphorisms work: “an absent anchor only further disturbs an unmoored heart”. But many of them are superb: “Talent, vision, luck, work – all are necessary for a career, but not sufficient. An artist falls short if he cannot master the art of indifference.”Engaged in their separate discourses against obscurity, John and Percherette fail to master the art of indifference. Their passionate self-scourgings form a counterpoint to the eerily calm and patient gathering-in effects of Li’s prose. The result is pure readerly pleasure – posterity (and this might be what Li, in this novel of half-forgotten artists, is suggesting) be damned.Late in the novel there is a brief reflection on the loss of a child. Li herself, of course, haswritten about the loss of her two sons, Vincent and James, to suicide. The subject is not dwelt on at length in Music Against the Night. It forms merely part of a piercing argument about the passions of life versus the austere and indifferent values of art. The aphoristic narrator remarks: “Death is a subject that rewards minor artists.” But “Life? It requires major talent to convey that.” Li conveys life without apparent effort. Major is the word.Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li is published by 4th Estate (£20).To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: Aberfan: From Darkness to Light review – Mealor’s requiem offers hope amid the tears | Classical music | The Guardian
description: A thoughtful and moving concert – with Paul Mealor’s new choral work its centrepiece – commemorated the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster
Author: Rian Evans
Headline: A thoughtful and moving concert – with Paul Mealor’s new choral work its centrepiece – commemorated the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster
Content: Playful singing … children from Ynysowen Primary School and Ysgol Gymraeg Rhyd y Gru on stage for Aberfan 60 at Hoddinott Hall, Cardiff.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanView image in fullscreenPlayful singing … children from Ynysowen Primary School and Ysgol Gymraeg Rhyd y Gru on stage for Aberfan 60 at Hoddinott Hall, Cardiff.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanClassical musicReviewAberfan: From Darkness to Light review – Mealor’s requiem offers hope amid the tearsHoddinott Hall, CardiffA thoughtful and moving concert – with Paul Mealor’s new choral work its centrepiece – commemorated the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disasterRian EvansMon 26 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAconcert requiem of hope is how composerPaul Mealordescribes his new choral work Aberfan: From Darkness to Light, commemorating the 60th anniversary ofthe disaster that killed 116 children and 28 adults. Heard first in the Aberfan Community Centre with the voices of children from today’s junior schools – Ynysowen Primary School and Ysgol Gymraeg Rhyd y Grug – joining the Ynysowen Male Voice Choir, the BBC National Chorus of Wales and an instrumental ensemble, this second performance, again conducted byTimothy Redmond, had the full weight of the BBC National Orchestra of Wales. While the focus on hope coloured the whole, it was – not surprisingly – the bright, shining voices of the children, their every syllable crystal-clear, which made one well up.Setting words by Grahame Davies, whose poetic sequence of narrative and verse balanced remembrance with reflection, the piece was, at its heart, a celebration of life and the culture of the valley. Both librettist and composer were guided by Aberfan people themselves who asked that the spirit of hope and renewal be invoked, and that present and future be implicit alongside recognition of the tragic past.With Mark Lewis Jones narrating, this then was a story simply told, neither shying away from the horror, nor from pointing a finger at those who might have prevented the disaster, and remembering the heroic bravery of the rescuers and of those who perished. A lyrical melancholy – especially from cor anglais and oboe – was present in the orchestral transitions yet, overall, Mealor’s achievement was in finding musical language, often vibrantly rhythmic and percussive, to carry the different facets over a span of 40 minutes without sounding sentimental or maudlin, and making the children’s playful singing feel the most natural thing in the world. At the end, a member of the audience was heard to say that they could not have imagined the piece would have such joy.By way of preface, Anna Clyne’s This Moment – inspired by the calligraphy of the Buddhist monk, Thich Nhat Hanh – had meditated on death and life, on rain and tears. Together with movements from symphonies by Haydn and Mozart and a stirring performance of Vaughan Williams’s Toward the Unknown Region, setting Walt Whitman’s poem on spiritual death and rebirth, a concert which might only have represented grieving also invited a deeper kind of contemplation.Broadcast onBBC Radio 3on 29 OctoberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicBBC National Orchestra of WalesWalesAberfan disasterreviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Pianist review – Władysław Szpilman’s Holocaust memoir retold with his own music | Musicals | The Guardian
description: This adaptation is perhaps too smooth but is well-staged and performed, and draws strong feeling from the pianist’s compositions
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This adaptation is perhaps too smooth but is well-staged and performed, and draws strong feeling from the pianist’s compositions
Content: Chamber piece … Daniel Krikler as the Polish pianist Władysław Szpilman and Mischa Jardine as Janina in The Pianist.Photograph: Richard SouthgateView image in fullscreenChamber piece … Daniel Krikler as the Polish pianist Władysław Szpilman and Mischa Jardine as Janina in The Pianist.Photograph: Richard SouthgateMusicalsReviewThe Pianist review – Władysław Szpilman’s Holocaust memoir retold with his own musicPark theatre, LondonThis adaptation is perhaps too smooth but is well-staged and performed, and draws strong feeling from the pianist’s compositionsArifa AkbarMon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe idea of turning the survival story of the Polish pianist Władysław Szpilman into a musical might, on paper, seem distasteful given the stark subject matter of the Holocaust. There is risk of triteness, too, in the light ofRoman Polanski’s acclaimed film, starring Adrien Brody,based on Szpilman’s celebrated memoir.But those who are acquainted with both those retellings of Szpilman’s second world war experiences will still find something new and affecting here. The form of the musical becomes meaningful through its use of Szpilman’s own compositions. Thom Southerland, who has adapted Szpilman’s book and directs, creates an atmospheric chamber piece, with actors playing instruments, including a piano that twirls on and off stage.View image in fullscreenOut of body experience … Malcolm Forbes-Peckham as Szpilman’s wartime self with Krikler, and Oliver Grant as Hosenfeld.Photograph: Richard SouthgateSzpilman (Daniel Krikler, elegantly otherworldly) is narrating his own story, seeing not just the ghosts of his family drift back to life but also himself (played by Malcolm Forbes-Peckham, the show’s musical director). This wartime self is always before the piano, playing Chopin (Nocturne in C-sharp minor) and Szpilman’s compositions, as Krikler’s haunted version watches on. It is a good way to portray out of body experience; he is a man removed from himself, judging himself, too.Not all the songs suit the subject matter; there is a warm, nostalgic 1930s glow to some numbers that show Warsaw just before and after its surrender, when Szpilman is working for Polish radio. Music accompanies the story in a way that verges on sentimental.View image in fullscreenAn exceptionally musical family … Krikler with Szpilman’s mother, played by Rosalind Ford.Photograph: Richard SouthgateThe piece is too smooth, the savagery of the world outside Szpilman’s own seen only in glimmers. But that is also the point, especially in the first part when we see the exceptionally musical family to which he belonged, from Szpilman’s father (TJ Holmes), who uses his cello to escape reality, to his quietly determined mother (Rosalind Ford) and brood of siblings. The actors are accomplished musicians and strong in their roles.Family of man who inspired The Pianist film win defamation appealRead moreSzpilman’s arguments with his brother Henryk (Nitai Levi) too emphatically hash out the question of an individual’s responsibilities in wartime: whether to resist and protest, as Henryk would have it, or to stay together and just survive, as Władysław does for the main. The place of music is also tacitly explored, though again this could be more penetrating.The production is good at drawing out class distinctions and the family’s privilege at this point, as well as Szpilman’s survivor’s guilt. It shows effectively the slide into totalitarianism, with denials and disbelief, even as the family’s world narrows. The scene when Szpilman separates from them, just as they arrive at Auschwitz, is terrible, the back wall of Andrzej Goulding’s set design suddenly resembling a cattle truck. There are other chillling moments: when he sees a boy bludgeoned to death; when the person who has been hiding him orders him to leave his home.The pace just slackens too much in the second half when Szpilman is alone and in hiding. The musical interludes seem protracted, perhaps because Szpilman’s music is being honoured in fullness. It is still a handsomely orchestrated production, and moving, too, when finally Krikler sits down to play the piano himself in Out of the Darkness. A survivor, finally inhabiting his music.AtPark theatre, London, until 28 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMusicalsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: John Anderson obituary | Country | The Guardian
description: American country singer and songwriter who took the music genre back to its unvarnished roots
Author: Garth Cartwright
Headline: American country singer and songwriter who took the music genre back to its unvarnished roots
Content: John Anderson performing in Nashville, Tennessee, in 2013.Photograph: Mark Zaleski/APView image in fullscreenJohn Anderson performing in Nashville, Tennessee, in 2013.Photograph: Mark Zaleski/APCountryObituaryJohn Anderson obituaryAmerican country singer and songwriter who took the music genre back to its unvarnished rootsGarth CartwrightMon 26 Oct 2026 16.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 16.22 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJohn Anderson, who has died aged 71, reinvigorated country music in the 1980s by returning the genre to its unvarnished roots.His breakthrough came at a time when country was in a lull, with lush productions that made its stars sound increasingly soporific. By contrast, Anderson harked back to the simpler days of the 50s, purveying strong songs with feeling.His adoption of what became known as “New Traditionalism” was so successful that he scored 40 hits on the Billboard country charts in the US, five of which made No 1 – and his work inspired a new generation of singers inNashville, including George Strait, Randy Travis and Dwight Yoakam, all of whom followed his credo and went on to enjoy great success.Although he never won a pop/rock crossover audience, Anderson’s sales were impressive. His 1983 singleSwingin’, an uptempo celebration of first love, sold more than 1.4m copies in the US – the biggest country hit in Warner Brothers’ history – and won the Country Music Association’s single of the year award. His 1992 album, Seminole Wind, which addressed environmental issues and Native American history, sold in excess of 2 million.Anderson’s final No 1 country hit,Money in the Bank, came in 1993, and the LP from which it derived, Solid Ground, was the last of his albums to sell in large numbers. But he kept recording and performing for many years afterwards.Born in Apopka, Florida, John was one of the six children of George, a landscaper, and Juanita, a homemaker. At 13 he began singing in a band playing Rolling Stones numbers, but two years later heard aMerle Haggardalbum and decided that country music was his vocation.In 1972, aged 17, he moved to Nashville with a view to making a living as a musician, arriving at his sister Donna’s flat there unannounced. Initially he took whatever work he could find – including as a labourer helping to refurbish the roof of theGrand Ole Oprytheatre, vowing from his eyrie that he would appear there on stage one day – which indeed he did.Soon he and Donna were working as a duo in Nashville clubs, and in 1974 he began recording for the small Ace of Clubs label, releasing three 45s that failed to chart. However, the quality of his voice and songs, allied to his cherubic features, persuaded Warner Brothers to sign him in 1976.Determined to establish Anderson as a new voice in country music, the company pushed his singles on the radio but refused to let him record an album until he had enjoyed a sizeable hit. That came in 1980, withShe Just Started Liking Cheatin’ Songs, which reached No 13 on the country chart and was swiftly followed by his eponymous debut album, which won widespread praise.His 1981 album, John Anderson 2, featured two Top 10 hits and inspired a number of commentators to compare him to Lefty Frizzell andGeorge Jones, two of country’s finest male vocalists. His fourth album, Wild & Blue (1982), spawned two No 1 hits –the title trackand Swingin’ – and established him as one of country music’s most popular artists.Thereafter Anderson continued to release strong material. But by 1986 his sales were sliding, prompting him to fire his manager and leave Warner Brothers for MCA. His 1987 MCA album, Blue Skies Again, demonstrated what an expressive ballad singer he was, yet it only reached No 41 on the country charts, and the decline continued with Too Tough to Tame (1989), which failed to make it into the charts at all.He then signed with BNA, for whom his Seminole Wind album gave him his greatest success, both critically and commercially. His fortunes continued to rise with the Solid Ground album and its associated Money in the Bank single, but though he released material regularly thereafter he made little further impression.Anderson slowed down after a health crisis in 2010, until in 2019 he was approached byDan Auerbach, guitarist and vocalist of the indie rock band the Black Keys. The two began writing together, a venture that led Auerbach to produce Anderson’s 2020 comeback – and final – album, Years. The Auerbach connection won him his widest media attention in decades, although Years is not considered one of his stronger offerings.In 2022 the album Something Borrowed, Something New: A Tribute to John Anderson, featured 13 country and Americana artists, includingJohn Prineand Gillian Welch, each recording a favourite Anderson song.In 2024 he was inducted into theCountryMusic Hall of Fame.Anderson is survived by his wife, Jamie (nee Addikison), whom he married in 1983, their daughters, Alexa and Brionna, and several grandchildren.John David Anderson, singer and songwriter, born 13 December 1954; died 21 October 2026Explore more on these topicsCountryFloridaNashvilleobituariesShareReuse this content

title: Allotmentcore: why everyone is dressing like Barbara in The Good Life | Fashion | The Guardian
description: Clogs, chore jackets, straw hats and woven baskets are the look of the season. But are the brands and people embracing this aesthetic really doing any gardening?
Author: Leah Harper
Headline: Clogs, chore jackets, straw hats and woven baskets are the look of the season. But are the brands and people embracing this aesthetic really doing any gardening?
Content: Felicity Kendal as Barbara Good in The Good Life.Photograph: taken from picture libraryView image in fullscreenFelicity Kendal as Barbara Good in The Good Life.Photograph: taken from picture libraryFashionAllotmentcore: why everyone is dressing like Barbara in The Good LifeClogs, chore jackets, straw hats and woven baskets are the look of the season. But are the brands and people embracing this aesthetic really doing any gardening?Leah HarperMon 26 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLately, it feels like you can’t move for clogs. Everywhere you look, it’s straw hats, dungarees, floaty dresses, chore jackets and basket bags – and that’s in city centres, not garden centres. This is the rise of “allotmentcore” – somewhere between the linen-clad luxury of the “coastal grandmother” and the whimsical outdoorsiness of “cottagecore” – and it’s coming for all of our autumns.“I’d describe it as Little House on the Prairie meets Felicity Kendal in The Good Life, meets Bill and Ben,” says Mal James, professor of fashion design at the University of Edinburgh. “With the overall style of an imaginary love child of Monty Don and Pamela Anderson, the reinvented queen of garden chic.” It’s true that Anderson – once most famous for sporting a high-leg red swimsuit – has more recently become a pioneer of the allotmentcore style, living “romantically” in midi dresses and bandanas, frequently clutching floral bouquets. Popular brands include the family-run Carrier Company from Norfolk, Danish designers Skall Studio and Welsh-founded lifestyle label Toast. As online fashion publicationWho What Wear put it: “If it looks like you’re ready to sport a pair of pruning shears at any moment, you’ve got the look right.”View image in fullscreenThe full monty … Don gardens in style.Photograph: PA Images/Alamy Stock Photo/Alamy Live News.It’s easy to see the appeal – even if you don’t have an actual allotment. “I am not afraid to say I don’t own a handbag, only baskets,” saysJessica Stokes, a florist, gardener and writer based in Wiltshire. If that sounds whimsical, it’s worth pointing out that every piece in thevintage basket collectionatStraw London, a lifestyle and homeware brand that specialises in allotmentcore staples, is currently sold out.View image in fullscreenCan you dig it? Clothing from Norfolk’s Carrier Company.Photograph: Carrier Company“A heavy cotton workwear jacket with generous pockets is another favourite,” says Stokes. “It’s practical enough for a day outdoors, but can look equally good thrown over a white dress.” She’s often photographed sporting frilled gingham shirts, knitted tank tops and floral dresses (including particularly dreamy numbers from nightwear brandIf Only If), all while surrounded by luscious greenery. But, she insists, durability is key. “Gardening and floristry is physical, messy and often hard on your clothes, so anything that you wear needs to earn its place,” she says. “The lovely thing is that practicality doesn’t have to mean unattractive.”View image in fullscreenAllotment queen … Pamela Anderson.Photograph: Pamela AndersonClogs – and particularly theGardanasmade by Plasticana, another Straw London bestseller – may have been an early indicator of fashion’s blossoming love-affair with allotmentcore, but for London-based gardenerMel Zulu, you can’t beat a Blundstone steel toe-cap boot. “I also wear a lot of denim and woven fabrics because, if you’re rose-pruning and you’re wearing knitwear or something delicate, it is more likely to get ripped,” she says. Rather than a straw hat, she tends to opt for a cap – “which keeps my hair in and offers a bit of protection from both the sun and any branches that might get caught”.It’s not just womenswear that’s been taking inspiration from the green-fingered of late;Errol Reuben Fernandes, a horticultural consultant and head of horticulture at the Horniman Museum and Gardens in southeast London has noticed it, too. “I can comment less on the floppy hats and billowing frocks, and more on the practicality of having a pair of slip-on garden clogs by the back door or a good, waxed cotton tote bag for a quick dash down to the veg patch,” he says. “This style is purpose-led and practical, and that is what allotments are all about. Less flounce and more utility. There is something nice about a well-designed item like a secateur holster or gilet that is by your side for years – and genuinely useful.”View image in fullscreenThe Good Life meets Bill and Ben … threads by If Only If.Photograph: IfOnlyIfHave real-life allotments become veritable catwalks in light of fashion’s horticultural infatuation? “I would say that I definitely don’t follow the trend, although if I can wear a pair of dungarees then I feel very chic,” says Molly Kampmann, who acquired a plot within Glasgow’s Sir John Stirling Maxwell AllotmentGardenslast June. “I saw someone there looking super-stylish recently – but she had just stopped by to lightly water on her way home from a lunch out, so it depends on the kind of activity you’re undertaking. My friend also has an allotment and her style will usually just be jeans, a sweater and something waterproof – which maybe doesn’t fit with the allotmentcore aesthetic but is definitely a must in Glasgow.”But James is sceptical about whether the allotmentcore look has life beyond social media. “I haven’t seen anyone actually garden in it, that’s for sure,” he says. “It’s trending because everyone wants to be seen to be in harmony with nature, driven by the ongoing interest in sustainability. Suddenly, caring about your garden and growing your own veg is cool. It’s wholesome and timeless to be planting dahlias and wearing natural fibre fabrics.” For him, allotmentcore is safe, homey and unthreatening – and not necessarily in a good way. “It’s a quick snooze among the tall grasses, the sounds of lawnmowers, bees and birds; it’s the background noise to fashion’s ‘party-core’; it’s about sitting on fashion’s proverbial (garden) fence.”Explore more on these topicsFashionGardensAllotmentsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: A job that changed me: I was a rookie tour guide for art lovers – no one goes harder than active seniors in search of cultural enrichment | Travel | The Guardian
description: I spent time in some of the greatest art institutions with groups of self-funded retirees. But a vacation it was not
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: I spent time in some of the greatest art institutions with groups of self-funded retirees. But a vacation it was not
Content: I’ve written a cosy crime book about a hapless tour guide enlisting his travellers to steal the three separated panels of a 16th-century triptych and reunite them, writes Jonathan Biggins.Composite: Guardian design/Getty Images/SuppliedView image in fullscreenI’ve written a cosy crime book about a hapless tour guide enlisting his travellers to steal the three separated panels of a 16th-century triptych and reunite them, writes Jonathan Biggins.Composite: Guardian design/Getty Images/SuppliedA job that changed meTravelA job that changed me: I was a rookie tour guide for art lovers – no one goes harder than active seniors in search of cultural enrichmentI spent time in some of the greatest art institutions with groups of self-funded retirees. But a vacation it was notRead more in thea job that changed me seriesJonathan BigginsMon 26 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 19.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn 2012 I was living in Sydney, halfway through the shelf life of our annual theatric political satireThe Wharf Revue,although I didn’t know that at the time. I was also doing some work for the Art Gallery of New South Wales, hosting panel discussions and interviews, when a colleague asked if I would be interested in co-leading a guided tour to New York, focusing on art and theatre. Of course I said yes.Handling the art side of things was my gallery colleague Brian Ladd and together we landed in a wintry Manhattan in January with about 25 guests largely, shall we say, a certain demographic who were keen to sample the cultural delights of the great metropolis.A job that changed me: On midnight shifts as a Subway ‘sandwich artist’, I served clubbers, cops and sailorsRead moreAnd let’s face it, there’s no shortage of them. We took in the Metropolitan Museum and the Cloisters, MoMA, the Frick, the Whitney, Radio City, the Brooklyn Museum, the Guggenheim, the High Line, half a dozen shows and several exhaustive bus tours from one end of the island to the other with our indefatigable local guide Frederique. We even managed a backstage tour of the Met, led by a volunteer who actually paid for the privilege of conducting them! A full-on schedule but, let me tell you, no one goes harder than an active senior in search of cultural enrichment. By the end of the 10 days, we were desperately in need of a holiday.In 2014, it was just me and Frederique leading guests through Chicago and New York. I went solo in 2016 for New York and Philadelphia, braving the second-biggest snowstorm on record to hit the east coast. Broadway went dark, the subways stopped running and at midnight we saw a guy swooping down Fifth Avenue on skis. It was the most exciting part of the trip – Al Pacino struggling and largely failing to remember his lines in the new David Mamet play didn’t come close.Since then, I’ve done Canada, the UK and another trip to New York. One scheduled for earlier this year was cancelled due to a curious reluctance among art lovers to travel to the United States. Mind you, I probably wouldn’t get through customs anyway; it wouldn’t take long to track down evidence of me being less than polite to the president.But a vacation it is not. I was on call constantly. I now know more than I probably need to about breakfast vouchers, bus charters, lost or hospitalised guests, wheelchair hire, a higher than anticipated beverage spend, ticket allocation, gallery docents who know even less about art than I do, and the vagaries of group dynamics on a 36-seater coach stuck in traffic on 45th Street with no restroom in sight.double quotation markThink The Italian Job with mobility scooters instead of Mini CoopersSpending so much time in some of the greatest art institutions in the world with groups of self-funded retirees, and the social connection I still maintain with many of them, has inspired me to make tentative steps along a new career path. I’ve written a cosy crime book about a hapless tour guide enlisting the help of his regular travellers to steal the three separated panels of a 16th-century triptych and reunite them as a symbolic protest against the modern desecration of artistic integrity. Think The Italian Jobwith mobility scooters instead of Mini Coopers.My work as a tour leader has opened my eyes to two things: the fun that can be had in organised group travel; and the almost infinite richness of art history held by the world’s great galleries. Especially with a view to the possibility of pinching something. Not that I ever would, of course, and my research has shown that the most successful thieves target the second tier of institutions with less security anyway. Besides, robbing churches in Europe is even easier, just saying.Jonathan Biggins is the author ofNear Death in Venice, available now through Simon & Schuster (A$34.99)Explore more on these topicsTravelA job that changed meNew York holidaysUnited States holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: I thought testing bread makers would be easy. 36 loaves later, I may have lost the plot | Bread | The Guardian
description: Our tester pushed her love of bread, and freezer space, to the limit in pursuit of the perfect homemade loaf. Plus, the best Kindles for every budget
Author: Danielle Amato
Headline: Our tester pushed her love of bread, and freezer space, to the limit in pursuit of the perfect homemade loaf. Plus, the best Kindles for every budget
Content: Loaf and behold: bread makers lined up for testing.Photograph: Danielle AmatoView image in fullscreenLoaf and behold: bread makers lined up for testing.Photograph: Danielle AmatoGuardian journalism is independent. We earn a commission if you buy something through an affiliate link.Learn more.The Filter UK newsletterBreadI thought testing bread makers would be easy. 36 loaves later, I may have lost the plotOur tester pushed her love of bread, and freezer space, to the limit in pursuit of the perfect homemade loaf. Plus, the best Kindles for every budgetDon’t get the Filter delivered to your inbox? Sign up hereDanielle AmatoMon 26 Oct 2026 06.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHow much bread is too much bread? I found myself wondering this while testing nine of thebest bread makersfor the Filter. You see, while one hot, crusty loaf is a cause for celebration, 36 feels like a cry for help.Because yes, that really is how many loaves I made to rigorously test these machines. The number might even be closer to 45 if you count the weird experiments and loaves that collapsed due to user error. As you succumb to flour-induced delusions, at some point you begin to lose count.At least bread makers have shrunk in size considerably since they first gained popularity in the 90s. Most are now half the size of your standardair fryer, with twice as many features. This was a welcome change from the space taken up by July’sice-cream makermadness – leaving me more room for all that bread.And size isn’t the only improvement these machines have seen. The things you can now do with a bread maker are impressive – including the sheer number of settings for bread alone. I became giddy thinking of all the different types of bread that were at my fingertips, along with all the pasta dough some bread machines can mix and knead for you (which I told myself I was absolutely, definitely going to get round to).Bread, but not as you know itView image in fullscreenLoaf actually: some of the bread produced during testing.Photograph: Danielle Amato/The GuardianGraef’s bread makerwas a perfect example of this. It wowed me with its enticingly original bread types, including yoghurt-honey bread, a carrot grain loaf and the rather intriguing “dough for bread on a stick” setting (pretty self-explanatory but unexpected nonetheless). And the resulting bread tasted as good as it sounded – though, for the sake of finishing the test this year, I decided not to work my way through all 36 of its settings. I’m sure my stomach thanked me for that, too.My top award ultimately went to thePanasonic mini bread maker. While small, it consistently produced tasty loaves – including a delicious mini gluten-free loaf with a wonderful texture. And while carrying it to a friend’s house for some cross-kitchen testing, I came to realise it’s very portable too – it even has a handle. Funnily enough, this particular model also doubles as a compact ice-cream maker – which regular readers may remember isanother love-hate relationship of mine.Now, you might be wondering what happened to all that bread. Of course, one person couldn’t possibly eat 40-plus loaves all to herself, as much as she might try. But fear not, bread lovers: I detest food waste and ensured my fare was put to good use.Many of the loaves are now residing in my freezer, alongside some long-lost ice-cream remnants. These will be used as toast or homemade breadcrumbs for many months to come. The rest of the loaves went to friends and neighbours … whether they wanted them or not.This week’s picksHow I Shop with Bill Bailey: ‘Could be a life-saver in an apocalypse’The best Kindles for every bookworm and budget – testedThe best gifts for nine-year-olds, picked by nine-year-olds and parents‘Outrageously good’: the best (and worst) supermarket ready-made custard, tasted and ratedEditor’s pickView image in fullscreenUnder cover: a checked rain hood keeps showers at bay.Photograph: Hannah Rochell/The GuardianFrom disposable ponchos to flimsy umbrellas, a lot of wet-weather gear seems destined for landfill. So how can you protect yourself from the rain while also protecting the planet – and still look stylish? Hannah Rochell has rounded up the bestsustainable ways for women to keep dry, from surprisingly attractive recycled polyesterwaterproof trousersto anall-season macthat’s designed to be recycled.Monica HorridgeDeputy editor, the FilterIn case you missed it …View image in fullscreenBright start: sunrise alarm clocks bring a little light to winter wake-ups.Photograph: Pete Wise/The GuardianGetting out of bed during the dark mornings of winter is no joke – but asunrise alarm clockcan make it that tiny bit easier. Pete describes them as “kickstarting your circadian rhythm before you get out of bed”. He also writes: “As a lifelong reluctant riser, I’ve found the experience of testing these devices a gamechanger.” His verdict? “I’m now using one daily. title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for crab and spring onion fried rice | Food | The Guardian
description: So good that I make this comfort blanket once a week
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: So good that I make this comfort blanket once a week
Content: Georgina Hayden’s crab and spring onion fried rice.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and Prop Styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex JorgeView image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s crab and spring onion fried rice.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and Prop Styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex JorgeQuick and easyFoodGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for crab and spring onion fried riceBatch-cook a load of rice, cool it, then whip up this comforting shellfish fried riceGeorgina HaydenMon 26 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis gently seasoned rice has become such a comfort blanket that I now make it at least once a week at home. That’s quite surprising, really, given that I’m guilty of drowning most of my food in chilli crisp oil, but this rice is so delicate yet flavourful that it’s just the gentle hug I need. The key is to cook the aromatics slowly and quietly in the oil, to soften and infuse, but not colour too quickly. Cook the jasmine rice in advance, if you like – it fries better once it has been cooked and cooled. Alternatively, packs of pre-cooked microwave rice work brilliantly.Crab and spring onion fried ricePrep10 minCook15 minServes44 tbsp neutral oil4 garlic cloves, peeled and finely sliced30g ginger, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks1bunch spring onions, trimmed and cut into 1cm slices500g cooked jasmine rice¼ tsp white pepper2 tbsp fish sauce1½ tbsp soy sauceSea salt2 large eggs, whisked150g white crab meatPut the oil in a wok or large frying pan and add the garlic, ginger and spring onions. Pop on to a low heat and leave for eight to 10 minutes – you want to infuse the oil slowly, so the spring onions turn tender and the garlic and ginger are lightly golden. Turn up the heat to medium-high, add the cooked rice and fry for a minute. Stir in the white pepper, fish sauce and soy sauce, and fry for two minutes, so it’s all combined and the rice is piping hot.Season the whisked eggs and pour over the top of the rice. Give them a minute to start setting, then drag the eggs through the rice – you don’t want clumps of egg, rather a ripple of it throughout the dish. Fork through the crab meat, cook for a further minute, then take off the heat. Check the seasoning, and add more salt, soy or fish sauce as you wish. Serve straight away.The Guardian aims to publish recipes for sustainable seafood.
