title: The pet I’ll never forget: Clement was hit by a car and left to die in a ditch – then found his beautiful purpose | Life and style | The Guardian
description: Before being rescued, he had an extremely traumatic experience. You’d never know it though, from the joy his patience and sunny nature bring to those who most need him
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Before being rescued, he had an extremely traumatic experience. You’d never know it though, from the joy his patience and sunny nature bring to those who most need him
Content: The gift of affection … Clement.Photograph: Courtesy of Stephanie IsraelView image in fullscreenThe gift of affection … Clement.Photograph: Courtesy of Stephanie IsraelThe pet I'll never forgetLife and styleThe pet I’ll never forget: Clement was hit by a car and left to die in a ditch – then found his beautiful purposeBefore being rescued, he had an extremely traumatic experience. You’d never know it though, from the joy his patience and sunny nature bring to those who most need himStephanie Israel, as told to Farryn StockMon 26 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn December 2024, my kerry blue terrier, Magnus, died suddenly from a stroke at the age of nine. Devastated, I started looking at rescue dogs on Facebook and came across Clement, who was being looked after by a shelter in Romania. It wasn’t his appearance that caught my attention, but his heartbreaking story.An eight-year-old mixed-breed rescue, Clement had spent most of his life with a woman living with Alzheimer’s. One day, she accidentally let him out. He was hit by a car, attacked by two large dogs and left in a ditch for three days in the snow before being rescued by chance. When I read this, I knew I had to take him in.On 11 June 2025, exactly six months after Magnus died, Clement arrived on what I called the “happy bus” from Romania.He was small, with long black fur, a greying beard, and pointy ears that stood to attention. With a gentle and calm demeanour, Clement was the perfect fit alongside our three other dogs. He settled into our family straight away.Despite the difficult time he’d had, Clement loved being around people and other dogs. His gentle nature made me think he would make a fantastic therapy dog, particularly with elderly people. After six months with us, I decided to register him. Passing his therapy dog assessments, Clement soon began working with Ashfields care home in Norwich.They had been looking for a therapy dog for years and Clement instantly enriched the lives of those within the home, just as he had ours. Walking around the communal spaces, you can see that spending time with him brings the elderly residents comfort and gets them talking about their own former pets.Due to his experience in Romania, Clement came to us with limited motion. Although it doesn’t stop him getting around, I bring a stool with me to help him climb up and sit beside people. Often, he will sit for a minute or two before moving on – but on our last visit he sat with a woman, who had been quite upset all day, for five minutes without moving. It was as though he knew she needed him.Not only has Clement brought joy to those in Ashfields care home, but he has taught me a lot in life. He has shown me that no matter your circumstances, we each have something to give to this world. No, he might not win dog shows, but that’s not his purpose. His gift is giving affection and companionship to people who need it most, and he does it beautifully.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleThe pet I'll never forgetPetsDogsDementiaMental healthHealthfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The one change that worked: I told the men in my life I loved them – and my world opened up | Men | The Guardian
description: At first I felt uncomfortable telling my dad, brother and friends how I felt. But I soon found it liberating, and once I started, I couldn’t stop
Author: Ioan Marc Jones
Headline: At first I felt uncomfortable telling my dad, brother and friends how I felt. But I soon found it liberating, and once I started, I couldn’t stop
Content: ‘It might seem like a small change, but to me it felt terrifying’ … Ioan Marc Jones.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘It might seem like a small change, but to me it felt terrifying’ … Ioan Marc Jones.Photograph: Martin Godwin/The GuardianThe one change that workedMenThe one change that worked: I told the men in my life I loved them – and my world opened upAt first I felt uncomfortable telling my dad, brother and friends how I felt. But I soon found it liberating, and once I started, I couldn’t stopIoan Marc JonesMon 26 Oct 2026 02.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleUntil my thirties, I didn’t tell my brothers or my dad that I loved them. I had never told my friends, whom I love, that I loved them. Not in person, at least. Certainly not sober. I had no problem expressing love to women: my partner, cousins, a mate I sort of liked, the neighbour’s cat. “Love you, Mum,” I’d say, waving goodbye. “And see you later, Dad.” The barrier to intimacy between brothers, male friends, fathers and sons, felt natural, a fact of life. It seemed to be a trait of modern men, one that I’d never betray.Then, in 2023, I made the mistake of reading books on masculinity. It started withJJ Bola, Ivan Jablonka,Rebecca Solnitand RW Connell, then I got carried away with Simone de Beauvoir, Judith Butler and Audre Lorde. But one book performed a small act of sorcery: it made me question my life. The Will to Change bybell hooksfelt revolutionary, full of generosity towards men, particularly tough men or men who performed toughness. It spoke of the need for us to break barriers and practise intimacy. “It is not true that men are unwilling to change,” hooks writes. “It is true that many men are afraid to change.”So I decided to change. It might seem like a small change, but to me it felt terrifying: I’d start telling the men I love that I loved them. I started as soon as I’d finished the book. I felt so uncomfortable on the first few attempts that it activated my autonomic nervous system, triggering a fight-or-flight response. “I love you,” I declared to one of my best mates, near the barriers of Shepherd’s Bush tube station, then I ran inside and never looked back.View image in fullscreenIoan Marc Jones (right) and his friend Daniel.Photograph: Courtesy of Ioan Marc JonesI would sometimes mumble the words under my breath. “Did you say something?” a friend asked. I shook my head. I’d say “Love ya” instead of “I love you” because it felt less intimate, less of a declaration. On one occasion, I whispered the words into a friend’s ear while we hugged. I pulled out of the hug and scurried away, not waiting to see his reaction. It felt effortlessly creepy, like an arrestable offence.Reactions proved equally hilarious. One friend asked whether I was feeling OK, as if I’d been felled by an undiscovered ailment. Another stared at me, in confusion, as though I’d posed a riddle. A few mates said it back, out loud, with aplomb. Jesus, I thought, aren’t you emotionally equipped! My brothers didn’t say it back, not at first. I remember one sort of nodding, as if I’d given him a reasonable price on a secondhand car. My dad – a stoic man, much like his dad and his dad’s dad, dad infinitum – surprised me by saying it back, unabashed. It was as if I’d given him license to say it.Others have never said it back. That’s OK. I remember being struck by this line in Connell’sMasculinities: “Men are not permanently committed to a particular pattern of masculinity. They make situationally specific choices from a repertoire of masculine behaviour.” What I understood that to mean is that masculinity is a learned thing. Our fear of intimacy is learned. That means we can unlearn and learn anew.I hoped that saying “I love you” might help the men I love. But it mostly helped me. I found that saying three little words made me more comfortable in my vulnerabilities. I noticed that I talked more about feelings as I spoke to friends. Declaring love seemed a gateway to openness. It felt liberating. I could not stop. I opened up a little, then a little more, now I have become very open, too open, annoyingly open. I’ll talk to the lads about anything. They find it a bit gauche, I think. But I know that openness opens, and intimacy begets intimacy, because I’ve noticed a few of them opening up, too.Saying “I love you” still feels uncomfortable. But I’ve realised it’s a small and secret superpower. I hope it reminds me and the men around me that vulnerability is a virtue – a contagious one that often nudges the world in the right direction. I still tell the men I love that I love them, still with a hangover of discomfort, but now I say it loudly and unapologetically.Explore more on these topicsMenThe one change that workedFriendshipFamilyShareReuse this content

title: Stung with a parking fine for an 18-second airport stop to tackle a wasp | Consumer affairs | The Guardian
description: No matter what the cause, airports are ruthless in issuing PCNs if a car stops in a red zone. But there is a get-out clause
Author: Anna Tims
Headline: No matter what the cause, airports are ruthless in issuing PCNs if a car stops in a red zone. But there is a get-out clause
Content: Warning signs at an airport which means stopping for just seconds could cost £100.Photograph: Avpics/AlamyView image in fullscreenWarning signs at an airport which means stopping for just seconds could cost £100.Photograph: Avpics/AlamyConsumer championsConsumer affairsStung with a parking fine for an 18-second airport stop to tackle a waspNo matter what the cause, airports are ruthless in issuing PCNs if a car stops in a red zone. But there is a get-out clauseAnna TimsMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleI had to stop my car for 18 seconds in a red zone at Leeds Bradfordairport to deal with a wasp. It was buzzing in front of my face and making safe-driving impossible.The result was a £100 parking charge notice (PCN) sent to my wife (the registered keeper) byVehicle Control Services(VCS).I’ve explained the circumstances to VCS, whose CCTV footage shows Ionly stopped for seconds and never left the car, but it won’t listen.AW,Hebden BridgeIts hearing improved when I contacted the airport, which ordered VCS to refund the charge as “goodwill”. The airport tells me that if you had contacted it directly, it would have intervened. However, it is evidently worried that its actions in this case will open the floodgates to wasp-ridden drivers.“Stopping in this area remains enforceable,” it says sternly. “And due to the safety-critical nature of the road, we would not be able to consider cancellation of any future penalty notices for stopping in this area.” VCS did not respond to a request for a comment.‘Cheap’ parking at Stansted airport cost me hundreds of poundsRead moreParking operators are infamously ruthless when enforcing airport no-stopping zones. Drivers have been charged forstopping at temporary lights,or waiting in traffic queues.By remarkable coincidence,SMof Pontyclun in Wales also stopped for 18 seconds in an airport red zone. She was billed £100 by VCS, via her husband, who is the vehicle’s registered keeper.In her case, the airport was Bristol, and she stopped to read the terms and conditions on a sign planted in the no-stopping area.“I had prepaid £103.60 for three days in the short-stay car park,” she writes. “At the entrance was a prominent sign stating that payment was on exit, and including several lines of information. Confused, I wanted to make sure I was at the right place.”Her appeal was rejected by VCS, which argued that it is “the motorist’s responsibility to ensure they are familiar with the terms and conditions displayed on the signage” – which is ironic given that SM was doing just that.It was also rejected by the Independent Appeals Service, which concluded that red-route restrictions prohibit stopping under any circumstances.“Is it reasonable to expect a motorist to read a substantial amount of car park information while their vehicle is moving, particularly when that information is relevant to determining whether they are entering the correct car park?” asks SM.There are 24 lines of information, in varying sizes of font, on the sign SM was studying.Drivers enter a contract when using a car park and are assumed to have agreed the terms and conditions, or else risk a PCN. It was therefore imperative SM read the notice, and not unreasonable she stopped to do so safely.Bristol airport says: “The customer did not contact us to make us aware of the situation and that she had pre-booked parking. After the circumstances were reviewed, the penalty charge was refunded by the enforcement company.” VCS was contacted for a comment.View image in fullscreenA No Stopping sign at Bristol Airport.Photograph: Richard Wayman/AlamyIn fact, neither AW nor SM were obliged to pay the charge because of a loophole in the law. Airports are “statutory land” governed by bylaws, and are not subject to the Protection of Freedoms Act 2012, which governs private parking enforcement in England and Wales.The act allows private parking operators to pursue the registered keeper of a vehicle for charges. There is no such keeper liability on statutory land, so if the keeper declines to confirm who was driving, the parking operator is powerless. Operators don’t, of course, want you to know this.The clue is in the small print of PCNs sent to the spouses of AW and SM which “invite” them to pay up or name the driver. Anyone else in this situation should reply stating that as an airport is statutory land, they are not liable as the vehicle keeper and not obliged to name the driver.Motorists penalised for reasonable stops on land that does fall under the act may have a future get-out clause.The government’snewly announced crackdownon private parking charges means that when the new official code of practice takes effect (we don’t have a date yet), charges will be cancelled on appeal for things such as stopping briefly because of a medical emergency (potential wasp stings, hopefully, included).Explore more on these topicsConsumer affairsConsumer championsConsumer rightsMotoringAir transportShareReuse this content

title: Is it true that … toothpaste is an effective spot treatment? | Life and style | The Guardian
description: It might dry out a pimple, but it could make things worse, so it’s worth exploring other solutions
Author: Kate Lloyd
Headline: It might dry out a pimple, but it could make things worse, so it’s worth exploring other solutions
Content: Illustration for 'Is it true' column Oct 24th 2026Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianView image in fullscreenIllustration for 'Is it true' column Oct 24th 2026Illustration: Edith Pritchett/The GuardianIs it true that …Life and styleIs it true that … toothpaste is an effective spot treatment?It might dry out a pimple, but it could make things worse, so it’s worth exploring other solutionsKate LloydMon 26 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe idea that toothpaste can be used to treat spots has been around for years. But does it actually work – or could it make things worse?“A spot happens when a sebaceous gland gets plugged and inflamed,” says Dr Rosalind Simpson, a consultant dermatologist and associate professor at the University of Nottingham. Acne develops through a combination of blocked pores, increased sebum production and changes inCutibacterium acnes, bacteria that naturally live on the skin.The thinking is that ingredients such as baking soda or alcohol can dry out a pimple, making it appear smaller. But that doesn’t mean toothpaste is good for skin.double quotation markHydrocolloid acne patches have been shown to help reduce lesion size, redness and inflammation“One or two of the ingredients can temporarily dry out the skin a little bit,” says Simpson. “But the flipside is that other ingredients, such as menthol and sodium lauryl sulfate, are highly irritant to skin and could make the problem worse by increasing inflammation and worsening scarring and pigmentary change.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toInside SaturdayThe only way to get a look behind the scenes of the Saturday magazine. Sign up to get the inside story from our top writers as well as all the must-read articles and columns, delivered to your inbox every weekend.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIs it true that … houseplants freshen the air in our homes and offices?Read moreShe would not recommend treating a spot with toothpaste. Instead, she says, hydrocolloid acne patches can help reduce lesion size, redness and inflammation. Also, avoid picking or squeezing spots, which increases the risk of scarring; apply a warm cloth to the area; and use an over-the-counter topical treatment such as azelaic acid.“Topical treatments for acne need to be used for a long time, usually 12 weeks, to start getting the best anti-inflammatory effects,” she says, and prevention is better than cure. So ensure your skincare routine includes products that reduce inflammation and have antibacterial properties.Simpson recommendsAcne Supportandthe British Association of Dermatologistsfor information. If acne is not responding to simple skincare measures, she advises seeing a doctor.Explore more on these topicsLife and styleIs it true that …SkincareBeautyfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Meet my new après buddies!’: a joyous group skiing trip in Les Deux Alpes, France | Skiing holidays | The Guardian
description: One large ski chalet in the French Alps and 17 strangers. An organised trip for solo travellers is a leap into the unknown
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: One large ski chalet in the French Alps and 17 strangers. An organised trip for solo travellers is a leap into the unknown
Content: Some of the chalet group.Photograph: Andrew DayView image in fullscreenSome of the chalet group.Photograph: Andrew DaySkiing holidays‘Meet my new après buddies!’: a joyous group skiing trip in Les Deux Alpes, FranceOne large ski chalet in the French Alps and 17 strangers. An organised trip for solo travellers is a leap into the unknownAndrew DayMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEveryone had their reasons for joining the trip. Louisa from south London was putting her life back together after a split from her partner; first-timer Tim was strapping on ski boots following years of hesitation; and Lexi from Bristol had a classic case of the non-skiing boyfriend.I was there because I needed a ski gang. None of my friends ski, and my brother was out of action with an injury. Not only that, I needed a good night’s sleep. I love my two-year-old son dearly, but I have somehow spawned an insomniac – still waking four times a night. Weary from bedtime battles, Holly, my partner, bluntly pointed out we could both benefit from “a temporary break from family life”. In other words: separate holidays.Holly arranged a walking trip with friends; I opted for a week’s skiing in the French ski resort of Les Deux Alpes withFriendship Travel, a specialist operator in solo travel for more than 20 years. They find a chalet, fill it with solo skiers, provide travel, most meals and group ski lessons – that’s the basic service.View image in fullscreenThe chalet.Photograph: Andrew DayWe were staying in a comfortable, largeish chalet just back from the resort’s mile-long drag. Entering a group holiday with strangers is a leap into the unknown. I was greeted by Sam and Mike, our (thankfully) low-key hosts, shown to my private room (you can save by bunking up with a same sex stranger), then introduced to my fellow holidaymakers. It turned out that there were 17 of us – nine women, eight men – and we were whisked into the lounge for a briefing and welcome drink. The atmosphere was upbeat and easy, and we gathered round one large table for an excellent three-course dinner.double quotation markWhat was once viewed with hesitation is now celebrated, and solo holidays have become one of the fastest-growing segments in the industryMost Friendship Travel guests are aged between 35 and 65, and our group was at the top end of that range. There was Vivienne, a retired nurse from Cumbria who had just lost her partner, and Adriana, a “silver splitter” relishing retirement. For a few – myself included – it was the first such holiday, but many were inveterate solo travellers, with Ivyon, a former production operator from Bridgend, clocking up more than 90 trips.The first morning, we set off to our ski lockers at the bottom of the slopes (tip: I booked my equipment hire in advance, saving €40). The group naturally fragmented, allowing small cliques to form – people relaxed as they started to identify potential après buddies.I skied with Elaine, Clemmie, James and our guide, Luke, in the “level 4 advanced” group (we were asked to rate our ability beforehand). The backbone of Les Deux Alpes, the new Jandri 3S cable car, whisked us up to an altitude of 3,200 metres in 17 minutes – instead of the previous 40. Above broken clouds, we paused to admire the astonishing jagged peaks of theÉcrins national park.View image in fullscreenAndrew, Luke, James, Elaine and Clemmie.Photograph: Andrew DayWe blasted down a mixture of broad blue and red runs, plus some not overly challenging blacks. Although none of us had met before, we quickly settled into a rhythm, looking out for one another as the snow fell softly. There’s safety in numbers, especially on the off-piste sections. “I’d never have tried that alone,” said Clemmie.double quotation markAt times, group etiquette could be a minefield: is it rude to always sit in the same seat at breakfast?Afternoons brought more skiing, followed by hands-in-the-air après atSkandal– reopened in 2025 following an extension – with a DJ on a packed terrace. Around sundown, the chalet WhatsApp group would start to ping. “Polar Bear Pub, anyone?” would be a typical message, often sent by Mícheál from Armagh, a dependable partner for a pint.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSolo travel has undergone a perception shift in recent decades, according to Colum McLornan, who founded Friendship Travel in 1999. “Travelling alone was often seen as unconventional, and for many it carried a stigma. But travellers are increasingly seeking independence, flexibility and personal growth. What was once viewed with hesitation is now celebrated, and solo holidays have become one of the fastest-growing segments in the industry,” he said.View image in fullscreenClemmie, Elaine and Andrew hit the slopes.Photograph: Andrew DayAt times, group etiquette could be a minefield: nobody likes waiting for latecomers (me); is it rude to always sit in the same seat at breakfast? (probably); is it OK to peel away from the group and ski by oneself? (up to a point); will I look like a skinflint if I buy my own wine? (absolutely, but life’s too short for plonk).Honourable mention to Steve, a jolly retired doctor from north London. I enjoyed his vivid stories of cruising the Yangtze River, and skiing with his father in Austria during the late 1950s. Despite our age gap, we struck up a bond that lasted all week. Naturally, not all guests are interesting and fun. One seemingly endless dinner conversation about printer cartridges had me dreaming of Netflix in my room.Then, suddenly, I found myself hugging my ski gang goodbye, bound for the train. Would I go solo again? Yes. Our hosts were helpful without being intrusive, the skiing superb (especially the high-altitude stuff on Glacier de Mont-de-Lans) and I met people I will stay in touch with. Best of all, I finally got some sleep.The trip was provided byFriendship Travel. A seven-night packagewith a private room in a shared chalet, daily breakfast and afternoon tea, dinner with wine on five evenings, and six days of group ski lessons inLes Deux Alpes, costs from £1,820pp. Return rail travel from London to Grenoble was provided byEurostarExplore more on these topicsSkiing holidaysFrance holidaysGroup tripsEurope holidaysAlps holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Did you solve it? A magical melody from the Mozart of math | Mathematics | The Guardian
description: The solution to today’s puzzles
Author: Alex Bellos
Headline: The solution to today’s puzzles
Content: Terence TaoView image in fullscreenTerence TaoAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleMathematicsDid you solve it? A magical melody from the Mozart of mathThe solution to today’s puzzlesAlex BellosMon 26 Oct 2026 13.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEarlier today, I set a puzzle by UCLA professor Terry Tao, who is widely regarded as one of the world’s top mathematicians.Here it is again with solutions.The magic money plantIn an online game, you earn coins by harvesting from plants. There are two types of plant:a regular plant produces a single coin per daya mother plant produces a single coin and two seeds per day. (A seed will grow into a regular plant the following day.)At the start of the game, a player has a certain number of mother plants, regular plants and coins, but not more than nine of each.Suppose that I begin on Day 1 withamother plants,bregular plants andccoins.1.How many coins do I have in total at the end of days 2 and 3?2. Find an expression for how many coins I have at the end of Day X.3.At the end of Day 10 I have 427 coins. What area,bandc?Solution1.Day 2: 4a+ 2b+c.Day 3: 9a+ 3b+cWorkings: At the end of day 1 the number of coins is isa + b+c.Each mother plant has also produced 2 seeds, but these have not yet grown into regular plants. On day 2, these plants produce a coin each, so there are 2aof these, added to anotherafrom the mother plant and theafrom day 1, makng 4a.The regular plants produce another coin each, makingbin total to add to thebfrom day 1. This gets us 4a+ 2b+cfor day 2, and the same reasoning gets us the above expression for day 3.2.aX2+bX +cWe calculated for X = 1, 2 and 3. You hopefully saw the pattern emerge. The number of coins produced by the mother plant and her descendants is the square of the day.3.a = 4, b = 2, c= 7.When X = 10, there are 427 coins. Thus100a +10b+c= 427. Soa, bandcmust be 4, 2 and 7. The answer was in the question!Tao said he suggested this puzzle because he likes the way it naturally introduces algebraic ways of thinking as the most efficient way to solve a problem.“It turns out that the number of coins at day X is given by a polynomial,aX2+bX +c. In modern algebra, we have realized that polynomials are very similar to numbers in many ways: for instance, one can add and multiply two polynomials together much as one can add and multiply numbers. For this problem, it is more than an analogy: on day 10 (X=10), the value of the polynomialaX2+bX +cis just the three-digit numberabc(assuming thata,b,andcare at most nine). So one can now read off the desired unknownsa, b, cjust by inspecting the digits 4, 2, and 7 of the given coin value 427.”The idea that polynomials behave like numbers is one of the themes of Tao’s first book for a general audience,Six Maths Essentials.I hope you enjoyed today’s puzzle. I’ll be back in two weeks.Six Maths Essentials by Terence Tao is out tomorrow. You can buy it at theGuardian Bookshop.I’ve been setting a puzzle here on alternate Mondays since 2015. I’m always on the look-out for great puzzles. If you would like to suggest one,email me.Explore more on these topicsMathematicsAlex Bellos's Monday puzzleShareReuse this content

title: ‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults | China | The Guardian
description: Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’
Content: A social media post advocating raising a brick, in which it said among other things: ‘Those seemingly meaningless little things actually make you realise that, besides spending money, you can have a lively, ever-changing corner for free.’Photograph: xiaohongshu.comView image in fullscreenA social media post advocating raising a brick, in which it said among other things: ‘Those seemingly meaningless little things actually make you realise that, besides spending money, you can have a lively, ever-changing corner for free.’Photograph: xiaohongshu.comChina‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adultsFaced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’Amy Hawkinsin BeijingMon 26 Oct 2026 05.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYoung adults inChinalooking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having children or pets have found an answer: raising bricks.Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.Raising “brick babies” is easier than caring for house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day then waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article described the bricks as being “practically immortal”. “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on the Chinese social media platform Weibo.View image in fullscreenSocial media users document their brick’s changes over a year, with hashtags including #healing and #stress relief.Photograph: @South/xiaohongshu.comChinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick “parent” told Chinese media the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”Young people in China are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society, such as having children and working long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students,are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the unemployment rate much higher.China’sbirthrateis in decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of intensely competitive studying, many young people are choosing to shun the rat race and opt instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low-effort, low-stress lifestyle; one well-suited to raising bricks.The trend has become so popular that Chinese media have started to warn about the health risks.Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of itchy eyes and runny noses. Xuedong Li, a retired professor of moss from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged people to keep their bricks in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.Additional research by Yu-chen LiExplore more on these topicsChinaAsia PacificPopulationYoung peopleHobbiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: I saw a drone suddenly descend towards me. My heart started pounding and I thought, ‘Is this the end of my life?’ | Journalist safety | The Guardian
description: Photographer Zeinab Faraj, 21, found herself buried under rubble beside a dying colleague while reporting in Lebanon. She had never expected to be the target of an Israeli missile attack
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Photographer Zeinab Faraj, 21, found herself buried under rubble beside a dying colleague while reporting in Lebanon. She had never expected to be the target of an Israeli missile attack
Content: Photojournalist Zeinab Faraj explains how she survived an Israeli drone attack - videoUnder fireJournalist safetyI saw a drone suddenly descend towards me. My heart started pounding and I thought, ‘Is this the end of my life?’Photographer Zeinab Faraj, 21, found herself buried under rubble beside a dying colleague while reporting in Lebanon. She had never expected to be the target of an Israeli missile attack.Supported byAbout this contentElsy Moufarrej in TyreMon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 08.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIt was mid-April and after a month of deadly airstrikes across Lebanon, Israelagreed to a ceasefire. Much of the bombing had focused on southern Lebanon, where entire villages had been demolished. But with the truce, people were hopeful of being able to return to their homes or to see what remained.Zeinab Faraj, a 21-year-old photojournalist, decided to join Amal Khalil, 42, a newspaper reporter inLebanon, on a trip to an area in the south of the country to document the aftermath of war. The two had worked together on a number of assignments after Khalil had seen Faraj’s work on social media and contacted her.“I expected it to be like every other time. Amal and I would go out, take some footage and then leave. I had absolutely no sense of fear. We could hear some gunfire and artillery, but as a videographer, you find those things important to document and capture,” says Faraj, who was freelancing alongside finishing her degree in radio and TV.View image in fullscreenPhotojournalist Zeinab Faraj, left, with Amal Khalil, a newspaper reporter in Lebanon. The two worked together on a number of assignmentsBy the time they reached the village of al-Tiri on the afternoon of 22 April, Faraj began to look out the window and reminisce. She was born and grew up in the nearby city of Bint Jbeil. “My whole life revolved around this area. As we say, a fish suffocates when it’s taken out of water. That’s how we feel whenever we leave Bint Jbeil.”Ahead of them was a car carrying Ali Nabil Bazzi, 27, a municipal official in Bint Jbeil, and Mohammed Hourani, 37, a friend of the mayor. They had met them by chance earlier in the day at Tebnine governmental hospital, which had become a gathering point because people considered it relatively safe and would base their movements from there. Bazzi was due to sign a marriage contract that evening, but was still keen to join the trip.Faraj says she did not hear the missile coming, just the sound of Khalil screaming and then the sight of the car in front of them on fire. The two women got out of their car.“I do not know how I managed to stay so calm. The only thing I could think was: if I come closer, I will be able to see Ali. Maybe I will be able to pull him out.”Khalil kept repeating: “Oh God, they’re gone.” Slowly, Faraj began to understand what was going on. “I could see their bodies torn apart.”Then the drones appeared.“When the drones came, my heart started pounding in a terrifying way. The drone started coming very close to my face. I tried to cover my face, but whenever I did, it would fly back up. That was when I really felt the real danger.”Map showing locations of Israeli drone attacks on Lebanon since the start of the US-Iran warThe drones flew low and close as Khalil and Faraj frantically made phone calls to emergency services who repeatedly assured them that help was on its way. Faraj says the assurances were “like an anaesthetic”, something that briefly numbed the reality that no one was rescuing them.One of the paramedics on a call told them to get into their car and try to drive back up the road, as ambulances were being preventing from driving to where they were. But as they tried to get into the car, it was struck by a missile.Both of them were thrown backwards, with Khalil wrapping her arms around Faraj. As the drone continued to circle overhead, Khalil said she hoped it would “think we were dead”.With the nearby car engulfed in flames, they decided to take shelter in a nearby house. Khalil had visible injuries, with blood on her face, hand and leg. Faraj says she sent her sister a last message before her phone died: “There’s no hope left. Forgive me.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every fortnightSign up toGlobal DispatchGet a different world view with a roundup of the best news, features, opinion and photography, curated by our global development teamEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionView image in fullscreenA paramedic pulls Faraj out of the rubble after the attackInside, they sat on a bathroom floor. Khalil was unable to move, so Faraj says she crawled to a position from where she could watch the road. Suddenly a drone descended towards her.“It had been high up and suddenly it came down. The way it descended was terrifying. My heart stopped.” Soon after this, Faraj says she came back inside and began to feel tired and detached from what was happening. “I felt alone.”Then came the sound of a missile falling. “I’ve never heard anything like it in my life. I’ve heard so many strikes and drones, but this was completely different. It was terrifying and Amal was screaming,” she says.She does not remember what happened next, but when she opened her eyes an enormous weight was pressing down on her body. Everything was black and she could barely breathe. She was trapped underneath rubble. “I couldn’t bear the weight. It felt like something was pushing me down, crushing me. All I cared about was being able to breathe.”Faraj says she then heard a voice and thought it was her father, but it was a paramedic who had managed to reach the scene of the attack. As he held her by the shoulders, Faraj says she instinctively clung to him and refused to let go. “I told him: ‘Don’t leave me. I’m afraid to stay alone.’” He stayed beside her while a second paramedic cleared the rubble.As the sound of drones returned once more, the paramedics quickly pulled Faraj free as she screamed from the pain. At about the same time, Faraj says she heard a stun grenade dropped by the drone. As they drove away in the ambulance, she repeatedly mistook the sound of the vehicle for a drone. “They’re going to hit us. We’re not going to make it,” she says she kept repeating.3:33NGOs say Israel bombed a journalist and appeared to attack ambulances trying to aid her – explainerAfter they got to a hospital, Faraj says she started to ask about Khalil. At first the nurses tried to reassure her. But eventually, she says, they fell silent. “That’s when I knew she was gone.” Khalil isbelieved to have diedabout an hour before the paramedics had been allowed to return to the area again after rescuing Faraj.The Israeli military justified their attack saying they had identified saboteurs violating the ceasefire. However, human rights groupscalled it a war crime. As Khalil and Faraj took refuge in the building the Israeli military received repeated messages urging them to allow a rescue operation. A week before the attack, an Israeli military spokesperson shared a video of Khalil published by her newspaper and described it as “terrorist media”. Khalil had also received death threats from Israeli numbers.Today, as Faraj prepares to return to university, she still struggles to walk properly and has visible injuries to a hand. An injury to her face has affected the movement of one eyebrow; others are hidden by her clothes and hijab. Her limp is especially hard to bear. “I was always on the move. I lost that. Even climbing stairs can be hard,” she says.A graph showing that almost 600 people have been killed by Israeli drones in Lebanon since the start of the the US-Iran warAt first she was in shock, she says, but now more symptoms are starting to appear. She wakes at night screaming and buries herself in the pillows as if a missile is going to strike. The sound of drones and warplanes put her on edge.Returning to frontline journalism feels uncertain and she says she is repeatedly haunted by the image of Hourani lying on the ground after the first missile attack. “His head was turned towards me. His eyes open and looking at me. That is something I will never get out of my head.”Explore more on these topicsJournalist safetyUnder fireLebanonIsraelMiddle East and north AfricaWar reportingWomen in journalismWar crimesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Protests, tourists and the Kremlin: Georgia at a crossroads – photo essay | Georgia | The Guardian
description: Citizens want greater democracy, while tourists seek out Soviet-era nostalgia, but could Russia’s war on Ukraine be the ultimate decider of country’s fate?
Author: Alessandro Gandolfi
Headline: Citizens want greater democracy, while tourists seek out Soviet-era nostalgia, but could Russia’s war on Ukraine be the ultimate decider of country’s fate?
Content: A large crowd of local young people and tourists gathers in Europe Square in central Batumi, Georgia, to watch the 2026 World Cup final between Argentina and Spain. Photograph: Alessandro GandolfiCitizens want greater democracy, while tourists seek out Soviet-era nostalgia, but could Russia’s war on Ukraine be the ultimate decider of country’s fate?ByAlessandro GandolfiMon 26 Oct 2026 10.02 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn the heart of Tbilisi’s Armenian quarter, Avlabari Square is where crowds gather for the “Saturday March”. Every weekend, protesters head towards the Bridge of Love, reach Freedom Square and march towards parliament, chanting slogans against Irakli Kobakhidze’s government.View image in fullscreenDemonstrators in Tblisi take part in the Saturday March, when pro-European parties and movements march through the historic centre to protest against the policies of the ruling Georgian Dream party, which critics accuse of being pro-Russian.View image in fullscreenFor years, the target has been the same: Georgian Dream, the ultraconservative party in power since 2012, accused of growing authoritarianism and, through its decision to suspend EU accession talks, moving the country closer to Moscow again. Georgia wasgranted EU candidate statusin 2023.Monday marks two years since the contested parliamentary elections on 26 October 2024 that ignited the political crisis. Protests began two days later and peaked on 28 November, when the government announced it would not put the opening of EU negotiations on its agenda before the end of 2028.View image in fullscreenA woman walks along one of the bridges connecting three Soviet-era towers on Nutsubidze Street in Tblisi.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTwo homeless people shelter in the decaying entrance to the Metallurgist sanatorium, an abandoned Soviet-era hotel. Formerly a famous spa town, Tskaltubo hosted 120,000 visitors a year, including Joseph Stalin, who came to enjoy its 22 sanatoriums. After the collapse of the USSR, the area fell into decline and most of the sanatoriums and hotels were abandoned. Today, only a few hundred tourists visit the town’s sole remaining spa centre.View image in fullscreenBooks lie scattered across rooms at the Museum of Local Traditions in Tskaltubo, Georgia, where the library is being rebuilt.Georgia is experiencing a curious paradox: while many of its citizen would like the country to be more democratic and form closer ties toEurope, Georgia is attracting growing numbers of tourists drawn to its historic sites, post-Soviet atmosphere and unspoilt landscapes.While the streets of Tbilisi have become the stage for one of the longest protest movements in recent history, in 2025 the country, according to data from the Georgian National Tourism Administration, recorded a high of more than 5.5 million international tourist visits: an 8.4% increase on 2024 and almost 10 times the number (about 560,000) who visited the country 2o years ago.View image in fullscreenA tourist walks through one of the rooms of the Joseph Stalin Museum. The Soviet dictator was born in Gori in 1878, and the museum was established in 1937 near his birthplace. Transformed into a museum glorifying Stalin in 1957, it remained open even after the collapse of the USSR and the 2008 war withRussia.View image in fullscreenTravellers come not only from Europe; many are from the Middle East, and large numbers come from Russia.After the full-scale invasion ofUkrainein 2022, tens of thousands of Russian citizens relocated to Georgia, bringing money and opening businesses, but also exerting strong pressure on the property market by buying homes across the country.This has fuelled discontent among a population that, mindful of the early 1990s wars against Russian-backed separatists in South Ossetia and Abkhazia, and the brief August 2008 war fought against Moscow, also in South Ossetia, continues to consider Russia an occupying power.View image in fullscreenAn abandoned Soviet-era building in Chiatura – one of Georgia’s most important mining towns, where manganese is extracted. The industry faces a severe environmental and economic crisis, which has prompted continuing protests by workers.View image in fullscreenAn inhabited Soviet-era building in Chiatura.The mythical land of the Golden Fleece and the Argonauts – the ancient Greeks called the journey to reach it “the longest possible voyage” – is now a republic roughly the size of Ireland, with a population of fewer than 4 million. Georgia emerged from the fall of the Soviet Union in 1991.Sandwiched between Russia and Turkey (alongside Armenia and Azerbaijan), it offers a wealth of attractions that draw tourists: quaint mountain villages scattered along the Georgian Military Road, ancient Orthodox churches overlooking rivers and valleys, fascinating post-Soviet cities with a decaying atmosphere, wine with a millennia-old history, a lively “Las Vegas” on the Black Sea (the port of Batumi) and a dynamic, cosmopolitan capital.View image in fullscreenVisitors relax on the pebble beach north of the historic centre in Batumi, with a large container ship heading into the port in the background. Home to numerous casinos and a rapidly growing tourist destination, Batumi is known as the ‘Las Vegas of the Black Sea’ and is also an important commercial port.View image in fullscreenTbilisi, with its rich underground scene and repurposed industrial spaces, is reminiscent of 1990s Berlin. One of its crown jewels, a true symbol of national independence, is the Rustaveli theatre, renovated 20 years ago by the billionaire who founded Georgian Dream in 2012: Bidzina Ivanishvili. Now in his 70s, Ivanishvili served as Georgian prime minister between 2012 and 2013 and made his fortune in Russia during the 1990s after the Soviet collapse.View image in fullscreenPeople on a train in Tbilisi. Opened in 1966 to facilitate travel in a city that stretches along the river and is built on steep slopes, the metro network was the fourth-largest in the Soviet Union. Today, the metro, which has two lines and 23 stations, carries 400,000 passengers a day.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenA woman takes a selfie overlooking Tbilisi from Mtatsminda Park.View image in fullscreenView image in fullscreenTourists take photos near the Leghvtakhevi waterfall in Tbilisi, while others capture the scenery from the funicular leading to Mtatsminda Park.View image in fullscreenGeorgians attend a concert at Mtatsminda Park. Founded in the 1930s, the park stands 770 metres above sea level and features restaurants, a rollercoaster, a concert venue, and a large ferris wheel visible from much of Tbilisi.Today, the relationship between Georgia and Russia is built on a contradiction that is difficult to resolve. After the 2008 conflict and the consolidation of Russian military control over Abkhazia and South Ossetia (regions accounting for approximately 20% of Georgian territory), diplomatic relations between the countries were severed.View image in fullscreenYet economically, Moscow remains a partner that is difficult to replace: trade, tourism, remittances and Russian capital, along with energy imports, prop up Tbilisi’s economy, which, despite strong growth – GDP rose by 7.5% in 2025, marking five consecutive years of expansion – continues to be affected by unemployment, low wages, widespread poverty and, in many rural areas, depopulation.But Georgia’s predicament extends beyond its domestic political crisis, reflecting wider geopolitical tensions.View image in fullscreenA woman picks flowers in the hills surrounding Gergeti Trinity church, beneath Mount Kazbek.View image in fullscreenWorshippers leave Gergeti Trinity church after mass on 16 July. The day marks the Gergetoba festival, also known as the Day of Spiritual Love.Relations with Brussels have deteriorated recently; the EU has criticised the Georgian government’s record on the rule of law and political repression. And many believe a strengthening of Moscow in the Ukraine war could significantly increase its ability to exert pressure on the Caucasus.Both of which make the question inevitable: does the future of a vulnerable Georgia – internationally isolated and with limited domestic support – also hinge on the fate of Ukraine?Explore more on these topicsThe Guardian picture essayGeorgiaEuropeUkraineRussiaEuropean UnionfeaturesShareReuse this content
