title: UK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’ | Global development | The Guardian
description: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze
Author: Mark Townsend
Headline: Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freeze
Content: Armed defectors from the Rapid Support Forces arrive to surrender to the Sudanese military in Omdurman on 19 August.Photograph: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenArmed defectors from the Rapid Support Forces arrive to surrender to the Sudanese military in Omdurman on 19 August.Photograph: Ebrahim Hamid/AFP/Getty ImagesGlobal developmentUK sanctions Sudanese military leaders implicated in El Fasher ‘campaign of rape’Commanders suspected of sexual violence during the largest and fastest slaughter of civilians in more than 30 years have been subjected to travel ban and asset freezeSupported byAbout this contentMark TownsendMon 26 Oct 2026 11.07 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSenior Sudanese commanders implicated in a “campaign of rape” have been targeted by the UK on the first anniversary of amass atrocitythat saw tens of thousands of civilians killed over several days.A year after thefall of El Fasher, the British government said it had sanctioned military leaders from both sides in the country’s ongoing conflict whom it suspected of sexual violence during the siege of the city.A total of 15 commanders from the military groups – the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and the Sudanese Armed Forces (SAF) – have been subjected toa travel ban and an asset freeze.The Foreign Office said it hoped the action would ensure “the horrors that took place at El Fasher will be known to the world”.During the RSF’s takeover of the city, up to 10,000 men, women and children are believed to have been slaughtered over two days – thefastest and largest massacre of civilians this century. Another 40,000 remain unaccounted for.The killings came at the end of an 18-monthstarvation siegeby the RSF, which was allegedly backed by the United Arab Emirates (UAE). The UAE continues to deny supporting the RSF.Fewer than 70,000 people are believed to remain in El Fasher, compared with a prewar population of more than 1 million. Life inside the city continues to be horrendous,with testimony indicatingroutine detention, torture and unlawful killings.Individuals targeted by the UK’s latest sanctions include Hussein Abu Jalak, an RSF colonel linked to atrocities during the siege, which forced hundreds of thousands of civilians to live off animal feed.Another is Al-Nour Ahmed Adam – also known as “Al-Qubba” – who was identified as playing a prominent role in the attack on the city.A Guardian investigation earlier this year revealed internal US and UKwarnings were sidelinedin the run-up to the RSF attack on El Fasher, and that action that might have saved lives was not taken.A statement to mark the anniversary of the massacre fromthe Coalition on Atrocity Prevention and Justice for Sudansaid: “The victims will not be forgotten, survivors will be heard, and we will continue to pursue accountability for those responsible.”During the 12 months since the fall of El Fasher, Sudan’s ruinous conflict – which hasforced 14 million people to flee their homes– has developed increasingly into a drone war.Thelatest strikessaw the RSF causing mass power outages across east Sudan after targeting power stations with a coordinated drone attack.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSudanAfricaMiddle East and north AfricaWar crimesRape and sexual assaultViolence against women and girlsnewsShareReuse this content

title: US forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El Niño | Global development | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?
Author: Mark Townsend
Headline: Exclusive: Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?
Content: A colonel from US special operations in Somalia with a soldier from a branch of the Somali army trained by US special forces, in Mogadishu in 2023.Photograph: Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA colonel from US special operations in Somalia with a soldier from a branch of the Somali army trained by US special forces, in Mogadishu in 2023.Photograph: Jonathan Torgovnik/Getty ImagesGlobal developmentUS forces accused of ‘weaponising’ Somalia’s floods by trapping women and children in the path of El NiñoExclusive:Coordinated airstrikes on territory held by al-Shabaab are driving the civilian population to find refuge alongside a river where rising water levels are a threat to safety. Is it a deliberate military strategy?Supported byAbout this contentMark Townsendin KismayoMon 26 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe water was rising rapidly. It had already reached Cayni Ali’s waist. Her home, five metres from the flooded River Juba in southernSomalia, never stood a chance. There was nowhere to go. Ali’s city of Jilib was under attack. Repeated airstrikes, said the mother of six, were pinning its population beside the rising river.“The drones come all the time,” said the 27-year-old. “We hear them constantly. They kill animals, civilians. The town is big but destruction is everywhere.”View image in fullscreenCayni Ali with her child Mandeq at a health centre in Kismayo, Somalia.Photograph: Hugh Kinsella CunninghamAsho Omar from Malenda, a village near Jilib, described “constant” airstrikes that had forced people towards the banks of the Juba.“The airstrikes are everywhere; it is difficult to move. So many people have been killed.”Their testimony offers a rare glimpse of life inside the stronghold ofal-Shabaab, the Islamist militants who control 30% of Somalia. Closed off from the outside world, residents describe a city dealing with significant civilian casualties. Bodies, some said, lay in the streets.The ongoing conflict is a legally ambiguous, shadowy war coordinated by the United States in eastAfrica, in which there is little accountability for harm to Somali civilians.TheUnited States Africa Command(Africom) would not share “operational security” details of a seemingly accelerating campaign that has also raised questions over potential covert US strikes. But there is, perhaps, an even darker dimension to the offensive on al-Shabaab’sde facto capital.Sources say the military strategy appears to be seeking to drown those living in al-Shabaab territory by “weaponising” arapidly strengthening El Niño, forecast to intensify Somalia’s rainy season from this month.View image in fullscreenAn aerial view of the Juba River, close to the town of Kismayo.Photograph: Hugh Kinsella Cunningham“The airstrikes are forcing people to go close to the river. It’s an extremely aggressive offensive, exploiting El Niño as a weapon of war to push the population into flood-prone areas,” said a source monitoring the Juba floodplain in southern Somalia.Pinning the population – which includes large numbers of women and children – on the river’s floodplain has raised concerns of large-scale deaths in the months ahead.“The official line is that they are targeting military positions and al-Shabaab, but because al-Shabaab is embedded within the community, it’s difficult to avoid collateral damage,” added the source.When El Niño last struck Somalia in 2023, it caused theworst floods seenin the country for a century, displacing more than1.2 million people. Analysts have questioned the ethics of the US military allegedly using mapping data from flood-prone areas – conceived to mitigate civilian casualties – to inflict harm.Jethro Norman, a senior researcher with theDanish Institute for International Studies, said: “A weaponisation of El Niño is a reversal of process – using humanitarian remote sensing to inflict casualties rather than to mitigate harm. You capture the cumulative impact of a sustained airstrikes campaign in an El Niño flooding context.”View image in fullscreenThe aftermath of the 2023 El Niño in Luuq district, Jubaland, which caused the worst floods ever seen in the country.Photograph: Feisal Omar/ReutersUS officials deny exploiting climatic factors. A spokesperson said: “Africom does not target civilians, conduct operations for the purpose of displacing civilian populations or use weather or flooding as a method of warfare. Africom targets lawful military objectives and takes feasible measures to mitigate civilian harm.”Nevertheless, many wonder if the opportunity to weaken al-Shabaab using the weather was too tempting to ignore, offering a catastrophic drowning event blamed on asupercharged El Niño.Like many cities, Jilib’s location has been found wanting in an era of extreme weather. On a low-lying plain, the city ischronically vulnerableto flooding. In 2023, vast swathes of farmland were submerged. Halimo Abdikadir from Kamsuuma, south of Jillib, described the destruction of her home, 6 miles (10km) from the river. “The waters came quickly at night – when they left, everything was mud. A lot of animals drowned.”Arbey Famu from Ahmed Yare, another village outside Jilib, expects this El Niño to befar worse than 2023: her crops of maize and sorghum are underwater.“In Jilib, there is big flooding already,” said the 70-year-old.US defence officials will know the early indicators of El Niño’s impact in al-Shabaab’s heartland. UN agencies say the Juba River basin is of “particular concern”. TheInternational Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC), meanwhile, foresees “severe flooding”.View image in fullscreenArbey Abdi Famu, a resident of the Dalhiska displacement camp in Kismayo.Photograph: Hugh Kinsella CunninghamAttacking Jilib using ground forces carries much risk. Airstrikes can yield triumphs such as thedeath of a senior al-Shabaab commanderon 1 October, but are unable to overrun a city of 100,000.Ali Adan Ali, the commissioner fordisplaced people in Jubaland, is worried. In his Kismayo office, Ali identified 327 regions prone to flooding. By October, El Niño warnings had only been issued to half.His chief concern is the lack of boats. Without them, he says, thousands in al-Shabaab territory risk being trapped on the east side of the river, unable to reach help in Kismayo, at the mouth of the Juba.View image in fullscreenPeople on the streets of Kismayo, where long-term drought and USAID cuts have brought misery.Photograph: Hugh Kinsella CunninghamThree years ago, during the last El Niño, Ali says, 19,000 people were stranded for a week without food. “We are running out of time,” he says.The absence of boats sums up Somalia’s funding woes. In 2023, the country’s aid budget was $2.2bn. Now it stands at about $300,000. Flood protection investment has dwindled.Compounding concerns is al-Shabaab’s lack of preparedness in the area it controls. Ali has not received a response from the militants regarding El Niño readiness. Cayni Ali said there are no sandbags or flood defences deployed yet in Jilib. Earth walls were erected along the river but have proved insufficient.“They are not big enough,” she said. Thelatest flood advisoryfor the River Juba urges communities to “reinforce” weak riverbanks.Corroborating testimonies describe a prolonged – and seemingly indiscriminate – campaign of airstrikes against al-Shabaab that appears to have killed many civilians. The US would not share details of potential civilian fatalities “to protect US and partner forces and preserve operational security”.Farhan Ahmed, who lived in Jilib until fleeing last month, described constant terror. “There were airstrikes every day, all the time.” One strike flattened five homes in his neighbourhood. Ahmed, 35, described bodies littering the city streets.Fadumo Abdi claimed the airstrikes were largely failing to target militants. “The attacks are mostly killing civilians. Some were buried, but some were not,” she said.Abdikadir, from Kamsuuma, added: “The drone attacks on Jilib are too much. So many people die.”Yusuf Siidi, 27, from Araare near Jamame in al-Shabaab territory, witnessed three teenagers killed in one strike. Maryan Salah was at home near Jamame when a drone sent a shard of burning metal 20cm long into her back yard, landing next to her two-year-old daughter.“It was so close. I am very angry. I’m not part of the conflict.”Salah’s near miss predates the current offensive. She can recall only that it happened in “mid-March”. The US admits a drone strike near Jamame on 19 March, but no other data is provided.View image in fullscreenA mother takes her baby to a Somalia Red Crescent Society health centre in Kismayo to check for symptoms of malnutrition.Photograph: Hugh Kinsella CunninghamAlthough eyewitness accounts detail an extraordinary number of strikes in Jilib,official US recordsconfirm only one airstrike in Jilib during August. Six took place last month. Between the start of August and now,the US saysit conducted a total of just 11 strikes.Allegations of ambiguity increasingly characterise US operations in Somalia. It is an opaque approach that raises questions over whether Africom has authorisedcovert airstrikesin the region.Records from the nearest hospital indicate intensive airstrikes or fighting. TheICRChas treated 205 patients with “weapon-related” injuries in Kismayo this year, a 43% increase on last year.David Sterman, analyst at theNew Americathinktank, said: “The possibility that we are seeing covert US strikes always looms large when there are strikes without clear attribution.”View image in fullscreenA malnourished three-month-old baby in Kismayo hospital’s intensive-care ward in September.Photograph: Hugh Kinsella CunninghamThe US, however,said it publicised“all airstrikes conducted under its authority in Somalia. We do not maintain an undisclosed or unannounced strike count.”Turkey has alsoused dronesto target al-Shabaab in Somalia. Operating alongside Africom, Turkey rarely divulges any details of its strikes or military operations in Somalia.Beyond airstrikes and floods, the primary concern forSomalis is hunger. Those fleeing the Juba valley – local authorities are offering humanitarian help to those who escape – say there is insufficient food to sustain them.Omar’s family of 13 survives on one fish a day. How big is the fish? Omar held her hands less than 30cm apart.Habiba Ali, 55, from Jamame, said her family – like many – shares one daily meal of maize. Time in between is spent hiding from conflict. “When the fighting stops, we wait for it start again.”In Kismayo, too, long-term drought andUSAID cutshave brought misery.Shukri Ahmed, 32, the president of Galbeed refugee camp, estimates that 6,000 might have died in Kismayo’s network of displacement sites since the Trump administration abruptlyshut USAIDlast year. Overnight, two children had died in makeshift shelters from diarrhoea.El Niño will “deepen [Somalia’s] hunger levels”,warns the UN-backed bodyresponsible for identifying famine.Zakaria Mohammed, head nurse at Kismayo’sICRC-supported hospitalfor five years, says children from al-Shabaab territory arrive every day so severely malnourished or weak they cannot be saved. Cases of child malnutrition rates have risen 40% this year.Xaawo Nacdoor made it just in time.Al-Shabaabhad blocked her leaving Jamame to receive treatment for her baby. But her 14-month-old daughter Faadumo was dying, so Nacdoor fled at night.View image in fullscreenFadumo Abdi with her 14-month-old baby, Maryan, in the infant intensive-care unit in Kismayo hospital.Photograph: Hugh Kinsella CunninghamFor three days, with just a bottle of water, Nacdoor walked with her daughter strapped to her back. On the second day, the toddler lost consciousness.“She was severely dehydrated, but I kept going.” Arriving at the hospital, Faadumo weighed 4.1kg. Three days later: 4.4kg. She survived.Most patients here vow never to return home, saying life under al-Shabaab meant no school, education, healthcare or food. For the thousands of families straddling the Juba River – often the poorest – things are about to get much worse.Explore more on these topicsGlobal developmentSomaliaAfricaMiddle East and north AfricaEl Niño southern oscillationInternally displaced peopleFloodingfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Sudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern states | Sudan | The Guardian
description: Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Rapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese army
Content: Displaced people in Gedaref city. The UN has said attacks on power stations threaten the health of millions of people in Sudan, who are already facing extreme hunger.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenDisplaced people in Gedaref city. The UN has said attacks on power stations threaten the health of millions of people in Sudan, who are already facing extreme hunger.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesSudanSudan paramilitary drone strikes cause mass power cuts in eastern statesRapid Support Forces strike five power stations in three states controlled by Sudanese armyAgence France-Presse in KhartoumMon 26 Oct 2026 05.59 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 13.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSudan’s paramilitary Rapid Support Forces have launched a coordinated drone attack against five power stations, causing mass power outages across the country’s east, a government official said.The drones hit two power stations each in the states of Al-Jazira and Gedaref and one in White Nile state, “resulting in power outages across large parts of these three states”, the official said on condition of anonymity.All three states are controlled by the Sudanese army, which has been at war with the RSF, its former ally, since April 2023.The United Nations has repeatedly warned that regular attacks on power stations threaten health and services for millions of people who are already facing the world’s largest hunger crisis.Babiker Youssef, a resident of Al-Fao, in Gedaref, said the power had been out there since early morning.“My son is diabetic, his insulin has to be stored in the fridge,” he said over the phone, adding that he feared he would not be able to replace the medication if it spoiled. “We have no idea when the power will come back,” he said.Electricity has been cut for days at a time after past paramilitary drone strikes on power stations and hydroelectric dams.Sudan’s war is currently being fought primarily via drones, with both sides launching sophisticated attacks across the country, killing dozens of civilians at a time.In the first three weeks of October, drone strikes killed more than 300 people and injured hundreds more, according to a UN tally.Africa’s third largest country, home to an estimated 50 million people, has been ravaged by the war, which aid workers estimate has killed more than 200,000 people.The majority of Sudan’s hospitals have been forced to close, at least 8 million children are out of school and swathes of the country cannot access basic services.Abdelhafez Daafallah, a 54-year-old farmer, said by phone from Al-Junaid town in Al-Jazira: “The electricity had just started to improve three months ago, the power station the militia had destroyed was just repaired and we had hope our irrigation pumps would finally start running again.“We hoped we would be able to finally get back to farming, but now the station has been hit,” he said, frustrated after nearly four years unable to work his land.Sudan’s RSF committed crimes against humanity in El Fasher, Amnesty saysRead moreFarmers in Al-Jazira have struggled to rehabilitate and replant their land since the army recaptured the state from the RSF last year.To the east, in Gedaref, Ibrahim Mohammed, 37, a grocer, said he was “already facing power cuts for hours before the strike”. “Now I have chicken in the fridge, we either lose our entire stock, or will be forced to sell it off at any price, which is still a loss,” he said.Sudan is also grappling with unprecedented inflation and its currency has lost more than 25% of its value in recent weeks.Explore more on these topicsSudanAfricaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: UK poised to miss reduced aid spending target of 0.3% of national income  | Foreign policy | The Guardian
description: Calculations from the Center for Global Development say spending next year is likely to be £410m less than anticipated
Author: Rowena Mason
Headline: Calculations from the Center for Global Development say spending next year is likely to be £410m less than anticipated
Content: People queue for food aid in February during severe drought conditions in Kenya.Photograph: Patrick Ngugi/APView image in fullscreenPeople queue for food aid in February during severe drought conditions in Kenya.Photograph: Patrick Ngugi/APForeign policyUK poised to miss reduced aid spending target of 0.3% of national incomeCalculations from the Center for Global Development say spending next year is likely to be £410m less than anticipatedRowena MasonWhitehall editorMon 26 Oct 2026 02.59 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe UK is on course to miss its target of spending 0.3% of national income on international aid by an estimated £400m by the end of next year.Calculations from the Center for Global Development (CGD) found the UK was on course for a large shortfall in promised official development assistance at the end of 2027.The researchers said the central forecast from the Treasury’s comparison of independent experts implied UK aid would be £410m less than anticipated – at only 0.29% of national income.However, they said it was “very plausible” that the shortfall would be £580m, at only 0.28% of national income. Even the most conservative forecast implies a £250m shortfall, according to the estimates.Ian Mitchell, a senior fellow at the CGD and co-director of its Europe programme, described these as “material shortfalls in the spending power of UK aid”.Making up a shortfall of even £400m would be enough to halve cuts toAfricathat are likely to cost thousands of lives and mean the UK’s de facto exit from the south and east of the continent, he said.Conservative plans to slash aid budget would ‘irreparably damage’ UK’s global credibility, charities sayRead moreThe CGD attributed the shortfall to higher than expected inflation, which means national income will be higher than forecast at the spending review, and a 2025 policy change around theForeign, Commonwealth and Development Office(FCDO) budget.The researchers called on ministers to consider allocating additional funds to international aid in this week’s budget, to avoid the embarrassment and criticism from missing a target.The 0.3% spending target for 2027 is far below the 0.7% promised in Labour’s election manifesto, having been downgraded by Keir Starmer to boost spending on defence.Fleur Anderson, a former minister who sits on the foreign affairs select committee, said she would like to see higher spending on development aid in the budget.She said: “I’d like to see this government going further and reversing these cuts altogether in time, but at the very least we should be hitting the reduced target that was set.“Falling short isn’t an abstract accounting issue. It means communities not having clean water, girls pulled out of school, vaccines that don’t get delivered, peace programmes in war zones cut.“The upcoming budget presents real opportunity for the Treasury to address this and for the government to show that its words on Britain’s place in the world are matched by action.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toFirst EditionOur morning email breaks down the key stories of the day, telling you what’s happening and why it mattersEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionCharities have repeatedly said that the government’s deep aid cuts will hit children’s education and increase the risk of disease and death in some African countries.The latest figures released by the FCDO in September showed that British aid cuts under Starmer’s governmenthit the world’s poorest countries the hardest, while higher-income countries’ share of aid increased. The data showed a 6.7% decrease in funding to the least-developed and low-income countries, amounting to cuts of £118m.The UK’s overall official development assistance (ODA) budget in 2025 decreased to 0.44% of gross national income, compared with 0.5% in 2024, a drop of £987m.The government has prioritised spending through multilateral agencies such as the World Bank’s development arm, the International Development Association, and the global vaccines initiativeGavi. It has also continued to fund humanitarian support.The Conservative party and Reform UK havepledged to slash aid even further, from about £9bn a year to £1bn – a level that would leave the UK unable to cover existing contributions to the UN and World Bank.An FCDO spokesperson said: “The publication of the FCDO multi-year ODA allocations in March 2026 set out our spending plans and priorities for the next three financial years based on GNI [gross national income] at the time of the 2025 spending review.“Moving to a fixed budget reduces volatility and provides the necessary stability to deliver high-impact aid programmes.”Explore more on these topicsForeign policyLabourAidBudget 2026AfricaForeign, Commonwealth and Development OfficeBudgetnewsShareReuse this content

title: Brazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passports | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering case
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: Far-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering case
Content: Flávio Bolsonaro makes a statement in Brasilia after he lost the presidential runoff to Lula on Sunday.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenFlávio Bolsonaro makes a statement in Brasilia after he lost the presidential runoff to Lula on Sunday.Photograph: Xinhua/ShutterstockBrazilBrazil: defeated Flávio Bolsonaro ordered to surrender passportsFar-right senator banned from leaving country as supreme court judge’s ruling makes reference to money-laundering caseTiago Rogeroin BrasíliaMon 26 Oct 2026 19.02 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe far-right senator Flávio Bolsonaro was banned from leaving Brazil and ordered to surrender his passports just hours after his dramatic loss in the presidential election to the leftist presidentLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva.The ruling was issued by supreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes, the same justice who oversaw the trial of the senator’s father, the former president Jair Bolsonaro, for attempting a coup.Bolsonaro posted a video saying the decision was based on an interview his brother, Eduardo Bolsonaro, gave last Friday urging his brother to leaveBrazilif he lost the election.On Monday night, Bolsonaro’s party issued a statement acknowledging the election result, saying: “We recognise the presidential result proclaimed by the electoral court, but believe that the questions raised need to be properly clarified through a balanced and democratic political debate.”Bolsonaro, like his father four years ago, has still not conceded defeat to Lula.How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in BrazilRead moreThe court’s brief ruling regarding his passport only refers to a criminal case in which the federal police are investigating Flávio Bolsonaro over his possible involvement in amoney-laundering scheme. The ruling orders him not to have any contact with his friend Willer Tomaz, a lawyer linked to betting companies that police suspect were being used to launder about £680m.It also cancelled all of Bolsonaro’s passports, including the diplomatic one he holds as a congressman, and ordered him to hand them over within 24 hours.Bolsonaro was the first to speak publicly about the matter, before Brazilian media were even aware of the judge’s decision.In avideoposted on social media, he said he had just left a visit to his father, who is under house arrest in Brasília, when “Lula’s federal police were at his door and in the middle of the street, and I was served with an order to hand over my passports and I am also prohibited from leaving the country”.He added that, although his brother – who is in self-imposed exile in the US –tolda US podcast on Friday that he favoured the senator leaving Brazil if he lost the election, “I never said that”.2:54How students and social media delivered Lula a historic comeback in Brazil – videoWhen his Senate term ends early next year, Bolsonaro will be out of public office for the first time in 24 years, and therefore without the special jurisdiction afforded to officeholders.He is under investigation in another criminal case, too, over what happened to the £20m he was captured on tape asking a disgraced banker accused of corruption to provide for a biopic about his father.The Folha de S.Paulo newspaperreportedthat Flávio Bolsonaro had been persuaded to drop his plan to seek to annul the election, which he had announced after the result was declared on Sunday night.Bolsonaro had claimed that the two-hour extension of voting – intended to allow voters who had been unable to access the mandatory free public transport to cast their ballots – had harmed the election, despite the fact that his own campaign had also argued for an extension.According to the newspaper, allies and lawyers told him his argument was legally weak.Bolsonaro had still not publicly reversed his demand for an annulment, and in the same video he said he would file another case to have Lula’s ticket disqualified over alleged abuse of economic power, a similar case to others his legal team brought during the campaign.Explore more on these topicsBrazilFlávio BolsonaroLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaAmericasnewsShareReuse this content

title: How the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in Brazil | Brazil | The Guardian
description: A viral WhatsApp channel and student-led protests played a key role in the veteran Brazilian leftist’s election victory
Author: Tiago Rogero
Headline: A viral WhatsApp channel and student-led protests played a key role in the veteran Brazilian leftist’s election victory
Content: Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, addresses supporters after winning the presidential runoff election, in São Paulo on Monday.Photograph: Alexandre Meneghini/ReutersView image in fullscreenLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the Workers' Party (PT) candidate for re-election, addresses supporters after winning the presidential runoff election, in São Paulo on Monday.Photograph: Alexandre Meneghini/ReutersBrazilAnalysisHow the streets and social media drove Lula to a historic comeback in BrazilTiago Rogeroin Brasília andTom Phillipsin São PauloA viral WhatsApp channel and student-led protests played a key role in the veteran Brazilian leftist’s election victoryMon 26 Oct 2026 13.56 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.49 EDTShareAfter the first round of the Brazilian presidential election three weeks ago, the leftist incumbent Luiz Inácio Lula da Silvareportedlytold allies he could not understand how he finished second after a government he considered the best of his three terms.A mood of dismay swept Brazil’s left, and because 9 million voters for the other candidates, all of them on the right, were expected to mostly transfer to senator Flávio Bolsonaro, analysts widely saw the far-right senator’s victory as certain.Then, on the night after the election, students from the Fluminense Federal Universitytook to the streetsof Niterói, a city of 480,000 across Guanabara Bay from Rio de Janeiro, to protest against the return to power of a member of the Bolsonaro family, whose patriarch, former president Jair Bolsonaro, Flávio’s father, is under house arrest for attempting a coup.Two days later, another student protest took over downtown Rio and, in the days that followed, similar ones spread across the country in organic demonstrations that analysts and Lula himself agree gave new life to his campaign and played a decisive role in his historic comeback in the runoff.‘Democracy always’: Lula vows no return to dictatorship in Brazil after election winRead more“I want to thank the generosity of Brazil’s young people who took to the streets to defend democracy,” Lula said in his victory speech on Sunday night after defeating Bolsonaro.Political scientist Fábio Vasconcellos said Lula’s victory, in which for the first time in Brazil’s democratic history a second-placed candidate overturned a first-round defeat in the runoff, could be explained by a combination of the streets, social media and the machinery of government – in recent weeks, Lula approved a “package of benefits” at the limits of what electoral law allows, including increasing and bringing forward payments from the main cash-transfer programme for poor families.“The streets and social media almost overlap,” said Vasconcellos, a researcher with the Representation and Democratic Legitimacy group at the Federal University of Paraná.Two days after the first round, congressman André Janones, a Lula ally, created a WhatsApp channel called “Lula’s Army”, where Janones sent audio messages, videos – often beginning with shouts of “Guys, urgent!” – and dozens of daily instructions on how to make pro-Lula content perform well on social media.The channel had 60,000 followers by the end of its first day and, by election Sunday, more than 10 million, and Lula’s digital reach overtook Bolsonaro’s.In his victory speech, Lula called Janones “our general”, who had the role of “raising the morale of our troops every day”. The congressman’s relentless efforts, which included a 24-hour YouTube live stream on the eve of the vote, led to him being admitted to hospital last week – the only day the WhatsApp channel went silent.Lula’s campaign also overhauled his online communications, and the incumbent, who turns 81 on Tuesday, began recording selfie videos despite not owning a mobile phone. On Sunday night, he said he had been given a phone and that “from now on I’m going to talk a lot to the Brazilian people, many times a day, directly”.With the streets and social media, “the mood of defeat was gradually replaced by hopes of a comeback over those three weeks,” said Vasconcellos.Camila Rocha, a political scientist who studies Brazil’s new right, said Lula’s comeback also represented “a broad rejection of the Bolsonarista project for Brazil”.Lula supporters celebrate shock election victory – in picturesRead moreShe has been interviewing undecided voters since May and said “the fear voters had, workers had, of losing rights and also of a possible concentration of power in Bolsonaro’s hands was very clear”, which meant that even people who did not like Lula voted for him this time.Bolsonaro had won 56.1m votes in the first round and received 3.7 million more in the runoff. Lula, by contrast, went from 53.9m to 64.2m. The more than 10m-vote increase came both from persuading voters to turn out after historically high abstention in the first round and from convincing voters from other candidates, including Bolsonaro.“Some undecided voters we interviewed said Bolsonaro was a playboy who sided with big business, while at the same time spontaneously saying that, if he won, there would be a dictatorship in which people would lose rights,” said Rocha.Bolsonaro was also embroiled in several controversies recently, including saying he would use the new, even more conservative congress to change the constitution and “re-democratise” Brazil, as well as the two federal police inquiries in which he is under investigation over alleged corruption and money laundering.Many analysts have also pointed to the weight of Lula himself. “If it were another candidate, Bolsonaro would already have won in the first round,” said political scientist Helcimara de Souza Telles.Marco Aurélio de Carvalho, Lula’s campaign manager, answered without hesitation when asked what explained the historic election fightback: “President Lula. We have a great statesman on our team. We have a star player. That’s what absolutely made the difference. I haven’t the slightest doubt about it.”The question already occupying the minds of Brazil’s left is what happens next, given that Lula has said this was his last election.“That is a very big challenge because, in the polling on this, Lula’s dominance is still very strong. There is no one in his party with the same leadership,” said Rocha.Vasconcellos believes Lula’s re-election campaign, “from what we saw on the streets, offered the Brazilian left an opportunity for renewal”.“Lula’s party can learn from what happened and find better ways to connect with young people and urban voters who feel their concerns are not being heard,” he added.The Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions about the election and the future of Brazil from 1500 GMT on Tuesday 27 October as part of ourConversationsseries. title: Brazil runoff as it happened: world leaders congratulate Lula on historic election win as Bolsonaro refuses to concede | Brazil | The Guardian
description: Leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated the far-right senator and was elected president of Brazil for a fourth non-consecutive term
Author: Adam Fulton
Headline: Leftist president Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva defeated the far-right senator and was elected president of Brazil for a fourth non-consecutive term
Content: 05.18 EDTWhat you need to know about the historic Brazilian election voteIt has just gone past 06:15am in Brasília and 09:15am in London, where I am blogging from. Here is a quick recap of the main updates from one of the most significant and bruising elections in Brazilian history:Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, the 80-year-old Brazilian president, has staged a dramaticelection comeback, defeating his far-right opponent,Flávio Bolsonaro, to claim a historic fourth term in power.Lula secured51.79%of the votes compared with Bolsonaro’s48.21%, according to Brazil’s Superior Electoral Court – about4.4mmore votesFlávio Bolsonaro, the eldest son of former PresidentJair Bolsonaro, refused to accept the election result, and has called for it to be annulled.The 45-year-old senator called into question a late-Sunday decision by a Lula-appointed supreme court justice that extended voting by two hours over alleged voter transport irregularities.His refusal to concede defeat has echoes of his father’s reactionafter losing to Lula in 2022. Jair Bolsonaro never accepted his loss and was later sentenced by the supreme court to 27-years in prison for plotting a coup to remain in power.Lula, who highlighted a track record of falling poverty and inequality during his campaign, becomes the first president in Brazilian history to win a fourth term.It is also the first time, since Brazil’s return to democracy in 1988, that a candidate who lost the first round of voting went on to overturn the result and win the presidency. Lula’s new term is set to begin on5 January 2027.The leftist president’s victory is a blow for the US president, who had been hoping Bolsonaro would become the latest in a series of pro-Trump leaders to take power in South America.Numerous world leaders have congratulated Lula for his dramatic election win, but so farDonald Trumphas remained silent.You can read more in this insightful recap from my colleagues,Tom PhillipsandTiago Rogero:Lula wins historic fourth term as Brazilian president in defeat of far-right Flávio BolsonaroRead moreShareUpdated at05.28 EDT

title: Japanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing woman | Japan | The Guardian
description: Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of Okinawa
Author: Ramon Antonio Vargas
Headline: Devin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of Okinawa
Content: Devin Jacob Ballard, a US marine, leaves a police station to be sent to prosecutors over the killing of a Japanese woman in Okinawa, Japan, on 5 October 2026 in this photo taken by Kyodo.Photograph: KYODO/ReutersView image in fullscreenDevin Jacob Ballard, a US marine, leaves a police station to be sent to prosecutors over the killing of a Japanese woman in Okinawa, Japan, on 5 October 2026 in this photo taken by Kyodo.Photograph: KYODO/ReutersJapanJapanese prosecutors charge US marine suspected of robbing and killing womanDevin Jacob Ballard, 20, denies charges that he fatally strangled Anna Yagi, 39, in a hotel on the island of OkinawaRamon Antonio Vargasand agenciesMon 26 Oct 2026 09.41 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 08.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleProsecutors inJapanhave filed formal charges against aUSmarine suspected of murdering and robbing a woman while stationed on the country’s island of Okinawa, according to Japanese media.Devin Jacob Ballard, a 20-year-old lance corporal assigned to Marine Corps Air Station Futenma in Okinawa, is charged with fatally strangling Anna Yagi, 39, at a hotel in the city and stealing from her a backpack containing a wallet, the public broadcasterNHK reported.Ballard had initially beenarrestedin Yagi’s killing on 4 October, about a day after she was found dead in Naha, Okinawa’s capital. Prosecutors indicted him in the case on Sunday, and he has reportedly denied the charges.Japan PM leads outcry after US Marine arrested over alleged killing of woman on OkinawaRead moreNHK and other Japanese media outlets had previously reported that Ballard was arrested after surveillance camera footage from near the scene of Yagi’s killing showed a man entering a room with a woman and later leaving the scene with her belongings.Ballard evidently matched the description of the suspect seen in the footage, was confronted and agreed to accompany investigators voluntarily to a local police station, Japanese media reported.While being questioned by police, Ballard denied having a hand in Yagi’s killing, saying, “I don’t know anything about it,” NHK reported. But during subsequent questioning Ballard was alleged to have “made statements that partially hinted at his involvement”, the broadcaster reported.A statement reported by NHK and reported to Yagi’s family on Sunday expressed a hope that Ballard “will confront what he has done and make amends commensurate with what he has done”.“She lost her life at the young age of 39,” the statement from Yagi’s family added. “She … wanted to live much, much longer.”Yagi’s killing prompted protests in Okinawa and the Japanese capital of Tokyo, with political leaders publicly condemning her killing. It also triggered a curfew and alcohol ban forUS militarymembers stationed in Okinawa, where most of the 54,000 US troops in Japan are based.Crimes committed by US troops in Japan – including rape, assault, hit-and-run and drunk-driving – have long strained relations between the countries, which are close military allies.A Japanese court in June 2025 sentenced US marine Jamel Clayton, then 22, to seven years in prison after he was convicted of choking and sexually assaulting a woman in her 20s.In 2017, a former US marine and civilian military base worker named Kenneth Shinzato was sentenced to life in prison for the rape and murder of a local Okinawa woman.US military forces in Japan that same year banned all personnel from consuming alcohol after an intoxicated US marine crashed his vehicle into a mini-truck, killing a local driver, age 61.The Yomiuri Shimbun newspaper reported that about 6,000 US military personnel have been arrested since the US returned Okinawa to Japan after the second world war in 1972.There were 80 such arrests in 2024, constituting a 20-year high.After Ballard’s arrest, Shinjiro Koizumi, Japan’s defense minister, said: “Incidents and accidents involving US military personnel cause great anxiety among the local community and must not be allowed to happen.”Reuters and Agence France-Presse contributed reportingExplore more on these topicsJapanUS militaryUS crimeAsia PacificnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adults | China | The Guardian
description: Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’
Author: Yu-chen Li
Headline: Faced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’
Content: A social media post advocating raising a brick, in which it said among other things: ‘Those seemingly meaningless little things actually make you realise that, besides spending money, you can have a lively, ever-changing corner for free.’Photograph: xiaohongshu.comView image in fullscreenA social media post advocating raising a brick, in which it said among other things: ‘Those seemingly meaningless little things actually make you realise that, besides spending money, you can have a lively, ever-changing corner for free.’Photograph: xiaohongshu.comChina‘Zero-energy companionship’: bizarre hobby takes seed among China’s stressed young adultsFaced with a stagnant jobs market, many are spurning children or pets in favour of ‘raising bricks’Amy Hawkinsin BeijingMon 26 Oct 2026 05.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleYoung adults inChinalooking for a cheaper, low-maintenance alternative to having children or pets have found an answer: raising bricks.Bricks may not be as cuddly as cats or as life-affirming as human offspring, but they also cost next to nothing. “No cats, no dating, I started raising a brick,” wrote one brick parent on social media.Raising “brick babies” is easier than caring for house plants, involving spraying them with water a few times a day then waiting for moss spores already present in the atmosphere to attach themselves and grow. One Chinese media article described the bricks as being “practically immortal”. “If you forget to water them, the moss goes dormant. If you remember to water them again, the greenery returns.”A hashtag related to the trend has attracted more than 5m views on the Chinese social media platform Weibo.View image in fullscreenSocial media users document their brick’s changes over a year, with hashtags including #healing and #stress relief.Photograph: @South/xiaohongshu.comChinese commentators have linked the trend to young people looking for low-effort routes to finding meaning in life. One brick “parent” told Chinese media the hobby created “a sense of accomplishment no less than completing a long-term project”.One user on Xiaohongshu, an Instagram-like platform, also known as Rednote, posted a picture of their rusty-coloured brick, saying “no output required, no KPIs to hit, no need to beg it to bloom [and] no comparing its growth with others”.Another user wrote: “My friends asked if I’d lost my mind. I said no, I’m just starting to raise a brick.“A brick gives me a sense of certainty that feels way more grounded than a lot of relationships. Psychologists call this ‘zero-energy emotional companionship.’ It fulfils your need for company without demanding any obligation to give love in return.”Young people in China are increasingly shunning the traditional expectations of society, such as having children and working long hours in strenuous jobs, assuming they can find one in the first place. Nearly one in five 16- to 24-year-olds, excluding students,are unemployed, according to official statistics. Some estimates put the unemployment rate much higher.China’sbirthrateis in decline and fell to a record low last year. Faced with a sluggish job market after years of intensely competitive studying, many young people are choosing to shun the rat race and opt instead for “lying flat” – pursuing a low-effort, low-stress lifestyle; one well-suited to raising bricks.The trend has become so popular that Chinese media have started to warn about the health risks.Cultivating moss could lead to the spread of mould, with some “brick parents” reportedly complaining of itchy eyes and runny noses. Xuedong Li, a retired professor of moss from Beijing’s Capital Normal University, urged people to keep their bricks in an enclosed environment. “It is best to wear disposable gloves and a mask during handling to reduce spore inhalation and skin contact,” Li told Chinese media.Additional research by Yu-chen LiExplore more on these topicsChinaAsia PacificPopulationYoung peopleHobbiesnewsShareReuse this content

title: Xi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leaders | China | The Guardian
description: The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty
Author: Amy Hawkins
Headline: The fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyalty
Content: People say an oath of loyalty in front of a flag of the Communist party of China on the 105th anniversary of its founding in Beijing in July.Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPeople say an oath of loyalty in front of a flag of the Communist party of China on the 105th anniversary of its founding in Beijing in July.Photograph: Kevin Frayer/Getty ImagesChinaXi Jinping’s corruption crackdown in the spotlight as China prepares for meeting of top leadersThe fifth plenum comes against a backdrop of years of purges that have had some analysts wondering if the issue is corruption or a lack of loyaltyAmy Hawkinsin BeijingSun 25 Oct 2026 20.58 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhenXi Jinpingcame to power in 2012, he pledged to stamp out corruption all through the ranks of the Communist party. More than a decade later, the pace of investigations has not slowed. Last year, China’s disciplinary authorities opened investigations into more than 1 million people, including more than 100 officials at or above ministerial or provincial level.As Chinese Communist party (CCP) officials kick off an important meeting this week, discipline – and party loyalty–is high on the agenda. For those who try to read the tea leaves of elite Chinese politics, concern about the apparent lack of discipline is dominating CCP discussions.The “fifth plenum” began on Monday and is set to focus on “major issues on advancing the party’s full and rigorous self-governance”, according to a Chinese state media. In party-speak, “governance” is a byword for discipline, loyalty andanti-corruption.Taiwan charges five men over plot to run over comedian for his Xi Jinping jokesRead moreAs Xi continues to crack down on corruption, the fact that investigations nearly always result in a conviction begs the question over whether targets are truly guilty of corruption, or are they just political rivals to the people in charge.Kerry Brown, director of the LauChinaInstitute at King’s College London, explained that in Xi’s worldview, which is obsessed with discipline and loyalty, there may not be much difference between the two. “If you’re corrupt, you’re not politically loyal. If you’re politically loyal, you’re not corrupt,” Brown said.He added that in the CCP system, “corruption is not just material things”, but also “spiritual corruption”, which includes political disloyalty.Some analysts argue that the reason that the anti-graft drive is so enduring is because corruption is a feature rather than a bug of an authoritarian, top-down political system with a sprawling bureaucracy that governs 1.4 billion people.Neil Thomas, a senior fellow at the Asia Society thinktank, said: “Xi has made the party less corrupt and strengthened his control, but he knows that tougher punishment cannot fully resolve the problem of officials putting their own interests ahead of the party’s.View image in fullscreenXi Jinping at a gathering at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing last week.Photograph: Xinhua/Shutterstock“Xi’s answer is to keep tightening discipline, making anti-corruption a permanent method of governing with no obvious point at which he can declare the job done,” Thomas said.The job may be never ending, but the plenum is an opportunity to refocus the party’s energy on discipline. The fifth plenum is the fifth of seven gatherings that normally happen in every five-year cycle between CCP congresses. The plenums bring together more than 300 members of the CCP’s Central Committee, the most senior officials in the party hierarchy.The meeting is particularly significant because it is likely to be the last substantive meeting before next year’s 21st Party Congress, where a new Central Committee will be chosen, and where Xi is expected to be anointed for a fourth term as the head of the CCP.Eliminating anyone who poses a risk to his authority or to the party’s credibility is a key priority for Xi. And potential threats are everywhere. Nearly 15 years after Xi took office, according to CCP proclamations and a host of recent investigations, the problem is still not stamped out. “It is a deeply ingrained part of [Xi’s] worldview,” said Brown. “Everyone else is corrupt”.In the past, Xi has warned that the party could “lose its ruling status and inevitably be eliminated by history” if it could not get its house in order. “This is by no means an exaggeration,” he said.The current focus on party governance comes amid a host of high-profile investigations against senior party and military leaders.In January,Zhang Youxia, China’s top general and a man second only to Xi in the military hierarchy, was placed under investigation; he was expelled from party last month, having already been removed from the military’s top ruling body, the Central Military Commission (CMC)Ahost of other purgesmeans that the CMC, which normally has seven members, has been reduced to just two: Xi and Zhang Shengmin, the CMC’s head of discipline.Other recent scalps include Ma Xingrui, the former party secretary for Xinjiang, and Huang Qifan, the former mayor of Chongqing.Huang had long been known as the ultimate survivor in Chinese politics because of his connections to the scandals in the early 2010s in which Xi’s political rival, Bo Xilai, the former Party boss for Chongqing, was embroiled in the death of the British businessman Neil Heywood. Bo was ultimately convicted of bribery and embezzlement, for which he is serving a life sentence, but Huang survived. No longer.Some China analysts have asked whether the recent purges, which have reached the highest echelons of the Party and military ranks, indicate instability in the regime. But Xi likely sees it differently. Corruption investigations demonstrate who is in charge. Plus, Brown added, they are “the most easy and natural tool by which to enforce unity and discipline”.Explore more on these topicsChinaAsia PacificXi JinpingnewsShareReuse this content

title: The chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costs | Australian economy | The Guardian
description: Australia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woes
Author: Patrick Commins
Headline: Australia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woes
Content: Protesters attend an authorised demonstration organised by labour unions in Paris against the cost of living and rising fuel prices on Saturday.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersView image in fullscreenProtesters attend an authorised demonstration organised by labour unions in Paris against the cost of living and rising fuel prices on Saturday.Photograph: Hannah McKay/ReutersAustralian economyAnalysisThe chaos in France is a ‘warning signal’ for Australia’s public spending and rising costsPatrick ComminsAustralia’s public debt may be well below that of France but there are lessons to be taken from its economic woesGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastMon 26 Oct 2026 18.45 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTShareThe explosion of discontent that led to major protests and violence inFranceand across Europe is a “warning signal” that Australia could follow the same path without an “honest conversation” about the budget, economists say.Hundreds of thousands marchedin cities across France on Saturday to protest against school underfunding, as complaints of insufficient teacher numbers and dilapidated infrastructure mingled with broader discontent about cost-of-living pressures.Here, and across the developed world, people are struggling to cope with the affordability crisis as households grapple with high and rising prices.The scale of the challenges in individual countries may be of a different order of magnitude but the grievances are common.Luke Hartigan, a senior economics lecturer at the University of Sydney, said it was clear there was no single factor behind the discontent in France but soaring energy costs were having a major impact.Sign up for Guardian Australia’s Politics, really newsletter hereFuel prices are up 36% this year in France, or three times the increase in Australia. The US-Israel war on Iran has sent European gas prices soaring as the northern hemisphere approaches winter.Jim Chalmers faces a world of hard choices where the solution to one problem makes the other worseRead moreMore fundamental, however, is that France’s finances are buckling under its generous welfare state.France’s high public debt, stagnant economy and universal social security benefits have created a “binary” situation, Hartigan said, where citizens’ demands for better services and cost-of-living help are clashing with the country’s increasingly dire fiscal position.France has not balanced its budget since 1974. Meanwhile, total public debt as a share of the economy has swelled to nearly 120%, according to the International Monetary Fund.Chart showing total government debt as a share of GDPAustralia’s total government debt pile looks benign in comparison at 53%. But a decade ago our debt was 40% of GDP, and a decade before that it was just under 10%.Hartigan said France’s lacklustre economy had compounded its fiscal problems, underlining how Australia needed to work hard to boost productivity.double quotation markThe federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no moneyBob Breunig“If you think about trajectories, they [France’s challenges] give us an idea of where we could potentially be if we continue down this path,” Hartigan said.“It’s a warning signal.”Bob Breunig, the director of the ANU’s Tax and Transfer Policy Institute, said there was a growing gap between what voters believed the government should be able to do, and what politicians were able to deliver.“One thing that is happening everywhere is this narrative that the government should be able to solve all your problems, and that narrative has probably been pushed further in Europe than it has here. It’s failing in both places but it’s pointier there than here,” Breunig said.Chart showing total government spending as a share of GDPThe evidence of this growing demand for government intervention is that French public spending now accounts for 58% of the economy, the IMF data shows.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionIn contrast, Australia’s total public spending is equivalent to 40% of our national output – the highest in data stretching back to 1990, outside the pandemic, and at similar levels to the United States and the United Kingdom.“All these protesters are asking the government to help them out, but the government has maxxed out the credit card,” Breunig said, who said France’s debt was “reaching levels that are unmanageable”.1:44Police and protesters exchange teargas and fireworks in demonstrations across France – video“The federal government here can still borrow and has a lot of flexibility, and the French just have no money.”President Emmanuel Macron’s decade in power has been marked with failed attempts to rein in spending.“There’s a real sense that people don’t know what to do,” Breunig said.The bond marketreflects growing alarm with France’s fiscal trajectory.France typically has to pay a higher interest rate on its 10-year debt than fiscally prudent Germany, and the gap between the two rates is a measure of financial markets’ confidence in France’s fiscal position.That gap is now at its widest since the European debt crisis in 2011.Amid structural pressures on the budget from an ageing population, the NDIS, higher interest rates, and the push for greater spending on national defence, Breunig agreed there were lessons for Australia in not allowing the country to drift too far and for too long.“We need an honest public conversation about what the government can be expected to do and what it can’t, and then a conversation about how much that would cost and whether we are willing to pay for that.”While the opposition has attacked what it sees as the deadening effect of high government spending on economic dynamism, Breunig said he was broadly “agnostic” whether repairing the budget involved lower spending or higher taxes.“At the end of the day, making these decisions is exactly what democracy is for.”Patrick Commins is Guardian Australia’s economics editorExplore more on these topicsAustralian economyAustralian politicsFranceanalysisShareReuse this content

title: Man found dead in Queensland floods named as former councillor and One Nation candidate | Queensland | The Guardian
description: Fraser coast mayor described Hansen as ‘always ready to help others, contribute to the community and advocate strongly’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Fraser coast mayor described Hansen as ‘always ready to help others, contribute to the community and advocate strongly’
Content: A man’s body found in flood waters following an unusual weather system has been identified as a former councillor, One Nation candidate and dairy farmer, James Hansen.Photograph: Fraser Coast Regional CouncilView image in fullscreenA man’s body found in flood waters following an unusual weather system has been identified as a former councillor, One Nation candidate and dairy farmer, James Hansen.Photograph: Fraser Coast Regional CouncilQueenslandMan found dead in Queensland floods named as former councillor and One Nation candidateFraser coast mayor described James Hansen as ‘always ready to help others, contribute to the community and advocate strongly’Get ourbreaking news email,free appordaily news podcastAustralian Associated PressMon 26 Oct 2026 16.55 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 02.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJames Hansen, a formerQueenslandcouncillor, has been identified as the man who died in flooding on the state’s Fraser Coast.Hansen, 57, was a dairy farmer and fourth-generation resident of the area. He served as a councillor for the Fraser Coast regional council between 2012 and 2024.George Seymour, the mayor of Fraser Coast, paid tribute to Hansen, saying he was someone “who was always ready to help others, contribute to the community and advocate strongly”.“His passing is a great loss to our community and my thoughts are with his family and friends as they come to terms with this sudden tragedy,” Seymour wrote on Facebook. “He was one of a kind and will be missed.”Hansen, 57, also served as a councillor for the Woocoo Shire council from 2004 to 2008. He ran for One Nation in 2017, challenging a sitting MP, but finished second.Paul Truscott, the division 3 councillor for the Fraser Coast regional council, said he was shocked and saddened by Hansen’s death.“James and I worked together on Council for eight years,” Truscott wrote in a statement. “He was pretty old fashioned at times, a man who always spoke his mind, someone who you knew where you stood with, and a bloke who would give you a hand if you needed it.“Through plenty of challenging times on Council, it was always good to be able to share a laugh with James along the way and I’ll always remember him as someone who stood up for what he believed in, and stood up for the farmers and the ‘little guy’”.Emergency services were called to a creek at Boompa on Queensland’s Fraser Coast shortly after 11am on Monday after reports a man had been found unresponsive. The man was declared dead after being found in Smothering Creek on Boompa Road, Queensland police said.An investigation into his death has begun, with police to prepare a report for the coroner.Further south, six campers were rescued after becoming stranded by flood waters at a public campground in Leyburn in Queensland’s Southern Downs.Queensland Fire and Rescue Swiftwater crews responded to the call for help at 7.45am on Monday. They rescued three men aged 71, 47 and 26 and two women aged 68 and 26 without incident at about 11.15am.Sign up for the Breaking News Australia emailTorrential downpours across Queensland between Thursday and Monday left many rivers and roads flooded across the state’s south and east.Flash flooding hit Laidley Creek and Glenore Grove in the Lockyer Valley, west of Brisbane, closing some roads, Queensland police said on Monday.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When neededSign up toBreaking News AustraliaGet the most important news as it breaksEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe highest recorded four-day totals were spread across the state, with Blackdown Tableland, near Rockhampton, recording 439.4mm to early Monday.Lower Springbrook, near the Gold Coast, recorded 325.2mm, while Nambour, near the Sunshine Coast, copped 314.2mm.Brooweena, inland of K’gari, received 299.6mm.Meteorologist Angus Hines said the system behind the downpours was unusual.“The widespread rain bands with heaps of cloud cover, much cooler temperatures, and then the storms in that situation are really driven by what’s going on in the higher parts of the atmosphere,” he said.The Bureau of Meteorology said Queensland’s weather was set to return to more typical spring conditions as the week continued.Hot and humid days are expected to give way to more subdued afternoon showers and storms.Explore more on these topicsQueenslandAustralia weathernewsShareReuse this content

title: iPhone Duo owners report cracks in Apple’s first foldable handset | iPhone | The Guardian
description: Company says small number of devices affected by display glitch after posts appear on Reddit and social media
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Company says small number of devices affected by display glitch after posts appear on Reddit and social media
Content: A broken iPhone Duo. Apple confirmed some devices had been affected by a display glitch.Photograph: Surya MangiView image in fullscreenA broken iPhone Duo. Apple confirmed some devices had been affected by a display glitch.Photograph: Surya MangiiPhoneiPhone Duo owners report cracks in Apple’s first foldable handsetCompany says small number of devices affected by display glitch after posts appear on Reddit and social mediaDan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 26 Oct 2026 15.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 18.07 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleOwners of the new foldableiPhoneare reporting cracks in the device’s screen, as Apple confirmed an issue with a “small number” of units.Reports of cracks have emerged on Reddit and social media platforms since the handset went on general sale globally on Friday. Experts said there had been too few examples to determine whether there was a more serious problem with Apple’s first foldable device, which retails from $1,999 (£1,499).Apple confirmed some devices had been affected by a display glitch.“We are aware of an issue impacting the inner display on a small number of iPhone Duo units. If users experience issues with their iPhone Duo display, they should contact AppleCare for a replacement,” it said.One user in Australia reported that their Duo had cracked within six hours of taking ownership of it andposted their experience on Reddit.“I was showing it to a friend, and as I opened it, I felt something around the internal hinge, underneath the screen,” they wrote alongside an image of the phone showing an apparent display malfunction where a white strip of light ran along one half of the screen.“As I continued opening it, I heard an audible crack, and the screen broke right along the hinge.”They said their local Apple store had replaced the phone immediately. The Guardian has been unable to verify the user’s claims. Another user in Australia posted that they had heard “almost a cracking noise” on their handset, which resulted in a similar screen malfunction.View image in fullscreenIPhone Duo handsets on display at an Apple store in London.Photograph: Kin Cheung/APA report by the Bloomberg news service also highlighted similar issues among users in the US and India.Apple believes the affected units are showing defects quickly after use. It said the response from early users had been “incredibly positive”.The company said demand had been “nothing short of extraordinary” for the iPhone Duo, its most high-profile product launch under the company’s new chief executive, John Ternus, whotook over from Tim Cook in September.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe device has sold out and the next round of shipments is not expected until January, according to a report in the Economic Daily, a publication based in Taiwan, the home country of Foxconn, Apple’s main device manufacturer.Francisco Jeronimo, the vice-president of data and analytics at IDC, a tech research company, said it was too early to tell whether the screen issue was significant. “This is quite common when a new product comes to market,” he said.Citingsimilar problems at Samsung in 2019, he said: “What matters now is how the company responds … Samsung experienced problems with the original Galaxy Fold in 2019, but it also showed that a fast and transparent response can contain the damage to a category.“Apple said that any customer with problems should ask for a replacement, which is the right first step.”Ben Wood, the chief analyst at the research firm CCS, said he was taking a very cautious view of the Duo screen problem and that there was as yet no evidence of a more widespread issue with the device.Explore more on these topicsiPhoneAppleComputingMobile phonesSmartphonesTelecommunications industryConsumer affairsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Endangered turtles and ‘exceptional’ coral at risk from Woodside’s gas drilling in WA, watchdog says | Woodside | The Guardian
description: Exclusive: EPA flags oil spill risk from proposed gasfield and threat to pygmy blue whales
Author: Peter Milne
Headline: Exclusive: EPA flags oil spill risk from proposed gasfield and threat to pygmy blue whales
Content: Scientists warn Woodside’s plan to develop the Browse basin off WA could damage the Scott Reef ecosystem and endangered green turtles.Photograph: Wendy  Mitchell/GreenpeaceView image in fullscreenScientists warn Woodside’s plan to develop the Browse basin off WA could damage the Scott Reef ecosystem and endangered green turtles.Photograph: Wendy  Mitchell/GreenpeaceWoodsideEndangered turtles and ‘exceptional’ coral at risk from Woodside’s gas drilling in WA, watchdog saysExclusive: EPA flags oil spill risk from proposed gasfield and threat to pygmy blue whalesFollow ourAustralian politics live blogfor latest updatesSign up for climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s free Clear Air newsletter herePeter MilneMon 26 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 21.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWoodside Energy’s plan to drill for gas off Western Australia’s north-west coast could significantly damage “exceptional” coral reefs and it may be impossible to reduce the risk of an oil spill to an acceptable level, according to advice from the state’s independent environmental watchdog.A draft letter from WA’s Environmental Protection Authority written in 2023, seen by the Guardian, sharply criticised Woodside’s proposal to develop the Browse gasfield, saying its plans to protect endangered turtles and blue whales near Scott Reef would be ineffective.Woodside, Australia’s largest fossil fuel company, is hoping to win approval next year to develop the Browse basin, about 300km off the Kimberley coast. Scientists have warned it could damage the Scott Reef ecosystem, which is home to more than 1,500 species, many unique to the area.Almost every shallow-water coral reef on the planet faces ecosystem collapse by 2075, UN advisors sayRead moreEPA staff presented the draft letter to the authority’s board for approval in December 2023. In February 2024, two months after it was discussed, the EPA sent a letter to Woodside saying its preliminary view was toreject development of the vast gas reserve.It was a significant setback to Woodside’s plan to drill more than 50 wells and pipe the gas 1,000km to its ageing North West Shelf gas export plant adjacent to the world heritage-listedMurujuga rock art.Download original documentThe company won approval last year to run the North West Shelf until 2070. But it needs the gas from the Browse basin – Australia’s largest undeveloped source of gas – to feed it. If the processing plant was to operate until 2070 it could lead to about88m tonnes of carbon dioxide being released into the atmosphere each yearafter the gas was burned.View image in fullscreenSeringapatam Reef, part of the Scott Reef system, off the coast of Western Australia. The area is home to more than 1,500 species. It sits over the underwater Browse gas basin.Photograph: GreenpeaceThe concerns presented in the letter to the EPA board show the pressure on authorities to recommend against the gasfield development being approved. The development is being assessed by both the state and commonwealth EPAs. Ultimate decision-making power lies with environment ministers.Sign up to get climate and environment editor Adam Morton’s Clear Air column as a free newsletterThe letter shows the EPA board was advised by its staff that there was a threat of serious or irreversible harm to turtles and whales and more generally due to oil spills. The threats were considered serious enough that the staff said the precautionary principle should be invoked. It meant the EPA should assume the worst possible outcomes could occur.Download original documentIn response to this near rejection of its proposal, Woodside added explosive-driven shear rams to its drilling plans, a step that could allow it to seal a leaking well in seconds. The company said this would reduce the “longest credible duration” of a “highly unlikely” well blowout, and potential oil spill, to about 12 hours.Not all companies have faith in shear ram technology. In 2024, fellow WA gas exporter Chevron rejected “pyrotechnic shearing” technology for its own wells, describing it as unproven and impossible to test in the field.A Woodside spokesperson said if the shear rams failed it would deploy a capping stack to stop the oil flow within 16 days.But the EPA was advised in 2023 that if a well leaked for 13 days it was possible there could be “irreversible consequences” to Scott Reef.View image in fullscreenGreenpeace activists protesting Woodside’s proposed Browse project on Scott Reef deploy a  banner at the company’s Scarborough gas platform off the coast of Western Australia on 17 October.Photograph: Greenpeace/ReutersThe draft letter said Sandy Islet, a part of Scott Reef considered critical to the survival of endangered green turtles, would be threatened if the seabed subsided after Woodside extracted gas from beneath it. It said a proposal to top up the sand on the islet, where about 1,000 turtles breed each year, was a “high-risk” measure and its success was “likely to be limited”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |When he publishesSign up toClear Air AustraliaAdam Morton brings you incisive analysis about the politics and impact of the climate crisisEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionWoodside said it would address this by changing its plans so that no wells would be drilled within 20km of Sandy Islet. It also said the flaring of gas, which produces bright light that can confuse turtle’s navigation, would be restricted.The EPA board was also told noise, traffic and vessel strikes would have a significant impact on pygmy blue whales migrating between Timor and southern Australia. Scott Reef is the only known whale feeding ground on the migration route, according to the draft letter.Woodside’s spokesperson said the company understood whales did feed at Scott Reef, but that this was opportunistic and the area was not as important as the ocean off Perth and other areas further south. Woodside agreed that Scott Reef and Sandy Islet had exceptional environmental value and it was important to protect them for future generations.‘Manifestation of creative genius’: Murujuga rock art in Western Australia placed on Unesco world heritage listRead moreGlenn Walker, Greenpeace head of nature, said Woodside’s plans to address the concerns raised by the EPA did not go far enough and relied on “fanciful and unproven technology” to prevent a catastrophic oil spill.“It would be a major backflip for both the WA EPA and the national EPA to now recommend approving this project,” he said. “It is now critical that these regulators maintain their independence from corporate and political influence and reject this destructive project.”Greenpeace last week nominated Scott Reef for national heritage listing based on its ecological and scientific values.Just two of the current nine-strong WA EPA board were in place when the watchdog told Woodside it was set to reject Browse.One of those – the current chair, Darren Walsh – said in a statement the assessment had been lengthy because it was a complex project in a sensitive area. He said a final state report and recommendations on the proposal would be provided to the WA environment minister, Matthew Swinbourn, when it was complete.
