There would then be a three-week public appeal period before a decision was made.A spokesperson for the national EPA said the development was being assessed under the national Environment Protection and BiodiversityConservationAct, and the “decision clock” had been paused while the agency waited on “further technical advice”.Issues that have to be considered under national law include the potential impact on pygmy blue whales, green turtles, the marine environment in commonwealth waters and Murujuga rock art near the gas processing facility.Explore more on these topicsWoodsideGas (Environment)Western AustraliaEnergy (Australia news)BusinessGas (Business)Energy (Environment)newsShareReuse this content

title: Protest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schools | France | The Guardian
description: Activists say struggle must go on until their ‘maximum’ demands are met over teacher shortages and building repairs
Author: Angelique Chrisafis
Headline: Activists say struggle must go on until their ‘maximum’ demands are met over teacher shortages and building repairs
Content: Representatives of Les Lycéens speak to reporters on Monday after meeting the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, in Paris.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenRepresentatives of Les Lycéens speak to reporters on Monday after meeting the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, in Paris.Photograph: AFP/Getty ImagesFranceProtest leaders urge French pupils to keep barricading their schoolsActivists say struggle must go on until their ‘maximum’ demands are met over teacher shortages and building repairsAngelique Chrisafisin ParisMon 26 Oct 2026 16.17 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFrench children should continue to barricade their schools and take part in street protests, a student union said on Monday after the government announced a package of education measures to try to stem the crisis.“Today we’re at the negotiating table, we’re able to negotiate with the government,” Pierre Sourzat of Les Lycéens toldFranceInfo television. “We’re in a power struggle and we still need to call for continued mobilisation to meet a maximum of our demands.”‘This is state violence’: Paris students rage at politicians and heavy-handed policingRead moreThe government told high school student representatives it would cap some class sizes and review the university application system. But Sourzat said: “We want measures, not half measures.”More than five weeks after the start of high school blockades in September, the government made the proposals to address the demands of what has becomethe biggest youth protest movementin years. It has been joined by trade unions and cost-of-living protesters in regular mass street demonstrations on Saturdays.High school pupils had demandedan end to teacher and staff shortagesand for repairs to decrepit school buildings that had collapsing ceilings, mould, broken toilets, a lack of chairs and windows that did not shut.The education minister, Édouard Geffray, said some schools were so dilapidated they were “not fit” for teaching. He announced a government loan of €4bn to regional authorities to begin repairs.View image in fullscreenEmmanuel Macron, kneeling centre, meets police officers in Marseille. He told them the authorities had ‘to hold the line’.Photograph: Aurélien Morissard/EPAResponding to complaints of overcrowded classes, Geffray said class sizes for 15-year-olds in the first year of high school would be capped at 28 in the 50% of schools in the lowest-income areas, increasing to all high schools next year. He said more teaching posts would be created and there would be a review of the French baccalaureate system.The university application platform, Parcoursup, which has been described as opaque and unfair, will be changed in 2027 and replaced by a new system in 2028, according to the government. Parliament will hold a debate on the issue on Wednesday.The higher education minister, Philippe Baptiste, said 15,000 extra student places would be created in higher education, focusing on vocational courses.Louis Letoublon, who attended a meeting with the prime minister, Sébastien Lecornu, on behalf of Les Lycéens, said: “Bravo to the high school students who have demonstrated. We’ve got something: the government is afraid and knows it must do something and listen to us. “Not all our demands were ⁠met. We’ll go on for as long as it takes.”Baptiste said the government’s door was “open” for more discussions.Several children have been maimed or seriously injured in the protests, allegedly by police explosive weapons. Hundreds of children have been arrested and held in police custody.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe authorities have increased security measures and placed restrictions on demonstrations after France saw itsworst day of violence in yearson 17 October, with looting, fires and vandalism of state buildings. Curfews have been put in place in certain cities, alongside protest bans. Protest routes were pushed to the outskirts of cities on Saturday when demonstrations passed off largely peacefully.The interior minister, Laurent Nuñez, said there had been a new phenomenon in cities such as Nice and Montpellier at the weekend with ultra-right groups arriving in “organised formations” and targeting protesters. Eleven suspects are to face charges.In a visit to Marseille on Monday,Emmanuel Macronsaid nationwide street protests were likely continue, and that the next day of street demonstrations on 31 October would also be a “day of risk”.The French president said the looting and vandalism seen on 17 October should never happen again. Speaking to members of the police, he said it was “not normal” for the country to be in “such a state of turmoil” six months before a presidential election.Macron steps down next spring and the far-right leaderMarine Le Penis leading the polls.Macron said: “We will continue to hold the line. If we all do our jobs well, this movement will subside – because we will address legitimate expectations, and because order will be maintained. But nothing is a foregone conclusion.”Authorities have admitted to security and intelligence failures that paved the way for the clashes on 17 October.Explore more on these topicsFranceProtestEmmanuel MacronEuropeYoung peopleSchoolsTeacher shortagesnewsShareReuse this content

title: No 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movement | Brexit | The Guardian
description: Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend
Author: Aletha Adu
Headline: Clarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekend
Content: Andy Burnham had indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about a closer relationship with the EU.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/Pool AFP/APView image in fullscreenAndy Burnham had indicated that staying out of free movement would no longer be a red line in discussions about a closer relationship with the EU.Photograph: Carlos Jasso/Pool AFP/APBrexitNo 10 clarifies Andy Burnham’s stance on freedom of movementClarification comes after PM fuelled speculation about EU-UK relationship in series of interviews at weekendAletha AduPolitical correspondentMon 26 Oct 2026 14.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleDowning Street has been forced to clarify Andy Burnham’s stance on whether the UK would return to having freedom of movement with the EU after the prime minister said an “honest discussion” was needed on the issue.Burnham fuelled speculation about a return to freedom of movement in an interview at the weekend, prompting questions about how close the UK could become to Brussels.Confusion deepened after further interviews were interpreted as leaving the door open to an eventual return to freedom of movement and another referendum on the issue.It forced a Downing Street spokesperson to say the prime minister was not proposing a return to freedom of movement, or any particular option.“He is saying that it’s time for us to discuss what kind of long-term relationship withEuropeis best for Britain and he is referring to the types of areas that that agreement and long-term future could cover,” she said.“He is crucially not leaning either way, and that will be for the British public to decide. And his focus for now is on next month’s summit and the practical arrangements that we hope to make there, which will add billions to the economy.”She said the government was not yet at the stage of confirming whether the public would decide on proposals for the UK to move closer to the EU.Asked whether Burnham accepted that returning to freedom of movement would mean Britain lost control over legal migration, the spokesperson said: “He’s not setting out a concrete position either way. What he’s saying is that he wants to have a conversation with the British public about what our long-term future with theEuropean Unionlooks like.”In an interview with the Sunday Times, Burnham indicated thatstaying out of free movement would no longer be a red linein discussions about how the UK can move closer to the EU.On Monday, Burnham ruled out the possibility of rejoining the EU within this parliament and indicated he could fight the next general election on a promise to take the UK back into the EU. He said: “I’m not going to move away from the red lines that were in theLabourmanifesto.”Hours later, Burnham told journalists “no” when asked if he would allow the UK to join the EU freedom of movement scheme without a referendum.When asked whether he wanted Britain to rejoin the EU, he said: “I’ve said I’m going to be honest and say, in my lifetime I would like to see that happen, but I am not going to move ahead of the public. I am not going to dictate in terms of my own opinions here, you have to make sure that the British public are the bosses.”Challenged on how his constituents in Makerfield would feel about his discussions about the EU, given 65% of them voted to leave, Burnham added: “I said we wouldn’t rerun the referendum and that’s not what I’m doing.“The British public, the people of Makerfield, will be the bosses here. They will decide what happens in relation toBrexit.”Burnham even ruled out an early general election on a manifesto change on this issue. He told GMB: “There is no election coming anytime soon. People may as well put that out of their mind.” However, he left the door open to a future fight on a promise to fully rejoin the EU.Burnham will be in Brussels for the UK-EU summit on 20 November, as he seeks to strike a better deal with the bloc. He believes the Brexit deal has “weakened our economy [and] weakened our control of immigration” and is not good enough for the country.Explore more on these topicsBrexitAndy BurnhamLabourEuropean UnionEuropeForeign policynewsShareReuse this content

title: Serbia’s Student List preparing for talks on forming government despite no clear leader | World news | The Guardian
description: Non-hierarchical movement is seeking to ‘rebuild society’ in Balkan country after years of authoritarian rule
Author: Jon Henley
Headline: Non-hierarchical movement is seeking to ‘rebuild society’ in Balkan country after years of authoritarian rule
Content: Young Serbians celebrate outside the national assembly building in Belgrade on Monday after Student List won the country’s parliamentary elections.Photograph: Armin Durgut/APView image in fullscreenYoung Serbians celebrate outside the national assembly building in Belgrade on Monday after Student List won the country’s parliamentary elections.Photograph: Armin Durgut/APWorld newsSerbia’s Student List preparing for talks on forming government despite no clear leaderNon-hierarchical movement is seeking to ‘rebuild society’ in Balkan country after years of authoritarian ruleJon Henleyand Ana Milosavljevic in BelgradeMon 26 Oct 2026 13.12 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.46 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleSerbia’s triumphant but untested Student List movement is preparing to start talks on forming a government capable of reversing 14 years of increasingly authoritarian nationalist rule, aftera seismic weekend election win.Supporters of the movement, which has no experience of government, took to the streets in the west Balkan country on Monday after the strongman former president, Aleksandar Vučić, was defeated in a historic landslide.Vučić conceded defeat late on Sunday, bringing his domination of Serbian politics to an abrupt end and capping two years of anti-government protests triggered by the collapse of a canopy at the Novi Sad railway station that killed 16 people.Cheers, fireworks and flags after Vučić concedes defeat in Serbian election – in picturesRead moreWith 100% of ballot samples counted, projected results from the Centre for Free Elections and Democracy in Belgrade showed the Student List on 53% of the vote, giving it 141 MPs in the 250-seat parliament, while Vučić’s Serbian Progressive party (SNS) won 39%, giving it 103. The remaining seats went to national minority party lists.As yet, there are few clues as to how the winning movement, built around collective decision-making, will actually govern. Its candidates included academics, actors and farmers as well as students, but it is deliberately leaderless with no hierarchy, so it is unclear who it will appoint as the prime minister and cabinet.Prominent Student List figures include: ​Ilija Srdanović, a cardiologist who headed the candidate list; Dejan Šoškić, a former central bank governor; and Radomir Saičić, a chemistry professor at Belgrade ​University who spoke on behalf ‌of the List after its ​victory.Much like Péter Magyar’s Tisza party, which ended Viktor Orbán’s 16 years of illiberal government in Hungary this spring, the List faces public institutions staffed with civil servants loyal to the outgoing regime, complicating the task of institutional overhaul.“Everyone in the student movement, and every candidate on the list, has a complete and very clear understanding of the weight of the responsibility before us,” said Ana Mirković, a university educationist, psychologist and Student List candidate.0:42Drone footage shows crowds in Belgrade celebrating defeat of Aleksandar Vučić – video“We do not see the election result as gaining power and privileges, but as taking on a historic debt to our own people and to our own children.”Mirković told the Guardian the movement’s first priority was “the social and psychological detoxification” of the country.Vučić’s 14-year rule has been described as a “textbook regime” of autocracy, with his party extending control over the media, judiciary and other state institutions and elections marred by registration irregularities, media bias and voter bribes.The students’ platform centres on a pledge to fight corruption and restore the rule of law, including creating an independent police unit accountable to prosecutors, not the interior ministry, and a purge of police officers linked to organised crime.View image in fullscreenStudent List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/APIt also aims to ban appointments of party loyalists to state-owned companies and to promote financial accountability and public scrutiny – by new independent bodies – of all major state infrastructure contracts ⁠to curb the misuse of public funds.Mirković said the new government would dismantle a “system of intimidation” that encouraged “fear and polarisation”, by “urgently opening up” the media, putting an end to pressure on public-sector workers and “stopping institutional violence”.She added that the aim was to “rebuild society from the ground up: full disclosure of all contracts and financial flows; depoliticising and strengthening the judiciary; renewing the education and healthcare systems”, and that state capture should “never again” be possible.The Student List deliberately kept divisive foreign policy issues, including relations with the EU and Russia, in the background. The Kremlin said on Monday it hoped the new leaders “understand that cooperation with Russia is in Serbia’s interests”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionDušan Vučićević, an analyst, said that, from the outset, the movement “insisted as much as possible that Serbia must first and foremost address domestic political issues – the literal dismantling of every institution, from the national to the local level”.The students’ win marks a profound political shift in Serbia and could potentially offer inspiration to other student movements that have cropped up acrossEuropein recent weeks demanding better education standards and prospects.However, Vučićević said it was distinct from other protests. “This experiment in grassroots democracy ultimately secured more than 50% of the vote,” he told Agence France-Presse, but it was “unclear whether a similar model could work in other countries”.Nikola Burazer, programme director at the Belgrade-based Centre for Contemporary Politics, said on Monday that the movement’s decision-making process also needed to “be sped up”, as its process for choosing candidates “actually took a long time – months”.‘This is a symbol for Europe’: streets of Belgrade resound with joy after Vučić defeatRead moreHe added: “After people are done celebrating and thinking about what happened yesterday, we will focus a bit more on what’s coming up, and how the government will look. Twenty-four hours ago that all seemed like a fantasy.”On Sunday, Vučić, who maintained close ties with Russia throughout his tenure, blamed his party’s defeat on “the direct support of various European countries and the US deep state, the one that is also against President Trump”.International leaders, meanwhile, joined a chorus of welcome to the students on Monday. “This is clearly a new chapter in the history of the country and its people,” said the Ukrainian president, Volodymyr Zelenskyy.“We wish ⁠Serbia success, real development, and warm ⁠relations with the European community. ​We in Ukraine thank Serbia for respecting our people, our state, and our independence. And we always celebrate our shared achievements.”The German chancellor, Friedrich Merz, said Berlin would “actively support Serbia’s European path” after the victory, saying the students “with their demand for the rule of law, fighting corruption and fundamental freedoms, have reached the people”.Serbia’s constitution requires the new parliament to convene within 30 days of the official election result, and sets a 90-day deadline after that for formation of the new government.The country must also hold new presidential elections before 27 December, since Vučić stepped down to run for prime minister.Explore more on these topicsWorld newsSerbiaEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Serbia wakes up to new reality after student-led movement ousts Vučić – as it hapepned | Serbia | The Guardian
description: Hopes raised for a reset in relations with EU and other partners following the defeat of authoritarian president
Author: Jakub Krupa
Headline: Hopes raised for a reset in relations with EU and other partners following the defeat of authoritarian president
Content: 05.00 EDTMorning opening: Serbia wakes up to new reality after VučićJakub KrupaSerbia wakes up to a new reality this morning after a grassroots opposition movement led by students ousted the country’s former authoritarian president Aleksandar Vučić, raising hopes for a new opening in relations with the EU and other partners.Opposition supporters celebrate at the parliament building after Aleksandar Vučić, represented by the silhouette, conceded defeat in the parliamentary election in Belgrade, Serbia.Photograph: Marko Đurica/ReutersWith 96.9% polling stations processed,the Student List has 52.6% of votes,well ahead of Vučić’s bloc at 39.22%.The latest CeSID projection suggestedthe students will have 140 seats in the new parliament, well clear of the 126 required for majority,with 103 for Vucic’s bloc. No other party crossed the 3% threshold, with national minority parties taking the remaining seven seats.We are likely to get more reactions to the vote today, withinternational observers set to present their preliminary report on the vote in the early afternoon.I will also pick up the latest onthe first round of the presidential vote inBulgaria,which saw a record-low turnout of just 22%. The second round will be held this Sunday.Elsewhere,I will be looking for updates fromFranceand Italy after another rocky weekend of protests.French PMSébastien Lecornuis going to meet with the student unions in the afternoon for what could be pivotal talks on the future of the demonstrations.AndE5 defence ministers – that’s France, Germany, Italy, Poland, and the UK – are meeting in Parisfor discussions onUkraine. Oh, and Slovakia’s foreign ministerJuraj Blanáris in Moscow for energy talks with Russia.It’sMonday, 26 October 2026, it’sJakub Krupahere, and this isEurope Live.Good morning.Share

title: Audi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearance | Germany | The Guardian
description: Gernot Döllner criticised for in-person announcement of major investment in US days before midterm elections
Author: Deborah Cole
Headline: Gernot Döllner criticised for in-person announcement of major investment in US days before midterm elections
Content: Donald Trump and the Audi CEO, Gernot Döllner, on stage at a rally in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday.Photograph: Edgar Su/ReutersView image in fullscreenDonald Trump and the Audi CEO, Gernot Döllner, on stage at a rally in Perry, Georgia, on Saturday.Photograph: Edgar Su/ReutersGermanyAudi boss under fire in Germany for Trump rally appearanceGernot Döllner criticised for in-person announcement of major investment in US days before midterm electionsDeborah Colein BerlinMon 26 Oct 2026 10.42 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.23 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe head of the luxury carmaker Audi is under fire in Germany for appearing at a rally withDonald Trumpjust days before the US midterm elections, to announce billions of dollars of investment in battleground state Georgia.Gernot Döllner joined Trump on stage after the US president gave a speech criticised by the head of an elected body of employees at Audi’s parent company, Volkswagen, as being full of “racism, sexism, transphobia [and] contempt for democracy”.Daniela Cavallo, the head of the VW works council, added that anyone who heard Trump’s speech and then saw that Döllner had become an active participant in the event must “sink into the ground with shame”, according to internal company communications released to German media.She said the investment deal and Döllner’s appearance showed VW’s management had allowed itself to be “turned into a puppet in the propaganda show of a highly dubious political figure”.Isabel Cademartori, the transport spokesperson for Germany’s Social Democrats – part of the country’s ruling coalition – called Döllner’s actions a “disgrace”. She added this was particularly so “in view of the history of the Volkswagen Group”, in an apparent reference toVW’s founding as a showcase company under the Nazis.A spokesperson for the German government declined to comment on the matter, calling it “a business decision regarding where the company invests and, in this case, where the company’s chief executive appears”.View image in fullscreenDöllner announced plans to spend $4bn and create 4,500 jobs in the battleground state of Georgia.Photograph: Mark Schiefelbein/APDöllner and Trump announced to the crowd on Saturday thatAudi would spend $4bn to build its first factory in the USand create 4,500 jobs, even asVW aims to slash tens of thousands of positions and close plantsin Germany.“We are planning to bring our ⁠biggest and most premium SUVs, and produce them here in Macon,Georgia,” Döllner said at the rally in Perry near Macon, in a highly unusual move for a European executive during a hard-fought US electoral campaign.He called the plans, which foresee factory construction starting next year and car production beginning in the 2030s, “a long-term investment because we believe in the American market”.Audi is the only premium car manufacturer without its own factory in the US, making it particularly vulnerable to Trump’s punishing 15% import tariffs, which cost it an estimated €1.2bn last year. The Macon plant would build 200,000 SUVs annually.The head of the powerful German trade union IG Metall, Christiane Benner, called Döllner’s US appearance “extremely embarrassing, politically unacceptable and unworthy of the company, but above all of Audi’s employees”.She accused Döllner of being in “flagrant breach” of the company’s code of conduct, “which expressly requires political neutrality in the run-up to elections”.She warned that any major investment like the Macon plant would have to go before VW’s supervisory board. Benner is the board’s deputy chair.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every daySign up toHeadlines EuropeA digest of the morning's main headlines from the Europe edition emailed direct to you every week dayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionVolkswagen is locked in a battle between management and labour over a push to cut as many as 100,000 jobs and close factories. It has blamed the downsizing on intense competition from Chinese carmakers, as well as US tariffs and the expensive transition to electric vehicles.Its German ​factories are under particular pressure to drive down costs, with Audi’s facility in Neckarsulm, which employs 15,000 people, among four VW plants threatened with closure from early next decade.“Each site must do its part in terms of competitiveness and the long-term strength of Audi,” a company spokesperson said.Trump isdeeply unpopular in Germanyand has riled its political mainstream byvocally backing the far-right Alternative für Deutschland. The AfD is the country’s most popular party, according to polls, and hasactively courted Trump’s support.The 3 November election in Georgia could be decisive inthe Democrats’ battle to regain a majority in the Senate. The incumbent senator, Jon Ossoff, is fighting a tough re-election battle against Republican challenger Mike Collins, in a state Trump won in 2024.Trump has argued ahead of the midterms that his tariffs on car imports arehelping the US economy.Explore more on these topicsGermanyAutomotive industryUS midterm elections 2026EuropeDonald TrumpVolkswagen (VW)GeorgianewsShareReuse this content

title: Jordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attack  | Jordan | The Guardian
description: Jordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in Karak
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Jordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in Karak
Content: Mourning relatives hold a framed portrait of a victim killed in the attack on 23 October on a Greek Orthodox church during a funeral ceremony in Karak, Jordan.Photograph: Raad Adayleh/APView image in fullscreenMourning relatives hold a framed portrait of a victim killed in the attack on 23 October on a Greek Orthodox church during a funeral ceremony in Karak, Jordan.Photograph: Raad Adayleh/APJordanJordan attacks militants in Syria in retaliation for last week’s church attackJordanian air force says it carried out strikes against ‘terrorist groups’ tied to killing of nine in KarakAssociated Press in AmmanMon 26 Oct 2026 18.08 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 19.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJordan has carried out airstrikes against armed groups in Syria in retaliation forFriday’s attack on a Greek Orthodox churchin the southern Jordanian city of Karak that killed nine people, the Jordanian air force has said in a statement.It said the operation “resulted in the killing and wounding of many members of these terrorist groups and the destruction of a number of their vehicles”. It did not specify who the groups were or the precise location of the strikes.Syrian state media reported that civilians had been killed in the strikes. The director of health in the southern province of Daraa, where the strikes took place, told the Syrian national news agency, Sana, that at least five civilians had been killed, including women and children and a 65-year-old man.Jordan’s armed forces said the operation was conducted in coordination with Damascus, but Syria’s government gave a contradictory account, saying it had launched an investigation into the ⁠Jordanian attacks, and stressed in a statement the importance of field and security coordination in border areas.In the aftermath of the strikes, Syria said it had closed the ⁠Nassib border crossing with Jordan, suspending ⁠traffic in both directions. Nassib is Jordan’s only passenger and commercial border crossing with Syria.Earlier on Monday, Jordanian authorities arrested three men for last week’s attack, which also wounded more than two dozen people. The arrests followed a dawn shootout, and all three men were wounded, officials said.The attack struck the Greek Orthodox church during a funeral in Karak, about 55 miles (90km) south of the capital, Amman, on Friday. Karak is home to a minority Christian population.The attack shocked the nation, and Jordan declared three days of mourning for the victims. No group immediately claimed responsibility for the attack; the attackers’ motive remained unknown.Later on Monday, Jordan’s Public Security Directorate identified the three arrested men as brothers Hazzah Zaidan Mohammad and Mishal Zaidan Mohammad, and their brother-in-law Ahmad Sami Hussein. All three are Jordanian; they were taken into custody in Karak, south of Amman.The agency’s chief described the gunmen as “takfiri”, a term used for Sunni militants, but said they were not tied to any organised group.“They only represent themselves,” Maj Gen Obaidallah Abd Rabbo Al-Maayta told a news conference. He also said a large cache of munitions was found in the abandoned house where Jordanian forces apprehended the men.Jordan’s interior minister, Mazen al-Faraya, said the attack by the three men was the result of “a terroristic, extremist way of thinking”.“If this way of thinking is not resolved, we will see incidents like this again,” he told reporters.Jordan’s King Abdullah II had ordered authorities to respond with “an iron fist” against what he called the outlaws of Islam and anyone attempting to undermine the unity of the Jordanian people.“We vowed the terrorists would not escape punishment, and no proponent of dark ideologies that divide Jordanians will be tolerated,” he said in a statement on Monday.Relatives of the victims said the arrests brought them some relief.“Despite the profound and immense tragedy, what happened today has eased our grief, and the grief of the Jordanian people – not just for us, the families of the martyrs,” Khaled al-Borqan, himself a survivor of the attack and a relative of three of the people killed, told Al-Mamlaka.“Despite the sadness and pain, the news brought us joy,” Fares Halaseh, an uncle of one of the victims and a survivor of the attack, told the TV station.But the pain remains, he added. “We will not forget this agony for years to come.”Explore more on these topicsJordanSyriaMiddle East and north AfricanewsShareReuse this content

title: British politicians among international delegates barred from entering West Bank | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Group was on visit to meet Palestinian children, farmers and civil leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces
Author: Sinéad Campbell
Headline: Group was on visit to meet Palestinian children, farmers and civil leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces
Content: The British MPs Clive Lewis and Lara Bird were among those detained and barred from entering the West Bank.Composite: WENN, PA/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe British MPs Clive Lewis and Lara Bird were among those detained and barred from entering the West Bank.Composite: WENN, PA/AlamyWest BankBritish politicians among international delegates barred from entering West BankGroup was on visit to meet Palestinian children, farmers and civil leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forcesSinéad CampbellMon 26 Oct 2026 17.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 18.43 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAn international delegation including British politicians has been barred from entering theWest Bankon a trip to meet Palestinian children, farmers and society leaders facing escalating violence from Israeli forces during olive harvest season.The delegation of 23 people, including four elected representatives, was drawn from countries including France, Spain, Luxembourg, Switzerland, Greece, Holland, Ireland and the US. It included the Labour MP Clive Lewis, the Scottish National party MP Lara Bird, the Scottish Greens MSP Kate Nevens and the former Labour MP Sam Tarry.Lewis told the Guardian: “We were detained, taken aside and then interrogated. I use the word interrogated because people were shouted at. We were asked why we were going in, what was happening, why our stories were one way or the other. The bottom line was it was a deeply unpleasant experience.”The delegates were set to participate in Progressive International’s Second Ramallah Congress, a gathering to oppose Israeli occupation inPalestine. The congress was organised by Progressive International in partnership with Birzeit University and includes a programme of meetings with Palestinian academics, students and civil society organisations.View image in fullscreenClive Lewis (left) and Sam Tarry were both denied entry to the West Bank at the border crossing checkpoint.Photograph: Global Justice NowTarry told the Guardian that he thought the delegation had a “genuine chance of going across” into the West Bank but they were detained at the Allenby/King Hussein Bridge by Israeli forces in Jordan for nine hours. “They made a political decision very clearly based on the fact they didn’t want people to witness what’s been going on in the West Bank, especially ahead of the elections,” he added.The exclusions occurred amid attacks by Israeli forces on Palestinian olive farmers and foreign press and activists in the region. International travel to parts of the West Bank is permitted but subject to military checkpoints. Earlier this month, Israeli media reported that the defence minister, Israel Katz, hadinstructed officials to pursue exclusion ordersagainst activists travelling to Palestinian olive-harvesting areas.Guardian reporter filmed masked militants seconds before West Bank attack on French mayorRead moreIn the first two weeks of October, the UN aid coordination officerecorded at least 160 Israeli settler attackslinked to the olive harvest, often under the protection or with the participation of Israeli forces.Israeli forcesattacked European diplomats and a French mayoraccompanying Palestinian farmers, while about 80 olive-harvest volunteers, including US congressional candidate Brad Lander,were also recently detained.Bird said in a statement: “I came to stand alongside Palestinians being attacked for harvesting olives on their own land. Instead, we were turned away at the border with no reason given.“It is more important now than ever that we bear witness and show our solidarity. But we were prevented from doing so. If Israel has nothing to hide, why is it so determined to stop us seeing what is happening in the occupied West Bank?”Laila Hazaineh, a political coordinator for Progressive International, said in a statement: “Despite escalating violence, our delegation remained determined to cross to Palestine to participate in the olive harvest, and actively engage with Palestinian communities and institutions. Every refusal of entry will only strengthen this determination.”The embassy of Israel has been contacted for comment.Explore more on these topicsWest BankMiddle East and north AfricaArab and Middle East unrestCivil liberties - internationalProtestPalestineIsraelnewsShareReuse this content

title: Netanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to election | Benjamin Netanyahu | The Guardian
description: Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls
Author: Emma Graham-Harrison
Headline: Israeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in polls
Content: Benjamin Netanyahu tours the Mahane Yehuda market in Jerusalem ahead of the national election.Photograph: Kevin Coombs/ReutersView image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu tours the Mahane Yehuda market in Jerusalem ahead of the national election.Photograph: Kevin Coombs/ReutersBenjamin NetanyahuNetanyahu reportedly pressured military to attack Iran in run-up to electionIsraeli prime minister increases alarmist rhetoric as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in pollsEmma Graham-HarrisonandJulian Borgerin JerusalemMon 26 Oct 2026 15.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleBenjamin Netanyahu has resorted to increasingly alarmist rhetoric and reportedly put pressure on Israel’s military to take action against Iran as his far-right coalition narrowly trails in the polls ahead of Tuesday’s close-run elections.What you need to know about the most consequential election in Israel’s historyRead moreThe Israeli prime minister posted an AI-generated image of a nuclear mushroom cloud destroying Tel Aviv, telling Israeli voters to choose him or risk nuclear annihilation.“Anyone who cares about their own physical existence, that of their family, and their loved ones should have a trembling hand before voting for [the opposition],” he wrote in asocial media postabout Iran’s nuclear programme.View image in fullscreenAn AI-generated image of a nuclear strike on Tel Aviv was posted on Netanyahu’s X account on Sunday.Photograph: X/Benjamin NetanyahuIsrael’s Channel 12 news reported that the prime minister and the armed forces chief of staff, Lt Gen Eyal Zamir, clashed in recent days over a directive to the military which could “potentially spark an immediate conflagration withIranat a very sensitive juncture”, by provoking a miscalculation by Iran.Zamir is reported to have requested the directive, the details of which were not specified, to be presented to him in writing.Netanyahu denied the report, and the defence ministry later denied any intention to carry out military operations against Iran.On Monday however, CNN reported that Netanyahu had tried to convinceDonald Trumpto launch a renewed assault on Iran in recent weeks, renewing the war both men started in February.The report, confirming an earlier account in the Financial Times, said Trump had ruled out any such action until US congressional elections next week.The Israel Defense Forces (IDF) issued a statement on Monday that stopped well short of a denial of the press reports. It simply insisted that its decisions were based exclusively on “security, professional, objective and national considerations”.Netanyahu’s warnings were a marked contrast with his triumphalism in the immediate wake of the wars on Iran that launched last year and this spring.In March Netanyahu said Israeli and US strikes haddestroyedIran’s ability to enrich uranium and produce ballistic missiles, and in 2025 he claimed a “historic victory” over Iran that would stand for generations.Gadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc and Netanyahu’s most likely challenger for the prime minister’s job, expressed his confidence in Zamir. “We won’t allow the IDF to be turned into a pawn in Netanyahu’s survival campaign,” said Eisenkot, who is a retired general.View image in fullscreenGadi Eisenkot, the leader of the opposition bloc, is the most likely challenger to Netanyahu as prime minister.Photograph: Abir Sultan/EPAMost polls suggest the mainly centre-right opposition bloc led by Eisenkot is poised to win more seats in Israel’s Knesset than the Netanyahu coalition, but neither would be able to muster the 61 seats necessary for a majority government.The opposition would most likely be able to gather a majority and topple Netanyahu in coalition with parties representing Palestinians with Israeli citizenship, roughly a fifth of the population. But conservatives inside the Eisenkot bloc have ruled out such a coalition, raising the prospect of a minority government, another round of elections and a possible Netanyahu resurgence.As the elections drew closer, Netanyahu framed the country’s choice as existential. He told Channel 14, which has acted as his lead cheerleader in the Israeli media: “There is a single fundamental issue here – our existence.”He described the opposition bloc as the “left” in alliance with Palestinians, and enemies of the country. “We see what is happening in Europe. The alliance between the left and Islam might destroy the state of Israel,” he said.The main opposition parties are rightwing or centre-right, sharing Netanyahu’s adamant opposition to the establishment of a Palestinian state, and who have largely supported the war in Gaza. Some opposition leaders have ruled out any kind of political alliance with Palestinian Israeli parties, who could emerge from the elections holding the balance of power in the Knesset. Palestinians in the occupied territories do not have the vote.The opposition bloc is held together more by its shared antipathy to Netanyahu, who has dominated the Israeli political scene over the past three decades and veered increasingly towards authoritarianism, seeking to limit the independence of the judiciary and turn the police and Shin Bet internal security service into political tools.The prime minister is also in the midst of a trial on corruption charges, and his legal jeopardy could increase if he loses his grip on power.View image in fullscreenBenjamin Netanyahu has been emphasising in his campaign the support he has from Donald Trump.Photograph: Ohad Zwigenberg/APIn the closing stages of the campaign, Netanyahu has also emphasised the overt support he enjoys from Donald Trump, who repeated his endorsement on Sunday in a social media post, saying “When you go to the Polls please remember that Bibi has been an outstanding warrior prime minister!”The Israeli outlet Walla News reported that this repeat endorsement was a result of relentless pressure from Netanyahu’s office. It is unclear, however, whether Trump’s support will carry any weight with the electorate. The US president’s earlier “total endorsement” on 18 October made no visible difference to the polls.In one survey, 64% of Israelis questioned said it would not influence their vote, and 17% said it made them less likely to back Netanyahu, against 12% who said it had deepened their resolve to support Netanyahu’s Likud party.In the closing stages of the closely fought campaign, Netanyahu has also forecast growing financial isolation, saying billions of dollars in annual military aid from the US would dry up soon, and drew a rare public rebuke from the central bank for a repeated claim that Israel could use cryptocurrencies to dodge escalating global sanctions.“Cryptocurrencies cannot serve as a means to circumvent sanctions,” the Bank of Israel said on Sunday evening. “The right course for the Israeli economy is to maintain economic relations with our primary trading partners and to focus on preventing sanctions and their negative impact on the economy.”Netanyahu had already laid out a forecast for a bleak, isolated future a year ago, when he said Israel might need to become a militarised “super Sparta”, then rowed back again in the face of fierce criticism from a horrified Israeli public.His return to this rhetoric and the tactics of fear, particularly after unexpected losses for far-right allies in Serbia and Brazil, raised questions about whether the ultimate political survivor may finally be on the ropes.Few among his allies or enemies expected his government to survive long after 7 October, much less complete its term. But the majority of polls have been clear for more than two years that his current coalition looks set to lose its slim majority.Explore more on these topicsBenjamin NetanyahuIsraelUS-Israel war on IranIranMiddle East and north AfricaDonald TrumpnewsShareReuse this content

title: Middle East peace held back by US insistence that Iran is a threat, Oman’s foreign minister says | Iran | The Guardian
description: Badr Albusaidi calls for security pact involving Gulf states, Iraq and Iran with US no longer primary provider of security
Author: Patrick Wintour
Headline: Badr Albusaidi calls for security pact involving Gulf states, Iraq and Iran with US no longer primary provider of security
Content: An actor portraying Donald Trump sits behind bars in a billboard installation resembling a prison cell in Tajrish Square, Tehran.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APView image in fullscreenAn actor portraying Donald Trump sits behind bars in a billboard installation resembling a prison cell in Tajrish Square, Tehran.Photograph: Vahid Salemi/APIranMiddle East peace held back by US insistence that Iran is a threat, Oman’s foreign minister saysBadr Albusaidi calls for security pact involving Gulf states, Iraq and Iran with US no longer primary provider of securityPatrick WintourDiplomatic editorMon 26 Oct 2026 15.12 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Middle East’s ability to solve its problems has been held back by America’s 50-year insistence that the Gulf states should view Iran as a security threat, Oman’s foreign minister said on Monday in a significant speech designed to break the deadlock over the region’s future.Badr Albusaidi called for a non-aggression security pact involving all six Gulf states as well asIranand Iraq. The US would in future no longer be the primary provider of security, he said.He was speaking on the day high-level defence and intelligence officials from Turkey, Pakistan andSaudi Arabiatravelled to Tehran in an attempt to prevent a renewed outbreak of fighting between the US and Iran.View image in fullscreenFrom left, Saudi Arabia’s defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, Pakistan’s army chief, Asim Munir, and Ibrahim Kalin, the head of Turkey’s intelligence service, at a meeting in Tehran on Monday.Photograph: Iranian Presidency Office/APTehran said the meeting also explored future security arrangements in the region. The high stakes were underlined by the sight of the Saudi defence minister, Khalid bin Salman, in Tehran weeks after Iran had struck Saudi infrastructure and as Iran-backedHouthiscontinue to send missiles towards Riyadh.Albusaidi is the first Gulf leader to break ranks so explicitly by calling for the mainly Sunni Gulf states to form a security alliance with Iran, a long-term aspiration of Tehran’s.Speaking at Girton College, Cambridge, he said the talks might be difficult and the proposal appeared counterintuitive, but “issues such as the strait of Hormuz have become impossible to resolve because external powers continue to define the terms of engagement, while regional powers are unable to take collective responsibility for making their own security arrangements and reach a consensus on them”.He added: “What holds us back is that issues which ought to be handled at a regional level by the states of the Gulf themselves, are made more complex, more intractable and sometimes simply impossible to resolve because the region’s security arrangements are insufficiently developed.“And they are insufficiently developed because they have relied for too long on the involvement of external powers.”He said that for half a century Iran “had been systematically excluded from playing any meaningful role in the security arrangements of the region”. This had led to “profoundly negative consequences, not just for Iran, but for the region as a whole”, including the imposition of priorities on the region by external powers such as “the entirely false perception that there is a fundamental regional antagonism between Iran and the Arab states of the Gulf”.He added: “Perhaps the most damaging of the priorities imposed on the region from the outside has been the requirement that Iran be excluded. Not just excluded. Worse. Positioned as the threat against which regional security had to be organised.”View image in fullscreenBadr Albusaidi, left, with Iran’s foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, in Tehran in August.Photograph: Iranian Foreign Ministry/APOman is on the southern side of the strait of Hormuz, with Iran on the northern shores. The two countries have reached a temporary agreement on how shipping traffic should be managed in the strait, but the plan is on hold until the US and Iran lift their respective blockades of the waterway.Albusaidi also indirectly challenged Donald Trump’s case for a further attack on Iran by saying he believed the previous round of talks between the US and Iran in February, which Oman mediated, were “making significant progress, and that an agreement was within reach. We still stand by that judgment today.”The Iranian foreign ministry has often proposed a security pact for the region in which Iran, as opposed to the US, plays a role. The US-Iran conflict may have reopened the debate among Gulf states about whether the heavy presence of US bases in their countries is a source of reassurance or insecurity. Oman is one Gulf state to have explored a regional security pact that includes Iran.No Gulf state openly supported the US-Israeli attacks on Iran last year or this February, but some have covertly cooperated in the operations. Iran has sought to defend itself by attacking US bases and energy infrastructure in the Gulf states.Iran threatens to strike oil and AI facilities across Gulf if US and Israel renew attacksRead moreThe meeting in Tehran was taking place against a backdrop of continued Pentagon briefings about a major US military buildup in preparation for a possible assault after the midterm elections. Qatari mediators spent much of Sunday in Tehran seeking terms for Iran to reopen the strait of Hormuz.Israeli media reports claimed that the country’s prime minister, Benjamin Netanyahu, has beentrying to browbeat the military into provoking a war with Iranbefore the Israeli elections on Tuesday.Donald Trump’s repeated call for Netanyahu to be re-elected only adds to the mood in the region that the US and Israel have the potential to be a long-term source of insecurity.The idea of a security pact with Iran will be resisted in large parts of the Middle East after the damage Tehran has been prepared to inflict on the economies of the region, either directly or through the use of intermediaries such as the Houthis. Iranian hardliners increasingly say Iran’s security best lies in trying to assemble a nuclear bomb.A pact that is likely to take many months to negotiate may also not be a solution to Washington’s demand that Iran reopen the strait of Hormuz before US sanctions are lifted.Explore more on these topicsIranUS-Israel war on IranSaudi ArabiaPakistanTurkeyMiddle East and north AfricaOmannewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homes | West Bank | The Guardian
description: Families forced to flee as Netanyahu tries to prove security credentials after two Israeli soldiers killed days before election
Author: Julian Borger
Headline: Families forced to flee as Netanyahu tries to prove security credentials after two Israeli soldiers killed days before election
Content: An Israeli checkpoint in the flattened area of Farsh al-Hawa, an entrance to Hebron, where two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in a shooting last Friday.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianView image in fullscreenAn Israeli checkpoint in the flattened area of Farsh al-Hawa, an entrance to Hebron, where two Palestinian gunmen killed two Israeli soldiers in a shooting last Friday.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianWest Bank‘It’s collective punishment’: nearly 2,000 Palestinians in Hebron displaced as Israeli forces take over homesFamilies forced to flee as Netanyahu tries to prove security credentials after two Israeli soldiers killed days before electionJulian Borger,Sufian TahaandQuique Kierszenbaumin HebronMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleHebron, the biggest city in the West Bank, had paid little attention to Israel’s looming elections until it found itself suddenly in the midst of them, a proving ground for Benjamin Netanyahu’s security credentials in the run-up to Tuesday’s vote.Agun attack on an Israeli military checkpointon Friday in which two soldiers were killed brought immediate televised visits from Netanyahu and his finance minister, Bezalel Smotrich, whose ruling coalition isnarrowly trailingwith two days of campaigning left.They vowed abrupt and sweeping retribution, and the prime minister warned of imminent military operations on a scale theWest Bankhas not seen in nearly 60 years of occupation.Within hours, the whole city of 250,000 people had been sealed off and the neighbourhood of Farsh al-Hawa, closest to the site of Friday’s attack, had been flattened. By Sunday morning, there was nothing left but rubble of an industrial area that had been full of car workshops, a big ceramics plant and other enterprises.Map of the West Bank, marking the Palestinian communitiesAs the bulldozers were at work there, another district a few kilometres away was being systematically emptied. Ein Deir Baha was allegedly home to at least one of the two men involved in the attack (both of whom were killed on the spot), and on Friday its residents paid the price.The imam from the local mosque, Fahed Ahmaro, was woken at about midnight by the loudspeakers from military vehicles patrolling the street, telling homeowners to vacate their homes immediately for their own safety.View image in fullscreenFahed Ahmaro, who was forced to flee his home in the Deir Baha area of Hebron by Israeli security forces, looks at his house from a distance.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianAhmaro had 30 members of his family living in his house. He rushed his frail mother and some of his grandchildren to his daughter’s house in another part of Hebron, and was on his way back in the hope of picking up some of his possessions when his neighbour phoned him.“He told me not to come back, and the army had blown up the gates to the house. I don’t know what they have done to it by now. I heard they destroyed the furniture,” Ahmaro said. “You don’t know what you have until you lose it. Now I realise how devastating it is to lose your home.”View image in fullscreenFahed Ahmaro’s house in Hebron, now a military position, with netting over its upper floorsPhotograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianAt midday on Sunday, he was in a Hebron market shopping for a change of clothes for his grandchildren, uncertain how long the family’s exile would last.He had heard that the house was being used as a base by Israeli soldiers and looking up at the house, perched on the side of a steep hill, he could see some lights on but no sign of life.The Hebron municipality said that 370 families, nearly 2,000 people, had been displaced by the army sweep through Ein Deir Baha. In its official comments, the Israeli army had said that the displaced population had left voluntarily, that “civilians who wished to evacuate were permitted to temporarily leave the area”.Ahmaro was outraged at the suggestion that he had any choice about fleeing.“Never, never, never. Why should I leave my house?” he asked.Abdul Halim al-Tamimi tried to stay put when the military came at 1.30am. The 77-year-old was told his family had only 10 minutes to vacate their home.“An intelligence officer told me if we didn’t go, they would displace us the same way they have done it in Gaza,” he said. “We stood there in front of the house, and we refused to leave until we were faced by three military vehicles and they forced us out.”By the time the Tamimi family left, it was 3am on Saturday morning. On Sunday morning their home was festooned with large Israeli flags and ringed with military vehicles. The army had turned the substantial villa into its headquarters.In its statement, the Israeli military claimed that 2,000 local people were from the Jaba’a clan, from which the gunmen were allegedly drawn, and which the army claimed was “associated with Hamas”.The claim drew consternation and derision from people in Ein Deir Baha. They numbered the extent of the Jaba’a clan at 150 at most, with no known reputation for radicalism.“We are from a completely different family. We are innocent people. We have nothing to do with the whole thing,” Tamimi said. “I don’t know what they are using it for, other than maybe election publicity.”Palestinians in the occupied West Bank have no vote in Tuesday’s elections, but their lives could be deeply affected by the outcome.View image in fullscreenWasam Sadi, a Palestinian driver, has difficulties with his vision after he was attacked in his truck by Israeli settlers near the entrance of Hebron.Photograph: Quique Kierszenbaum/The GuardianBy Sunday evening, all roads in and out of the city remained closed to cars, with heavy steel barriers swung across them. The only traffic was on foot, with taxi drivers squabbling for fares. The driver of a delivery truck, Wasam Sadi, pulled in at one checkpoint with the cab windshield smashed and glass fragments in his eyes. He had been attacked by settlers at a nearby junction, he said.“It’s collective punishment,” said Hebron’s mayor, Yousef al-Jabari. “They have dragged people from their houses, and they have prevented the media from getting into the district in order to cover up what is happening.“Netanyahu and his gang are using Palestinian land to displace Palestinian people, closing the city, closing the mosque, in order to achieve their political goals.”Explore more on these topicsWest BankIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricaBenjamin NetanyahuInternally displaced peoplefeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Unfair’ cliff-edge rule that punished carers to be abolished in budget | Carer's allowance | The Guardian
description: Controversial mechanism that hit unpaid carers with huge penalties to be scrapped following Guardian investigation
Author: Patrick Butler
Headline: Controversial mechanism that hit unpaid carers with huge penalties to be scrapped following Guardian investigation
Content: The new digital taper system will see just £1 of carer’s allowance payments removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit.Photograph: Andrew Bret Wallis/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe new digital taper system will see just £1 of carer’s allowance payments removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit.Photograph: Andrew Bret Wallis/Getty ImagesCarer's allowance‘Unfair’ cliff-edge rule that punished carers to be abolished in budgetControversial mechanism that hit unpaid carers with huge penalties to be scrapped following Guardian investigationPatrick ButlerandPippa CrerarMon 26 Oct 2026 18.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 19.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe controversial rule that led to unpaid carers being punished with penalties amounting to thousands of pounds is to be abolished, the Guardian can reveal.The chancellor,John Healey, is to announce a new digital taper system for carer’s allowance in Wednesday’s budget, effectively ending what is regarded as one of the UK benefit system’s most feared and unfair administrative practices.The scandal was highlighted in a Guardian investigation that revealed howhundreds of thousands of carershave, through no fault of their own, run up life-changing debts in recent years after overstepping weekly earnings thresholds by just a few pence.Those hefty debts were then ruthlessly chased down by welfare officials who pursued carers using legislation designed to recover funds from drug dealers and organised crime bosses. Some unpaid carers were convicted of fraud as a result.The cliff-edge rule dictates that if a carer earns even a penny more than the weekly earnings limit allowed – currently £204 – they forfeit their entire week’s carer’s allowance payment, currently £86.45. A carer who earned a penny over the limit for a year would breach it by 52p but would be asked to repay £4,495.40.Although the Department for Work and Pensions (DWP) was aware when carers breached earnings limits, it refused to warn them, insisting the onus was on carers to report any changes.Thousands of carers spent long periods unaware of the breach, in some cases for years, resulting in overpayment debts typically of £2-£5,000 but in some cases as much as £20,000.Under new rules set to be announced in the budget, the introduction of a tapered system instead of a cliff-edge means only £1 of carer’s allowance will be removed for every additional £1 earned above the earnings limit, meaning carers are no longer left financially worse off for working additional hours or receiving a pay rise.The announcement is one of five more “everyday fixes” announced by Healey ahead of his budget on Wednesday. His room for manoeuvre is severely constrained by the tight fiscal backdrop, a result of global events including the conflict in Iran.Treasury insiders have warned that the budget will be low-key, with difficult tax and spend decisions put off until the spending review next year. But there is anxiety among some Labour MPs over the scale of the announcements, after Andy Burnham came to power promising major change.Victims of carer’s allowance crisis ‘need speedier repayments’, say campaignersRead moreAmong the other measures to come is making higher tax-free mileage rates permanent – with the 55p per mile rate for the first 10,000 business miles locked in, and increasing the rate above 10,000 miles to 35p per mile. The Treasury said the move would benefit about 3 million people – employees and self-employed – who use their own vehicle for work.The chancellor’s intervention on the draconian cliff-edge rule comes after anaward-winningGuardian investigationwhich revealed how the DWP had for years known of theprofound distressit caused carers – including warnings from a DWP whistleblower – but did nothing about it.The Guardian’s reporting triggered a government-commissioned independent review of carer’s allowance overpayments by disability rights expert Liz Sayce,published last year. It found unpaid carers suffered depression and hardship on a huge scale after falling foul of a series of systemic injustices, including the cliff edge.In one case highlighted bythe review, a carer was penalised when the national minimum wage had increased at a faster rate than the earnings limit. This put her 15p a week above the limit, even though her hours had not changed. Months later, she was told she had incurred a £2,000 penalty for above-limit earnings totalling just £5.The review found the outdated design of carer’s allowance, coupled withlongstanding DWP failuresin its administration, meant about 180,000 carers ran up overpayment debts amounting to £300m between 2019 and 2025.Campaigners welcomed the decision, calling it a “long-overdue reform” although there was disappointment the technical demands of building a new digital system to run the taper means it will not be introduced before the end of the decade.Carers UKsaid the cliff-edge plays havoc with carers’ attempts to work part-time around their minimum 35 hours a week of caring duties, with many giving up paid work or refusing promotions, overtime or bonuses because of the risks.John Healey, the chancellor, told the Guardian the carer’s allowance system had worked against carers. “That means doing an extra shift or getting a small pay rise can actually leave someone worse off. That cannot be right.“So at this budget on Wednesday, we’re ending that cliff-edge. Carer’s allowance will instead taper as earnings increase, giving carers the freedom to work a little more and earn a little more without suddenly losing all their support.”As well as unpaid carers, Healey’s budget will benefit an extra 150,000 new parents – including self-employed fathers and partners who have previously missed out – with parental support worth up to £194 a week.Ministers are also removing import tariffs on more than 100 products, including baked beans, chocolate and gherkins, while also supporting farmers facing higher fertiliser bills and households that rely on paraffin.There will also be hundreds more Post Office drop boxes, bringing the total to 1,000, to make it more convenient for people to send and return parcels without having to queue.Healey will also reportedly raise the minimum wage by about 4% to about £13.20 an hour. However, in a sign of government concern over rates of youth unemployment, the chancellor is said to be about to raise youth rates by roughly the same amount, rather than the inflation-busting levels seen in previous budgets.Labour came to office in 2024 promising to raise the youth rate, which applies to workers under 21, to the same level as the full rate. But ministers have become concerned in recent months that raising the minimum wage for younger workers could be dissuading companies from taking on young employees.“We are taking on the big challenges facing the country. But that doesn’t mean losing sight of the everyday problems that cost people money or simply aren’t fair,” Burnham said.“If you’re a nurse driving to work, a parent spending those precious first weeks with your new baby, or an unpaid carer picking up an extra shift, these changes will make life a little easier and put more money back in your pocket.”Pat McFadden, the work and pensions secretary, said: “We have listened to [carers’] concerns about the cliff-edge built into the system which leaves them financially worse off for taking on a few more hours, or getting a modest pay rise, and intend to bring that to an end.”Kirsty McHugh, chief executive ofCarers Trust, said: “It is great news that the government is acting to remove the carer’s allowance cliff-edge. This is an important and long-overdue reform.“We would urge the government to use this change as a springboard for a wider and deeper reform of carer’s allowance – a benefit that remains stuck in the 1970s and must be made fit for the future.”Emily Holzhausen,CarersUK director of policy, said: “We have countless stories from carers who have shared their deep fears of going just a few pence over the earnings limit and losing all of their benefit.“It’s absolutely right that the chancellor is thinking of practical changes that will make their lives easier. A taper on the earnings limit should give families much more choice about working and still caring.”Explore more on these topicsCarer's allowanceBudget 2026CarersJohn HealeySocial careBudgetnewsShareReuse this content

title: Russell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and his bad behaviour was normalised, trial told | UK news | The Guardian
description: Brand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant alleges
Author: Emine Sinmaz
Headline: Brand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant alleges
Content: Russell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court with his wife, Laura, on Monday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenRussell Brand arriving at Southwark crown court with his wife, Laura, on Monday.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAUK newsRussell Brand had ‘insane sexual appetite’ and his bad behaviour was normalised, trial toldBrand, charged with rape and sexual assault, was ‘sleeping with people day and night’, former assistant allegesEmine SinmazMon 26 Oct 2026 16.08 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.58 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRussell Brand had an “insane sexual appetite” and his bad behaviour was “normalised and dismissed” by those around him, his former personal assistant has told a court.Helen Berger alleged she had seen Brand treat women badly and that she once had to stop his mother and girlfriend walking in on him having sex with someone in his dressing room.She also told the court she had overheard the comedian receiving oral sex in a toilet cubicle and once found a celebrity leaving his bedroom in the morning.Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault against six women, in allegations spanning 10 years from 1999. He denies all the charges.Wearing a grey suit and white shirt, Brand sat still in the dock as statements from prosecution witnesses were read to Southwark crown court on Monday.Berger worked for Brand from June 2006 to February 2007, when he was at the height of his fame. She said the job was one of the hardest she had had because Brand had “non-stop energy”, and she left because she was “sick of him” and burnt out.“Though I’d worked with celebrities before and seen a lot of people normalising bad behaviour, this was on another level. I think everyone else normalising and dismissing Russell’s behaviour made me think, I guess, this is just the way it is,” Berger said in a May 2024 witness statement to police.Describing his behaviour, she added: “He was always in his underwear, he loved walking around in his underwear with no shirt on. I remember Sadie Frost came over to interview him. He did the whole interview in his underwear and no shirt and an open robe.”At the time, Brand had filming commitments for Channel 4’s Big Brother as well as MTV and the BBC, a radio show, a national comedy tour, a weekly Guardian column, and was writing a book.“In addition to his busy work, he had an insane sexual appetite and was sleeping with people day and night. He was very open about what his needs were,” Berger said in the statement, which was read out by the prosecutor, Riel Karmy-Jones KC.“He never seemed happy after sex, more so depressed,” Berger alleged. “There were times when I was at his house and he would be on a deadline … and he would get antsy and joke with me: ‘May I go and have sex now?’”She recalled Brand turning to the website Myspace to find random women to sleep with and how women, including an unnamed celebrity, would often be at his flat in Camden, north London, for sexual liaisons. “He was like a peacock, women always approached him,” she said.When Brand was recording an MTV show, Berger alleged, he told her to ask women for their phone numbers, which she said made her feel uncomfortable.She alleged that on other occasions she had to keep Brand’s mother and girlfriend away from his dressing room because he was having sex, and she overheard him receiving oral sex in a women’s toilet. Berger described overhearing Brand talking and recognising his trademark cowboy boots in the cubicle next door.Berger recalled that when Brand was headlining the Edinburgh festival, he ended his show by asking that anyone with “a vagina and heartbeat” meet him at a pub afterwards. Many women showed up, Berger said, and she later found him having sex in the shower at the apartment he was renting.“I never witnessed Russell doing anything against the law,” she said, before adding: “I did see Russell treat women poorly.”She recalled how he was once “hitting on” a woman who revealed she had a boyfriend, before Brand “turned in a way” that startled his then PA. “He literally just switched off his charm and moved on to the next woman,” Berger said.The court also heard a witness statement from the manager of a woman who said she was sexually assaulted by Brand when she worked at Channel 4 in 2009. The manager said she recalled the alleged victim telling her that Brand’s associates Jack Bayles and Gareth Roy had “told her she had to give Mr Brand a massage” or he would not continue with the day’s recording.The manager recalled being told that Bayles and Roy “were both there the whole time and watched and laughed while Mr Brand sexually assaulted her right in front of them”.The sister of a woman who alleges she was sexually assaulted and then orally raped by Brand at a Soho bar in 2004 told the court she was “upset and almost in shock” the next morning.In 2023, the woman called her sister in tears and told the “full story” of what had happened, the court heard.“It sounded like she was struggling to catch her breath,” the witness recalled. “She said his [Brand’s] eyes had gone completely black and he was possessed or had been a completely different person.”The trial continues.Explore more on these topicsUK newsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Major clean-up under way after two storms cause havoc in Britain | UK weather | The Guardian
description: More strong winds forecast after Austen and Boelo kill two people and bring travel disruption and flooding
Author: Mark Brown
Headline: More strong winds forecast after Austen and Boelo kill two people and bring travel disruption and flooding
Content: Waves crash over a lighthouse at Newhaven harbour during Storm Austen.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenWaves crash over a lighthouse at Newhaven harbour during Storm Austen.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersUK weatherMajor clean-up under way after two storms cause havoc in BritainMore strong winds forecast after Austen and Boelo kill two people and bring travel disruption and floodingTell us: have you been affected by Storm Boelo and Storm AustenMark BrownNorth of England correspondentMon 26 Oct 2026 14.25 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.09 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA major clean-up operation was under way on Monday after weekend storms caused havoc, with forecasters warning of more strong winds to come.Two men were killed by falling trees after two named storms,Austen and Boelo,struck parts of the UK, and there was widespread travel disruption, flooding, power cuts and event cancellations.The Energy Networks Association, which represents operators in the UK and Ireland, said 90,000 customers were still without power on Monday morning. That figure was later down to 39,000.The association’s chief executive, Lawrence Slade, told BBC Radio 4’s Today programme that disruption had been widespread, with operators having to restore power to about 700,000 customers over the weekend.He said Friday, Saturday and Sunday had been particularly challenging. “It certainly was a tough one. One of the problems was how quickly Boelo followed after Austen,” he said.Another issue was that there was no letup in the strong winds, widely 50-70mph and up to 85mph in northernScotland. “Until that weather system passes we can’t safely get engineers out to replace poles, to get wires back up etc,” Slade said.Storm Boelo causes severe flooding in town centre of Largs, ScotlandThe weather was much milder on Monday but the Met Office said more strong winds were on the way andissued two yellow weather warnings. One is in place from 6pm until 3am on Tuesday, covering western coastal areas from Cornwall up to south-west Scotland. Gusts of up to 65mph could hit exposed coastal areas, accompanied by heavy rain at times. The Met Office advised people to take care near cliffs and be aware of strong waves.The second warning will be in place from 3am to 9pm on Tuesday and covers most of Scotland. Forecasters said winds of 50-60mph were likely to be quite widespread, with gusts up to 70mph in the far north. It warned of possible travel cancellations, road closures and more power cuts.The weekend storms led to two deaths, authorities said. A 60-year-old man was hit by a falling tree in Dumfries and Galloway, while a man in his 20s died in Finchley, north London.The 60-year-old was named on Monday afternoon as Richard Baines, the curator of Logan Botanic Garden near Port Logan.David Knott, the director of horticulture at the Royal Botanic Garden Edinburgh, said Baines would be remembered for his “passion and enthusiasm for plants … significantly increasing and expanding the plant collection at Logan”.There was flooding in several parts of Scotland, withdramatic footage from Largsshowing flood water cascading through the town centre. One resident said it was the highest she had ever seen in 36 years of living there.Staff at the Thai restaurant Tha-Tien-Thaishared a video of their kitchen overrun by waterwith the desperate caption: “There is nothing left.” They said its doors would be closed for the foreseeable future “due to larger flood restoration than originally planned”.Robyn Cryans, an executive assistant from Renfrew, is on holiday in Cyprus and woke to see pictures taken by a neighbour of her Nissan Micra Sport submerged back at home.“It is very upsetting, a bit stressful,” she said. “It was unexpected considering we’ve got a £10m flood barrier literally just down the road which is supposed to activate if the Clyde bursts its banks.”View image in fullscreenA downed tree in Gladstone Park, London, on Sunday after strong winds overnight.Photograph: Martin Evans/PAShe is scheduled to fly back on Tuesday and fully expects to find her flat damaged. “I’m obviously very upset about it, but at the end of the day it’s material objects. It could have been a lot worse.”In Aberdeenshire, 13 primary schools without power were shut on Monday, and Ellon academy was closed because of storm damage. Ten primary schools were shut in the Highlands.Scotland’s first minister, John Swinney, met senior politicians, emergency teams and forecasters on Sunday to discuss the ongoing response to the weather.Emergency services were called to a flooded care home in Saltcoats, North Ayrshire, on Sunday evening. Police Scotland said everyone at the care home was accounted for, road closures were in place and officers were expected to remain on site overnight to assist.There was also travel disruption, with flights diverted from landing at Leeds Bradford, England’s highest airport, and others cancelled. Most train services were getting back to normal but operators advised customers to check before they travelled.The storms brought a number of event cancellations including the Sunday racing at Aintree, abandoned because of the high winds. The Guardian’s live blog of the terrible tea-time Sunderland v Leeds goalless drawsummed up the action: “And the winner is … the wind.”Explore more on these topicsUK weatherScotlandEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: FTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customers | US news | The Guardian
description: Suit that cites 2025 Guardian investigation alleges ‘pattern of inaccurate pricing’ that ‘affects millions of purchases’
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Suit that cites 2025 Guardian investigation alleges ‘pattern of inaccurate pricing’ that ‘affects millions of purchases’
