Content: A Dollar General store in Windsor, North Carolina.Photograph: Cornell Watson/The GuardianView image in fullscreenA Dollar General store in Windsor, North Carolina.Photograph: Cornell Watson/The GuardianThe price we payUS newsFTC and 20 states sue Dollar General, accusing bargain chain of overcharging customersSuit that cites 2025 Guardian investigation alleges ‘pattern of inaccurate pricing’ that ‘affects millions of purchases’The price we pay is supported byAbout this contentBarry YeomanMon 26 Oct 2026 19.22 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 20.55 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe Federal Trade Commission and 20 states have sued Dollar General, the nation’s largest dollar-store chain, for persistently overcharging customers at its more than 20,000 stores across the United States.Thelawsuit, filed in federal court in Nashville, cites a Guardianinvestigationpublished last December.“Dollar General has for years engaged in deceptive conduct that harms the very consumers it claims to serve,” the 95-page legal complaint claims.“Although Dollar General promises convenience, low prices, and value, the company has routinely charged customers more at the register than the prices displayed on shelves, price tags, and advertisements. This pattern of inaccurate pricing has persisted for years and affects millions of purchases across the country.”How the dollar-store industry overcharges cash-strapped customers while promising low pricesRead moreThe lawsuit says the scope of the retail chain’s “pricing misconduct” is “staggering”.The FTC is the federal agency charged with protecting consumers from deceptive, unfair and anticompetitive business practices. State authorities from Mississippi to Ohio to Nebraska to Utah have joined the case as plaintiffs.Dollar General did not respond to questions for this story, but has previously said that it was “committed to providing customers with accurate prices on items purchased in our stores”.The FTC’s allegations are consistent with the Guardian’s December 2025investigation, which found that Dollar General stores failed more than 4,300 government price-accuracy inspections in 23 states over a three-year period. That article “was the subject of significant internal deliberation and discussions” within the company, the lawsuit said.The agency noted in the lawsuit that Dollar General has policies in place that are supposed to align register prices with shelf prices. For example, it directs employees to remove and replace outdated labels on certain days of the week. Workers told the Guardian that, because of understaffing, they are often too busy to change those labels.“Dollar General’s on-paper policies to update pricing achieve little in practice,” the lawsuit said, because “they do not track whether the printed labels are actually affixed to shelves.”The FTC cited a Guardian interview with a lead sales associate in Louisiana who said: “I threw away tags sometimes, to keep me or a co-worker out of trouble.”Dollar General told the Guardian in 2025 that it is “disappointed” any time it fails to deliver on its commitment to accurate shelf pricing. In court documents in Ohio, Dollar General’s lawyers have argued that “it is virtually impossible for a retailer to match shelf pricing and scanned pricing 100% of the time for all items. Perfection in this regard is neither plausible nor expected under the law.”In a statementaccompanyingthe FTC lawsuit, the federal agency noted that Dollar General markets itself as a low-cost alternative to other retailers, and that low- and fixed-income customers rely on the accuracy of its price labels.“Dollar General has betrayed the trust of millions of American consumers and imposed significant financial harm on communities and consumers who are already struggling to make their paychecks last,” said Christopher Mufarrige, director of the FTC’s bureau of consumer protection.In a separate case, the New York attorney general, Letitia James,announcedearlier this month that Dollar General had agreed to a $1.875m deal to settle allegations that it had repeatedly overcharged customers across the state.Explore more on these topicsUS newsThe price we payConsumer affairsRetail industrynewsShareReuse this content

title: Massachusetts lesbian bar makes frantic effort to find new owners after relaxing masking policy | Massachusetts | The Guardian
description: Last Ditch bar announced it would ‘soft close’ after it went viral following a story on its attempt to relax Covid rules
Author: Lucy Campbell
Headline: Last Ditch bar announced it would ‘soft close’ after it went viral following a story on its attempt to relax Covid rules
Content: The Last Ditch, located in Greenfield, Massachusetts, said it is looking for new co-owners on social media.Photograph: Sophie ParkView image in fullscreenThe Last Ditch, located in Greenfield, Massachusetts, said it is looking for new co-owners on social media.Photograph: Sophie ParkMassachusettsMassachusetts lesbian bar makes frantic effort to find new owners after relaxing masking policyLast Ditch bar announced it would ‘soft close’ after it went viral following a story on its attempt to relax Covid rulesLucy CampbellMon 26 Oct 2026 18.39 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 19.03 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAMassachusettslesbian bar that went viral for loosening its Covid mask policy last month announced plans to “soft close” on Monday as it seeks new ownership.The Last Ditch bar, in the small city of Greenfield, saidin an Instagram postthat it was searching for co-owners, new owners or a full sale, and that it would “soft close effective immediately”, with “only booked events” continuing while it closes this winter. It had opened just last year as a bar for “dykes, transsexuals, gender freaks, workers, and their friends”.Last month the bar went viral followinga Boston Globe storydocumenting a masking dispute after the owners attempted to relax the bar’s Covid mask-wearing policy for one night a week in a bid to drive up Saturday business. The bar had been struggling to raise revenue while adhering to a strict policy of mask-wearing, but the proposed change prompted a backlash from customers who accused the owners of ableism and abandoning immunocompromised people.There was then a backlash to those critics, with people piling on and mocking customers’ concerns about contracting Covid.The publicity did also attract some support to the bar, but evidently, not enough. “We put our lives on hold to foster networks of care, resources and a home base for organizing. It’s time we pass it on,” the bar said on Instagram.“We’ve been fighting since the beginning to fill out the team, and we still don’t have a board/leadership to manage workers’ owned co-op transfer. We are soft closing effective immediately; all booked events will continue; otherwise, we are closed.”In seeking new ownership, the bar noted that the sale would include the furniture, equipment, inventory and social media pages, to an estimated value of $70,000.As set out in the Globe’s article, the bar was already in financial trouble before the masking furor, and two of thethree original ownershad dropped out of the project. The remaining owner was left with the responsibility of repaying the $50,000 loan the three took out to open the bar and was living out of her truck and working several jobs to try to keep it running.The Guardian has reached out to the Last Ditch bar for comment.Explore more on these topicsMassachusettsLGBTQ+ rightsBars, pubs and clubsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industry | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability
Content: Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, in Bengaluru, India, on 16 February 2026.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, in Bengaluru, India, on 16 February 2026.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersAnthropicAnthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industryMarket debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viabilityBlake MontgomeryandJohana BhuiyanMon 26 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropichas publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom.Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT,confidentially filedwith US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.“We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’sinvestor prospectusreads. Anthropic researchers and executives have trumpeted the transformative power of AI while simultaneously warning of its potential to cause human extinction.Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030Read moreA leader in the race to create powerful artificial intelligence models and a bellwether of the American AI boom, Anthropic’s chatbot Claude is its flagship product, which offers text generation features as well as advanced coding and cybersecurity capabilities. CEODario Amodeifounded the company after quitting OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.Anthropic’saudited filingswill offer the first public glimpse of its financial health, which have been the object of intense speculation in recent months as questions of apotential AI bubble swirl.The company detailed rapidly rising revenue in the prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.Despite the increasing revenue,Anthropicdisclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.Anthropic has focused on businesses as its primary paying customers, unlike OpenAI, which has courted everyday consumers for ChatGPT. As of 30 September, Anthropic said it had more than 14,000 enterprise customers – 11,900 of which had $100,000 or more of revenue, more than 1,900 that had $1m or more revenue and about 250 enterprise customers that had $10m or more revenue.“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” Anthropic executives wrote.The filing contains some of the hyperbolic language characteristic of AI companies predicting the miraculous potential of their technology. Describing the potential of AI agents, semi-autonomous chatbots that can carry out tasks on behalf of users, Anthropic executives wrote: “The result is something without historical precedent: what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a datacenter, available to every organization and sector of the economy.”Investing in Anthropic and the development of a model that the company claims could revolutionize knowledge work across industries comes with a great deal of risk. Anthropic listed more than 90 pages of potential to its business. For one, a “substantial portion” of the company’s revenue comes from a limited number of customers, and losing any of them could put a huge dent in their revenue. A quarter of Anthropic’s revenue comes from its top five customers, though no single customer represents more than 10% of its business.The company also has incurred $6.2bn in debt as it built out its infrastructure and spends billions yearly on computing power provided by third parties, according to the filing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI modelsRead moreThe misuse of AI and Claude in particular also poses a considerable risk to Anthropic’s business. When it comes to AI, there are four categories of potential risk, executives wrote: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. Anthropic’s most capable models have “capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote. The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended.”Amodei has called for a slowdown of AI’s development, citing existential risk. Anthropic’s stock market listing may elicit a rush of investment in the company and the AI sector more broadly, which could speed up the pace of the industry further.The company disclosed that in September 2025, staffers documented what they believe was the first large-scale cyber-attack that didn’t rely on significant human intervention. Anthropic “detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”.Donald Trump’s administration may also be a risk to the company. Anthropic has been embroiled in a feud with the Trump administration over the use of the startup’s products in warfare, which culminated in the designation of the company as a supply chain risk, a first for an American company. This prevents any military agency from contracting with Anthropic. The company has challenged the blacklisting.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicStock marketsUS marketsAI (artificial intelligence)Dario AmodeiChatbotsIPOsnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so far | US midterm elections 2026 | The Guardian
description: As the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under Trump
Author: Lauren Aratani
Headline: As the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under Trump
Content: Illustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenIllustration: Guardian Design/Getty ImagesUS midterm elections 2026Explainer‘We don’t have inflation’? Five charts show the US economic reality of Trump’s second term so farAs the US midterm elections approach, we take a look at data to see a true picture of the US economy under TrumpLauren Arataniin New YorkMon 26 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWith themidterm electionsfast approaching, many Americans have theeconomyon their minds.US voters areexhaustedby years of higher prices.Donald Trumpwon the presidency in 2024 on promises to lower inflation and undo the damage he said the Biden administration had inflicted on the economy.Too little, too late: Trump takes on gas prices as fuel costs hamper his midterm hopesRead moreIn Trump’s view, his plan is working. At a recent rally in Montana, Trump boasted about the current economy, framing it as a booming time for Americans. “We’re richer now,” he said. “We don’t have inflation.”Economic data paints a different picture.Inflation, especially gas prices, has soared over the last year. The job market has been in stasis, and higher interest rates have meant it’s more expensive for Americans to borrow money for loans and mortgages.These fluctuations have a concrete impact on the lives of Americans. A recentHarris pollfor the Guardian found that a majority of Americans, including some Republicans, disagree. Nearly two-thirds said they believe the country is experiencing a recession, and many said higher prices had been a pain point. Americans are reporting having trouble saving, and a third polled said one surprise bill could sink them financially.Here’s what the data shows us about Trump’s second term so far.InflationThe rate of price increases has dramatically cooled since its peak in 2022, when the pandemic’s economic stimulus packages found their way into consumer prices. Inflation peaked at 9.1%, a 40-year high, in June 2022.In January 2025, the month when Trump started his second term, inflation was down to 3%. By April 2025, it would be 2.3% – the lowest rate since 2021.A line chart US inflation rateThat’s when things start to get bumpy. After Trump placed tariffs on nearly everything that the US imports, inflation started to heat up again, climbing back up to 3% in September 2025. After many of his tariffs were paused and eventually found to be illegal, prices started going down again. In January and February 2026, inflation was back down to 2.4%.The Iran war, specifically its impact on oil prices, has brought inflation back up to levels not seen since 2023. In May, inflation reached 4.2% and has hovered above 3.4% since.It’s been nearly six years since Americans have seen inflation at a manageable 2% level. Price increases build up over time and can put a squeeze on budgets, which is why it’s such a sensitive point for voters during a crucial election.Gas pricesIn the Guardian’s recent poll with the Harris Poll,gas priceswere the most common pain point for Americans, with 83% saying they are making a dent in their current finances.A line chart showing average gas prices in the USSoon after the war in Iran began, the strait of Hormuz, a key route that a fifth of the world’s oil typically passes through, was blocked off. Its closure has pushed up prices all around the world. Though the US itself is a major oil producer, prices have still surged since the war. The average price of gas was $4.32 per gallon in mid-October, according to AAA, nearly $1.30 a gallon higher than a year ago.Even for an oil-producing state like Texas, a gallon of gas is $3.81 compared with $2.64 a year ago. Meanwhile, drivers in California, a state that imports much of its gas from overseas, are paying $6.21 per gallon.Monthly job figuresThe labor market is another metric used to measure the health of the economy, and while the US job market has seen some growth since Trump took office again, figures have fluctuated over the last year. In 2025, altogether 181,000 new jobs were added to the economy, compared with 2.2m jobs in 2024.A bar chart showing monthly change in US jobsEmployers have been dealing with a mixed landscape for hiring: harsher immigration policies, uncertainty from tariffs and higher prices for supplies have all meant slow job growth. The unemployment rate has remained low, though, at just over 4%. Economists call this a “low-hire, low-fire” economy, in which employers are neither hiring nor dismissing workers.S&P 500Though many Americans report struggling in today’s economy, a small group have never been wealthier. The stock market has continued to soar since Trump took office, recovering from dips seen during his initial tariff announcement and the early days of the Iran war.Economists largely see AI investment as the leading factor in the stock market’s acceleration. Tech companies are spending billions of dollars investing in datacenters and for chips that are needed to power AI.A line chart showing the latest S&P 500 figuresWhile many Americans are invested in the stock market through their retirement and pension funds, this growth has really been a boon for the top 1% wealthiest Americans, whoownnearly half of the stock market investments.Economists say higher prices paired with an exuberant stock market have led to aK-shaped economy, where the wealthier have never felt richer while everyday Americans continue to deal with tightened budgets from high prices.Interest ratesInterest rates are often not as noticeable to consumers as gas or grocery prices, which they come across every day. The impact that higher interest rates have on the economy takes longer to appear and runs deep. Interest rates shape how much Americans pay to borrow money – to run their businesses, pay off car loans and buy their homes.For the Federal Reserve, shifting interest rates is the tool it uses to balance the economy. Raising rates can cool the economy, bringing prices down, though at the risk of hurting the job market. Lowering rates can stimulate the economy at the risk of leading to more inflation.A line chart showing federal interest rateWhen Trump entered office in January 2025, the Fed was in the middle of a series of interest rate reductions. Officials said they were seeing inflation cooling and slower growth in the labor market. Interest rates were at a range of 4.25% to 4.5% – 1% lower than they were a year ago.Uncertainty around Trump’s new tariffs would ultimately lead officials to pause the reduction, though the president was still demanding lower rates. As tariffs proved to have less of a long-term effect on prices, the Fed started lowering rates again in fall 2025.For months, the Fed held off on changing rates as the economic impacts of the war of Iran bore out. But in September, the Fedhiked ratesfor the first time since 2023, by a quarter point. The Trump-appointed Fed chair, Kevin Warsh, said that “inflation is too high and has been for too long”.Higher interest rates have already had an impact on mortgage rates, which had dipped down to below 6% (for a 30-year mortgage) for the first time since 2022, in February, but are now up past 7%.Explore more on these topicsUS midterm elections 2026US economyInflationUS gas pricesUS unemployment and employment statisticsStock marketsUS interest ratesexplainersShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic files for stock market IPO; Meta announces $95bn fundraising drive to pay for AI expansion – as it happened | Business | The Guardian
description: Meta says share sale will support its “continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”, as Elon Musk warns some AI cloud computing firms face ‘guppy-level death’
Author: Graeme Wearden
Headline: Meta says share sale will support its “continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”, as Elon Musk warns some AI cloud computing firms face ‘guppy-level death’
Content: 07.41 EDTMeta to raise $95bn to help fund AI plansBoom! Meta has just announced plans to raise up to $95bn to help pay for its massive AI ambitions.The company behind Facebook, Instagram and WhatsApp is kicking off a new fundraising drive to fund “its core business and emerging AI opportunities”.The fundraising comes in two parts.First, Meta plans to raise $35bn through new “underwritten public offerings” – a sale of company stock.This offering has some big name backers –Nvidia,AMDandBroadcomhave all shown interest in taking part, Meta says. These ‘cornerstone investors’ could buy up to $5bn of the stock on offer.Second, Meta also plans to launch a $60bn “at-the-market offering” – in which it will sell new common stock to investors at the going market rate in future.The Silicon Valley giant says these plans will support “Meta’s continued investment in AI infrastructure and personal superintelligence”.It also says it is “investing with financial discipline,” saying:double quotation markAI is creating significant opportunities for Meta across its core business and new products and services. Meta’s AI investments are already generating tangible returns through increased engagement, improved advertising performance and increased monetization. Meta is also pursuing new opportunities across personal superintelligence, consumer and business agents, enterprise products, and AI glasses.The ‘at the market offering’ involves selling Meta’s new Class C Stock, which it announced last week it is creating. These Class C shares don’t have voting rights, so can be sold without diluting founder Mark Zuckerberg’s control of the company.Meta strikes deal with Mark Zuckerberg to help him foot billionaire tax billRead moreInternal forecasts last week showed that Meta needs to raise “hundreds of billions of dollars” over several years to fund its AI plans.Share

title: European gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fears | Gas | The Guardian
description: Jump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike Iran
Author: Lauren Almeida
Headline: Jump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike Iran
Content: Oil, gas and fuel storage units in Grays. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores across Europe.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAView image in fullscreenOil, gas and fuel storage units in Grays. The UK has some of the smallest gas stores across Europe.Photograph: Neil Hall/EPAGasEuropean gas prices soar to four-year high over winter supply fearsJump fuelled by fears of further Middle East supply disruptions amid reports of US-Israeli plans to strike IranLauren AlmeidaMon 26 Oct 2026 06.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEuropean gas prices have jumped to levels not seen since 2022 as fears continue to grow around the continent’s supply this winter and the conflict in the Middle East.Wholesale gas prices hit €97 (£81) a megawatt-hour on Monday, as temperatures across Europe fell and traders priced in stronger demand for heating.The UK’s month ahead contract also rose by 4% to 240p a therm, its highest level since December 2022 when prices were rocketing after Russia’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine.The jump in gas prices comes as fears grow that there could be further supply disruptions in the Middle East, amid reports theUS and Israel have drawn up plans for renewed strikes against Iranafter the US midterm elections.Those reports helped send the oil price as high as$117 a barrelon Friday. The international Brent crude benchmark retreated about 2% on Monday but remains at nearly $115 a barrel.Europe is also facing a shortage of stored gas reserves as it heads into winter with stores at their lowest level in more than a decade owing to a slowdown in exports from Qatar and an increase in consumption in the summer to power refrigeration and cooling. European storage is now about 75% full, against a seasonal average closer to 80%.Britain’s energy regulators have said the country isexpected to pay some of the highest energy costs in Europethis winter amid a reliance on imports to ensure a steady supply.The UK has some of the smallest gas stores in Europeafter decades of relying on homegrown production from the North Sea.The UK paid a record £4bn on power imports over the year ending in August, according to figures from the Office for National Statistics, of which half was spent on electricity imported from France.It has also made near-record payments over the past year to fire up gas plants while wind and solar farms have been paid to turn off because of bottlenecks in the grid.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toBusiness TodayGet set for the working day – we'll point you to all the business news and analysis you need every morningEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionMeanwhile, British households face growing energy bills, which arepredicted to rise 16%in January to reach the equivalent of about £2,000 for the typical annual dual fuel bill.European stock markets rose slightly on Monday on the weaker oil price, with the Stoxx Europe 600 – which tracks the biggest companies on the continent – up by 0.3% in early trading on Monday. The UK’s blue chip FTSE 100 rose by 0.4%.Explore more on these topicsGasCommoditiesOilEnergy billsEuropenewsShareReuse this content

title: Should we tip on takeout? We weighed all angles and the answer is … | Social etiquette | The Guardian
description: Adding gratuity doesn’t always make sense, but the obligation to has been entrenched as a societal norm
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Adding gratuity doesn’t always make sense, but the obligation to has been entrenched as a societal norm
Content: ‘Maybe it was a mistake to imagine that there’s one explanation for tipping rather than many of them – and that they change across time and place.’Photograph: lechatnoir/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘Maybe it was a mistake to imagine that there’s one explanation for tipping rather than many of them – and that they change across time and place.’Photograph: lechatnoir/Getty ImagesSocial etiquetteShould we tip on takeout? We weighed all angles and the answer is …Adding gratuity doesn’t always make sense, but the obligation to has been entrenched as a societal normWard Farnsworth and Saul LevmoreMon 26 Oct 2026 07.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.53 EDTShareYou arrive at a pizza place to pick up your order. The credit-card screen asks if you would like to tip and gives some choices. It seems strange to tip the cashier, who did nothing but hand over the pizza. But it also seems a little harsh to select “no tip” instead of one of those more generous options.What’s the right thing to do?Start with the situations where our instincts are clearest. Tipping is normal at restaurants, in taxis or after haircuts. We don’t usually tip when we buy fast food, ride on a bus or have the plumbing fixed.What explains the difference? One way to think about it is through economics. A server’s pay, in effect, is split in two: a salary paid by the restaurant, and a tip paid directly by you, the customer. But why do you get a say in the server’s pay when you don’t have that role in other cases?The logic is simple: you’re in a better position than the restaurant owner to judge the quality of the service.double quotation markYou know something the employer doesn’t. And that gives you a role in deciding how much the worker gets paidYou know whether the server was fast or slow – so your tip rates it as baseline, above baseline or below baseline. A low tip, though, can feel confrontational: you’re delivering your verdict in front of the person you’re judging.And it’s not just restaurants. A cab company knows how far the driver went, but not how well the car was driven. You know that, so you leave a tip. The owner of a hair salon knows how many customers were served, but not whether they were served well. Or take housekeepers at a hotel: you don’t watch them work, but you still know something the hotel doesn’t know: how big a mess you left behind.The common thread is that you know something the employer doesn’t. And that gives you a role in deciding how much the worker gets paid.But what about the places where we don’t tip?You don’t tip the cashiers at a fast-food restaurant. Why? The company trains the staff to say the same things every time, then watches them. You don’t see much that the company doesn’t. And the cashier works behind a counter where the pressure to keep moving is already strong.Gen Z wrestle with shame from ordering delivery food: ‘This economy is not for the weak’Read moreWhen you ride the crosstown bus, you don’t usually see anything important the bus company doesn’t, and the prospect of being tipped probably wouldn’t change what the driver does. So you don’t tip.Or a company sends you a plumber. You might know whether the problem got fixed, but not whether the plumber worked efficiently or cut corners. Since you don’t know anything the boss doesn’t, there’s no reason to give you a direct role in setting the agent’s pay.Compare this with a case where the plumber has to climb long stairs to reach you or face off against a scary dog. Here, you do know about hidden hardships – hidden from the plumber’s boss, that is – so tipping is a sensible economic gesture as well as a kind one.Still, the theory only gets us so far. Why don’t people usually tip employees of airlines, front-desk workers at hotels or baggers at the grocery store?Maybe it was a mistake to imagine that there’s one explanation for tipping rather than many of them – and that they change across time and place. In some cultures, there’s little or no tipping, and a tip might even be considered an insult.In fact, our theory above was a better fit in the United States 20 years ago than it is today, because invitations to tip have become more common in places where customers know little that management doesn’t already know.So why is the pizza place asking you for a tip in the first place?Some people imagine that the business is trying to get out of paying its clerks what it should; it’s foisting that job on to its customers. But that’s probably the wrong way to look at it. Clerks decide whether to take jobs and keep them based on the total pay they take home, wherever it comes from. Adding tips to their pay, in the long run, will probably hold down the base salaries that they’re paid.Look at it this way: if all tipping were banned tomorrow, you’d expect the base pay of servers to go up soon afterwards, along with prices on the menu. Otherwise the loss of tips would just be a pay cut; and if restaurants could pay less to their servers without losing them, they’d presumably (alas?) be doing it already.More likely, the takeout place just needs to somehow raise its prices. They think you’ll react better to an invitation to tip than you would to a more expensive menu, though it comes to the same thing. You’ll use the menu to decide what to buy and won’t think about the tip. Then when tipping is invited at the end, you won’t tell yourself the cafe raised its prices. You’ll just think the culture is changing: everyone wants a tip nowadays! But in effect, the invitation to tip is just a price hike that the owner is hoping you won’t view that way.There’s another oddity: the timing of the request. An unfamiliar invitation to tip sometimes comes early, when some of the work you’re buying hasn’t been done yet. This might give the server a chance to see your tip before performing and then retaliate on the spot with sluggish service if you seem ungenerous, or do a good job if you’ve been nice.This order of operations isn’t very consistent with the idea that you’re tipping in order to rate the quality of the work done.So what should you do when the screen asks you to tip?In those new settings – bakeries, coffee shop, fast-food places – your choice can function as a kind of vote – not on the quality of service, but on tipping itself. Leaving a tip accepts the invitation to help set the pay and encourages the arrangement to continue. If you don’t tip, you’re saying that you’re against using tips as a way to divide decisions about pay in this situation.But once tipping is customary – not auditioning for acceptance, but entrenched – then you should tip, at least usually. The obligation isn’t set by law, but you consent to it when you eat at the restaurant. The owner is saying, in effect: your obligation to pay for this meal will be a combination of laws (that make you pay the check) and norms (that make you pay the tip).‘It’s out of control’: the fight against US ‘tip-creep’Read moreYou should play by the rules that the business has set or not play at all, even if the rules might seem to defy your theory, or any theory, of when tipping serves a good purpose. But when deciding what to order or where to eat, just remember: 20% of the cost (or whatever the customary tip might be) isn’t shown on the menu.To put this more generally: if you run into a norm that you aren’t sure you like, ask whether you’re in a position to help shape it or whether you can only decide whether to go along with it.The bottom line: tipping for takeout doesn’t make sense as a custom. It should be resisted unless it’s entrenched, at which point it’s best viewed as part of the bargain.Put differently, we would vote against the idea; but having lost the vote, we go along with it.Ward Farnsworth is a professor at the University of Texas school of law, and Saul Levmore at the University of Chicago law school. This is an edited excerpt from their new book,Should You Tip for Takeout? Solving the Puzzles of Everyday Life, out nowExplore more on these topicsSocial etiquetteShare

title: Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warns | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Australian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Australian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’
Content: The ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, says ‘we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment’.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, says ‘we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment’.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warnsAustralian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’Follow ourAustralian politics live blogfor latest updatesGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerMon 26 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 20.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralians should prepare for more basic and important online services to go offline unexpectedly, the nation’s signals intelligence agency has warned, urging that “system security must be prioritised over system availability”.The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) also says businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarm that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever.In its annual cyber threat report, the ASD warns hostile foreign governments, criminals and hackers are using AI to gather intelligence, disrupt critical infrastructure and steal money, and that Australians should fight fire with fire.Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staffRead more“We need AI tools to help automate our defences to stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers,” the ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, said on Monday.“Australia must accelerate the modernisation of its technology and cybersecurity foundations to protect the systems we rely on every day.”The annual threat report, released on Tuesday, revealed that ASD had responded to 1,500 cybersecurity incidents in the 2025-26 year, an increase of 20% from the previous year. It also notified external entities – including businesses, governments and critical infrastructure – of more than 4,400 potential malicious cyber incidents, up 80% in a year. AI is expected to accelerate those dangers in future.ASD said government and private networks in Australia experienced “persistent” breach attempts from state-based actors last year, and claimed such actors “in the Indo-Pacific” could be launching attacks to prepare for potential future conflicts – including “future intelligence collection or disruption activities”.The agency said the increasing availability of AI was creating positive opportunities but also allowing cybercriminals and state-based actors to find vulnerabilities and launch attacks faster and more effectively. ASD warned “all network owners are facing elevated threat levels”, saying cybersecurity was now a “core business risk and leadership responsibility” for all organisations, no longer only a technical concern.The report said integrating AI tools into cybersecurity functions could help find potential weaknesses or suspicious behaviour, and improve responses.“To strengthen our cyber defences, we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment,” Bradshaw said.She has spoken previously about ASD having access toAnthropic’s Mythos model, the powerful AI tool the frontier lab said it could not release publicly because it could identify unknown flaws in IT systems. While the use of AI by malicious actors is on the rise, Australian government agencies believe having access to such frontier models and collaborating with leading AI labs is critical to bolstering cybersecurity.“To stay ahead, Australians must enhance their cyber defences while harnessing AI’s benefit,” the defence minister, Richard Marles, said on the report’s release.Tony Burke, the minister for home affairs and cybersecurity, said the government was “positioning Australia to respond to the evolving threats and opportunities presented by emerging technologies”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBradshaw said “legacy technology”, such as outdated systems or devices that were no longer supported with new updates by their creators, were among the biggest risks and most attractive targets for hackers. ASD called for Australia to modernise technology and cybersecurity capabilities, and said all organisations must take stronger action to ward off new threats.The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on | Peter LewisRead moreLast week,newly discoveredvulnerabilities in PHP – a programming language thatunderpins most websites– triggered a rush by governments and businesses to fix the problem.ASD urged organisations to update their systems, seek help from ASD and report suspicious incidents.Bradshaw and Marles said organisations should prioritise the security of their systems over keeping them online, which could mean more services are forced to go offline while they are secured.“In a threat environment transformed by AI, collective action is our strongest defence,” Bradshaw said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Potential WNBA finals decider to be played at 12.30pm on a Thursday | WNBA | The Guardian

Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: Game 6 between the Valkyries and the Dream will tip off at 9.30am on the west coast because an NBA game in Atlanta on the same day could not be moved
Content: Angel Reese and the Atlanta Dream will play Game 6 of the WNBA finals at State Farm Arena, but not in primetime.Photograph: Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAngel Reese and the Atlanta Dream will play Game 6 of the WNBA finals at State Farm Arena, but not in primetime.Photograph: Rich von Biberstein/Icon Sportswire/Getty ImagesWNBAPotential WNBA finals decider to be played at 12.30pm on a ThursdayValkyries-Dream Game 6 to tip at 9.30am on west coastGame moved to larger State Farm Arena in AtlantaHawks’ NBA game on same day could not be movedAssociated PressMon 26 Oct 2026 14.47 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.56 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleGame 6 of the WNBA finals between the Atlanta Dream and theGolden State Valkyrieswill be played at State Farm Arena on Thursday at 12.30pm ET, the league has announced. That means Valkyries fans in California will be watching the game at 9.30am local time.Dream guard Allisha Gray said it didn’t matter what time the game was played.“I mean, it’s the finals. You just gotta do what you gotta do,” she said. “We’re locked in on winning Game 6. I don’t care if we’re playing at 8am, 10am, midnight. We’ve got a championship to win.”TheWNBAworked hard with the NBA to move the game to State Farm Arena – home of the Atlanta Hawks – where Games 3 and 4 of the championship series were played. Game 5 will start at 8pm ET in San Francisco on Monday.Quick GuideWNBA finals 2026ShowScheduleBest-of-seven series. All times US Eastern Daylight Time (EDT).Sat 17 OctGame 1:Golden State 68, Atlanta 64Mon 19 OctGame 2:Atlanta 79, Golden State 65Wed 21 OctGame 3:Atlanta 97, Golden State 71Sat 24 OctGame 4:Golden State 67, Atlanta 62Mon 26 OctGame 5: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm (USA/CNBC)Thu 29 OctGame 6: Golden State at Atlanta, 12.30pm (USA/CNBC)Sat 31 OctGame 7: Atlanta at Golden State, 8pm* (USA/CNBC)*-if necessaryHow to watchIn the US, the series will air on NBC, USA Network and CNBC, with all games streaming on Peacock. In the UK, it will be carried by Sky Sports. In Australia, fans can watch through WNBA League Pass, with selected coverage also available through ESPN.Was this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.The Hawks have a game against the Cleveland Cavaliers on Thursday night that couldn’t be moved to another date or place. The only way they could make it work was to play in the early afternoon game. The Hawks game was moved back an hour.“The sellout crowds and extraordinary atmosphere at State Farm Arena for Games 3 and 4 were a tremendous success, and we’re excited to give thousands more fans the opportunity to experience Game 6 with a championship on the line,” WNBA commissioner Cathy Engelbert said in a statement. “We thank the NBA, Dream, Valkyries, Hawks, State Farm Arena and USA Network for the collaboration and flexibility that made this move possible. We look forward to delivering another unforgettable Finals experience in Atlanta.”skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly for the 2026 WNBA seasonSign up toWNBA 30A limited run women’s basketball newsletter dedicated to the league’s historic 30th season.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe WNBA finals are a basketball wonderland – unless you’re part of the Maga machineRead moreBy playing Game 6 in State Farm Arena, the Dream can have more than 17,000 fans as opposed to their normal home of Gateway Center Arena, which seats about 3,500. Game 3 was moved up a day to last Wednesday and Saturday’s contest started at 1pm ET so the Hawks could still host their home opener that night against Houston.That game was moved back 30 minutes to allow more time for the arena staff to change the building over for the Hawks contest. title: Creaking, smug … and a contender? Aaron Rodgers may yet get his Super Bowl farewell | Aaron Rodgers | The Guardian
description: The 42-year-old remains a polarizing figure. But the Steelers have a formidable defense and a quarterback who has seen it all before
Author: Melissa Jacobs
Headline: The 42-year-old remains a polarizing figure. But the Steelers have a formidable defense and a quarterback who has seen it all before
Content: Aaron Rodgers and Cameron Heyward walk off the field after Sunday’s win.Photograph: Todd Rosenberg/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenAaron Rodgers and Cameron Heyward walk off the field after Sunday’s win.Photograph: Todd Rosenberg/Getty ImagesAaron RodgersCreaking, smug … and a contender? Aaron Rodgers may yet get his Super Bowl farewellThe 42-year-old remains a polarizing figure. But the Steelers have a formidable defense and a quarterback who has seen it all beforeMelissa JacobsMon 26 Oct 2026 04.20 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.34 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAaron Rodgers is nowhere near this NFL season’s MVP conversation. At times in his second season with thePittsburgh Steelers, the almost-43-year-old has shown glimpses of the player he was in his prime, slinging the ball with zest and precision, able to suss out any coverage. Other times he has looked like, well, a guy in his 40s playing a young man’s game.Rodgers looked more like prime Rodgers in the Steelers’ gritty 16-10 win over the New Orleans Saints in Paris. He wasn’t satisfied with his side of the ball, telling reporter Molly McGrath, “I don’t think we played very good on offense today.” But Rodgers did enough to secure the win, including a 51-yard strike to DK Metcalf in the second quarter.He later scrambled for a first downon third-and-six to secure the win.Sure, there were points left on the table – the Steelers had several stalled drives and scored only one touchdown in four red-zone trips – and 16 points against a two-win team isn’t impressive. But the Steelers left France with a win, a 5-2 record and a ton of upside.So here’s a crazy thought: could Rodgers win a Super Bowl in his finalNFLseason?But when you consider the parts around Rodgers, perhaps it’s not so crazy. As competent as Rodgers was against the Saints, the defense stole the show. It smothered Saints quarterback Tyler Shough, and shut down the Saints’ run game as Steelers linebacker Patrick Queen had predicted. This Steelers run defense is punishing and only improving. In Weeks 1 through 4, it allowed 4.5 yards per carry. Over the last three weeks, that has dropped to 2.8 yards per carry. All told, Pittsburgh’s defense has allowed just three touchdowns in the last 15 quarters. That is some 2025 Seahawks-level domination.Offensively, Rodgers is no worse than Sam Darnold was last year when the Seahawks won the Super Bowl. He’s thrown 13 touchdown passes and five interceptions for 1,699 yards through his first seven games – Darnold had 12 TDs, four picks and 1,754 yards over the same span in 2025. Saints linebacker Kaden Elliss likened Rodgers to a point guard, noting the advantage he has over other NFL quarterbacks. “Even though he’s up there in age, I think that’s an advantage to him, his mind,” Elliss said after Sunday’s game. “And I think he used that today.”Maybe Rodgers’s football IQ could catapult Pittsburgh to a deep playoff run in the AFC. Yes, there are the perennial Super Bowl contenders like Kansas City and Buffalo, but no AFC team this season is a winning machine like the Patriots in the Brady-Belichick era.And, after a ho-hum Super Bowl from a star power perspective, a Rodgers return to the big stage would set off fireworks.Of course, Rodgers comes with plenty of baggage due to his commitment to his “own research” during the pandemic, his ridiculous antipathy towards Anthony Fauci and his habit of calling out coaches and teammates. Recently, though, he appears to have realized keeping his opinions to himself is probably the best course of action. His worst take over the weekend was appearing to think Peaky Blinderswas set in France rather than England. He’s not exactly likable, but considering what he’s said in the past, his recent behavior seems like progress.Not that he’s completely quiet. In Paris, when asked about the International Series, he let it be known that NFL owners had considered a 16-game schedule with two byes and an entire international week, where teams play all over the world. Instead,according to Rodgers, they opted for the 17-game schedule to rake in extra cash. Rodgers added that the league “may be a little tight on money”, a refreshing level of shade that will win him some fans.Realistically, Rodgers and the Steelers will need a good deal of luck to make it to the Super Bowl this year. But that’s the case for plenty of teams. A run to the title game would send Rodgers’s smugness off the charts, but you have to admit that his final game coming on Super Bowl Sunday would be interesting.MVP of the weekView image in fullscreenJoe Burrow walks off the field after Sunday’s win over the Ravens.Photograph: Stephanie Scarbrough/APJoe Burrow, QB, Cincinnati Bengals.Down 13-0 at the half, the Bengals looked destined for an infuriating loss, an art they specialize in. They had mustered just 49 passing yards, and were struggling to sustain drives. Meanwhile, the supposedly retooled Bengals defense couldn’t get the Ravens off the field. At the half, Baltimore, led by a backup quarterback, had dominated the time of possession 22:20 to 7:40. Yet again, Cincinnati looked like a fringe playoff team not meeting their full potential. And after locking up star receivers Ja’Marr Chase and Tee Higgins for Joe Burrow in his prime, being a fringe playoff team isn’t acceptable.Chase’s half-time team talk seems to have worked. “I told our offense [that] we can’t look at our defense the whole time. We’ve got to step this shit up and make something work,” he said after the game. Burrow, who is chasing his first league MVP, duly played out of his mind. He was essentially perfect after the break, dicing up the Ravens secondary for four touchdowns on four drives with 243 yards and an 89% completion percentage. Burrow made it look effortless as he tends to do at his best.Stat of the week64. How do the Tampa Bay Buccaneers win a game 43-13 when Baker Mayfield threw for only 64 passing yards? They faced a Carolina Panthers team who were a walking comedy of errors. Mayfield threw just 11 passes in his first game back from dislocating his thumb, and did connect with Tez Johnson for a score. The damage unsurprisingly came on the ground – Tampa rushed for 258 yards and three touchdowns, including two from Bucky Irving, who eclipsed 100 yards. The Bucs also strip-sacked Bryce Young and returned it for a touchdown. Imagine the score if Mayfield was slinging the rock.Video of the weekAllow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.bsky.app. We ask for your permission before anything is loaded, as the provider may be using cookies and other technologies. To view this content,click 'Allow and continue'.Allow and continueBo Nix came into Sunday’s game with just 37 rushing yards all season. So when the Broncos quarterback nearly doubled that total in one play – a62-yard touchdown runthat gave Denver a late second-quarter lead over Arizona – hell yeah, he was going to add a flourish.The spin move at the goalline might not have been necessary, but it must have been cathartic. Nix has been criticized for not providing an offensive spark, even though Denver entered the game at 4-2 after negotiating one of the league’s toughest schedules. But Nix looked far more comfortable – and at times electric – in Sunday’s 30-16 win. He finished with the one long rushing touchdown, and 222 passing yards.Elsewhere around the leagueView image in fullscreenJaxon Smith-Njigba was brilliant again on Sunday.Photograph: Steph Chambers/Getty Images-- The Chiefs were undefeated going into their game with the Super Bowl champion Seahawks but weknewKansas City had flaws. Patrick Mahomes has been good rather than great, the receiving corps is ravaged, and their schedule was soft to start the season. On Sunday Night Football, they were overwhelmed by Seattle, whose defense became the first unit this season to make former Seahawk Kenneth Walker III look human. And Seattle’s Jaxon Smith-Njigba was terrifying once again, hauling in 150 receiving yards in his team’s 20-3 win. “One hell of a game from Sam Darnold,” Smith-Njigba said, slightly underplaying his own contribution.–- The Miami Dolphins are no longer winless after humiliating the New York Jets 28-25 at MetLife. Geno Smith was outplayed by Malik Willis, who played clean football and was able to scramble at will, especially in the first half. Jeff Hafley outcoached Aaron Glenn, not a hard feat. Given New York’s talent advantage, they have no business losing at home to a 0-5 team with severe salary cap issues. But when the Dolphins have the ball for the final nine minutes of the first half and Glenn enters the break with all three timeouts remaining, winning is difficult. The Jets’ star receiver, Garrett Wilson, has cut a frustrated figure recently and was targeted just three times Sunday. CBS cameras caught him yelling on the sidelines, although he later denied his anger was directed at his quarterback, Geno Smith. “We were collaborating,” Wilson said. “I don’t even think I was talking to Geno.”This fan on Reddit summed it up best.–- The Minnesota Vikings moved to 6-0 after an ugly 16-10 win over the Indianapolis Colts. This was not the game that will leave the rest of the NFL believing the Vikings are a juggernaut. Colts kicker Spencer Shrader missed two field goals, and Minnesota sealed the win after Daniel Jones delivered a ball right to safety Harrison Smith. But the Vikings are the only undefeated team left in the league, something few would have predicted at the start of the season.–- The Houston Texans fell to 2-5 after a 27-21 overtime loss to the New York Giants, who move to 4-2-1 and are very much in contention in a weak NFC East. It was a masterclass by the Giants’ offensive line and running backs against a Houston team who were favored by 10.5 points. Cam Skattebo tore through the Texans line with 17 carries, 124 yards and a touchdown, a week after being benched. In his first start for New York, JJ McCarthy was sensational. While he had no passing touchdowns, McCarthy (20-of-28, 252 yards and no turnovers) was comfortable in the pocket and able to anticipate coverage under pressure. One bright spot amid the disappointment for Houston: Tank Dellcaught his first pass in 673 days. Dell suffered a torn ACL, MCL, LCL and a dislocated kneecap in late 2024, and his return is miraculous after a plethora of surgeries.–- The Atlanta Falcons handed the San Francisco 49ers their first loss of the season. The Falcons were opportunistic in the 29-20 win after a series of miscues by the 49ers. Brock Purdy threw two interceptions, including one on a pass he meant to be thrown away. The absence of the injured Mike Evans was felt keenly, and Christian McCaffrey missed a chunk of the game with a thigh injury, though he did return. Given the thin wide receiver corps in San Francisco,perhaps there’s an unhappy camper they can pursue.Explore more on these topicsAaron RodgersPittsburgh SteelersNFLUS sportsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: The horse that ushered in Manchester United’s 21-year tragic arc | Manchester United | The Guardian
description: There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment
Author: Jonathan Wilson
Headline: There’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected moment
Content: Manchester United’s success has been limited since the Glazers took over the club in 2005.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenManchester United’s success has been limited since the Glazers took over the club in 2005.Composite: Guardian Design, Getty ImagesSoccer with Jonathan WilsonManchester UnitedThe horse that ushered in Manchester United’s 21-year tragic arcThere’s plenty of blame to go around at Old Trafford. Like all downfalls it started with a seemingly small, unconnected momentSign up for our free newsletter hereJonathan WilsonMon 26 Oct 2026 10.43 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.29 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnd so here we are again, at that point as the nights draw in and Manchester Unitedprepare to sack a manager. Autumn: season of mists, mellow fruitfulness and a crisis at Old Trafford.Sunday’s 3-0 home defeat to Bournemouth, coming on the back of last week’s 4-1 reverse against Como, made clear what many had feared from the moment Michael Carrick was given the job on a permanent basis: that he isn’t up to it.But then, who could be? When you’ve burned through a long list of managers in 13 years, it’s perhaps worth considering whether the manager is really the problem. Could some blame perhaps go to the director of football, Jason Wilcox, or the chief executive, Omar Berrada, the people making the appointments? Or perhaps to Sir Jim Ratcliffe, the cost-cutting tax exile and minority shareholder with responsibility for sporting operations? Or to the Glazer family, who plunged the club into debt with a leveraged buyout in 2005 and have since made calamitous decision after calamitous decision, reducing the most successful club in English league history to a mid-table laughing stock with a roofthat leaks symbolically?It’s worth remembering where all this began. The United story has taken on the aspect of a classical tragedy and, like all good tragedies, it begins with a small, seemingly unconnected moment, amplified by pride, that ends up bringing the whole edifice crashing down.In 1999, Mull of Kintyre, a horse owned by the Irish millionaire John Magnier, won the Gimcrack Stakes at York. Traditionally, the winning owner would give a speech at the Gimcrack Dinner, but Magnier was a shy man who hated public speaking so he asked his friend, the United manager Alex Ferguson, to give the speech on his behalf. The racing establishment, though, refused: it had to be the owner. To spite them, Magnier named Ferguson as the owner of another horse, Juniper. The following year, Juniper was narrowly beaten in the Gimcrack Stakes. Magnier, though, was determined. So the year after that, he made Ferguson the owner of Rock of Gibraltar, which had won its first three races. Rock of Gibraltar won the Gimcrack easily and Magnier, waving a metaphorical two fingers at the racing authorities, watched Ferguson give the speech.Magnier was largely making mischief, but he was also happy to do a favor for a friend, to give Ferguson a better experience of racing, and he benefited from the association of the horse with such a famous name. In addition, Ferguson did not get on well with the United chairman, Martin Edwards, and had a sense that football clubs were becoming good investments. Accordingly Magnier and his associate JP McManus bought shares in United. (The full storyis explored by the journalist David Walsh here).It turned out, though, that Rock of Gibraltar was a much better horse than anybody had realized, winning seven Group One races in a row. The stud fees would be worth tens of millions of pounds. Ferguson believed the verbal deal was that he could choose 50% of the prize money won by Rock of Gibraltar (about £800,000) or 50% of the stud fees, which ended up being worth tens of millions. He went for the latter. Magnier’s recollection was rather different: 5% of the prize money or one stud nomination a year.Ferguson sued and, with his name on the ownership documents, probably would have won had it gone to trial. But then rumors started to spread about some of Ferguson’s financial dealings at United. Paid actors at United’s annual general meeting raised awkward points, then Magnier and McManus sent a list of 99 questions to the United board, which mysteriously found their way into the Daily Mail. United were highly embarrassed. Fans began to demonstrate against Magnier and McManus at race meetings. A settlement was reached, with Ferguson paid £2.5m to drop the action. But the damage was done.Magnier and McManus had decided to sell their shares in United, and another shareholder was ready and waiting: Malcolm Glazer. Ferguson backed Glazer, who launched his leveraged buyout. Magnier and McManus sold up in 2005 for £260m, a profit of a little under £100m. Had they waited for Ratcliffe, who bought a similar stake in 2024, they would have received roughly £1bn more than that. For Ferguson, a threat had been dealt with.The problem was that Glazer and his family would provesome of the worst club ownersin English history. For 20 years, United have been addled by debt and have made consistently terrible footballing decisions. Ferguson’s team was good enough, and his personality big enough, that United won five league titles and a Champions League after the takeover, but once his genius had gone, there was nothing left.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice weeklySign up toSoccer DeskJonathan Wilson and Guardian journalists bring expert analysis and reporting on the biggest stories in soccer.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionA mismatched squad built up over seven flawed managerial appointments and a multiplicity of conflicting approaches will not readily be sorted out. Carrick is the latest victim of a crisis 21 years in the making. For the want of a horse a club was lost.This is an extract from Soccer Desk, a newsletter from the Guardian US.Subscribe for free here.Explore more on these topicsManchester UnitedSoccer with Jonathan WilsonMichael CarrickUS sportsHorse racingThe Glazer familyfeaturesShareReuse this content

Content: Jalen Williams leaves the court on a stretcher after his injury on Sunday.Photograph: Kyle Phillips/APView image in fullscreenJalen Williams leaves the court on a stretcher after his injury on Sunday.Photograph: Kyle Phillips/APOklahoma City Thunder‘We’re not doing great’: Gilgeous-Alexander in tears after Williams suffers gruesome leg injuryGuard stretchered off court after apparent serious injuryTeam will learn more about status on MondayGuardian sportand agenciesSun 25 Oct 2026 23.06 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 09.37 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleShai-Gilgeous Alexander scored 34 points and theOklahoma City Thunderstayed undefeated but they lost All-Star guard Jalen Williams to what appeared to be a serious leg injury during their 108-101 victory over the Los Angeles Clippers on Sunday night.Oklahoma City won their third straight game to start the season but lost three players to injury, including Williams, who went down hard on a drive to the basket with 1:14 left. title: Doubles players sign open letter pleading with tennis chiefs to ‘protect’ format | Tennis | The Guardian
description: More than 150 doubles players on the men’s ATP tour have signed an open letter addressed to the ATP board, imploring the men’s tennis governing bodies to reconsider controversial doubles reforms
Author: Tumaini Carayol
Headline: More than 150 doubles players on the men’s ATP tour have signed an open letter addressed to the ATP board, imploring the men’s tennis governing bodies to reconsider controversial doubles reforms
Content: Francisco Cabral, of Portugal, and JJ Tracy, of the US, react in the men’s doubles final match against Lucas Miedler and Neil Oberleitner, of AustriaPhotograph: Shi Tang/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenFrancisco Cabral, of Portugal, and JJ Tracy, of the US, react in the men’s doubles final match against Lucas Miedler and Neil Oberleitner, of AustriaPhotograph: Shi Tang/Getty ImagesTennisDoubles players sign open letter pleading with tennis chiefs to ‘protect’ formatPlans to slash games by half and prize money criticised‘Hard for players to build and sustain a doubles career’Tumaini CarayolMon 26 Oct 2026 11.55 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 16.24 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 150 doubles players on the men’s ATP tour have signed an open letter addressed to the ATP board and management imploring the men’s tennis governing bodies to reconsider controversial doubles reforms and “protect” the format in professional tennis.The subject of potential reforms to the ATP has been a significant issue since players were informed in a meeting during Wimbledon that the ATP was conducting a review of its doubles regulations and potential changes could see doubles draws being halved at the ATP events in 2028. Under these proposals, ATP Masters 1000 events would host only 16 doubles teams and the main draws at ATP 500 and 250 events would accommodate only eight teams.Women’s tennis tour announces prize money parity with men in ‘major milestone’Read moreThe proposals could also lead to the total prize money distributed to doubles players being halved from 20% to 10%, with the remaining money allocated towards singles players. The news provoked significant criticism from a large group of doubles players at Wimbledon, and they have spent subsequent months organising to resist the reforms. In addition to more than 150 active players, the letter has been signed by more than 20 national federations and legends of the sport.In the open letter, the players state: “The current plans would shift about $20m (£15m) in prize money from doubles to singles, while cutting a significant number of professional opportunities for doubles specialists. That shift would make it much harder for talented players to build and sustain a doubles career. A healthy professional sport cannot rely solely on a small group of top stars; it needs pathways for players to develop, compete and earn a living.”View image in fullscreenNetherlands’ Sem Verbeek and Czechia’s Katerina Siniakova during their mixed doubles final at Wimbledon in 2025.Photograph: Kirill Kudryavtsev/AFP/Getty ImagesSem Verbeek, the 2025 Wimbledon mixed doubles champion and one of the players spearheading the campaign, told the Guardian that the doubles players feel the ATP’s potential reforms threaten the future of doubles and that the ATP has not sought to collaborate with doubles players to shape the future of the discipline.“The A to B with these proposals is really threatening not only the history, but also the present and future of the whole discipline of professional men’s doubles,” he said.“The livelihoods of a lot of players are at stake here, and not only that, I think also the dreams of any young player that wants to pursue a doubles career are really in big jeopardy.“I think that one of the big reasons that we have so much support for this open letter is to really provide the ATP with a platform to get in touch with us and make this more of a collaboration rather than a one-sided review that they keep saying is ongoing. But any real data and real numbers and real requests that we have have not been answered so far. And I think that’s why a lot of active players are so frustrated with this because we have a lot of ideas.”The ATP management views doubles as an unsustainable loss leader, and it intends to redistribute some of the money currently reserved for doubles to singles players, an initiative doubles players believe pits singles and doubles players against each other despite the fact that they are all members of the same association.“The main message that we want to send is the ATP really has to ­balance short-term economic growth with the legacy that it has built,” Verbeek said. “We understand that the ATP and ­tennis as a whole is entertainment, is a business but you also have a responsibility to all of your fans worldwide to protect and grow the legacy of both disciplines of your sport.“It’s been clear so far I think for a lot of people, if you look at how inaccessible doubles is from a viewership standpoint, that the ATP has under-invested and under-marketed the discipline so far. So we really just want to invite the ATP to really meaning­ful collaborations and meaningful discussions on how we can grow this part of the sport without damaging the future of it and allowing people to have a celebratory career in doubles. And I think that’s part of the reason that so many legends have signed on.“For some reason the generation of decision makers that are in the ATP right now feel like a doubles career is not a real tennis career. And that to us is ludicrous. It should be celebrated. It’s a discipline that has provided a lot of history and should provide a lot of future and it shouldn’t be looked at as, let’s say, a failed singles career or something like that.”This month the ATP announced widespread reforms to the calendar, schedule and rule book. In a Q&A attributed to the ATP chief executive, Andrea Gaudenzi, on the ATP website, the men’s tennis governing body addressed its potential doubles reforms. “Doubles will continue to be a core part of the ATP Tour,” ­Gaudenzi wrote. “The review is focused on identifying a model that gives the discipline a sustainable long-term future, works effectively for tournaments and fans and supports the wider player pathway.”Explore more on these topicsTennisnewsShareReuse this content

title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement  | La Liga | The Guardian
description: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at the Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points
Author: Sid Lowe
Headline: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at the Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points
Content: Real Madrid’s players converge after Kylian Mbappé’s late winner at Camp Nou.Photograph: Albert Gea/ReutersView image in fullscreenReal Madrid’s players converge after Kylian Mbappé’s late winner at Camp Nou.Photograph: Albert Gea/ReutersLa LigaMourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statementIt was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three pointsSid LoweMon 26 Oct 2026 12.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJosé Mourinho had already done thepor qué?,the printoutand the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in theclásicoon Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists.He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out.Davide Ancelotti wants to make a name for himself – will he do it at Lille?Read more“We have the best goalkeeper in the world, but none of us cried because Thibaut couldn’t play,” Mourinho said. Plenty might have felt like it, more reason to be fearful. But the coach called Andriy Lunin, the substitute goalkeeper so serious that he bought a roll of artificial turf and spent the pandemic diving round the living room of his flat, and told him this was his moment: “You train to play, not to sit on the bench, so go on.” As for the rest of them, the manager told them nothing changes: the plan remains in place. By the time they headed back to the dressing room, “Fucking get in!” echoing along the Camp Nou corridor, so it had proved.Thirteen years later, Mourinho was back in Barcelona for aclásicoand he had guided Madrid to a 2-1 win. It wasn’t supposed to be like this, or maybe it was. Barcelona, the team who had won nine in a row,banging in 4.3 goals per game, had been beaten by Madrid, the team who had lost twice already and, truth be told, were mostly just not very good. The night it could have been all over, the title race done when it’s not even in November, was instead the night it finally started. “If you leave here nine points behind, it’s very heavy psychologically; if it’s six, it’s more balanced; if it’s three, that’s different,” Mourinho said.View image in fullscreenJosé Mourinho returned to where it all began to continue his unbeaten streak against Barcelona.Photograph: Joan Monfort/APThis was different, and so is the season now. Counting theclásicosall those years ago, Mourinho racked up his sixth consecutive meeting withBarcelonawithout defeat, and there had been no parked bus, nor many lumps kicked. They didn’t just desperately hang on, although there was a moment when Dean Huijsen saved a shot with his face. Nor had they just waited for a moment, resisting and then robbing it, even if João Cancelo did insist: “That’s Madrid; they don’t have many chances but they score them.” The final shot count said 18-10 to Barcelona, and possession was 62% Barcelona’s.“The way we won is important: you can win luckily or by defending a lot. But we won with calmness and totally deservedly. We did it by being organised, concentrated and having the courage to come out from the back,” Mourinho said. And if that might have been pushing it a little – and, let’s face it, the analyses might be different had Lunin not made an astonishing save from Gerard Martín or Lamine Yamal’s second-half shot not faded just past the post – he had a point.Barcelona were not at their best. They had been hurried and imprecise, Rodri telling his teammates to lower their “pulse rate” as they came out for the second half. Lamine Yamal somehow missed an extraordinary chance just before the break. And when they did tighten the screw in the second half, they couldn’t break the wall. Xavi Espart was forced off, yet another injury at the back, the failure to sign a centre-back in the spotlight again. Yet this was still a faster, more aggressive, tighter Madrid than anyone expected. Asked to define it, Lunin went for “discipline and attitude”. And if that is partly about occasion, the least you can ask for, it’s more than you sometimes get.View image in fullscreenAndriy Lunin stepped up for Real Madrid in the absence of the ill Thibaut Courtois.Photograph: Jose Breton/APBesides, it was also more than that. More than Marc Cucurella getting under Lamine Yamal’s skin, although he certainly succeeded. They went for the space beyond Barcelona’s full-backs: superb in his firstclásico, aged 19, Yan Diomandé –the left winger– got more touches than any Madrid player, and protected his full-back as well. But it was more than that, too. More than the wonderful winning goal, a flash of inspiration with Jude Bellingham going all Nureyev, the ball flitting between his feet and Gabriel Jesus’s legs, pirouetting to release Eduardo Camavinga. This was a team with an idea and a victory that vindicated their manager, some kind of resurrection.Before the game, Rodri said that one of Madrid’s tricks is to convince you that they’re not that good, but insisted he wouldn’t fall into that trap. Still he felt that plan particularly. Pedri did too. Bellingham dealt with Rodri, Bernardo Silva with Pedri. Pressed and tired too, according to Hansi Flick, neither truly took control. The inclusion of Arda Güler and Silva – the surprise in the middle, starting his first league game in six weeks – underlined an intention for Madrid to keep the ball when they could. They actually had a midfield, which was new. From the back they tried to build, draw Barcelona in. And if a time came when they had to wait, to put bodies in before the ball, well, they would do that too. Six times Barcelona shots were blocked. At least twice more, shots were taken from their toes. At the other end, meanwhile, Madrid attacked with an intent and an incision that probably drew the clearer chances: the xG showed 1.19 v 1.94.Quick GuideLa Liga resultsShowAlaves 1-1 Malaga, Rayo Vallecano 0-3 Elche, Racing Santander 2-1 Espanyol, Valencia 1-2 Villarreal, Atlético 1-0 Deportiva A Coruna, A Bilbao 4-0 Getafe, Celta Vigo 0-0 Real Betis, Real Sociedad 2-1 Levante, Barcelona 1-2 Real MadridMonday:Sevilla v OsasunaWas this helpful?Thank you for your feedback.Victory puts Madrid three points behind Barcelona and, Federico Valverde claimed, “will give us a kickstart”. It has taken 10 weeks but it’s game on.Hay liga, as they like to say. There is league. There is Madrid, too. Something has shifted,starting in Rome, where 70 dreadful minutes gave way to 20 pretty good ones, another inexplicable comeback actually having something of an explanation, too.
