could see one of the matches broadcast free-to-air on Channel 5.The Guardian has learned thatChannel 5is also in advanced talks with Cricket Australia over a highlights package for the eight-match tour, with the ­terrestrial broadcaster also in discussions over securing live rights for one of the five T20 ­internationals.­Channel 5 has live rights for two home men’s and two women’s T20s each summer in a four-year deal that began this year, but has never broadcast an England match from overseas.While the finer details are still being discussed, the opening T20 of the five-match series in Melbourne on 21 November is the game of ­greatest interest to Channel 5, as the start time of 8.15am on a Saturday is likely to attract the biggest UK audience.If the deal is completed it would be the first time an England overseas game has been broadcast FTA since Channel 4 picked up the rights for a Test series in India in 2021 during the final Covid-19 lockdown.TNT Sports has broadcast ­England’s past three Ashes series in Australia so its decision to bid for a white-ball tour, that also attracted interest from Sky Sports and Dazn, comes as little surprise.Channel 5’s involvement is an intriguing development, however, which raises the prospect of more cooperation between the two over sports rights given that they are both owned by the US media giant ­Paramount Skydance.Channel 5 also picked up a highlights deal for the Commonwealth Games in the UK last summer with the event broadcast exclusively live on TNT Sports.Brendon McCullum’s white-ball squad fly to Australia at the start of next month following a brief return home after the conclusion of the one‑day international tri-series that is ­taking place in Pakistan, where England are struggling to reach the final after due tosuccessive defeatsto the hostsand Sri Lankaover the past seven days.After criticism of their preparation for last winter’s Ashes series the England and WalesCricketBoard has scheduled a 50-over warm-up game at the WACA on 7 November ahead of a three-match series that begins at the Perth Stadium on 13 November, with five T20s beginning the week later.The value of overseas cricket rights has fallen in recent years with the result that most of England’s winter tours have only been sold at the last minute.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe SpinSubscribe to title: NFL today: How to watch Cowboys v Eagles, TV channels & live stream Monday 26 October | Dallas Cowboys | The Guardian
description: How will Dallas and Philadelphia fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Author: Alex Kirshner
Headline: How will Dallas and Philadelphia fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream options
Content: The Eagles are likely to blitz Dak Prescott regularly on Monday night.Photograph: Sam Hodde/APView image in fullscreenThe Eagles are likely to blitz Dak Prescott regularly on Monday night.Photograph: Sam Hodde/APNFL watching and streaming guideDallas CowboysNFL today: How to watch Cowboys v Eagles, TV channels & live stream Monday 26 OctoberHow will Dallas and Philadelphia fare today? Here is what to know, including kick-off time, TV channels and live stream optionsAlex KirshnerMon 26 Oct 2026 16.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 16.11 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThere is “reeling”, and then there is whatever theEaglesare doing heading into Monday Night Footballagainst the Cowboys. Philadelphia have lost four games in a row to fall within a whisker of last place in the NFC East.Jalen Hurts’s blood clotsrapidly escalated and have probably knocked the franchise QB out for the season. Backup Tanner McKee has inherited a legitimate crisis. And it’s not as if all was hunky-dorybeforeHurts went out. The Eagles had already blown a 10-point fourth-quarter lead to the Rams and let the Jaguars come back on them in shocking fashion in London before the Hurts news.The Cowboys have their own enormous issues. Former Eagles assistant Christian Parker joined up as defensive coordinator, aiming to fix a bad unit, but the Cowboys are still struggling to keep teams from racking up big point and yardage totals. Facing the Cowboys defense has been a salve for struggling offenses, as when a Packers team who couldn’t convert a third down for their life suddenly converted nine of their first 10 against Big D last weekend.Despite these issues, both teams are within reach of the first-place Giants in the East. This is a critical game even though it is mainly compelling for the anxieties on both sides of the rivalry.Date:Monday 26 October 2026Time:8.15pm ET/5.15pm PT/12.15am GMT (Tuesday)Stadium:Lincoln Financial Field (Philadelphia, Pennsylvania)How to watchUnited States:Watch onESPN or ABC, or stream throughFuboorESPN Unlimited. Fubo’s ABC availability depends on location.Canada:Stream onFubo Sports ProorDAZN. Fubo Sports Pro includes NFL Game Pass on DAZN.United Kingdom:Watch onSky Sports NFL or Sky Sports Main Event, or stream withNOWorNFL Game Pass on DAZN.What to watch forFor Philly, McKee’s comfort level will be the most important thing. In his first 2026 outing, last week’s 25-14 loss to the Panthers, McKee threw 45 passes and prioritized getting the ball out quickly to leave less time for bad things to happen. McKee averaged 3.1 completed air yards per attempt, which ranks 40th in theNFLso far this season, according to Pro Football Reference. (The idea there: McKee did not successfully complete many passes more than a few yards beyond the line of scrimmage.) Most troublingly, the Eagles got just 2.9 yards after the catch per completion, a comically low rate that would have McKee last among regular starters.The Cowboys will be on high alert for blitzes from Eagles defensive coordinator Vic Fangio, who has surely observed Dak Prescott’s trouble against the blitz over his past two games. Fangio is one of the least-blitzy defensive coordinators in the league this season, but teams have drastically escalated their blitzing against Prescott, who has poor numbers against it (no touchdowns and a passer rating of 67when blitzed in his last two games). Could it be that the much greener McKee is not the only QB to have an ugly time in this one?Explore more on these topicsDallas CowboysNFL watching and streaming guidePhiladelphia EaglesUS sportsNFLnewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in US | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Latest example of unauthorised behaviour shows AI model bypassed paywall to access data as part of statistics project
Author: Dan Milmo
Headline: Latest example of unauthorised behaviour shows AI model bypassed paywall to access data as part of statistics project
Content: Anthropic said its AI model found a loophole in an old version of the Georgia state agency’s website.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersView image in fullscreenAnthropic said its AI model found a loophole in an old version of the Georgia state agency’s website.Photograph: Dado Ruvić/ReutersAnthropicAnthropic’s Claude AI model accessed Georgia voter data in USLatest example of unauthorised behaviour shows AI model bypassed paywall to access data as part of statistics projectAnthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis songs to train AI modelsDan MilmoGlobal technology editorMon 26 Oct 2026 07.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.42 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropic’s Claude model accessed voter data in the US state of Georgia, the AI company has confirmed, in the latest example of unauthorised behaviour by the technology.The AI model managed to bypass a paywall to reach data that is publicly available but is typically accessible only after paying a fee. Claude accessed aggregate vote counts as part of a statistics project at Anthropic, which is preparing for a$1.5tn (£1.1tn) flotation.“Claude did not access the state’s voter registration system, change any voting records, or pull any individual voter records,” Anthropic said.Anthropic said the AI found a loophole in an old version of the state agency’s website, discovering that it issued a digital entry pass – an “access token” – to visitors. It then requested a token and gained access to the information.The AI developer said it had since put in place guardrails to prevent similar actions happening again. The incident was first reported by the news website Axios.Anthropic had pointed out the unauthorised behaviour earlier in the month when it said in a blogpost that it had found examples of ​Claude “working around a restriction to reach data that ‌was ⁠gated by a token or a fee” and that some of these cases involved websites run by US ​government agencies. At the time, it said the incidents had “minimal real-world impact”.The unintended actions flagged by Anthropic included a model submitting a fake tip about an unsolved murder to the Philadelphia police department. The US state department also revealed this month that an Anthropic model had filed 19 visa applications in August.Examples of unauthorised behaviour by AI agents – programs powered by AI models that carry out tasks autonomously – have been mounting since OpenAI, the company behind ChatGPT, revealed in July that its bots hadhacked an AI startup.Since then, it has emerged that an OpenAI agent hacked theAustralian healthcare system, and the UK’s AI security institute revealed that Anthropic agents had carried out a hacking campaign against real peopleduring a cybersecurity test.This month, the UK’s AI minister said he expected an AI-driven cyber-attack similar to the Australia hack, describing such an incident as likely, “if not inevitable”. Kanishka Narayan said the government wouldconsider using the cyber security and resilience billas a vehicle for introducing AI safety regulations, including making it mandatory to report AI safety incidents.In the US, the White House’s newly formedSuper Intelligence Force– a federal body overseeing AI development – is mandating that all AI companies report security incidents involving their technology.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicAI (artificial intelligence)Technology sectorComputingGeorgianewsShareReuse this content

title: Anthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industry | Anthropic | The Guardian
description: Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability
Author: Blake Montgomery
Headline: Market debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viability
Content: Dario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, in Bengaluru, India, on 16 February 2026.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersView image in fullscreenDario Amodei, the CEO of Anthropic, in Bengaluru, India, on 16 February 2026.Photograph: Priyanshu Singh/ReutersAnthropicAnthropic files for potentially record-breaking stock market valuation in key test for AI industryMarket debut of firm behind Claude chatbot will be one of largest in US history, a test of AI boom’s financial viabilityBlake MontgomeryandJohana BhuiyanMon 26 Oct 2026 12.22 EDTFirst published on Mon 26 Oct 2026 09.12 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAnthropichas publicly filed for a stock market listing in what is slated to be one of the largest debuts in history. The company’s float on the US market will serve as a test of the financial viability of the multitrillion-dollar AI boom.Analysts and investors have valued the San Francisco-based company, founded in 2021, at more than $1.5tn. The company, which will will list under the symbol ANT,confidentially filedwith US financial regulators for an initial public offering in June.“We believe AI is one of the most consequential technologies in human history,” the company’sinvestor prospectusreads. Anthropic researchers and executives have trumpeted the transformative power of AI while simultaneously warning of its potential to cause human extinction.Anthropic researchers say AI could cause human extinction by 2030Read moreA leader in the race to create powerful artificial intelligence models and a bellwether of the American AI boom, Anthropic’s chatbot Claude is its flagship product, which offers text generation features as well as advanced coding and cybersecurity capabilities. CEODario Amodeifounded the company after quitting OpenAI, the maker of ChatGPT.Anthropic’saudited filingswill offer the first public glimpse of its financial health, which have been the object of intense speculation in recent months as questions of apotential AI bubble swirl.The company detailed rapidly rising revenue in the prospectus: $41m in 2023, $386m in 2024, $4.585bn in 2025 (an increase of more than 1,000%), then $16.286bn in the first six months of 2026 alone. The company disclosed that, as of the end of June, it had raised $141.1bn.Despite the increasing revenue,Anthropicdisclosed a net loss of $80bn for the first half of 2026.Anthropic has focused on businesses as its primary paying customers, unlike OpenAI, which has courted everyday consumers for ChatGPT. As of 30 September, Anthropic said it had more than 14,000 enterprise customers – 11,900 of which had $100,000 or more of revenue, more than 1,900 that had $1m or more revenue and about 250 enterprise customers that had $10m or more revenue.“The speed and depth of our enterprise customer adoption are powerful evidence of Claude’s position at the frontier of AI,” Anthropic executives wrote.The filing contains some of the hyperbolic language characteristic of AI companies predicting the miraculous potential of their technology. Describing the potential of AI agents, semi-autonomous chatbots that can carry out tasks on behalf of users, Anthropic executives wrote: “The result is something without historical precedent: what we refer to as a country of geniuses in a datacenter, available to every organization and sector of the economy.”Investing in Anthropic and the development of a model that the company claims could revolutionize knowledge work across industries comes with a great deal of risk. Anthropic listed more than 90 pages of potential to its business. For one, a “substantial portion” of the company’s revenue comes from a limited number of customers, and losing any of them could put a huge dent in their revenue. A quarter of Anthropic’s revenue comes from its top five customers, though no single customer represents more than 10% of its business.The company also has incurred $6.2bn in debt as it built out its infrastructure and spends billions yearly on computing power provided by third parties, according to the filing.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toTechScapeA weekly dive in to how technology is shaping our livesEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionAnthropic sued for allegedly using 274 Elvis Presley songs to train AI modelsRead moreThe misuse of AI and Claude in particular also poses a considerable risk to Anthropic’s business. When it comes to AI, there are four categories of potential risk, executives wrote: misuse by bad actors, loss of control, authoritarian abuse and economic disruption. Anthropic’s most capable models have “capabilities that could provide meaningful assistance to malicious actors seeking to develop chemical, biological, or other dangerous weapons”, the company’s executives wrote. The company deploys technical safeguards, “but such safeguards are incomplete, may be outdated in light of evolving threat models, have been and may in the future again be circumvented, or may fail to operate as intended.”Amodei has called for a slowdown of AI’s development, citing existential risk. Anthropic’s stock market listing may elicit a rush of investment in the company and the AI sector more broadly, which could speed up the pace of the industry further.The company disclosed that in September 2025, staffers documented what they believe was the first large-scale cyber-attack that didn’t rely on significant human intervention. Anthropic “detected and assessed with high confidence that a Chinese state-sponsored hacking group manipulated our Claude Code tool into attempting infiltration into roughly 30 global targets, including large technology companies, financial institutions, chemical manufacturing companies, and government agencies”.Donald Trump’s administration may also be a risk to the company. Anthropic has been embroiled in a feud with the Trump administration over the use of the startup’s products in warfare, which culminated in the designation of the company as a supply chain risk, a first for an American company. This prevents any military agency from contracting with Anthropic. The company has challenged the blacklisting.Explore more on these topicsAnthropicStock marketsUS marketsAI (artificial intelligence)Dario AmodeiChatbotsIPOsnewsShareReuse this content

title: Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warns | AI (artificial intelligence) | The Guardian
description: Australian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’
Author: Josh Butler
Headline: Australian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’
Content: The ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, says ‘we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment’.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, says ‘we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment’.Photograph: Hollie Adams/ReutersAI (artificial intelligence)Australians should prepare for online services to go down unexpectedly as threats rise, cyber agency warnsAustralian Signals Directorate chief says advanced AI tools are needed to defend against ‘AI-enabled attackers’Follow ourAustralian politics live blogfor latest updatesGet ourdaily political email,free appordaily news podcastJosh ButlerMon 26 Oct 2026 07.30 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 20.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAustralians should prepare for more basic and important online services to go offline unexpectedly, the nation’s signals intelligence agency has warned, urging that “system security must be prioritised over system availability”.The Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) also says businesses and critical infrastructure must use cutting-edge AI models to defend against digital threats, raising alarm that artificial intelligence is enabling more dangerous threats than ever.In its annual cyber threat report, the ASD warns hostile foreign governments, criminals and hackers are using AI to gather intelligence, disrupt critical infrastructure and steal money, and that Australians should fight fire with fire.Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staffRead more“We need AI tools to help automate our defences to stay ahead of AI-enabled attackers,” the ASD director general, Abigail Bradshaw, said on Monday.“Australia must accelerate the modernisation of its technology and cybersecurity foundations to protect the systems we rely on every day.”The annual threat report, released on Tuesday, revealed that ASD had responded to 1,500 cybersecurity incidents in the 2025-26 year, an increase of 20% from the previous year. It also notified external entities – including businesses, governments and critical infrastructure – of more than 4,400 potential malicious cyber incidents, up 80% in a year. AI is expected to accelerate those dangers in future.ASD said government and private networks in Australia experienced “persistent” breach attempts from state-based actors last year, and claimed such actors “in the Indo-Pacific” could be launching attacks to prepare for potential future conflicts – including “future intelligence collection or disruption activities”.The agency said the increasing availability of AI was creating positive opportunities but also allowing cybercriminals and state-based actors to find vulnerabilities and launch attacks faster and more effectively. ASD warned “all network owners are facing elevated threat levels”, saying cybersecurity was now a “core business risk and leadership responsibility” for all organisations, no longer only a technical concern.The report said integrating AI tools into cybersecurity functions could help find potential weaknesses or suspicious behaviour, and improve responses.“To strengthen our cyber defences, we must harness the technologies that are reshaping the threat environment,” Bradshaw said.She has spoken previously about ASD having access toAnthropic’s Mythos model, the powerful AI tool the frontier lab said it could not release publicly because it could identify unknown flaws in IT systems. While the use of AI by malicious actors is on the rise, Australian government agencies believe having access to such frontier models and collaborating with leading AI labs is critical to bolstering cybersecurity.“To stay ahead, Australians must enhance their cyber defences while harnessing AI’s benefit,” the defence minister, Richard Marles, said on the report’s release.Tony Burke, the minister for home affairs and cybersecurity, said the government was “positioning Australia to respond to the evolving threats and opportunities presented by emerging technologies”.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Every weekdaySign up toPolitics, reallyOur political team brings you up to speed on the stories that really matter and what they mean for youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBradshaw said “legacy technology”, such as outdated systems or devices that were no longer supported with new updates by their creators, were among the biggest risks and most attractive targets for hackers. ASD called for Australia to modernise technology and cybersecurity capabilities, and said all organisations must take stronger action to ward off new threats.The biggest threat from AI is the sense that we have no say in it. To that I say game on | Peter LewisRead moreLast week,newly discoveredvulnerabilities in PHP – a programming language thatunderpins most websites– triggered a rush by governments and businesses to fix the problem.ASD urged organisations to update their systems, seek help from ASD and report suspicious incidents.Bradshaw and Marles said organisations should prioritise the security of their systems over keeping them online, which could mean more services are forced to go offline while they are secured.“In a threat environment transformed by AI, collective action is our strongest defence,” Bradshaw said.Explore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)newsShareReuse this content

title: Microsoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cuts | Microsoft | The Guardian
description: Tech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reports
Author: Gaya Gupta
Headline: Tech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reports
Content: The Microsoft campus in Mountain View, California.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenThe Microsoft campus in Mountain View, California.Photograph: David Paul Morris/Bloomberg via Getty ImagesMicrosoftMicrosoft to reportedly offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in latest cutsTech company offers buyouts in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of AI, according to reportsGaya GuptaMon 26 Oct 2026 14.44 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.54 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMicrosoft announced that it would offer buyouts to 60,000 employees in an effort to reduce costs amid the rising use of artificial intelligence, according to reports, the latest example of how AI is reshaping tech companies and the greater workforce.This is the latest of several trimmings Microsoft has made to its workforce this year. The company announced in April that it was offering voluntary retirement to about 7% of its US workforce, which consisted of about 125,000 employees at the time. Its global workforce is made up of about 223,000 workers globally.Some of Microsoft’s most recognizable divisions – including Xbox, Windows and Copilot, its AI tool – will be participating in the offer, Bloomberg reported on Monday. Employees in certain divisions, including in cybersecurity, datacenters and marketing, would not be eligible for the offer, it said.“This offer gives eligible employees who may be considering a future outside the company a new choice to make that transition now with support. It also gives participating organizations another way to adapt their workforce to changing needs,” Amy Coleman, Microsoft’s executive vice-president and chief people officer, said in a statement. The company did not respond to a request for comment on further details about the offer.Multiple tech companies have announced layoffs due to the rise of AI and increased investment in the technology this year. Meta, the parent company of Facebook and Instagram, announced plans in April to cut 10% of its personnel, or about 8,000 employees, to boost efficiency. Amazon has madeseveral cuts to its workforce, most recently in its retail division. And in June, Oracle shed its workforce by nearly 13%, cutting 21,000 jobs,as a result of AI.But it’s unclear whether these workforce-reduction measureshave translated yet into greater efficiency,and some companies, including Meta, have scaled back their layoff plans. A top leader of Microsoft, Ryan Roslansky, recently complained about “AI slop” in the workforce on social media.The National Bureau of Economic Research also recently published aworking paperwhich found that among the 9,000 senior executives it surveyed from around the world, 90% said AI had yet to result in greater productivity at their companies.Explore more on these topicsMicrosoftAI (artificial intelligence)Job lossesTechnology sectornewsShareReuse this content

title: Sunlight at night: US startup’s demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws criticism | California | The Guardian
description: Company imitates reflection of sun from mirrors, prompting pushback from some scientists, environmentalists and California locals
Author: Oliver Milman
Headline: Company imitates reflection of sun from mirrors, prompting pushback from some scientists, environmentalists and California locals
Content: ‘A coalition of environmentalists and astronomers are far less excited about Reflect Orbital’s ambitions.’Photograph: Reflect OrbitalView image in fullscreen‘A coalition of environmentalists and astronomers are far less excited about Reflect Orbital’s ambitions.’Photograph: Reflect OrbitalCaliforniaSunlight at night: US startup’s demonstration of lighting Earth from space draws criticismCompany imitates reflection of sun from mirrors, prompting pushback from some scientists, environmentalists and California localsOliver MilmanMon 26 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.39 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleLocals in a rural area ofCaliforniawere recently startled to see dazzlingly bright light shining down from nearby mountains at night, illuminating a swathe of the desert below.Unbeknown to them, the strange nocturnal illumination was the latest step in a company’s plan to erect thousands of giant mirrors in space to reflect sunlight on to the Earth during night-time.The night-time light demonstration, near the town of Lone Pine in the Sierra Nevada region, was conducted by a US startup calledReflect Orbital, which has an almost sci-fi aim to launch 50,000 satellites into space in the next decade to illuminate parts of the world at night.In July, the Federal Communications Commission (FCC)approvedReflect Orbital’s proposal to launch an initial demonstration satellite next year, which will orbit the Earth and, via a 59ft-diameter mirror, reflect sunlight in 3-mile-wide beams in strengths from moonlight up to the brightness of the sun at noon.The demonstration in California, undertaken earlier this month, showcased what this would look like on the ground, to the bewilderment of locals, one of whomcalledthe lights “blinding”. Large mobile lights were erected near Mount Whitney, with Reflect Orbital comparing the radiance to that of a full moon.This provided, the company said, a realistic simulation of one of the benefits of this technology: to help search-and-rescue teams and other emergency responders at night. Other planned uses include bathing crops in sunlight, replacing broken streetlights and even providing solar power for military operations, all summoned by the tap of a button on an app.“Search-and-rescue teams are expected to be our first customers, so this was a real-world test conducted alongside teams who would use our technology,” said a spokesperson for Reflect Orbital, which partnered with a local search-and-rescue team for the demonstration.“We’ll keep working closely with local communities and authorities wherever we operate, and are excited to show how this technology can help save lives.”View image in fullscreen‘The demonstration in California, undertaken earlier this month, showcased what this would look like on the ground.’Photograph: Reflect OrbitalA coalition of environmentalists and astronomers arefar less excited about Reflect Orbital’s ambitions, however. These groups have criticized the company and the FCC for threatening a harmful change to the separation of night and day that will affect everything from people’s sleep to wildlife and the ability to see the stars from Earth.“This is an idiotic project,” said Jan Hasselman, a senior attorney with Earthjustice, an environmental group. “There are a huge number of unresolved questions and significant potential impacts. Literally all of life on Earth evolved based on the rhythm of day and night and there is a ton of data showing that messing with this is not a good idea.”“There needs to be some sort of discussion and analysis before we grant these people the right to fundamentally alter the night sky,” he added. “The proposal for 50,000 of these satellite mirrors is crazy and would really end the night sky as we know it.”Bomb the Arctic, dam the Mediterranean and build a second moon: five outlandish plans to remodel our climateRead moreIn August, four groups represented by Earthjusticeasked the FCC to reconsider its approval, citing concerns that opening up the skies to mirrored satellites, which would ascend to about 400 miles (645km) above the Earth’s surface before reflecting light back, would cause a litany of problems.Animals such as birds, insects and mammals rely on the reliable change between day and night to feed, shelter and mate, with any change to this being potentially disastrous for some species.Astronomers, meanwhile, have complained that this night-time glare would worsen existing light pollution and spur an overall rush to add more satellites to orbit – Elon Musk’s SpaceX plansto place 1 million celestial datacenters around Earth– that will obscure the stars and cause more space debris that could descend as pollution back to our world.There are also concerns that the scrambling of night and day will harm people’shealthby disrupting their circadian rhythms as they sleep. Looking directly at the unusual glaring sunlight at night would also, much like doing so during a solar eclipse, harm people’s eyes.Reflect Orbital has said its technology will actually aid the environment by boosting the energy output of solar panels when sunlight is pointed at them during night-time, thereby reducing reliance on fossil fuels.But some climate scientists have warned against meddling with the amount of sun’s energy reaching Earth. Proposals forsolar geoengineering, in which particles are sprayed into the atmosphere to deflect sunlight away from Earth instead of toward it,have also prompted fierce opposition.“Global warming is happening because the Earth has a radiative imbalance due to the massive amounts of greenhouse gases we’ve dumped into the atmosphere,” said David Ho, a climate scientist at the University of Hawaii.“Some people are promoting the already unhinged idea of installing space mirrors facing away from the Earth to reflect the sun’s energy in order to decrease global warming. Imagine wanting to turn those mirrors around so that the Earth gets hotter.”Reflect Orbital said it has had “substantive discussions” with scientists and astronomers on the use of its technology so that areas such as astronomical sites, national parks and other wildlife-rich areas are avoided.“We welcome oversight and want to play a role in shaping it,” a spokesperson said. “We believe it is our responsibility to work alongside governments, scientists and regulators rather than ahead of them.”Explore more on these topicsCaliforniaSpaceSatellitesThe sunGeoengineeringTrump administrationWest CoastfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Lula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in peril  | Jordana Timerman | The Guardian
description: After the rejoicing, it will be vital to learn the lessons. The rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible, but progressives cannot rest for a moment, says commentator Jordana Timerman
Author: Jordana Timerman
Headline: After the rejoicing, it will be vital to learn the lessons. The rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible, but progressives cannot rest for a moment, says commentator Jordana Timerman
Content: Supporters gather to watch Lula speak in São Paulo on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenSupporters gather to watch Lula speak in São Paulo on 25 October 2026.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersOpinionBrazilLula miraculously beat the Brazilian far right and Donald Trump. But have no doubt: the region is still in perilJordana TimermanAfter the rejoicing, it will be vital to learn the lessons. The rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible, but progressives cannot rest for a momentMon 26 Oct 2026 11.11 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 20.15 EDTShareThe impossible happened. President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silvawon a fourth termin Sunday’s runoff election in Brazil, overturning Flávio Bolsonaro’s first-round lead in a historic comeback. No candidate has ever lost the first round and won the second, until now. Grassroots mobilisation, alongside social welfare policies, helped turn the contest into a referendum on Brazilian democracy, rallying voters against a candidate seeking to restore the legacy of his father, Jair Bolsonaro,imprisoned for plotting a coupafter his 2022 defeat. Lula’s victory suggests that defending democracy can still be a powerful electoral argument against the ascendant right.Having already consolidated most of the leftwing vote, Lula had limited room to attract supporters of other candidates after his first-round defeat. His best chance lay in mobilising abstainers and reconnecting with working-class voters. The Workers’ party intensified its grassroots and digital campaigns, using social media influencers and messaging networks to reach supporters. Nearly 3 million more Brazilians voted in the runoff, and Lula gained ground across the country, particularly in major cities and his north-eastern strongholds. He also appealed to voters’ immediate economic concerns, drawing on a record of reducing poverty and inequality, andincreasing benefits under Bolsa Família, the landmark welfare programme he launched in 2003. Lula framed the election as a choice between protecting social gains and democratic institutions, or returning to the Bolsonaro family’s attacks on both, warning that his opponent would compromise Brazil’s sovereignty by aligning himself with Donald Trump.The implications extend far beyond Brazil. Lula’s victory interrupts a regional trend: rightwing candidateshave won seven presidential electionsacross Latin America in the past 18 months. Two decades ago, Lula was among the leaders of Latin America’s pink tide, a succession of leftwing governments that reshaped the region’s politics and sought greater autonomy from Washington. Today, he finds himself resisting a new regional wave moving in the opposite direction, without a comparable coalition of allies.Lula’s victory is welcome, but we shouldn’t forget that Flávio Bolsonaro wonmore than 48%of valid votes, demonstrating the enduring strength of a movement with substantial representation in an increasingly rightwing congress. His proposals on security and the economy appealed to voters frustrated by high living costs, including working-class Brazilians who had traditionally supported Lula. This mirrors the success of authoritarian-leaning rightwing candidates across the continent. Frustration with crime, economic insecurity and established political parties has propelled a new right promising tougher security policies and attacking progressive social agendas. From Nayib Bukele in El Salvador, to Javier Milei in Argentina, to the recentelection of Abelardo de la Espriellain Colombia.The emerging rightwing alliance is, in many ways, the mirror image of the pink tide, developing in close alignment with Trump and his ambitions to reassert US dominance over the hemisphere.The relationship is mutually reinforcing: rightwing leaders who gained ground through domestic discontent look to Washington to consolidate their power, while the US relies on those same governments and movements to advance its strategic interests. In his victory speech, Lula said the surge of street support in recent weeks “was a demonstration that this country refuses to be anyone’s back yard”. His declaration directly challenges the so-calledDonroe doctrine, which asserts an expanded US role in policing the region.Since returning to office, Trump has used endorsements, sanctions, tariffs and financial assistance to reward allies and put pressure on opponents. Hebacked rightwing candidatesin Honduras and Colombia. He has turned a blind eye to Salvadoran president Bukele’snegotiations with criminal organisations(Bukele denies having made an informal pact with these organisations). And ahead of Argentina’s 2025 legislative elections,he offered Milei a $20bn financial lifelinewhile warning that US generosity depended on the electoral outcome.Security provides a particularly powerful instrument for this alignment. The Trump administration has invoked the fight against “narcoterrorism” to expand its military role and apply pressure on governments to accept Washington’s priorities. Terrorist designations have helped justify the operation that captured Nicolás Maduro in Venezuela,threats of unilateral strikesagainst Mexican cartels andjoint military operationsin Ecuador. Washington has also discussed similar operations with Colombia. The designations do not themselves authorise military action, but they strengthen the administration’s justifications to intervene beyond US borders.Brazil demonstrates how this strategy can also serve Washington’s allies outside government. The Bolsonaro family had itselfsought Washington’s interventionagainst the Brazilian judiciary during Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The Trump administration imposed tariffs on Brazil and sanctions againstsupreme court justice Alexandre de Moraes. Following lobbying from the Bolsonaros, Washington also designated Brazil’s two largest criminal organisations as foreign terrorist organisations, reinforcing Flávio Bolsonaro’s campaign message that Lula was failing to confront organised crime.The stakes extend beyond the Bolsonaro family’s political fortunes. Washington has pressed Lulafor access to Brazil’s critical mineralsas it seeks to reduce dependence on China. Lula has defended Brazil’s freedom to trade with other partners.Brazil shows that Trump’s interventions can backfire. In 2025,Lula’s approval ratings roseafter Washington threatened punitive tariffs over Jair Bolsonaro’s prosecution. The president turned the dispute into a defence of national sovereignty, making resistance to foreign interference a defining theme of his re-election campaign. The electoral effect of Trump’s involvement is difficult to isolate, but the backlash helped Lula mobilise support. Combined with grassroots organising, appeals to democracy and social welfare policies, it offers one possible response to the regional right’s advance.Yet a defining feature of that resistance is that it has remained national. Brazil’s size gives it a capacity to resist Washington that none of its neighbours possess. Lula has also been pragmatic in keeping that resistance national, rather than attempting to forge a regional coalition against Trump’s hemispheric ambitions.He also faces a strengthened right at home. Flávio Bolsonaro hasrefused to concede, seeking to annul the election over a last-minute extension of voting hours that both campaigns had requested. Electoral authorities maintain that the extension did not affect the outcome.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe region’s rightward shift also obscures a fragmented political landscape. Across Latin America, deeply divided electorates have produced closely contested elections, complicating claims that either the left or the right has established a durable political hegemony.Brazilis a case in point: Lula’s victory interrupted the right’s advance, but nearly half of voters backed a candidate who embraced much of Trump’s agenda.Lula’s victory shows that the rightward shift is neither inevitable nor irreversible. But the movement retains substantial electoral support, influence over the political agenda and a powerful ally in Washington. Brazil may have stopped the blue tide at its borders, but it has yet to emerge as a regional bulwark against it.Jordana Timerman is a journalist based in Buenos Aires. She is the managing editor of The Ideas Letter and compiles the Latin America Daily BriefingThe Guardian’s Latin America correspondent Tom Phillips will be answering your questions about the election and the future of Brazil from 1500 GMT on Tuesday 27 October as part of ourConversationsseries. Email questions toconversations@theguardian.com.Explore more on these topicsBrazilOpinionAmericasLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroJair BolsonaroUS foreign policyDonald TrumpcommentShareReuse this content

title: Donald Trump has been a disaster for rural America | Steven Greenhouse | The Guardian
description: The president’s policies have taken such a toll on farmers that Republicans face trouble in deep-red states
Author: Steven Greenhouse
Headline: The president’s policies have taken such a toll on farmers that Republicans face trouble in deep-red states
Content: ‘When Trump plunged the US into the Iran war and his many trade wars, he showed little concern about what those decisions might mean for rural America.’Photograph: Charlie Neibergall/APView image in fullscreen‘When Trump plunged the US into the Iran war and his many trade wars, he showed little concern about what those decisions might mean for rural America.’Photograph: Charlie Neibergall/APOpinionDonald TrumpDonald Trump has been a disaster for rural AmericaSteven GreenhouseThe president’s policies have taken such a toll on farmers that Republicans face trouble in deep-red statesMon 26 Oct 2026 08.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.25 EDTShareDonald Trump’s policies have been a disaster for the nation’s farmers, so much so that a near electoral miracle may soon happen: Kansas, one of the deepest red, most rural states, may electits first Democratic senator in nearly a century.Since Trump won farm country handily in 2024, many rural voters in Kansas, Iowa and elsewhere have soured on him because the price of diesel fuel, a key input for farming, has soared by nearly 70%, because farm bankruptcies have surged and because Trump’s trade wars have significantly reduced agricultural exports.Rural voters are so upset with Trump that polls show that Republican Senate candidates stand a good chance of losing in Kansas, Iowa, Nebraska and Texas, even though Trump won those rural states by 13 percentage points or more in 2024. No wonder Trump is hopscotching madly across Kansas, Iowa, and other states in the midterm campaign’s final weeks.America must reverse Trump’s moral squalor | Robert ReichRead moreNo one is saying that Trump deliberately hurt farmers, but when he plunged the US into the Iran war and his many trade wars, he showed little concern about what those decisions might mean for rural America. It was nearly inevitable that Trump’s moves would batter farmers – by pushing down soybean and other farm exports and by pushing up the price of fuel, fertilizer and farm equipment. Not only that, Trump’s proudest legislative achievement, his “big, beautiful bill”, further hammered farm country with its major cuts to food assistance and its$1tn in Medicaid cuts, which will cause anestimated 1.8 million rural Americansto lose health insurance.“He has sold out rural Americawith his policies,” said Jon Tester, a third-generation Montana farmer and former US senator.Even the Cato Institute, a Republican-friendly, conservative thinktank, slammed Trump over what he has done to farmers. A Cato commentary stated that while Trump calls this a “golden age” for farmers, the fact is that Trump’s “tariffs are inflicting serious damage”on farmers, increasing their input prices and causing their exports todecline by billions of dollars.This helps explain whyfarm bankruptcies have jumped by 85%over two years ago.Little wonder that a recent KFF/AP poll found that roughlysix in 10 rural voters disapproveof how Trump is handling the economy, while about halfbelieve the economy is in worse shapethan when Trump returned to office.Indeed, many rural voters have turned against Trump – whilenearly two-thirds backed himin 2024, now less than half, 49%, of rural voters say they support GOP candidates this fall,according to a Fox News poll.At a recent news conference in Washington, John Hansen, president of the Nebraska Farmers Union, sought to convey the pain and anger many farmers feel. “Because of the misuse of tariffs, record high agricultural input costs, soaring fertilizer costs”, and “high interest rates”, Hansen said, farmers “arefacing the worst economic and financial crisissince the farm crisis of the 1980s”, when many farms went under because of sky-high interest rates.In a direct slap at Trump, Hansen added: “Just when farmers need to expand markets for their products, the president seems to be at war with our nation’s top three trading partners: Mexico, Canada and China. When trade wars break out,farmer noses always bleed first and worst and longest.”Many rural voters backed Trump in 2024 because he promised to cut prices, including energy prices, and vowed not to plunge the US into unnecessary, expensive wars overseas. But now many feel betrayed because Trump began an unnecessary, expensive war against Iran that caused diesel fuel – which farmers rely on for their tractors and combines – to soar toa record $6.52 a gallonin late September, before declining somewhat(to $6.32).This price spike – dieselaveraged $3.75 a gallonbefore the war – cost most farmers thousands of extra dollars when many were barely breaking even.“Compared to last year,our fuel bill is $50,000 higher,” Vance Ehmke, a Kansas farmer, told the Hastings (Nebraska) Tribune, while “fertilizer, that’s going to be at least another $20,000 or $40,000 increase. That’s all due to Trump and his war in Iran. We are madder than hell about it.“I want to tell you that I am a Republican, and I’m pissed.”Last month, the American Farm Bureau Federation ran a bad news article saying “the record-high input cost environment”, meaning high diesel and fertilizer prices, means that “no major row crop”, such as soybeans or corn, “is projected to clear break-even” this year”.In Texas, Kansas, Nebraska and other farm states, ranchers are fuming that Trumpannounced plans to import roughly 660m lb of tariff-free beefwith the aim of cutting beef prices by 25% – one of the many ways Trump’s tariffs angered consumers was by pushing up beef prices.The National Cattlemen’s Beef Association voiced dismayabout Trump’s beef imports, saying the move would undercut the struggling industry’s stability.The North Carolina farmer Matt Bell had a warning for Republicans.Bell, who voted for Trump in 2024, told CBS News: “Everything we touch has gone up. We’re in a position now where we’re mad and ready to be heard.”With rural America in deep pain, Bell and many other farmers who traditionally backed Republicans want to send a message to the party that controls the White House, Senate and House. Many are angry that GOP lawmakers haven’t sought to protect farmers by fighting against Trump’s tariffs and war against Iran.“We need to get some other voices in thereto push back a little bit on this stuff,” Nancy Danner, a soybean and corn farmer in Iowa, told the Wall Street Journal. “We need as many changes as we can get.” Danner said she planned to vote only for Democrats in November.A Wall Street Journal headline had bleak news for the GOP, saying: “Republicans arefacing the worst political environmentin farm country in decades.”All this dismay could go far to elect Democratic Senate candidates in rural states:Josh Turek in Iowa, Adam Hamilton in Kansas, Roy Cooper in North Carolina and James Talarico in Texas, not to mention the independent progressive Dan Osborn in Nebraska.John Tsitrian, a South Dakota business executive who writes about rural America, didn’t mince words about who’s to blame.“Farmers are hurtingthanks to Trump’s apocalyptic screw-up,” he wrote. Perhaps the biggest screw-up, in Tsitrian’s view, has been the loss of global markets caused by Trump’s never-ending trade wars, which he said had caused long-lasting “structural damage” to US farmers.Before Trump’s first term, the US and Brazil each provided about 40% of China’s soybean imports. But as a result of Trump’s repeated trade wars with China and China’s search for more reliable, less antagonistic trading partners, theUS now provides just 23% of China’s soybeans, with Brazil providing over 60% and Argentina 10%. With China importing around$60bn worth of soybeans annually, that means a painful loss of $10bn a year in US soybean exports.Trump has long been known to seek to shovel money, often lots of money, to people who are angry at him. Just look at his shameless plan tohand out $5,000 to every American adult.Seeing how upset farmers are about sky-high diesel prices, Trump announced a new handout on Monday at a rally in Kansas – he promised$8bn in emergency aid to US farmersin what he called the Harvest Fuel Relief Program. It seemed like a desperate, last-ditch effort to rescue Kansas’s incumbent Republican senator, Roger Marshall. That came after Trump announced a previous $12bn bailout of farmers last December.While acknowledging that farmers need emergency aid, South Dakota’s Tsitrianwrote, “Today’s tough farm economy, in regular need of federal cash infusions, is the result of a disaster that has a specific name attached to it: Donald Trump. Unlike most disasters, this one wasutterly foreseeable.”Across rural America, there is fast-increasing frustration, dismay and anger about economic conditions, Trump’s policies and GOP lawmakers whom farmers have long supported.“This Republican-led Congress has not donetheir job,” said Hansen, the Farm Union president. “They have not helped our nation’s farmers in our time of need, and it is time for a change.”Steven Greenhouse is a journalist and author, focusing on labor and the workplace, as well as economic and legal issuesExplore more on these topicsDonald TrumpOpinionUS midterm elections 2026Trump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: If Democrats win big, will they learn the right lessons from their victory? | Jan-Werner Müller | The Guardian
description: No election outcome ever interprets itself. So how will Democrats interpret these results once they are known?
Author: Jan-Werner Müller
Headline: No election outcome ever interprets itself. So how will Democrats interpret these results once they are known?
Content: Democratic candidate for Michigan’s Senate seat Abdul El-Sayed. ‘As the joke goes, every gas station display of prices has become an ad for Democrats.’Photograph: Robin Buckson/Detroit News/APView image in fullscreenDemocratic candidate for Michigan’s Senate seat Abdul El-Sayed. ‘As the joke goes, every gas station display of prices has become an ad for Democrats.’Photograph: Robin Buckson/Detroit News/APOpinionDemocratsIf Democrats win big, will they learn the right lessons from their victory?Jan-Werner MüllerNo election outcome ever interprets itself. So how will Democrats interpret these results once they are known?Mon 26 Oct 2026 06.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.12 EDTShareWhichever metaphor one prefers – landslide, earthquake, wave – it seems increasingly like theDemocratscan expect a significant victory in themidterms.As the joke goes, every gas station display ofpriceshas become an ad for Democrats; what’s more, some of them have managed to connect the relatively abstract issue of corruption to the daily misery of many Americans.But, in the end, no election outcome ever interprets itself;Democratsshould not rest content with the conclusion that only what moderate leaders (and consultants) like to call kitchen table issues really mattered.They have a historic opportunity to dislodge the image of theRepublicansas the party of national security and the party best trusted with the economy.After 2024, Republicans massively benefited from elite actors – Silicon Valley oligarchs, no less than many journalists – reading a globally important “vibe shift” into the presidential election outcome; we now know that what political scientists politely call “low-information voters” were simply fed up with inflation, as opposed to a large majority thirsting for a far-right agenda.But Trumpists turned the perception to their advantage; and to be sure, successful politicians are entitled to interpret a vote as they see fit.Democrats could stay relatively timid and read the outcome as simply a rejection ofDonald Trumpand the most egregious elements of his misrule since January 2025; they certainly should make the point that the spectacular cruelty of ICE and the incitement to hatred in which Stephen Miller and JD Vance regularly engage is deeply unpopular with the public. But it would be a mistake to see the outcome as only a referendum on Trumpism.True, the US president’s catastrophic record in foreign policy is partly explained by conduct the old Republican establishment could never have imagined: recklessly alienating allies, with the result that the US maynever be trusted by Nato countries again; massively destroying soft power by mistreating foreign students and undermining the capacity of American universities to attract talent internationally; blatant interference in elections to favor the global far right.double quotation markAs soon as Democrats are in charge, Republicans discover debt constitutes a national crisisBut the Iran war shows continuities with the George W Bush era that neoconservatives probably find uncomfortable to contemplate: an inability to think strategically and an apparent indifference to loss of human life. In fact, a line can be drawn from the torture memos to the murders at sea and the plans for a public execution under the US secretary of defense, Pete Hegseth.Yet the Republican party still lives off an image that the party of Ronald Reagan is supremely competent in matters of national security. The right response is not that Democrats should not enter a competition of how often they can use the word “lethality” in one sentence; they should simply point out how shameful it is that Republicans, some murmuring on the part of has-beens likeThom Tillisaside, have betrayed Ukraine; how damaging the loss of bases in the Middle East will turn out to be; and that, from the very beginning of Trump 2.0, it was a sign of deep unseriousness to put a second-rate TV host in charge of the world’s most powerful military force. There might be monuments to both Trump and Hegseth in Moscow and Beijing one day; after all, they effectively capitulated to the former and sped up the rise of the latter.The Republican party has also long benefited from the notion that, as the party of business, they are best qualified to boost the economy (no doubt, some low-information voters still buy into the myth of Trump as the great entrepreneur).The actual record has long shown something different: not just when it comes to Trump and his string of bankruptcies, but for the party as a whole. Since Trump engaged in policies so irrational and damaging that the old Republican establishment would never have contemplated them – tariffs being the obvious example – it is again easy to overlook continuities.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Weekly, plus breaking news alertsSign up toThe Stakes 2026A weekly guide to what really matters in the US midterms, plus breaking news alerts.Enter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe party that claims to be deeply concerned about debt and deficits (one of Elon Musk’s disingenuous justifications for Doge’s chainsaw massacres) has given us Reagan, Bush and Trump – all of whom managed massively to increase the national debt. The reason is, of course, that they pushed through enormous tax cuts that overwhelmingly benefited the wealthy.In the postwar period, economic growth, job creation and even stock market returns have on the wholebeen higher under Democratic administrations; it just seems that average gains are not enough for the uber-wealthy, who can buy themselves tax cuts by donating massively to Republicans.Needless to say, as soon as Democrats are in charge, Republicans discover that the very debt they were instrumental in causing constitutes a national crisis and requires deep cuts to social security.Conventional wisdom has it that the Biden administration overreached: too woke, too ambitious a Green New Deal, too harsh in its criticisms of Maga Republicans (with the next claim usually being that such overreach made a “backlash” inevitable and, so the implication goes, at least somewhat legitimate).But what if the opposite is true? What if Joe Biden’s mistake was to assume that there were still many Republicans who cared about policy – as opposed to endless culture war performance a la Hegseth – and long-term success for the country?What if Democrats seized the opportunity to discredit their opponents in the way Franklin D Roosevelt made the most of the Great Depression (as opposed to pining for bipartisanship); what if they showed people that all the Republicans who will soon be running away from Trump were not just complicit in the misrule, but that the misrule has been part of a larger story predating Trump?Explore more on these topicsDemocratsOpinionUS midterm elections 2026RepublicansDonald TrumpTrump administrationUS politicscommentShareReuse this content

title: In a rush to lure AI companies, the Australian government risks undoing a creative ecosystem that has taken decades to build | Dan Guthrie | The Guardian
description: If proposed copyright reforms proceed, Australia will become a global IP-laundering paradise. Why would a UK business license its TV shows here if they can be scraped at will?
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: If proposed copyright reforms proceed, Australia will become a global IP-laundering paradise. Why would a UK business license its TV shows here if they can be scraped at will?
Content: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. ‘They buy electricity. They buy talent. They buy water,’ Dan Guthrie writes. ‘Why should content be the only thing they get for free?’Photograph: Jason Redmond,ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenOpenAI CEO Sam Altman and Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei. ‘They buy electricity. They buy talent. They buy water,’ Dan Guthrie writes. ‘Why should content be the only thing they get for free?’Photograph: Jason Redmond,ludovic Marin/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionAI (artificial intelligence)In a rush to lure AI companies, the Australian government risks undoing a creative ecosystem that has taken decades to buildDan GuthrieIf proposed copyright reforms proceed, Australia will become a global IP-laundering paradise. Why would a UK business license its TV shows here if they can be scraped at will?Mon 26 Oct 2026 18.21 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 18.37 EDTShareAustralia and the UK have always had a shared love of creativity. We consume each other’s TV, news, music and books. Our chefs appear on each other’s TV channels and quite frankly I was bereft when the ABC’s The Newsreader ended its run in the UK.That shared love though, appears not to be reciprocated by the Australian government. Its rush to attract AI investment from big US tech, and the extreme copyright reforms that it believes need to go along with it, threatens a creative ecosystem that has taken decades to build.The Albanese government’s proposed reforms would give US big techunrestricted access to Australian and international content. This would allow AI companies to get access to everything Australians and their global fellow creators create online under an“opt out” model.Everything Australians put online could be scraped for AI under proposed new rules. How will you be affected?Read moreWe have been there in the UK. Our government had a similar idea. It believed it could attract AI investment and deliver copyright reform at no cost to the UK creative sector. This is not a zero-sum game. Weaken copyright and you weaken the creative industries. There is a massive trade-off. A one off, short-term investment will damage the potential of the creative sectors for future generations.We know our colleagues in the Australian creative economy are incredibly worried, and so they should be. The ability to decline a transaction is a fundamental feature of any functioning market. If a seller cannot realistically say no, their ability to negotiate a fair price is significantly diminished. The same principle applies to creative works. By requiring creators to make their works available unless they successfully opt out (which they can’t, as opt-outs don’t work in practice), the proposal risks weakening both creators’ rights and the market value of their work. Experience in the European Union suggests that opt-out systems are failing at scale.There is more at stake, though. If Australia goes ahead with its reforms it would become the global IP-laundering paradise of creative content. Why would a UK creative business license its TV shows in Australia if they can be scraped at will? Why would a global news publisher syndicate its news into Australia? That would mean less investment in Australia and less choice for Australians, and put Australia at odds with many of its international treaty commitments. It could also fuel piracy, exposing Australians to malware.This doesn’t mean we are anti-AI. In fact, we are the opposite. The UK’s creative sector is one of the most advanced adopters of AI. We want that to be responsible adoption, though. We also want sovereign AI capabilities to ensure we can protect national security, but that doesn’t happen by being a vassal of US big tech. National security begins with economic security, and throwing the creative sector under the bus doesn’t do that.The solution is for AI firms to license the content that their models don’t work without. They buy electricity. They buy talent. They buy water. Why should content be the only thing they get for free? Large AI firms are shopping around the world trying to sell their snake oil and the price is copyright reform. International creative businesses are looking at Australia and cannot believe the government has been duped, as the UK government so nearly was.We urge the Australian government to slow down, to look in more detail at the economics of what they are proposing and choose an Australian way, rather than one dictated by US tech. Maybe then we might even get that elusive fourth series of The Newsreader.Dan Guthrie is the director general of the Alliance for Intellectual Property in the UKExplore more on these topicsAI (artificial intelligence)OpinionIntellectual propertycommentShareReuse this content

title: As students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed Serbia | Novak Simin | The Guardian
description: After freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning state, says Novak Simin, a member of Serbia’s Student List movement
Author: Novak Simin
Headline: After freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning state, says Novak Simin, a member of Serbia’s Student List movement
Content: Student List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/APView image in fullscreenStudent List supporters in Belgrade react to the rightwing Serbian Progressive party conceding defeat on Sunday.Photograph: Marko Drobnjaković/APOpinionSerbiaAs students we never sought power – here’s how we reclaimed SerbiaNovak SiminAfter freedom, we want to give our people something radical: a normal, functioning stateMon 26 Oct 2026 15.04 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.56 EDTShareTwo years ago, I harboured no political ambition whatsoever. I was a student at the faculty of technical sciences in Novi Sad, my home town, pursuing a PhD in human resources and simply living my life. That was until thecanopy collapse at the newly renovated train stationin Novi Sad in November 2024, which killed 16 people. I took part in street protests and rallies in response to this shocking event, and like many others, realised that it needed to be a turning point.This was not an unavoidable tragedy. Systemic corruption and a culture of entrenched impunity were obvious factors in the collapse. But instead of ordering a full and impartial investigation and coming clean on official failings, the authorities began pushing back against us for demanding justice. We werevilifiedand attacked in the streets but law enforcement did nothing. So we took refuge in our lecture halls and schools, barricading ourselves inside faculty buildings, ready for a long haul.Democratic principles have long been ignored in Serbia but we made sure we observed them in our gatherings. As our coordination developed, we made sure we had the same clear goal for every demonstration we organised: pressuring a corrupt government to meet our demands. And these were demands that in any free country would have been accepted automatically. We wanted, for example, all the documentation concerning the renovation of Novi Sad railway station to be made public, without redaction, and that everyone responsible for the works be held to account. We demanded that those who assaulted us in the streets be arrested and prosecuted. Instead of agreeing, state officials beganbrandingusfascists and traitors.I was personallytargetedfor speaking out. As I handled media relations and communications, this often meant giving interviews to the country’s few remaining independent outlets. For this, I was accused by the regime’spropaganda machineof money laundering “millions” and conspiring with foreign powers. Others had to leave the country after being accused of high treason; some spent months in detention on manufactured, illegally obtained evidence. Many of us were placed under surveillance, our parents threatened, and many were fired from jobs and dragged through the mud in the pro-government popular press.But none of that intimidation broke us; rather it hardened our resolve. And eventually, when it became clear the regime would never concede, we opted to enter the electoral arena ourselves. That was the genesis of theStudent List. Through open, democratic plenary sessions, we nominated individuals of integrity and competence, people who were committed to justice and freedom for a silenced society.Our aims were clear and never wavered: we wantedSerbiato be governed by the rule of law, independent public institutions, transparency and solidarity in a fractured nation. We marched thousands of kilometres across Serbia, campaigning relentlessly and in doing so helped, I believe, to rekindle hope among the broader public. State propaganda could not hope to drown out that much unfiltered grassroots momentum.Now the regime has fallen, our collective effort to rebuild Serbia begins. True, sceptics may argue that we have filled parliament with political novices. The truth is that we have filled it with people eager to serve and willing to learn. Our newly elected representatives are professors, doctors, lawyers, farmers and scientists, all experts in their fields. Each has an established record of honest work and civic integrity. They may lack traditional political backgrounds, but they have spent the past two years studying the realities of governance and public trust. That very lack of direct political involvement is why the Serbian people have placed their faith in us: they did not vote for slick rhetoric or cynical manoeuvreing. They voted for clean hands.We are neither promising, nor expecting overnight miracles as a result of this victory; rather we hope for something fundamentally radical for Serbia: normal, functioning institutions.This mandate must first of all dismantle the culture of impunity. That requires verifiably independent prosecutors, fully transparent public procurement processes, and legal accountability for anyone who treated state resources as private spoils. For too long our teachers, healthcare workers and civil servants have seen their expertise subordinated to party loyalty cards. We want to restore the dignity of these dedicated public servants.We have taken our country back, and are proud to stand as free citizens of Serbia. If this historic turning point proves anything, it is that this country does not belong to an untouchable ruling elite. It belongs to all of us. We have proven that dignity is non-negotiable. Now, the real work begins. This victory marks the end of institutional fear. For the first time in years, we can breathe freely.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionNovak Simin is a member of Serbia’s Student List movementDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
