title: We’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music too | Sadiq Khan | The Guardian
description: We’ll revive the in-person shopping experience with a transformation of the area, inspired by the John Lewis and Selfridges founders who first set up there, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Author: Sadiq Khan
Headline: We’ll revive the in-person shopping experience with a transformation of the area, inspired by the John Lewis and Selfridges founders who first set up there, says London mayor Sadiq Khan
Content: An architectural illustration for the transformation of the Oxford Street areas, with pedestrianised zones, grass and trees.Computer-generated: AVR LondonView image in fullscreenAn architectural illustration for the transformation of the Oxford Street areas, with pedestrianised zones, grass and trees.Computer-generated: AVR LondonOpinionLondonWe’ve made Oxford Street traffic-free – and that’s just the start. Soon there’ll be green spaces for arts and music tooSadiq KhanWe’ll revive the in-person shopping experience with a transformation of the area, inspired by the John Lewis and Selfridges founders who first set up thereSadiq Khan is the mayor of LondonMon 26 Oct 2026 02.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.56 EDTShareAt around 8pm on Sunday evening the last car made its way down Oxford Street, marking the start of a momentous new era for our nation’s high street. Today, after decades of discussions and deliberations, the action we’ve taken means almost one kilometre of Oxford Street is now officially traffic-free – just in time for Christmas. But this is only the start of a much bigger transformation, and the first step towards a bright new future for this historic thoroughfare.Walk down Oxford Street, and you’re passing through hundreds of years of British history and culture. In 1864, an ambitious young draper called John Lewis opened his first shop on the street. Forty-five years later, the American entrepreneur Harry Gordon Selfridge arrived with a radical idea: to transform shopping from a mundane necessity into an unforgettable experience. He filled his store with dazzling window displays, world-class entertainment, restaurants and lounges. He even installed women’s toilets – a rarity in Edwardian England – giving women a newfound freedom to make the most of the city. As he opened the doors to his first customers, he told them “everyone is welcome”.That spirit has been at the heart of Oxford Street’s success ever since. We love it because it feels as if it belongs to all of us. It’s where teenagers come for their first shopping trip with friends. Where families marvel at the magic of festive lights and decorations. And where generations of Londoners and visitors have come to discover the latest music, fashion and trends. It’s also the beating heart of British retail – pumping billions into our national economy, with the surrounding area accounting for an incredible1% of the UK’s total economic outputin 2022.But in recent years this iconic streethas started to lose some of its sparkle. Changing consumer habits and the legacy of the pandemic have taken their toll. Footfall has fallen. Some of our best-loved stores have closed their doors, only to be replaced by vape shops and candy stores. And, too often, the experience of visiting a chaotic, congested Oxford Street has felt more like an ordeal to survive than a day out to enjoy.View image in fullscreenOxford Street and South Molton Street, visualised by architects for the transformation of the iconic shopping thoroughfare.Computer-generated: AVR LondonIf we’re to restore this beloved street to its former glory, we must rediscover the pioneering spirit of Harry Gordon Selfridge and create a space for everyone to enjoy, breathing new life into the high street and bringing back big brands. And that’s what our bold plans – backed by the overwhelming majority of Londoners and businesses – are all about. And with household names like Ikea, Puma and Clarks investing in new stores, there’s already excitement for what Oxford Street can become.People need a reason beyond simply buying something to visit their high street. And in an age when almost anything can be delivered right to our door, that principle matters more than ever. Coming to Oxford Street should feel like a positive experience. Somewhere you want to spend time, as well as your hard-earned money. A place where you’re not choked by tailpipe fumes or deafened by the noise of passing motorists. And that starts with reclaiming it for pedestrians, not traffic – rebalancing the relationship between cars and people in the centre of our city.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toMatters of OpinionGuardian columnists and writers on what they’ve been debating, thinking about, reading, and moreEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionEveryone hates Oxford Street. Will pedestrianisation save it?Read moreThat’s why I’m so delighted that, thanks to our efforts, the road stretching between Orchard Street and Great Portland Street is now officially traffic-free. But removing cars is just the beginning. Imagine an Oxford Street where you can stroll at your own pace, take a break from shopping with a coffee under the trees, or stumble across some live music, a fashion show, a sports exhibition or a cultural event. We’re determined to put Oxford Street not just on par with top global shopping destinations like Times Square, the Champs-Élysées and La Rambla, but make it even better.And while it’s a process – we’re deliberately keeping disruption to a minimum over the busy Christmas period – by next spring, visitors can expect to see new trees, new seats and new public plazas, alongside improved lighting and signage. This ambitious project has been far from straightforward or easy. As usual, we’ve had to overcome opposition from a vocal minority, and 14 years of a previous government that didn’t back the plans. But with seven in 10 Londoners expressing support for our vision, after extensive consultation, I knew we owed it to our city and to our businesses to deliver these improvements, which will help to boost jobs, growth and investment as we build a fairer, safer, greener and more prosperous London for everyone.View image in fullscreenThe first John Lewis shop, which opened in 1864, on Oxford Street.Photograph: John Lewis/PAOf course, we’ll continue to listen to Londoners. Many of the initial changes are temporary, and we’ll use real-time feedback to help refine the final designs in a test and review period throughout 2027. But for centuries, Oxford Street has reinvented itself, adapting to changing times and helping shape British culture along the way. And now it’s in need of its next great transformation. One that honours its extraordinary past while creating new possibilities for the future. A future where new memories are made, new businesses flourish and new chapters of British history are written.Today marks the beginning of that journey – and I encourage everyone to come to explore this newly transformed street, as we work together to ensure its best days are still to come. In the words of Harry Gordon Selfridge – everyone is welcome.Sadiq Khan is the mayor of LondonExplore more on these topicsLondonOpinionSadiq KhanShoppingcommentShareReuse this content

title: Could Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU? | Catherine De Vries | The Guardian
description: Anger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives better, says political scientist Catherine De Vries
Author: Catherine De Vries
Headline: Anger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives better, says political scientist Catherine De Vries
Content: Police officers face protesters near Porte de Vincennes in Paris, 24 October 2026.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenPolice officers face protesters near Porte de Vincennes in Paris, 24 October 2026.Photograph: Nicolas Tucat/AFP/Getty ImagesOpinionProtestCould Europe’s autumn of discontent threaten the survival of the EU?Catherine De VriesAnger on the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself if it can’t show why cooperation makes people’s lives betterMon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.30 EDTShareEurope is living through an autumn of unusual discontent. What protesters from Paris toMilantoMadridshare is a deepening anxiety about the future and a growing anger at the gap between what they expect from their governments and what they feel governments are delivering, whether the issue is unaffordable housing, stagnant wages, the spiralling cost of living or failing schools.The electoral consequences of the failure to get a grip on this public anger are already with us. Spain goes to the polls next month in a snap electioncalled after parliament voted down key housing reforms. France begins the process of electing a new president in April, while Poland, Italy and a string of smaller states will vote before the end of 2027. The stakes could not be higher.At the same time, national leaders face mounting pressures from abroad. Issues such as Ukraine, uncertainty over US security guarantees and economic competition with China demand more European cooperation, even as national politics makes this increasingly difficult. Governments face popular demands to deliver security and prosperity, just as their capacity to do so independently is shrinking. This leavesEuropewith a difficult question: how can countries whose leaders are increasingly struggling at home find the common ground needed to act together abroad?If the EU did not exist, Europeans would have every reason to invent it. Together, its members form a market of 450 million people and an economy of almost €19tn, the third largest after the US and China. No individual EU country comes close to that weight on its own. Germany, the largest, has 84 million people and an economy about a sixth the size of the US’s. Twenty of the 27 member states have fewer than 12 million inhabitants, less than half of Shanghai’s. In a world of tariffs and export controls, it is scale that secures a seat at the table.But this rationale for cooperation does not make the EU’s survival inevitable. This political project has often been declared on the brink of collapse; the most recent crises include Brexit, the pandemic and energy shocks. Yet it has proved remarkably durable, responding with improvised solutions that previously seemed impossible.The very traits that infuriate Eurosceptics – slow decision-making, endless negotiations and messy compromises – are, counterintuitively, sources of strength for Europe. The dispersion of power between governments, parliaments, courts and EU institutions makes the system hard to capture and compromises tend to stick.The EU’s staying power lies in its capacity to adapt despite disagreements, while helping countries achieve what is termed “effective sovereignty”. Nominal sovereignty is the right to decide alone, even when deciding alone–as the UK has discovered to its cost since it left the club supposedly to regain its sovereignty–changes little. Effective sovereignty is the capacity to shape outcomes on energy, trade, migration or defence that no European state can control by itself. And the EU has itself adapted: its fully paid-up members remain the core but non-members such as Norway and Switzerland participate on defence, security, energy and economic policy. The EU has an interest in bringing Britain back into closer cooperation too, even if not exactly as it looked pre-Brexit.1:44Police and protesters exchange teargas and fireworks in demonstrations across France – videoBut the EU’s resilience should not be taken for granted.Negotiationsover the nextseven-year budget,worth almost €2tn, show just how hard it is to achieve consensus. While everyone agrees on the need for greater European security and economic competitiveness, countries can’t agree on who should foot the bill. France, for example, is pushing for new EU-wide taxes, which others resist.Even so, growing domestic political instability does not necessarily mean there will be paralysis in Brussels. Quite the opposite – it creates an impetus to act. With France’s presidential election approaching,Emmanuel Macron has urgedfellow leaders to strike a budget deal by Christmas, warning that political room for manoeuvre would shrink in the new year if Marine Le Pen succeeds him.Le Pen no longer talks about takingFranceout of the euro or a Brexit-style referendum. But her platform would undermine the union from within, turning the EU into a “Europe of Nations” and threatening cuts to France’s contribution to the EU budget.Whether political change comes through elections, protests or new compromises in Brussels, public discontent cannot simply be negotiated away. This brings us back to the streets. French, Italian and Spanish citizens want functioning public services, affordable housing, economic and national security, and a sense that they have some control over their futures.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThis is EuropeThe most pressing stories and debates for Europeans – from identity to economics to the environmentEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionThe Guardian view on Europe’s protests: the social contract has broken – and young people want solutions | EditorialRead moreYounger Europeans, in particular, facegrowing uncertaintyabout their economic prospects, from finding affordable housing to securing stable employment. So far, this pessimism has not translated into widespread rejection of the EU.Recent pollingsuggests that young Europeans remain among the EU’s strongest supporters, with 90% favouring greater unity among member states and 78% wanting the EU to have more resources to act.This gives Europe an opportunity, but also a responsibility, to turn that support into tangible improvements in their lives. That is the real test in the years ahead. Decisions about defence, industrial policy and social protection will involve difficult trade-offs, and not everyone will benefit equally. But if European cooperation becomes better at preserving institutions than at responding to citizens’ concerns, the discontent now spilling on to the streets could increasingly turn against the EU itself. The EU has repeatedly shown that it can survive political crises. Now it must ensure that the people living through them can do more than merely get by.Catherine De Vries is professor of political science at IE University in Madrid. She is the co-author with Alexandros Kentikelenis ofHow Europe SurvivesExplore more on these topicsProtestOpinionEuropean UnionFranceSpainItalyEmmanuel MacronMarine Le PencommentShareReuse this content

title: The Guardian view on Lula’s comeback: a victory for Brazil and the world, as well as a Trump rebuff | Editorial | The Guardian
description: Editorial: A fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working people
Author: Editorial
Headline: Editorial: A fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working people
Content: Lula celebrates with his wife, Rosangela ‘Janja’ da Silva, and vice-president Geraldo Alckmin in São Paulo after winning the election on Sunday.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersView image in fullscreenLula celebrates with his wife, Rosangela ‘Janja’ da Silva, and vice-president Geraldo Alckmin in São Paulo after winning the election on Sunday.Photograph: Brian Snyder/ReutersOpinionBrazilThe Guardian view on Lula’s comeback: a victory for Brazil and the world, as well as a Trump rebuffEditorialA fourth presidential victory gives Lula another chance to defend democracy, protect the Amazon and deliver for Brazil’s working peopleMon 26 Oct 2026 14.40 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.48 EDTShareLuiz Inácio Lula da Silva’s win inBrazil’s presidential electionis a triumph for him, his country and the world. The 80-year-old incumbent snatched victory from the jaws of defeat, blocked the rise of the far right and saved the planetary air-conditioning system of theAmazon from irreparable destruction. Known universally as Lula, he made history by becoming the first candidate to win a presidential run-off after finishing second in the opening round. In triumphing against Flávio Bolsonaro, the leftist stopped what could have been the most dangerous consolidation of authoritarian rule in Brazil since military rule ended. A Bolsonaro presidency could have used a rightwing Congress toextend presidential termsand pack the supreme court, entrenching power for generations.Lula seemed to have been energised by his first-round defeat by Mr Bolsonaro. The three-time president initially pitted his extraordinary life and record against a 45-year-old senator married tocontroversy. But voters wanted answers to economic insecurity, rising prices and poor public services. Lula reversed course in the second round, offering immediate relief fromeveryday costsand indebtedness – including to the rising number of self-employedvoterswhom his rightwing opponent had been courting. Popular mobilisation transformed the runoff into a race to stop a Bolsonaro restoration withstudent protests, massdemonstrationsand a 10 million-strong “Lula’s Army” WhatsApp channel. It seemed to work. Nearly 5 million more people voted in the second round of the Brazilian election than the first.View image in fullscreenDonald Trump.Photograph: Yuri Gripas/EPAMr Bolsonaro’s desperate refusal to concede follows his father’s playbook. In 2022 then-president Jair Bolsonaro did the same, claiming fraud. The elder Bolsonaro’s attempted coup saw him jailed for27 years. This time Lula’s margin of victory – 4.4m votes – over the younger Bolsonaro was twice that achieved over the father. His win has also been recognised by rightwing regional leaders, conservative newspapers and even aprominent evangelical ally of the Bolsonaros. It may be significant that defeat denied Mr Bolsonaro a presidential shield from allegations ofcorruption and money laundering. Whether he remains in Brazil after his term as senator expires in February remains to be seen.After the Bolsonaro clan, the next biggest loser from the results of the Brazilian election is Donald Trump. Lula’s win broke a run ofseven rightwing presidential winsacross Latin America, a regional advance for which Mr Trump hadclaimed credit. While rightwing leaders in Chile, Paraguay and Peru congratulated Lula on his victory, the White House remained silent. The US president has only himself to blame: he tried to use tariffs topressureBrazil over the elder Bolsonaro’s prosecution and its courts’ enforcement actions against American tech companies. Mr Trump’s meddling handed Lula a winning argument for Brazil’s sovereignty.Brazil remains divided, with a rightwing Congress ready to obstruct Lula – particularly on the environment. But few are better placed to negotiate than the former trade unionist who founded theWorkers’ party. Lula’s victory provides an elected counterweight and that matters for labour rights, public services, Indigenous communities and global climate policy. The win shows the wider democratic left that a broad coalition can defeat the right. Can governing produce the secure livelihoods, strong state provision and meaningful opportunities that make that coalition durable? The next four years in Brazil may provide an answer.Explore more on these topicsBrazilOpinionLuiz Inácio Lula da SilvaFlávio BolsonaroAmericaseditorialsShareReuse this content

title: ‘My death was reported in Rolling Stone’: how the Zombies made Time of the Season | Culture | The Guardian
description: ‘A year after we broke up, we heard that two bands had started touring the US as the Zombies. One group said they were the originals but with a new singer – because I’d been killed in a car crash’
Author: Chris Broughton
Headline: ‘A year after we broke up, we heard that two bands had started touring the US as the Zombies. One group said they were the originals but with a new singer – because I’d been killed in a car crash’
Content: ‘A DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it’ … the band in 1964.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyView image in fullscreen‘A DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it’ … the band in 1964.Photograph: Pictorial Press Ltd/AlamyHow we madeCulture‘My death was reported in Rolling Stone’: how the Zombies made Time of the Season‘A year after we broke up, we heard that two bands had started touring the US as the Zombies. One group said they were the originals but with a new singer – because I’d been killed in a car crash’Interviews byChris BroughtonMon 26 Oct 2026 10.35 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleRod Argent, writer, Hammond L100 organ and backing vocalsOur first single,She’s Not There, was one of the first songs I wrote, when I was 18. It remained our only hit in the UK by the time we recorded our second album,Odessey and Oracle, in 1967 – this was only three years later but it felt like a lifetime. We’d recently signed to CBS and had been given £1,000, which even then was not a huge amount of money. We recorded pretty quickly in a few sessions spread over six months, producing ourselves for the first time.Time of the Season was the last song I wrote for the album. I was sharing a flat with our bass player Chris White, and we were going to each other’s rooms and playing the different things we had. I said: “I think I’ve just written a song that could be a hit.”The lyrics reflected the mood of the time. In 1967 there were pictures of war on TV, and people were seeing what a devastating thing it was and saying: “I’m not going to be part of this.” The “Who’s your daddy?” line was, in a way, going back to Gershwin’s Summertime, one of the first songs we performed together, but “Is he rich like me?” had kind of a double meaning: “rich” in the sense of understanding how to live.double quotation markIf you’re so bloody good, you come in here and sing itWe recorded at EMI Recording Studios, later known as Abbey Road. The Beatles were in before us making Sgt Pepper’s Lonely Hearts Club Band – we had the benefit of some of the same recording engineers, in particular Geoff Emerick. He found this special way of marrying the bass and the tom-tom sound. I suggested the clap before the beat and a vocal sound after, which became the exhalation.We soon used up our £1,000, but because of the tight timeframe we were working to, there was a spontaneity and freshness that was very valuable. It’s a method I try to preserve. It’s just much more fun.Colin Blunstone, lead and backing vocalsI was learning Time of the Season while we recorded it. Standing where the vocal mic had been set up, I was looking at this big red recording light with a clock underneath it while I tried to get it right. The studio was very strict about sessions finishing on time, and there were these guys with long brown coats moving equipment about. On one occasion, we were standing around a piano working out harmonies and they wheeled it out in the middle of a take.Rod always has an overview of his songs in his head – he can hear the drum track, what the bass should be playing and what the lead vocal should be doing. He’s extremely good at phrasing, so he was in the control room saying: “No, this phrase should be on the beat but the next phrase should be pushed …” Meanwhile, all the time I’m watching the big hand creeping towards five o’clock.Things got a little bit heated. I was saying, “If you’re so bloody good, you come in here and sing it,” and he said, “You’re the bloody lead singer, you stand in there until you get it right!” The language was probably richer than that. It makes me smile now to think I was breaking off from saying the most terrible things to Rod to sing these angelic lines: “It’s the time of the season for loving …”Rod likes to think I disliked Time of the Season, but I just thought there were more commercial songs on the album.Care of Cell 44, to me, sounded like the epitome of a hit single, but obviously I was wrong – it was released ahead of Odessey and Oracle and wasn’t successful. By the time the album came out in Terry Quirk’s misspelled sleeve, the band had split.View image in fullscreen‘I’ve never worked out how it can be both of its time and timeless’ … the Zombies in 1965: (l-r) Hugh Grundy, Colin Blunstone, Chris White, Rod Argent, Paul Atkinson.Photograph: Stanley Bielecki/ASP/Getty ImagesThe following year, Al Kooper left the American band Blood, Sweat & Tears and became a staff producer at CBS. He’d just visited London where he bought about 80 albums that weren’t available in the US, and later said Odessey and Oracle was the one that really stood out. On his first day at CBS he went to see the label’s president, Clive Davis, and said: “Whatever it costs, we have to get this album.” And Davis said: “We already have it. We were going to pass on it – it’s not commercial.”Al fought for it, and CBS released two singles that disappeared without trace. I think Time of the Season was only put out as a favour to Al, but one DJ in Boise, Idaho, would not stop playing it, and that was where our luck turned. It gradually picked up huge radio interest.By then, it was well over a year since we’d broken up and we were all doing other things, but we soon heard that a couple of other bands had started touring the US as the Zombies – one included two members of ZZ Top. The manager of one of these bands claimed they were the original members with a new singer, because Colin Blunstone had been killed in a car crash. It turned out my death was reported in Rolling Stone.The original Zombies didn’t play together again until 1997, when a box set was launched at the Jazz Cafe in London. I was singing with my solo band, but the other guys came up on stage and let it be known they wanted to play – we hadn’t planned it or rehearsed. We did She’s Not There and Time of the Season and it sounded really good. I thought: “You know what? There really was something special about that band.”Can you say a song’s got legs? Time of the Season wasn’t a success in the UK charts, but people know it. It’s often used in films set in the 1960s but also appears in commercials, where it sounds really current. I’ve never quite worked out how it can be both of its time and timeless.The Zombies release Continue Here, an album of remastered mono B-sides and singles, on 30 October. TheirBegin Here festivalis in St Albans, 30 October to 1 November.Explore more on these topicsCultureHow we madePop and rockfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle America | You Can See Everything | The Guardian
description: Nathan Fielder’s three-hour Elizabeth Holmes film has become a pop culture phenomenon but at a sold-out Times Square screening, no one was quite sure what to think
Author: Jesse Hassenger
Headline: Nathan Fielder’s three-hour Elizabeth Holmes film has become a pop culture phenomenon but at a sold-out Times Square screening, no one was quite sure what to think
Content: Advertising for You Can See Everything.Photograph: Todd Williamson/JanuaryImages for A24/ShutterstockView image in fullscreenAdvertising for You Can See Everything.Photograph: Todd Williamson/JanuaryImages for A24/ShutterstockYou Can See Everything‘A cultural moment’: smash hit doc You Can See Everything continues to dazzle AmericaNathan Fielder’s three-hour Elizabeth Holmes film has become a pop culture phenomenon but at a sold-out Times Square screening, no one was quite sure what to thinkIn You Can See Everything, it’s Elizabeth Holmes’s partner who makes for 2026’s timeliest villainSecrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the yearJesse Hassengerin New YorkMon 26 Oct 2026 10.37 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 17.16 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhen I see a film a second time during its theatrical run, it’s typically to take someone else who hasn’t yet seen it, at least in part hoping to witness their reaction to a piece of art that excited or moved me in some way. Seeing Lance Oppenheim and Nathan Fielder’sYou Can See Everythinga second time in New York City on a Saturday night was that impulse writ larger. This is a movie garnering a surprisingly sizable audience, and outsized audience reactions to go along with it; rewatching it in a full 300-seat auditorium offered the opportunity to re-experience that sense of discovery. Perhaps more to the point, almost everyone I knew had seen it already; all I could do was observe strangers.Secrets, lies and a shock A-list cameo: how You Can See Everything became the film of the yearRead moreThis documentary, peering into (and helping to create) a hall of mirrors around the famed med-tech scammer Elizabeth Holmes, has become the box office story of the fall, actually rising 25% on its second weekend to gross another $19.5m – a rare feat even given its expanded screen count. With over $45m in North America, it’s already one of A24’s biggest movies ever; it could wind up in the company’s top three, and way up on the list of the highest-grossing nonfiction features. If You Can See Everything isn’t quite anObsession-level cash cow, it’s probably even more surprising that a three-hour documentary whose existence was only announced about eight weeks ago is on track to make more money than high-profile new releases like Practical Magic 2, Verity and Street Fighter, among others. It’s also outgrossed co-director Oppenheim’s fellow A24 surprise hitPrimetime, which has the benefit of genuine movie star Robert Pattinson.A few of the viewers I spoke with following the 8pm showing ofYou Can See Everythingat New York’s AMC Empire (typically one of the highest-grossing venues in the country for any number of new releases, where Everything is currently showing on three to five screens depending on the time of day) had also seen Primetime, aware of the connection between the two films. Just as many, however, were not high-frequency moviegoers, at least not by New York standards. Despite an obviously youthful demographic – perhaps owing to the high tolerance for hustle and/or bustle required to trek out to Times Square, I couldn’t find anyone over 30 – there were several viewers who hadn’t been to the movies in months. (The answer to the question of what movie they last saw in theaters ranged from the month-old Primetime to the obligatory summer mega-blockbuster The Odyssey to, yes, Obsession.) Hardly anyone claimed to be a documentary aficionado, either; no one cited a recent documentary they had seen in theaters, saying they were more likely to catch that sort of thing on streaming, if at all.So what drew them to a big-screen experience featuring both an entertainer (Nathan Fielder) and a subject (Elizabeth Holmes) more closely associated with television? Most of the twentysomethings I spoke with had some combination of familiarity with Fielder’s more overtly comic work – one woman said this seemed “on brand” for him – and awareness of the notoriety of Holmes, the latter usually stemming from the non-documentary TV series The Dropout, which also figures into the film. Each seemed to provide a surprise hook for a big-screen feature – like a more thoughtful version of seeing a movie because it has Anne Hathaway or Spider-Man (not that there’s anything wrong with following either of those into the dark). To a cinema diehard, this seemed almost counterintuitive; were people really being enticed into theaters by faces they knew largely from couch-bound TV binges? Was this effectively serving as a three-hour crossover between The Dropout and The Rehearsal?‘You can’t make this stuff up’: why we remain fascinated by Elizabeth HolmesRead moreThere was a sense that this unexpected team-up was part of the sell, with the WTF nature of that idea intact. The extra promise, though, seemed to be that You Can See Everything would offer something more surprising and less easily spoiled than a typical streaming event. The 23-year-old sitting next to me said that she got the impression from social media – specifically, clips on Instagram and TikTok – that this was “a cultural moment”, as she put it. Multiple viewers echoed that sentiment about seeing a handful of clips via social media, and hearing buzz indicating that the movie simply was “unlike anything else out [at the movies]” and had to be seen firsthand to be believed - or at least to be experienced with the proper amount of spoiler-free, audience-vibing surprise. Remarkably, though the movie had been out for over a week and already discoursed at least halfway to death online, none of these twentysomething viewers reported having any idea about the unexpected pivot the movie made at its halfway mark – especially impressive given that it involves another marquee name added to the mix.During the movie itself, that mystery guest felt like she was winning fans in real time; she even got a round of spontaneous applause by describing Holmes’s partner,Billy Evans, as “batshit crazy”. But while early screenings had been described as meeting with rapturous audience engagement driven by the film’s surprises, this one felt more unpredictable in its alternating waves of laughter and murmuring discomfort. Early in the film, Holmes gets teary talking about the potential separation from her children as she prepares to leave for her prison sentence in a few weeks. Both times I’ve watched it with a full audience, Fielder’s reaction – “that must be hard” – drew one of the movie’s biggest laughs, seemingly for how flatly obligatory it sounds. Yet if this moment primed the audience for peals of cringe-comedy laughter or outright derision toward either Fielder’s affect or Holmes’s refusal to accept responsibility for her deception, that’s not exactly how the movie played out. The movie often cuts to Fielder lurking within proximity of the Holmes family during tense moments; though the mechanics of these de facto reaction shots are similar, sometimes they drew big laughs and sometimes what felt more like hushed suspense. It was as if viewers were deciding moment to moment whether they were watching dark comedy or something more menacing. Though the disparaging of Evans got an enthusiastically cathartic reaction, applause when the movie threw to its end credits was scattered and uncertain.View image in fullscreenNathan Fielder and Elizabeth Holmes in You Can See Everything.Photograph: Everett Collection Inc/AlamyIt’s not unprecedented for a movie to garner audibly mixed reactions. But something Oppenheim and Fielder seem to have cracked is allowing an audience to feel satisfied and impressed by those reactions, which would often serve as a death knell to a prospective blockbuster. When I asked people after the show for their immediate impressions of the film, one woman said it was “funnier than I expected”, while another was surprised by the sympathy she felt for Holmes at times despite feeling “on guard” about what to believe from her.You Can See Everything review – Nathan Fielder’s Elizabeth Holmes doc is a modern masterpiece of deceitRead moreThe most common reaction, however, was a kind of admiring confusion. They weren’t exactly sure what to think, a feeling that’s not traditionally music to a film executive’s ears. Because its initial release was in fewer than a thousand theaters, You Can See Everything hasn’t been subjected to the traditional and finicky CinemaScore polling that asks opening-night audiences for a grade, and seems to inexplicably augur disappointment with anything that’s not at least a B+. But PostTrak, another polling service, shows highly positive results. This could carry the movie past the $100m mark in North America, something only ever accomplished by one other documentary: Michael Moore’s hot-button Fahrenheit 9/11, which had the advantage of election-year currency and a film-maker coming off an Oscar win.Is this phenom, in conjunction with the surprise smash of Obsession and the less shocking but still staggering success of The Odyssey, indicative of movie audiences willing to grapple with more than they’ve been given credit for in the past? Or, along with the film’s three-hour runtime, is it more of an example of how traditionally TV-based projects are afforded a leeway that narrative films rarely receive from general audiences? As with the movie itself, clear answers haven’t emerged, and probably won’t. At very least, though, it offers some clear respite from the applause-mongering of the IP-driven, fan-focused era. Those movies won’t be banished byNathan Fielderand Lance Oppenheim, but by the time the next Avengers rolls around, they might feel, however slightly, like a narrower slice of the cinematic experience.Explore more on these topicsYou Can See EverythingDocumentary filmsNathan FielderElizabeth HolmesfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: LS Lowry review – matchstick men, or the broken denizens of a smog-filled hellscape?  | Art and design | The Guardian
description: With his heaps of mud, decaying sheds and chimney-filled skies, Lowry depicts northern England as a spirit-crushing dystopia
Author: Jonathan Jones
Headline: With his heaps of mud, decaying sheds and chimney-filled skies, Lowry depicts northern England as a spirit-crushing dystopia
Content: Withdrawn and wretched … Lowry’s Coming from the Mill.Photograph: © The Lowry Collection, SalfordView image in fullscreenWithdrawn and wretched … Lowry’s Coming from the Mill.Photograph: © The Lowry Collection, SalfordArt and designReviewLS Lowry review – matchstick men, or the broken denizens of a smog-filled hellscape?MK Gallery, Milton KeynesWith his heaps of mud, decaying sheds and chimney-filled skies, Lowry depicts northern England as a spirit-crushing dystopiaJonathan JonesMon 26 Oct 2026 12.03 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 12.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleWhile peoplequeue at the British Museum to see the Battle of Hastings, this excellent survey of LS Lowry at the MK Gallery in Milton Keynes takes you back to another, maybe more decisive part of our past – the age when Britain was the most industrialised society on Earth. Laurence Lowry was born in 1887 and worked for 41 years as a rent collector, a job that took him all over his native Greater Manchester observing its people and places. He had the city’s grime and grind in his soul. The MK wants to show him as a fully rounded artist, to uncover the Lowry with a song in his heart, but it’s the misery of his urban hell that holds and harrows you.In his 1930 painting Coming from the Mill it’s the end of the shift and scores of people emerge from a factory’s bleak yellow gatehouse as if leaving prison. Their daily captivity has left them broken and exhausted and the little abstracted figures hunch forwards as they walk without pausing to laugh or chat, going to their separate homes, each one withdrawn, wretched. They are not the painting’s protagonists – they are passive victims. The architecture of industry dominates the picture as it rules their lives. How can any of these little people, dwarfed by the mill that eats their time and energy, attain individuality? No wonder they all look the same except for minor variations in their drab clothes. They’ve been reduced by the Industrial Revolution tomatchstick people.View image in fullscreenLess well known dimensions to his talent … LS Lowry: The Theatre of Life at MK Gallery.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianLowry is the Franz Kafka of industrial Britain. He is not a naive artist who painted crudely because that’s the best he could do. Nor is he a patient social realist laying bare the injustices of capitalism – althoughFriedrich Engelswould surely have recognised his Manchester. He is a modern expressionist who finds his inner melancholy reflected in the industrial sublime. He drinks in its despair, feasts on its poetry of alienation. As you journey through Lowry’s North, you sink ever further into his personal slough of despond.Slough of Despond would make a good alternative title for his 1924 drawing The River Irwell at the Adelphi. Heaps of mud and ash choke the slow-moving river that runs through Salford, its shores lined with decaying sheds and slums against a smoggy, chimney-lined sky. It’s Lowry at his purest as he depicts the stunning, crushing presence of the city itself. He draws and paints the black, gnarled spires of urban churches with as much relish as those monstrous mills. In the second world war he was a fire-watcher with a privileged view of the blitz: a drawing of freshly bombed buildings in Piccadilly, Manchester shows husks of charred brick still wreathed in smoke.View image in fullscreenEerie … Lowry’s A Landmark.Photograph: © The Lowry Collection, SalfordThis show digs out other, less well known dimensions to his talent. But his paintings of the Lake District are even more chilling than his cities. Lake Landscape, painted in 1950, is a vista of low curving hills divided by silvery still water, receding in abstract, musical pulses of sadness. No people or animals inhabit this eerie world. When he paints people close up it’s even more disturbing: a young man with staring eyes, a father and sons who all seem equally desperate. He lightens up to paint his ideal woman with a simplified doll-like face apparently intended as his tribute to Pre-Raphaelite red-lipped beauties but the result is weirdly robotic. Her face is on the exhibition merchandise, perhaps because Halloween is coming.The most bizarre painting, however, is his 1963 work In a Park. At first glance it’s another city crowd scene until you realise everyone in this fenced enclosure has something different about them. A one-eyed face screams while people walk around the white-earthed, empty space with spinal deformities, facial palsies, amputated limbs. The catalogue gets itself in knots – is Lowry mocking the disabled or questioning how we define disability?skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toArt WeeklyYour weekly art world round-up, sketching out all the biggest stories, scandals and exhibitionsEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionFrieze review – you’ll see more avant garde wonders in the Bake Off tentRead moreBut this painting is not about disability in a political sense at all. It uses it as an image of humanity in general: all people are broken and alone, misshapen in Lowry’s hopeless universe.Lowry is a tricky customer. If it is pure snobbery to look down on him for being popular it is also patronising to see this troubled artist as a warmly sentimental nostalgist of the north. He is a painter of modern life in the age when that meant huge crowds staggering home in the shadow of smoking chimneys in cities blackened by carbon. At his best, Lowry is a great modern artist. His 1919 painting Pit Tragedy shows working-class people waiting for the worst news. They are statuesque, tragically posed in the grey dusty light. A woman turns towards us, her head veiled. Her pain is lost in the past but lives on here, observed and recorded by Lowry, visionary of the industrial age.LS Lowry: The Theatre of Life is at MK Gallery, Milton Keynes until 28 FebruaryExplore more on these topicsArt and designPaintingArtExhibitionsLS LowryreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I laughed so hard my Tampax fell out’: Michael Gambon’s pranks revealed by the stars he cracked up | Stage | The Guardian
description: He made Daniel Radcliffe’s Harry Potter fart, left Judi Dench unable to control herself and told a fry-up fantasy about Helen Mirren. A new biography details the star’s mischief
Author: Chris Wiegand
Headline: He made Daniel Radcliffe’s Harry Potter fart, left Judi Dench unable to control herself and told a fry-up fantasy about Helen Mirren. A new biography details the star’s mischief
Content: ‘I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby’ … Michael Gambon.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby’ … Michael Gambon.Photograph: Eamonn McCabe/The GuardianStage‘I laughed so hard my Tampax fell out’: Michael Gambon’s pranks revealed by the stars he cracked upHe made Daniel Radcliffe’s Harry Potter fart, left Judi Dench unable to control herself and told a fry-up fantasy about Helen Mirren. A new biography details the star’s mischiefChris WiegandMon 26 Oct 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.14 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleJasper Rees’s authorised biography ofMichael Gambon, published three years afterthe great actor’s death, has nuanced accounts of his performances in Shakespeare, Beckett and Pinter as well as The Singing Detective and the Harry Potter films. There are even chapters devoted to his hands (“the biggest you’ve ever seen on anybody” – Brian Cox) and similarly enormous feet. But, Gambon being Gambon, there are also dozens of accounts of tomfoolery on and off stage …‘One of the funniest people I’ve ever met’David Hare’s 1995 play Skylight is set in a draughty flat where a dish of spaghetti is cooked up on stage. Those kitchen cupboards proved useful for Lia Williams to hide when Gambon’s goofing got to her at theNational Theatre. Gambon would adopt a different accent or speak in tongues during a scene and “when he made me laugh it was hell on Earth because there was nothing I could do about it” said Williams, who called him “one of the funniest people I’ve ever met”. She continued: “One time I laughed so hard that my Tampax fell out and I had to deal with that for an entire act.”View image in fullscreen‘It was hell on Earth!’ … Michael Gambon and Lia Williams in Skylight at the National Theatre in 1995.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianDinner with Judi, Ken and NatashaIbsen’s Ghosts was a hot potato when it was first staged in 1882 thanks to its scandalous plot involving syphilis and incest. Gambon had some fun with the spuds when playing the self-righteous Pastor Manders in an 80s BBC TV version. Director Elijah Moshinsky envisioned a tense, sombre dinner scene and Gambon sat alongside Judi Dench and Kenneth Branagh. The potatoes were duly passed around byNatasha Richardson. “I’ll just have the usual eight,” requested Gambon. His co-stars’ corpsing led them to leave the set. “We couldn’t control ourselves at all,” confessed Dench.Dumbledore unleashes Fartis TemporusNot every actor’s biography includes “fart machines” in the index but toots fake and real are let off in several chapters. When Gambon took over the role of Dumbledore in Harry Potter and the Prisoner of Azkaban, he and Alan Rickman prankedDaniel Radcliffeby triggering a fart machine during a closeup of the young star when he was in a sleeping bag alongside fellow Hogwarts students. “I was initially really annoyed,” said Radcliffe, before concluding that if Rickman and Gambon had engineered it then “that is pretty funny”.A storm and a FoolWhen Gambon played King Lear for the RSC in 1982, Antony Sher sported a red nose as the clownish Fool. The poster presented themas a sort of double actand Sher was widely seen as stealing the limelight. Rees likens it to Gambon taking on what is often referred to as an “actor’s Everest” only to find another climber “clambering frantically up the same rope”. Adrian Noble, who directed the tragedy, said Gambon “joshed [Sher] mercilessly”. During the storm scene he reportedly bellowed: “Come on out, you little red-nosed fucker!”View image in fullscreenMichael Gambon and Robert De Niro in The Good Shepherd in 2006.Photograph: Ronald GrantThe fake De NiroWhen he was appearing on stage in Arthur Miller’s A View from the Bridge, Gambon kept a signed photo ofRobert De Niro– with words of admiration for Gambon’s work – on his dressing room table. The pair would appear together in the film The Good Shepherd in 2006 but had never even met by the time he was doing A View from the Bridge. The fake autograph and note – “I loved working with you Mike, you’re great – love Bobby” – were apparently written by Gambon himself.The play that changed my life: ‘Michael Gambon’s offstage anarchy as Falstaff made the show better’Read moreWink winkOne festive season in the late 60s, Gambon found himself starring in the Christmas show Hans, the Witch and the Gobbin at Birmingham Rep – much to his annoyance, remembered co-star Anthony Higgins. A prodigious swearer, Gambon decided to add to his stage makeup for a performance. “One night he’d written on one eyelid ‘fuck’ and on the other ‘off’,” said Higgins. Gambon blinked each eye to deliver the message to Higgins. Artistic director Peter Dews had to give him a word of warning.View image in fullscreenSurprise chocolate cake … Michael Gambon and Rupert Graves in The Caretaker at the Comedy theatre, London, in 2000.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The Guardian‘Rupert wet himself regularly’When Gambon played the tramp Davies ina 2000 revival of Harold Pinter’s playThe Caretaker, he revelled in repelling theatregoers – as well as the brothers played by Douglas Hodge and Rupert Graves. One night, according to Rees’s book, Gambon had his back to the audience and buried his hand in his trousers, where he had stowed away a serving of chocolate cake. He withdrew his smeared fingers and sniffed them, causing his co-stars to crack up. “Rupert was in terrible trouble,” remembered Hodge. “Rupert wet himself regularly.”A fry-up with CleopatraGambon loved to supply journalists with tall tales and see who believed him. He treated one interviewer to an “insight” into how he andHelen Mirrenprepared while in the wings for their roles as Antony and Cleopatra for the RSC. Mirren, he assured the journalist, got into character by performing a mime in which she prepared a dish of ham and eggs for Antony. “Absolute rubbish,” Mirren told Rees, though added: “It’s a lovely story.”Michael Gambon: The Authorised Biography by Jasper Rees is published by Century (£30). To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. Delivery charges may apply.Explore more on these topicsStageMichael GambonTheatreWest EndDavid HareDaniel RadcliffeHarry PotterfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: ‘Cocaine is the Gollum of drugs’ – and other things we learned from Anthony LaPaglia’s surprisingly juicy memoir | Books | The Guardian
description: The actor opens up about almost playing Tony Soprano, why Quentin Tarantino ‘flipped out’ at him and how he’s ‘pretty much broke’ now
Author: Sian Cain
Headline: The actor opens up about almost playing Tony Soprano, why Quentin Tarantino ‘flipped out’ at him and how he’s ‘pretty much broke’ now
Content: Anthony LaPaglia in Empire Records – the only set he ever walked off, he writes in his memoir, The Life We Choose.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyView image in fullscreenAnthony LaPaglia in Empire Records – the only set he ever walked off, he writes in his memoir, The Life We Choose.Photograph: Everett Collection/AlamyBooks‘Cocaine is the Gollum of drugs’ – and other things we learned from Anthony LaPaglia’s surprisingly juicy memoirThe actor opens up about almost playing Tony Soprano, why Quentin Tarantino ‘flipped out’ at him and how he’s ‘pretty much broke’ nowSian CainMon 26 Oct 2026 10.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 19.05 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaybe once a year we get a celebrity memoir that is as good on the juicy stuff – the Hollywood gossip – as the interior excavation; and boy does Anthony LaPaglia deliver both in his new memoir,The Life We Choose. “They say acting is the cheapest form of therapy,” writes the actor, best known for his roles in Without a Trace, Empire Records, Lantana and Frasier. “And that was lucky for me, because, coming up in the way I did, Christ knows I needed it.”The memoir reveals a lot about his abusive childhood inAdelaide, at the hands of his father, Egidio; and how he went from working as a shoe salesman to moving to the US, to work on Broadway and in Hollywood.Anthony LaPaglia: ‘There is not a role I didn’t get that I ever gave more than four hours of grievance to – even Tony Soprano’Read moreBut if you’re after name-drops, there are plenty. LaPaglia is a big fan of: Kiefer Sutherland (who he claims was once trailed by a “70-year-old ex-bov from London named Moe” whose sole job was to make sure Sutherland turned up on set when he was “shitfaced”); Arthur Miller; Allison Janney; Michael Keaton; Stanley Tucci; Mike Myers; the whole cast of Frasier but particularly Kelsey Grammer; Alan Arkin; Kerry Armstrong (“a genius actress and a complete nutcase”); and Hugo Weaving.LaPaglia has mixed feelings about: Val Kilmer (who he claims once deliberately poured coffee on him); John Landis (“aggressive and condescending”); the Empire Records director, Allan Moyle (the only time LaPaglia walked off a set); his youngest brother, Jonathan LaPaglia (“extremely boring company”);Harvey Weinstein(fair); and his third ex-wife, Alexandra Henkel (whom he won’t even name).Here are seven takeaways:1. He really does not like AdelaideLaPaglia had a tough childhood in the suburb Beefacres (now part of Windsor Gardens) in South Australia. He’s still not a fan of his home town: “There’s a bad energy running through it. Whenever I go back, I feel the same low-frequency unease that used to spook me as a kid … Maybe it was weird for a kid, but even during my school years I worried that if I didn’t one day leave Adelaide, I might never be happy.” Though he credits his childhood for helping him become an actor: “I estimate about 80% of the actors I know sprang from difficult beginnings and had poor relationships with their families … I believe nothing makes an actor better than the deep sense of anger and revenge that often accompanies suffering.”2. He loved cocaineIt wasn’t until 1993, when he was filming So I Married an Axe Murderer in San Francisco, that LaPaglia tried drugs for the first time in his 30s – and really liked them. The memoir includes some incredible lines, including: “Cocaine is the Gollum of drugs. You can go along on it for a while but there is a point where it just grabs you” and “I could buy a sandwich bag half-full of the stuff without putting a dent in my rent or grocery bill”. But he became a “bingeing addict” and went on “a four-day solo bender watching David Attenborough’s greatest hits”. One time, his kitchen drawer started talking to him.LaPaglia never went to rehab but eventually shook his addiction because he “couldn’t live with the stupidity”. He has dyscalculia and always struggled with numbers, “but for years after I quit drugs, I could remember my dealer’s phone number by heart”.View image in fullscreenAnthony LaPaglia in Frasier with Richard E Grant and Robbie Coltrane.Photograph: NBC/Getty Images3. He almost played Tony SopranoIn 1996, David Chase approached LaPaglia with the pilot forThe Sopranosand told him “he had me in mind when he wrote the character of Tony Soprano”. LaPaglia loved the script and tried to convince the former CBS chief executive Les Moonves to take the show on – but while Moonves also loved it, he said it was too racy for network television and that CBS would “gut” what made it great. As “David doggedly persisted and I kept trotting The Sopranos around”, LaPaglia was approved by Arthur Miller himself to play Eddie Carbone in A View from the Bridge on Broadway. “Almost as soon” as he committed to Bridge, HBO picked up The Sopranos – and James Gandolfini was cast as Tony instead.“James was far and away the best choice to play that part,” LaPaglia writes. “I’d have approached Tony Soprano entirely differently. In fact, David and I already had some disagreements about Tony’s personality and motivation. I wanted to portray a guy who’d escaped the mob only to be sucked back in after the death of his mother. I envisaged a more urbane, very reluctant mafioso.” In a weird coincidence, LaPaglia chose Allison Janney over Edie Falco to play Beatrice Carbone in the Miller production; Falco then went on to play Carmela Soprano, Tony’s wife, on the hit show.4. Tarantino ‘flipped out’ at himIn 2011, LaPaglia was invited to meetQuentin Tarantinoto discuss playing an Australian slave trader in Django Unchained. LaPaglia even read with Jamie Foxx for the role. But when production on the film was repeatedly postponed, LaPaglia committed to making Underground, a made-for-TV film directed by his friend – the Australian director Rob Connolly.“Finally, six months after it was supposed to begin production, Quentin was ready to start filming,” LaPaglia writes – but leaving Connolly’s film would have dashed its chance at funding. “It broke my heart to call [Tarantino] and say I couldn’t do it. The last thing I expected, though, was that he’d flip out: ‘What do you mean you can’t do it?’“Quentin was genuinely astonished that I would pass on a role in his movie to go and shoot some independent thing for Australian TV. I don’t think he was used to being turned down. ‘Can’t you get out of it?’ he said. ‘Jesus Christ, just get out of it.’” When LaPaglia persisted, he says Tarantino said “I don’t fucking believe this” and hung up on him.LaPaglia now calls his decision “a classic case of LaPaglia self-sabotage”: Django made $450m (A$646m) worldwide, while Underground was barely seen. “Would I have loved to be in the Tarantino family of actors?” he writes. “Sure, but I also know families can be overrated.” Tarantino ended up playing the Australian slave trader himself,if you’re being generous about the accent.View image in fullscreen‘You’ll never work again if you hit him’ … Anne Parillaud with LaPaglia in Innocent Blood.Photograph: Cinematic/Alamy5. He almost hit John LandisTarantino isn’t the only director LaPaglia had a falling out with. He hated working with Landis on the 1992 film Innocent Blood so much that he started having recurring dreams about the director dying violently: “What scared me most was how good I felt when I woke up from them.” While filming he even developed welts all over his body, which mystified his doctor: “I was convinced the hives were a result of intense work-related stress. I was allergic toJohn Landis.” LaPaglia even almost hit him during a disagreement over a take, but the actor Robert Loggia stopped him: “‘Don’t fucking hit him, kid,’ he breathed in my ear. ‘You’ll never work again if you hit him.’”Losing control at Landis reminded LaPaglia of his abusive father – so once shooting wrapped, he “booked a flurry of appointments” with his therapist.6. He called Harvey Weinstein a ‘prick’ to his faceWhile LaPaglia was dating “an up-and-coming young actress” decades ago, she told him “how she literally had to fight off the famed Miramax producer Harvey Weinstein when he tried to maul her in a hotel room”. Months later he met Weinstein at a charity event in Tribeca and confronted him. By LaPaglia’s telling, he called Weinstein a “prick” and told him he knew what he’d done to his girlfriend; Weinstein “smirked” and said, “What are you gonna do about it?”“I don’t have to do anything about it. It’ll catch up with you sooner or later,” LaPaglia replied, to which Weinstein retorted, “Fuck off … you’ll never work in one of my movies.”7. He’s ‘pretty much broke’ now“I never stopped spending like I had an unlimited supply of cash,” LaPaglia writes. Though he once owned houses around the world and had a taste for expensive watches, he now lives in a rented apartment in Santa Monica. “The properties I once owned have all been sold, as have the toys – the vintage motorbikes and the garage full of exotic cars. The only thing of value that remains is one Rolex watch. Other than that, I’m pretty much broke – cleaned out by three divorces and my long-term failure to take direct control of my finances.”He said after his accountant died in 2024, he had no idea where his money was – until the Internal Revenue Service caught up with him and “I realised how much trouble I was in”. He’s since paid back what he owed – but, he says, “don’t be like me”.The Life We Choose by Anthony LaPagliais published on 27 October (HarperCollins)Explore more on these topicsBooksAnthony LaPagliaTelevisionAutobiography and memoirQuentin TarantinoJohn LandisHarvey WeinsteinfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Aberfan: From Darkness to Light review – Mealor’s requiem offers hope amid the tears | Classical music | The Guardian
description: A thoughtful and moving concert – with Paul Mealor’s new choral work its centrepiece – commemorated the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster
Author: Rian Evans
Headline: A thoughtful and moving concert – with Paul Mealor’s new choral work its centrepiece – commemorated the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disaster
Content: Playful singing … children from Ynysowen Primary School and Ysgol Gymraeg Rhyd y Gru on stage for Aberfan 60 at Hoddinott Hall, Cardiff.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanView image in fullscreenPlayful singing … children from Ynysowen Primary School and Ysgol Gymraeg Rhyd y Gru on stage for Aberfan 60 at Hoddinott Hall, Cardiff.Photograph: Kirsten McTernanClassical musicReviewAberfan: From Darkness to Light review – Mealor’s requiem offers hope amid the tearsHoddinott Hall, CardiffA thoughtful and moving concert – with Paul Mealor’s new choral work its centrepiece – commemorated the 60th anniversary of the Aberfan disasterRian EvansMon 26 Oct 2026 10.36 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.44 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAconcert requiem of hope is how composerPaul Mealordescribes his new choral work Aberfan: From Darkness to Light, commemorating the 60th anniversary ofthe disaster that killed 116 children and 28 adults. Heard first in the Aberfan Community Centre with the voices of children from today’s junior schools – Ynysowen Primary School and Ysgol Gymraeg Rhyd y Grug – joining the Ynysowen Male Voice Choir, the BBC National Chorus of Wales and an instrumental ensemble, this second performance, again conducted byTimothy Redmond, had the full weight of the BBC National Orchestra of Wales. While the focus on hope coloured the whole, it was – not surprisingly – the bright, shining voices of the children, their every syllable crystal-clear, which made one well up.Setting words by Grahame Davies, whose poetic sequence of narrative and verse balanced remembrance with reflection, the piece was, at its heart, a celebration of life and the culture of the valley. Both librettist and composer were guided by Aberfan people themselves who asked that the spirit of hope and renewal be invoked, and that present and future be implicit alongside recognition of the tragic past.With Mark Lewis Jones narrating, this then was a story simply told, neither shying away from the horror, nor from pointing a finger at those who might have prevented the disaster, and remembering the heroic bravery of the rescuers and of those who perished. A lyrical melancholy – especially from cor anglais and oboe – was present in the orchestral transitions yet, overall, Mealor’s achievement was in finding musical language, often vibrantly rhythmic and percussive, to carry the different facets over a span of 40 minutes without sounding sentimental or maudlin, and making the children’s playful singing feel the most natural thing in the world. At the end, a member of the audience was heard to say that they could not have imagined the piece would have such joy.By way of preface, Anna Clyne’s This Moment – inspired by the calligraphy of the Buddhist monk, Thich Nhat Hanh – had meditated on death and life, on rain and tears. Together with movements from symphonies by Haydn and Mozart and a stirring performance of Vaughan Williams’s Toward the Unknown Region, setting Walt Whitman’s poem on spiritual death and rebirth, a concert which might only have represented grieving also invited a deeper kind of contemplation.Broadcast onBBC Radio 3on 29 OctoberExplore more on these topicsClassical musicBBC National Orchestra of WalesWalesAberfan disasterreviewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘I don’t give a damn what people think any more!’ Jimmy Webb on his wild days – and writing hits for Dolly, Glen and Frank | Music | The Guardian
description: From Wichita Lineman to MacArthur Park, he penned masterpieces. As the great hit-maker resurrects his lost songs, he recalls writing for giants – and the night Richard Harris stripped off and disappeared
Author: Dave Simpson
Headline: From Wichita Lineman to MacArthur Park, he penned masterpieces. As the great hit-maker resurrects his lost songs, he recalls writing for giants – and the night Richard Harris stripped off and disappeared
Content: ‘When I was 14, I was driving a tractor in a wheat field listening to a young Glen Campbell’ ... Jimmy Webb in 1971.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreen‘When I was 14, I was driving a tractor in a wheat field listening to a young Glen Campbell’ ... Jimmy Webb in 1971.Photograph: Michael Putland/Getty ImagesMusicInterview‘I don’t give a damn what people think any more!’ Jimmy Webb on his wild days – and writing hits for Dolly, Glen and FrankDave SimpsonFrom Wichita Lineman to MacArthur Park, he penned masterpieces. As the great hit-maker resurrects his lost songs, he recalls writing for giants – and the night Richard Harris stripped off and disappearedMon 26 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 07.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google‘Flat for 50 miles,” recalls Jimmy Webb, remembering the desolate stretch of Oklahoma that inspired his classic song, Wichita Lineman. “Nothing out there except endless railroad tracks and telephone poles. Then suddenly there’s a guy at the top of one of the poles. He’s got his phone, he’s talking to somebody and then … whoosh! He goes by. I never saw him again, but I never forgot him.”Webb immortalised the unknown telephone worker’s solitude (and imagined conversation with a distant lover) with a 1968 smash hit forGlen Campbell. “But you wouldn’t believe what some people thought it was about,” chuckles the songwriter, now a chatty, self-effacing 80-year-old, video-calling from his kitchen in Long Island. “One guy who wrote to me thought it was about a football lineman, and a woman thought the young man in the song gets electrocuted because ‘the Wichita lineman is still on the line’.”double quotation markFrank Sinatra took a drag on his Marlboro and said: ‘That song’s not quite baked yet, is it, son?’Webb also wrote By the Time I Get to Phoenix, Galveston and MacArthur Park, all 1960s classics that remain part of the culture. Only this year, Nick Cave and Flea recorded Wichita Lineman, Guns N’ Roses played it live and in February the octogenarian, who has three Grammys, was even involved in the 2026 awards after Kendrick Lamar’s TV Off, which samples a jazz version of MacArthur Park, won best rap song.View image in fullscreen‘I’m at an age where I don’t give a damn what people think’ ... Webb.Photograph: Kitty Williams“Another big moment for me was when Alysa Liu skated to an Olympic gold with MacArthur Park in the background,” smiles Webb. “She sort of took me along on this wonderful skate with her. I’m very fortunate, because I didn’t know I had a future.”He’d been “ready to hang up” his travelling shoes, “just maybe do some teaching or mentoring” when he noticed that his old friend and collaborator Art Garfunkel, 84, was booked to play the Royal Albert Hall in London. “I thought, ‘If Artie can do it …’,” Webb sniggers. So he has carried on touring and has a new, star-studded album, his first in 13 years, after producer Fred Mollin’s gentle reminder of how long it had been “hit me in the face like a cast-iron skillet”.The album, Yours for the Taking: The Found Songs of Jimmy Webb, contains new recordings of previously unheard songs that somehow got left behind when Webb was writing “three or four songs a week, too fast sometimes, but you feel the pressure of the marketplace.” That hustle left behind a trove of lost or unfinished songs that Webb felt could be improved. “Some were turned down by an artist,” he explains. “As a young songwriter, you don’t want to put those songs with your others. You want to take them outside and bury them in the back yard.”One such song, I Miss the Mistakes, was intended for Dolly Parton, while Webb originally penned the beautifully emotive Winter Clothes (sung withGraham Nash) for Frank Sinatra. “But as I was playing it to Mr Sinatra I was thinking, ‘Maybe this could be a little premature,’” the songwriter remembers. “He gently smiled, took a drag on his Marlboro and a shot of Jack Daniel’s and said, ‘Well, that one’s not quite baked yet, is it son?’ So I baked it all these years later.”View image in fullscreen‘That’s the guy I want to sing my songs’ ... Glen Campbell in 1967.Photograph: Donaldson Collection/Getty ImagesWebb, the son of an Oklahoma Baptist preacher, started writing songs for church but he talks about his subsequent celebrated career with a childlike marvel that it happened. “This sounds like something some genius publicist would make up,” he says, “but when I was 14 or 15 I was driving a tractor in a wheat field when Turn Around, Look at Me by a young Glen Campbell came on my transistor radio. There was something plaintive in his voice. I thought ‘That’s the guy I want to sing my songs.’” Six years later, by which time Webb had cut his songwriting teeth at Motown, Campbell’s recording of By the Time I Get to Phoenix sold a million copies.Webb vividly remembers how Campbell asked him for a follow-up. “He said, ‘I’ve got a pile of demos here and they’re all steaming crap,’” he smiles. “‘Could you write me another song about a town?’” Webb didn’t want to be known as “the guy who writes about towns” but wrote Wichita Lineman, which Campbell recorded before it was completed. “I said, ‘But Glen, it isn’t finished.’ He said, ‘It is now.’” Webb’s status as Campbell’s favourite songwriter was cemented by Galveston, an anti-war song penned during the Vietnam conflict. So how does one write a timeless classic?“By listening to other people’s songs and trying to copy them,” Webb shrugs. “Really, I wanted to be a film director, because all I do is watch films. I’ve had the pleasure of meeting guys like Steven Spielberg and Robert Altman and have been really surprised that they were people like me. I always thought they’d have a special aura. I think I could have made films because that’s the way I see things.” Hence his many film scores, but his pop songs haven’t done too badly.“Billy Joel used to take the stuffing out of me at the Songwriters Hall of Fame,” he remembers, and one year Joel deconstructed Wichita Lineman. “He said, ‘And I need you more than want you … that’s divorce, right?’ The audience were roaring. Then he got to ‘and I want you for all time’ and said, ‘Ultimately Wichita Lineman is about an ordinary man thinking extraordinary thoughts.’ And I got tears, you know. Some people think songwriters go around crying all the time, but most of us are lone eagles. We think of ourselves as tough but we’re not immune. Songwriting is like a hospital. We see the patients and the wounds.”View image in fullscreen‘She took me on this wonderful skate’ ... Alysa Liu celebrates winning Olympic gold skating to MacArthur Park.Photograph: Tom Jenkins/The GuardianSome of his greatest songs were driven by his own hurt. Breaking up with early love Susan Horton (who had already inspired By the Time I Get to Phoenix) fuelled 1967’s extraordinary, seven-minute MacArthur Park, which gave the legendary Irish actor Richard Harris a Top 5 hit (and Donna Summer a disco No 1 in 1978). “Richard and I were a perfect team,” Webb reflects of their two albums together. “He was like my older brother. Oh, the things we did. He showed me around Ireland during the Troubles. In Belfast we played in a club guarded by men with machine guns. I’d never had a drop of hard liquor before I met Richard, but before long I could have been on the Olympic drinking team.”One night, they were in the actor’s flat in Belgravia, central London, where Harris drank so much brandy he started taking off his clothes. “I thought, ‘I’m not staying around for how this ends’, so I went to bed,” Webb grins. Hours later, he was woken up by a cab driver, returning Harris, who was by this point wearing only underpants. “The cab driver said, ‘Excuse me guvnor, I found this gentleman on the King’s Road, where he was singing.’”Webb forged another great boozy friendship with singer Harry Nilsson, the pair even becoming embroiled inJohn Lennon’s infamous “lost weekend” bender. “You’d go out for a drink with Harry not knowing if you’d end up in Scotland,” Webb says, admitting that one of the downsides of reaching a ninth decade is outliving such gigantic figures in his life.View image in fullscreen‘He was like my older brother’ … Webb and Richard Harris in 1968.Photograph: Chris Walter/WireImage“I think about Harry twice a day, and Richard was so beyond the pale, so fearless. Sometimes, I’ll come up with a new song and for a moment I’ll think, ‘I gotta play this for Glen. Or Harry.’ And then it hits me all over again that there’s no Glen, no Harry, no Richard. But to me these people are still alive in one way or another and I think about them every day.”Webb, who has been teetotal since 2002, still likes to smell a Guinness, but concedes that getting old means “I don’t have to agonise about everything. When I was 23 I couldn’t go on stage without a couple of Jack Daniel’s and I didn’t play my first sober show until 24 years ago, but it’s made a big difference. I’m really proud of my voice now, but I used to get a lot of criticism of my singing because I was singing in some rarefied company. I’d pitch to Mr Sinatra or Tony Bennett, then I’d come out with my little midwestern squeaky voice. So I used to imbibe to build up dutch courage. Now I’m at the age where I don’t give a damn what people think about what I’m doing …” He flashes a warm smile. “But people seem to think it’s pretty good.”Today, Webb is one of the survivors of a golden age where hope, playfulness and stellar pop music became entwined. As a grandfather reflecting on decades on the planet, he argues that we have become obsessed with material things. “We’ve devalued some things that are really important and put other things in their place, which is symbolised by the leadership in my country. As an 80-year-old, I want this album to show the world that 80-year-old people can still be human beings. We can still love, can still feel and be sensitive to the plight of future generations, and we can be very active.”True to his word, he’s already written songs for another album. “Turning 80 doesn’t mean we have to sit around like lumps of coal.”Yours for the Taking: The Found Songs of Jimmy Webb is released on 23 October on Sun Records. A star-studded career celebration, Jimmy Webb: American Songwriter, airs on 30 October on PBS.
