title: As mega-hit Into the Woods wows the West End, what’s the secret weapon of this Sondheim spectacular? | Theatre | The Guardian
description: With its shimmering forest and its plunge into darkness and destruction, this fairytale romp bagged an Olivier for its lighting – and, reveals designer Aideen Malone, it wasn’t even finished
Author: David Jays
Headline: With its shimmering forest and its plunge into darkness and destruction, this fairytale romp bagged an Olivier for its lighting – and, reveals designer Aideen Malone, it wasn’t even finished
Content: Breathtaking … light breaks through the trees behind Oliver Savile and Rhys Whitfield in Into the Woods.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianView image in fullscreenBreathtaking … light breaks through the trees behind Oliver Savile and Rhys Whitfield in Into the Woods.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianTheatreInterviewAs mega-hit Into the Woods wows the West End, what’s the secret weapon of this Sondheim spectacular?David JaysWith its shimmering forest and its plunge into darkness and destruction, this fairytale romp bagged an Olivier for its lighting – and, reveals designer Aideen Malone, it wasn’t even finishedMon 26 Oct 2026 04.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 06.04 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a minute I worry that Aideen Malone might return her Olivier award. “It’s funny that I won an award for it, because I would say Into the Woods is one of the most unfinished pieces I have ever done,” declares the lighting designer. “There was a lot of detail we never got a chance to finish. We ran out of time – big time!”Luckily, the judges and audiences disagreed. If you want to see enchantment, take yourself toStephen Sondheim’s musical set in the twisted world of fairytale. Cinderella, Red Riding Hood and others bounce into the forest, which shimmers in a weave of powdery, gleaming branches and light angling through all the trees. Now transferred to the West End fromLondon’s Bridge theatre, it’s a breathtaking piece of design for a seriously playful musical.double quotation markInto the Woods offers a series of smoke and mirror surprises for which Malone uncages a misty spectrum of smoke and haze“This is a stunning piece, but it’s a monster,” Malone declares. “There was a lot of problem-solving.” From a lighting point of view, it is “about the passing of time, day and night. The woods are very luscious and inviting initially, and then become darker and more mysterious.” As tales old and new collide, and characters stumble far beyond their happy ever afters, design signposts the journey. After the initial quest into the woods, the characters return to find that arcadia has collapsed into “destruction and wasteland”.View image in fullscreenSending light through wheat fields in the Olivier-winning Fiddler on the Roof in London’s Regent’s Park.Photograph: Marc BrennerRangy and witty, the Irish designer arrives for our interview convinced that I’ll be chatting to all the “absolutely stunning” creatives behind Into the Woods; Jordan Fein (director), Tom Scutt (set) and Roland Horvath (video). “It’s a great team effort,” she insists. She previously sent light through Scutt’s wheat fields in their Olivier-winningFiddler on the Roof. Into the Woods offers a series of smoke and mirror surprises, for which Malone uncages a whole spectrum of smoke and haze: “A fog that’s quite dense but rises, and then a cool fog that stays low on the ground.” Light pierces the layers, especially when characters experience an epiphany (Red Riding Hood plucked from the wolf’s belly, Jack dismounting the beanstalk).What was her own career-setting epiphany? “Was I a little theatre kid?” she considers. “Not really.” A Dublin pantomime at an impressionable age was a turning point, while at her all-girls secondary school, the annual musical cast the tall Malone as swaggering blokes in Oklahoma! and The King and I. Acting beckoned – but her degree at Dublin Trinity and then Goldsmiths in London also covered backstage roles. “I fell upon lighting, and was definitely more comfortable with not being on the stage, collaborating with the whole team. I enjoyed how lighting is very technical and creative at the same time. I haven’t looked back since.”View image in fullscreen‘Devised work is nerve-racking’ …  A Monster Calls at the Old Vic, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianHer career in lighting began on the fringe and working on dance shows. She toured with dancer and choreographerAkram Khan, enjoying how dance let her “play with beautiful bodies in space. It’s very sculptural. Often you don’t need to worry about the faces, and you can play with angle.”View image in fullscreen‘A bit of magic’ … Aideen Malone.Photograph: Ian TaitTheatre then became her home turf. Do all directors understand lighting? “Not to name any names,” she grins, “but some are very visual, and some aren’t.” She prefers “somebody with nerves of steel who is prepared to try stuff” – like Sally Cookson, with whom she devised hit shows such asJane EyreandA Monster Calls. “Devised work is nerve-racking,” says Malone, “because you don’t know what you’ve got till the last week of rehearsals. You have to figure it out once you’re in the space.” Their2016 Peter Pan at the Nationalwas touch and go, she admits: “But we always get there for press night.”The pandemic prompted a long-contemplated masters in light and lighting at University College London. “I thought I knew a lot about colour,” Malone says, “but I learned so much about the detail of a light source, which makes a huge difference when you’re lighting skin tones.” This fascination carries back into her stage work. “Two people in daylight might look the same, but put them under theatre light and they’re quite different. One person needs 1% more magenta, and one needs 1% less. It’s a challenge.”View image in fullscreenTouch and go … Peter Pan at the National, London.Photograph: Tristram Kenton/The GuardianMalone has always been drawn to “the cool and warm natural colours of daylight” – a favourite venue is the Open Air theatre in London’s Regent’s Park, where she and Scutt designedCarouseland Fiddler. She also embraces projects blending architectural and theatrical knowhow, such as Sadler’s Wells East, which opened last year. A neon sign above the entrance proclaims: “You are welcome” – but glowing lighting through the building must sustain that welcome from morning to night.Although she is broadening her work, theatre retains its essential appeal for her. “You have a work light on and the space looks flat – then you put a spotlight on and it’s transformed. It’s a bit of magic.”Into the Woods is at theNoël Coward theatre, London, until 9 JanuaryExplore more on these topicsTheatreStagecraftStephen SondheimWest EndMusicalsOlivier awardsinterviewsShareReuse this content

title: Unions suspend planned V&A strike after improved pay offer | V&A | The Guardian
description: London sites to remain open as Prospect and PCS agree to ‘Acas-facilitated talks’ with museum management
Author: Matthew Weaver
Headline: London sites to remain open as Prospect and PCS agree to ‘Acas-facilitated talks’ with museum management
Content: V&A East in Stratford, one of the affected London sites.Photograph: Bailey-Cooper Photography/AlamyView image in fullscreenV&A East in Stratford, one of the affected London sites.Photograph: Bailey-Cooper Photography/AlamyV&AUnions suspend planned V&A strike after improved pay offerLondon sites to remain open as Prospect and PCS agree to ‘Acas-facilitated talks’ with museum managementMatthew WeaverMon 26 Oct 2026 10.25 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 10.51 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA planned strike at the V&A over half-term has been suspended after an improved offer from its management.Museum staff who were members of the Prospect and Public and Commercial Services (PCS) unions had voted to strike on Thursday and Friday in a dispute over pay and working conditions includinginadequate toilet and hydration breaks. The strike would haveclosedthe V&A’s main galleries in south Kensington, as well as V&A East, V&A Storehouse and Young V&A in east London.The strike was suspended on Monday pending last-minute talks with the Advisory, Conciliation and Arbitration Service, after the V&A management made an improved offer.In a statement PCS said it had suspended strikes planned for 29 and 30 October “to allow Acas-facilitated talks to take place, following an improved offer from the museum”. Prospect and the V&A also confirmed the strike had been suspended while negotiations continued.The unions are demanding a 4% pay increase for staff earning above the living wage, and for the V&A to become an accreditedLondonliving-wage employer within 12 months. They also want time-and-a-half pay for bank holiday working.On conditions, they are seeking improvements to working during heatwaves and better food at the museum’s east London sites. In July, when staff first voted to strike, a V&A spokesperson said “extensive measures” had been introduced to help staff during the heatwave. These included additional rest breaks and closing some galleries during the hottest periods.The dispute has previously involved two separate two-day strikes in September.View image in fullscreenV&A East Storehouse, east London. ‘All V&A museums will be open this week,’ a spokesperson said.Photograph: David Levene/The GuardianA V&A spokesperson said: “All V&A museums will be open this week, including all exhibitions, free displays and planned half-term activities. While we are working to reinstate as much of our public programme as possible, unfortunately some events may still be cancelled or postponed – visitors are encouraged to check our website before travelling.“We welcome this opportunity for constructive discussions with our trade union colleagues. Our latest pay offer delivers an average 4.18% pay rise and a 6.9% increase for our lowest-paid colleagues; increased bank holiday pay to 1.5, alongside a sector-leading bonus scheme and a subsidised food offer for staff at all V&A sites.”Paula Lamont, Prospect’s national secretary, said: “We will be entering talks in good faith and hope that a resolution to the dispute can be found.”Earlier this month, Prospect’s general secretary, Mike Clancy, called on the V&A’s director, Tristram Hunt, a former Labour MP, to get involved in the negotiations.He said: “Prospect members are dedicated to their jobs, and it is these dedicated staff who make the museum the world-class attraction it is. That Tristram Hunt can’t even be bothered to take part in the negotiations himself shows the level of disdain in which he holds his staff.”The London living wage is now £15.45 an hour. While the V&A has said all its staff are paid at least this rate, some of the museum’s outsourced contractors are not. V&A Dundee, which is not involved in the dispute, is an accredited living-wage employer.Explore more on these topicsV&AMuseumsLondonIndustrial actionTrade unionsLiving wagenewsShareReuse this content

title: Chris Brown given suspended sentence over bottle attack at London club | Chris Brown | The Guardian
description: R&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: R&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023
Content: A masked Chris Brown leaving Southwark crown court on Monday.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersView image in fullscreenA masked Chris Brown leaving Southwark crown court on Monday.Photograph: Chris J Ratcliffe/ReutersChris BrownChris Brown given suspended sentence over bottle attack at London clubR&B singer sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment suspended for 12 months over incident in Mayfair in 2023Press AssociationMon 26 Oct 2026 08.28 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 14.13 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe R&B singerChris Brownhas been given a suspended sentence after striking a man twice in the head with a tequila bottle in a central London club.Brown, 37,admitted affrayearlier this year after attacking a former friend with a “heavy” tequila bottle on the dancefloor at the Tape private members’ club in Mayfair in February 2023.Brown was sentenced to eight months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, at Southwark crown court on Monday. His vocal coach Omololu Akinlolu, 40, who joined the attack, was sentenced to four months’ imprisonment, suspended for 12 months, and both men were ordered to pay £1,500 costs.In front of a packed public gallery, the singer sat looking at the floor in the dock for much of the hearing.Judge Baumgartner called the attack “plainly dangerous” and warned that “commercial success does not attract preferential treatment” in court.In sentencing, he said: “The repeated use of a glass bottle in that way, especially aimed at the head, was plainly dangerous. It carried the risk of delivering a more serious injury than was ultimately sustained.”CCTV footage was shown in which Brown was seen striking Abraham Diaw four times with the bottle, connecting twice with his head and then hitting his shoulder.Heidi Stonecliffe KC, prosecuting, told the court Brown used a “heavy square-shaped tequila bottle” to “hit Mr Diaw twice over the left-hand side of his head”. He rained down “further blows” as Diaw turned away, the court heard.Stonecliffe said Akinlolu then grabbed Diaw in a “bear hug”. She said: “Mr Diaw falls to the ground and Mr Brown is also seen throwing punches.”In another clip, Brown, from California, could be seen being pulled away from the victim. The incident took place at about 3am and lasted about 20 seconds, the court heard.Explore more on these topicsChris BrownCrimeLondonEnglandnewsShareReuse this content

title: ‘Maxxing’ is Dictionary.com’s word of the year: ‘It’s cooler than saying you’re doing more’ | Language | The Guardian
description: As all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable - and experts predict it’s around to stay
Author: Matthew Cantor
Headline: As all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable - and experts predict it’s around to stay
Content: Guardian DesignLanguage‘Maxxing’ is Dictionary.com’s word of the year: ‘It’s cooler than saying you’re doing more’As all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable - and experts predict it’s around to stayMatthew CantorMon 26 Oct 2026 08.15 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.01 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMaxxing is not a new concept. Dungeons and Dragons players have been “min-maxing” character stats for years; Will Smith was maxin’ and relaxin’ in the 90s; as far back as the 40s, the term was used in game theory.But in the past few years, as all facets of our lives are optimized, the suffix has become inescapable. We’re personalitymaxxing to charm our peers and sleepmaxxing to get the best possible rest; the Pentagon brags about “lethalitymaxxing”.double quotation markPeople are proteinmaxxing their breakfast, tokenmaxxing their use of AI … cozymaxxing on a Friday nightSteve JohnsonThe explosion in the word’s use has made itDictionary.com’s word of the year for 2026.To choose each year’s word,Dictionary.comstaffers investigate search trends, social media and the news, “and then we ask ourselves what’s telling the most compelling story of the year”, says Steve Johnson, director of lexicography for the Dictionary Media Group. “This year, maxxing stood out because it really connects to so many different parts of life. People are proteinmaxxing their breakfast, tokenmaxxing their use of AI during the workday, cozymaxxing on a Friday night.”Who needs looksmaxxing when you’ve got Catholicmaxxing? The TikTok trend making religion great againRead moreWhile “maxxing” has been around in various forms for decades, it’s the phenomenon of “looksmaxxing” – putting your physical appearance above all other concerns, and going to extreme lengths to improve it – that has fueled the recent rise in the word’s use. The message board 4chan is responsible for a vast amount of current slang, according to the linguist Adam Aleksic, and looksmaxxing has roots in online “incel” communities that use it.But the suffix has emerged from the shadow of 4chan. As associate editor of Among the New Words, which tracks emerging terms in a quarterly journal, the linguist Kelly Wright and her colleagues havedocumented examplesof the term’s use since 1990, when it appeared in a D&D context, through looksmaxxing-related 4chan posts in the 2010s to YouTube discussions of “vibemaxxing” (“adding to my energy”) and Substack posts on “vocabularymaxxing” (“because there are some thoughts you’ll only have if you have the words for them”) in 2025.Wright sees the word as particularly creative – it can “apply to anything”.Dictionary.comdata bears this out: by August 2026, it was being used 19 times as often in digital media as its monthly average in 2025.And these days, it says far more about our social media-driven compulsion to optimize than it does about inceldom. “If there is an aspect of life that could be improved, it can probably be maxxed,” writes Jennifer Donnelly, a researcher at RCSI University of Medicine and Health Sciences, atthe Conversation.That comes with risks, she writes, as it suggests there is some kind of endpoint to the improvement process. “But health, wellbeing, social relationships and lifestyle habits aren’t really something we complete,” and maxxing can fuel “constant self-surveillance, self-criticism and the pursuit of an idealised ‘optimal’ self”.In fact, that obsession is emerging on both ends of the words we use: terms recently added to the dictionary include “prefixes that mean ‘much more’ – things like ‘hyper’, things like ‘ultra’, ‘super’”, Johnson says.The suffix benefits from being “infinitely customizable but instantly recognizable”, Daria Bahtina, a continuing lecturer in the UCLA department of linguistics, writes in an email. “You can attach the pattern to practically anything while still sounding like you are participating in a particular linguistic and cultural moment.” Saying you’re “proteinmaxxing” feels much cooler than just saying you’re eating more protein.Its popularity could also be, in part, simply related to its sound. “The sound structure of a word tells us a lot,” Wright says, “and maximalism is trending.” A similar string of sounds – “maxx” – “was maybe a little primed to get picked up”.Bahtina and Johnson agree that it’s unlikely most people using “maxxing” are thinking about any incel connections. Still, Bahtina wonders if its constant usage could help elevate its origins into the mainstream. “Someone encounters pheromone-maxxing or some other allegedly annoying but innocent version,” she writes, “and suddenly there is a linguistic breadcrumb trail into a much broader ideological ecosystem.”From hobbitmaxxing to Catholicmaxxing: how well do you know your maxxes?Read moreSo can we expect “maxxing” to stick around as a suffix – will it have the staying power of “-gate”, which has denoted scandal ever since Watergate, or will it go the way of “-licious”, which stretched from Bubblicious bubble gum to Destiny’s Child’s Bootylicious, but, as Johnson notes, has largely disappeared?It’s difficult to predict, the linguists say. Once a slang term gets a mainstream platform, it often loses its cachet. But “I don’t think it’s going to fizzle out,” says Wright. It’s not just young optimizers who’ve embraced it: “Middle-aged people really love this word. Corporate brands love this word. So it’s going to have some staying power.”Explore more on these topicsLanguageLinguisticsfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Eric Bauza, award-winning Looney Tunes voice actor, dies aged 46 | Culture | The Guardian
description: Bauza voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, along with hundreds of other characters. He died at home from hypertensive cardiovascular disease
Author: Emma Joyce
Headline: Bauza voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, along with hundreds of other characters. He died at home from hypertensive cardiovascular disease
Content: Eric Bauza at the Coyote vs. Acme Los Angeles premiere in August 2026.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Variety/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenEric Bauza at the Coyote vs. Acme Los Angeles premiere in August 2026.Photograph: Michael Buckner/Variety/Getty ImagesCultureEric Bauza, award-winning Looney Tunes voice actor, dies aged 46Bauza voiced Bugs Bunny, Daffy Duck and Porky Pig, along with hundreds of other characters. He died at home from hypertensive cardiovascular diseaseEmma JoyceMon 26 Oct 2026 02.24 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 02.26 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEmmy-award winning voice actor Eric Bauza, who was the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, has died at home from hypertensive cardiovascular disease, aged 46.The voice actor’s death was announced by his family, who shared a statement to the actor’sInstagram account. The cause of death was released by the Los Angeles county medical examiner.“Eric Bauza, Emmy award-winning voice actor and the modern voice of iconic Looney Tunes characters Bugs Bunny and Daffy Duck, along with dozens of other beloved cartoon characters, has passed away suddenly. More details to come,” his familywrote.Bauza worked forWarner BrosAnimation for 15 years and had more than 400 acting credits in his career, including voicing Porky Pig, Road Runner and Tweety.Coyote Vs Acme review – quirky comedy returns from the dead to flip Wile E Coyote’s slapstick-violent worldRead more“Eric Bauza was a unique voice talent who brought joy and laughter to millions around the world,” said Warner Bros Television Group and US Networks chair Channing Dungeyin a statement shared with Variety. “He followed in the footsteps of giants like Mel Blanc.“Eric said that carrying on the legendary legacy of the Looney Tunes was among the greatest honors of his life. In addition to his incredible talent, Eric was a treasured part of our animation family. Our hearts go out to his loved ones.”Bauza was born in Scarborough, Toronto, in 1979. Over his career he won three Emmy awards for his work on Teen Titans Go!, Bugs Bunny Builders and Looney Tunes Cartoons.This year he voiced characters in Rick and Morty, Superkitties, Minions & Monsters and Avatar: Seven Havens. At the time of his death, he was in pre-production for Bye Bye Bunny: A Looney Tunes Musical and The Dragon Masters.In August, Bauza attended the Los Angeles premiere of the live-action/animation hybrid film Coyote vs. Acme in California.Film producer, screenwriter and former voice actor Christopher DeFaria, who worked with Bauza on Coyote vs. Acme, told Variety the voice actor would be remembered for his “incredible impact”.“He’s a voiceover artist for animated characters that have historic precedents and roles, and somehow out of that, he carved out a place in this business,” said DeFaria. “And this past year, he had such an incredible impact, both on our movie, of course, but also on bringing attention to this amazing art form.”Explore more on these topicsCultureWarner BrosTelevisionChildren's TVnewsShareReuse this content

title: Bayeux tapestry becomes pop culture hit as young people more keen to see exhibition than top films | Bayeux tapestry | The Guardian
description: Monzo says 55% of its payments to British Museum in first hour of latest ticket release were by people under 35
Author: Rachel Hall
Headline: Monzo says 55% of its payments to British Museum in first hour of latest ticket release were by people under 35
Content: The museum’s second round of tickets sold out within three hours.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersView image in fullscreenThe museum’s second round of tickets sold out within three hours.Photograph: Toby Melville/ReutersBayeux tapestryBayeux tapestry becomes pop culture hit as young people more keen to see exhibition than top filmsMonzo says 55% of cardholders’ British Museum payments in first hour of latest ticket release were by people under 35Rachel HallMon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleA 1,000-year-old embroidery may be an unusual candidate for a pop culture moment, but young people are seemingly more willing to shell out for tickets for theBayeux tapestrythan spend money on Hollywood blockbusters.In the first hour that the second round of tickets toview the tapestry were available last Wednesday, payments from Monzo cardholders to theBritish Museumreached £14,100 and were 48 times that of a normal Wednesday morning. More than half (55%) of those buyers were aged under 35.This was double the opening mornings for this year’s blockbuster films: the critically acclaimedThe Odyssey, at £7,000, and the box office smash hitSpider-Man: Brand New Day, at £6,300, according to the bank’s spending data for its 16 million customers.Tickets for the Bayeux Tapestry, which is on display in England for the first time since it was taken to France in the 11th century, are significantly more expensive than the average cinema ticket, at £33 for standard adult peak tickets and £27 for off-peak. However, adjusting for the more expensive entrance fee – as well as the limited availability of tickets compared with a blockbuster movie – highlights the huge appeal of the tapestry.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toThe GuideGet our weekly pop culture email, free in your inbox every FridayEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionBayeux tapestrymania has gripped Britain. But what does it say about our own age of war and upheaval? | Charlotte HigginsRead moreAs a result, buyers spent five times more on average at the checkout than on Spider-Man’s opening morning, at £97 versus £19. By the time the Bayeux tickets had been on sale for two hours, Monzo customers had spent £30,500. Enthusiasm was such that many buyers were willing to travel from across the country for the once-in-a-lifetime event, with almost half of the buyers based outsideLondon, and the furthest purchases coming from Glasgow.Thousands joined an online queue to secure tickets when they went on sale at 10am on Wednesday, with spots selling out within three hours – beating the first wave, which sold out in 24 hours.The frenzy has drawn comparisons with big pop cultural events such as Glastonbury festival and the Oasis reunion tour. The British Museum said the response to the tapestry going on display last month had been “extraordinary”, leading it to make changes to addresslengthy queuesfor ticket holders, including banning visitors from taking photos.The exhibition has received rave reviews for its meticulous display of the woven record of the Norman Conquest, which is treasured for its impressive technical prowess, skilful storytelling and historical value. TheGuardian described itas “a stupefying, thrilling, horrifying masterpiece that shakes the earth”.Explore more on these topicsBayeux tapestryBritish MuseumExhibitionsMonzo bankLondonMuseumsnewsShareReuse this content

title: TV tonight: Idi Amin’s forced expulsion of Asians from Uganda | Television | The Guardian
description: People share their terrifying testimonies in this brilliant documentary. Plus: the remarkable stories of young people who had a stroke. Here’s what to watch this evening
Author: Hollie Richardson
Headline: People share their terrifying testimonies in this brilliant documentary. Plus: the remarkable stories of young people who had a stroke. Here’s what to watch this evening
Content: Ruling through fear … the military officer and dictator in Escaping Idi Amin.Photograph: bbc/Dragonfly Film And Tv Productions/Alamy/AllstarView image in fullscreenRuling through fear … the military officer and dictator in Escaping Idi Amin.Photograph: bbc/Dragonfly Film And Tv Productions/Alamy/AllstarTV tonightTelevisionTV tonight: Idi Amin’s forced expulsion of Asians from UgandaPeople share their terrifying testimonies in this brilliant documentary. Plus: the remarkable stories of young people who had a stroke. Here’s what to watch this eveningHollie Richardson,Jack Seale,Ali Catterall,Phil HarrisonandEllen E JonesMon 26 Oct 2026 02.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEscaping Idi Amin9pm, BBC TwoIn 1972, Uganda was home to 80,000 Asians. But 18 months after dictator Idi Amin came to power, he gave them 90 days to get out. In this deeply affecting two-part documentary, people who lived through this as children share their terrifying and complex testimonies – from curfews to daily radio countdowns, extreme street violence and abuse, and massacres.Hollie RichardsonThank You Sir Kev8pm, BBC OneRugby league legend Kevin Sinfield has raised millions of pounds for motor neurone disease since his best friend and fellow sports star Rob Burrow was diagnosed in 2019 (he died of the disease two years ago). Prince William leads the tributes to Sinfield while friends and family paint the full picture of the man and his achievements.HRClickbait Clinic with Stacey Dooley8.30pm, BBC OneDooley concludes her series on viral medical claims with the most emotive conundrum so far: can the dog deworming treatment, fenbendazole, cure terminal human cancer? Surely not, but questioning desperate people clinging to any sliver of hope is, as she discovers, not a pleasant task.Jack SealePierre9pm, Channel 4View image in fullscreenCampaigning for justice … Brenda (Cherrelle Skeete) in Pierre.Photograph: Channel 4/Olly CourtneyBrenda (Cherrelle Skeete) is arrested while fighting for justice over her nephew Michael’s death, and the more duty solicitor Pierre (David Harewood) “sniffs around”, the more resistance and threats he encounters. Meanwhile, was the attack on his son Eli a warning? “For God’s sakes, why would someone go to all this trouble to stop me digging around if there wasn’t something bigger going on?”Ali CatterallCrystal Lake9pm, Sky AtlanticWhat is a woman to do after mutilating two men to death and feeding their bodies to a bear? Go on a self-help retreat, of course! That’s what Pam (Linda Cardellini) has planned in episode two of the stomach-churning Friday the 13th prequel. Meanwhile, local cop Levon – who has the hots for Pam – finds the remains in the woods.HRTrauma: My Broken Brain10pm, Channel 4This series about young people dealing with the aftermath of strokes is a tough watch. However, seeing Dan (a dancer), Saskia (a social butterfly) and Dec (who has just begun a new relationship) deal with their changed realities is uplifting, too – the trio face a long road but their resilience is remarkable.Phil HarrisonFilm choiceBackrooms (Kane Parsons, 2026), HBO MaxView image in fullscreenTunnel vision … Chiwetel Ejiofor in a scene from Backrooms.Photograph: A24/APDirector Kane Parsons was just 20 when he shot this genre-redefining horror, based on the “creepypasta” YouTube series he had been developing since his mid-teens. Chiwetel Ejiofor stars as Clark, a failed architect who discovers an apparently endless liminal space behind the strip mall store where he works and, depressingly, also lives. Renate Reinsve is Clark’s therapist, Mary, a woman working through her own traumas around enclosed spaces, who nonetheless follows him into these backrooms to attempt a rescue. The wallpaper may be monotonously yellow, but there are scares of every shade here and, underlying it all, the heart-pounding thrill of pure originality.Ellen E JonesExplore more on these topicsTelevisionTV tonightfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li review – a virtuosic interrogation of the power of art | Books | The Guardian
description: What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality? Li examines the gulf between talent and genius through the marriage of two real-life musicians
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality? Li examines the gulf between talent and genius through the marriage of two real-life musicians
Content: Pure readerly pleasure … Yiyun Li.Photograph: Maria SpannView image in fullscreenPure readerly pleasure … Yiyun Li.Photograph: Maria SpannBook of the dayBooksReviewMusic Against the Night by Yiyun Li review – a virtuosic interrogation of the power of artWhat does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality? Li examines the gulf between talent and genius through the marriage of two real-life musiciansKevin PowerMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 03.06 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIn his recently publishedA History of the Novel in Britain, Philip Hensher makes a bold claim. Historical novels, he tells us, don’t last. However popular and prestigious a historical novel might be in its day, it will almost always get thrown overboard as the ship of literary culture sails on, piled high with novels of contemporary life. He might be on to something. Who now prefers Walter Scott to Jane Austen? The historical novel risks a double obsolescence, courting a future in which it has become an old-fashioned vision of an old-fashioned time.However much this news might dismay writers of historical novels, Hensher is untroubled: “As readers enjoying our contemporaries, we should not let our readerly pleasures be affected by the probability of ultimate oblivion.” Will the future, what there is of it, rate Wolf Hall as highly as we do? It doesn’t matter. Posterity, as Gore Vidal once wrote, is “a permanent darkness where no whistle sounds”. What matters is us, now, what we make of history and of our lives – in our novels and elsewhere.Posterity and its ironies form a central theme of Yiyun Li’s new historical novel. In several senses Music Against the Night isn’t, in fact, “a historical novel” – certainly not in the supermarket-own-brand sense of a cosplay adventure in which affable protagonists find themselves chatting with Byron or whoever. Readers of Li will already know that she soars far above the well-meant strivings of lesser writers, occupying a luminous realm of her own. She has the craft that makes craft invisible, and the art that makes art itself her obsessive subject. In Music Against the Night the art is music, as perceived through the lives, and the real and hoped-for afterlives, of two musicians.Real musicians, as it happens: a married couple, bound by a “contrapuntal fate”. The pianist and composer John Field, born in Dublin in 1782, is now remembered as the inventor of the nocturne, the form perfected by Chopin. There is a room in the National Concert Hall in Dublin called The Field Room. But to listen to Field’s nocturnes when you know Chopin’s is to ponder the gulf between talent and genius. In Li’s telling, Field himself compulsively ponders this gulf, as he becomes “a footnote in the life of Frédéric Chopin”. Li knows that footnote status is the fate of most artists. What does it cost, to live your life in the hope of immortality?In 1807 Field, by then living in Moscow, took on a student named Adelaide Percheron, an orphan raised by her grandmother in Pondicherry, French India. Adelaide too was a gifted musician, but her ambition was thwarted by the patriarchal strictures of the society into which she was born. John and Adelaide (she was known as “Percherette”), separately wrestling with the enemies of promise, married in 1810. It was not an auspicious union.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. Literary delights delivered direct to youEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotiondouble quotation markLi has the craft that makes craft invisible, and the art that makes art itself her obsessive subjectThe ordinary historical novelist starts there, and labours through the tempestuous marriage: Field’s drinking, his affairs, Percherette’s despair. But Li’s subject isn’t marriage. Music Against the Night is about the relationship between life and art; about what it means to sacrifice a life to art; and about what exactly is sacrificed, when such a sacrifice is made. Field and Percherette’s marriage is given to us in brief Muriel Spark-like flash-forwards. Long sections, split between Dublin and Pondicherry, follow Field and Percherette closely through late childhood and early adolescence; this is the bulk of the book. Childhood, for both, is short. Both are prodigies: Field on the pianoforte, Percherette as a kind of psychologist, perceiving the hidden truths of human behaviour. What they share is a “willingness to be rescued from an ordinary childhood”.Li’s narration is unapologetically omniscient, but she has no use for pastiche: she acknowledges she is writing in the 2020s, and yet there’s no historical-novel clutter about horses or furniture. Only that which impinges on her characters, or her theme, is noted. Her narrator is insistently aphoristic: “To be known is the desire that drives much of the world’s progress, also much of its destruction. History is a discourse against obscurity.” Not all the aphorisms work: “an absent anchor only further disturbs an unmoored heart”. But many of them are superb: “Talent, vision, luck, work – all are necessary for a career, but not sufficient. An artist falls short if he cannot master the art of indifference.”Engaged in their separate discourses against obscurity, John and Percherette fail to master the art of indifference. Their passionate self-scourgings form a counterpoint to the eerily calm and patient gathering-in effects of Li’s prose. The result is pure readerly pleasure – posterity (and this might be what Li, in this novel of half-forgotten artists, is suggesting) be damned.Late in the novel there is a brief reflection on the loss of a child. Li herself, of course, haswritten about the loss of her two sons, Vincent and James, to suicide. The subject is not dwelt on at length in Music Against the Night. It forms merely part of a piercing argument about the passions of life versus the austere and indifferent values of art. The aphoristic narrator remarks: “Death is a subject that rewards minor artists.” But “Life? It requires major talent to convey that.” Li conveys life without apparent effort. Major is the word.Music Against the Night by Yiyun Li is published by 4th Estate (£20).To support the Guardian, order your copy atguardianbookshop.com. title: War Is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman review – are we on the brink of world war three?  | Politics books | The Guardian
description: A foreign affairs expert’s bleak assessment of the state of global security
Author: Charlie English
Headline: A foreign affairs expert’s bleak assessment of the state of global security
Content: A tactical military exercise in Tainan, Taiwan, 2026.Photograph: Cheng Chia Huang/Getty ImagesView image in fullscreenA tactical military exercise in Tainan, Taiwan, 2026.Photograph: Cheng Chia Huang/Getty ImagesPolitics booksReviewWar Is Interested in You by Gideon Rachman review – are we on the brink of world war three?A foreign affairs expert’s bleak assessment of the state of global securityCharlie EnglishMon 26 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAre we on the brink of a new world war? This bleak subject is increasingly invoked by leaders, soldiers and officials, from Donald Trump to Vladimir Putin to the heads of our military and intelligence services. It’s an urgent theme, then, for the FT foreign affairs columnist Gideon Rachman to explore in his latest survey of global diplomacy. Rachman draws his title from the expression, sometimes attributed to Trotsky: “You may not be interested in war, but war is interested in you” – the idea being that conflict doesn’t much care whether we like to think about it or not: it will come knocking on our doors regardless.Clearly, humanity is in a particularly unsafe spot right now, but seeing our security issues laid out like this, catalogued and mapped and analysed, they seem almost overwhelming. To summarise: the most powerful, nuclear-armed states – the US, China andRussia– are led by unscrupulous, self-dealing “strongmen”, each of whom is playing with the nationalist “Great Again” politics epitomised by Trump. Democracy is being rolled back around the world, and even bastions of liberalism such as the UK, France and Germany seem vulnerable to takeover by the Putin-friendly far right. The so-called rules-based international order and its institutions – the UN, the WTO, Nato – are being deliberately undermined by the aforementioned strongmen, and are as weak now as they have ever been.double quotation markOf all the potential flashpoints, it is Taiwan that may offer the fastest route to a world warPutin has described the new world order with the term “might makes right”, and the result is that conflicts have been breaking out at a rate unprecedented in the postwar era. According to Rachman, there were 61 in 2024 alone, and 11 full-blown wars. This included Gaza as well as some conflicts far less visible in the west, such as the one in Sudan, which by mid-2025 had led to 150,000 battlefield deaths. In 2026 many “state-based conflicts” are ongoing, including the largest land war inEuropesince 1945 (in Ukraine) and the most disruptive in the Middle East for more than 20 years (Iran). Although these are mostly confined to their regions, they have begun to overlap and spread, as Russia deploys North Korean troops and tests Nato’s resolve, Iran throttles global shipping, and Ukraine advises Gulf states on drone use. And even as these grind on, others threaten to explode, including between India and Pakistan, North and South Korea, and China and Taiwan.Of these potential flashpoints, it is Taiwan that may offer the fastest route to a world war, since it could bring China and the US into direct conflict. For decades, Taiwan’s security was guaranteed by US naval superiority; now Beijing, after a massive military buildup, has more warships than Washington. It’s said that the single Chinese shipyard on Changxing Island has more capacity than all US yards combined. Still, Xi Jinping knows that if the US comes to Taiwan’s aid, the result would be a bloodbath, which is why US presidents have mostly been keen to emphasise the US’s commitment to Taiwan. But Trump has been far more ambivalent – declaring in May this year, for instance, that “I think the last thing we need right now is a war that’s 9,500 miles away” – which only increases the risk of China attempting an assault.It’s here, in the shifting power balance between China and the US, that the root of the new global insecurity lies. Whatever you think of American hegemony, the US maintained a sort of stability, after the cold war, in which victims could plausibly appeal to international law. The 2003 invasion of Iraq destroyed that system, and US failure there and in Afghanistan persuaded future presidents against intervention. Three times, between 2012 and 2015, Obama chose not to step in to address illegal acts by the Assad regime, Russia and China, which signalled an American retrenchment. The Trump administration has taken this further, reverting to the kind of isolationist, tariff-based protectionism that postwar institutions such as the UN security council and WTO were built to avoid. It’s hard not to spot echoes here of the 1930s – the time, incidentally, when the slogan “America first” was popularised.How to offset these risks? Rachman surveys a handful of mechanisms that have helped maintain the peace, and finds them wanting. The rules-based international order, for instance, barely functioned in its heyday; now, as Mark Carney put it plainly, it “no longer works”: we are living through a “rupture”. What about spreading democracy and economic stability as a path to peace – a principle exemplified by the “Golden Arches” theory, which states that no two nations with McDonald’s will wage war on each other? There’s no comfort here either, as that was proved wrong in the 1990s, and the number of democracies has been declining steadily since 2006. Then there’s deterrence, which still by and large keeps us safe. But it hasn’t stopped fighting between nuclear-armed India and Pakistan, and China and North Korea are rapidly expanding their atomic arsenals.What we’re left with, then, as American primacy declines, is a global version of Trump’s “Donroe doctrine”, in which each major power gets a “sphere of influence” where they call the shots. In this scenario, Washington rules over the Americas, Beijing over east Asia, and Moscow the old Soviet zone. Clashes are sorted out by one-to-one conversations between authoritarian leaders. But what if these rulers fall out? And anyway, who wants to live in the shadow of an overbearing neighbour?While the outlook of War Is Interested in You is undoubtedly gloomy, Rachman’s book is not. His writing is engaging and anecdotal, and he brings vast experience to bear on a vital subject. He won’t go so far as to say a new world war is inevitable, but the threat is becoming impossible to ignore.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |WeeklySign up toBookmarksDiscover new books and learn more about your favourite authors with our expert reviews, interviews and news stories. title: ‘Nothing worked for me until I was clean and sober’: Ashley Walters on acting, directing – and turning his life around | Movies | The Guardian
description: In Adolescence he proved himself one of the UK’s best actors. Now he has directed his first film, Animol. He reflects on the road from prison and addiction to soaring success
Author: Steve Rose
Headline: In Adolescence he proved himself one of the UK’s best actors. Now he has directed his first film, Animol. He reflects on the road from prison and addiction to soaring success
Content: ‘I’ve got eight kids, three grandkids, I’m paying a mortgage!’ … Ashley Walters.Photograph: Jamie Salmons/The GuardianView image in fullscreen‘I’ve got eight kids, three grandkids, I’m paying a mortgage!’ … Ashley Walters.Photograph: Jamie Salmons/The GuardianThe big interviewMoviesInterview‘Nothing worked for me until I was clean and sober’: Ashley Walters on acting, directing – and turning his life aroundSteve RoseIn Adolescence he proved himself one of the UK’s best actors. Now he has directed his first film, Animol. He reflects on the road from prison and addiction to soaring successMon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 11.52 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleAshley Walters seems to have lived his life on fast-forward. Before he turned 21 he had already had a No 1 hit, performed on TV and the West End stage, become a father and served seven months in prison. He has had another lifetime’s worth of incident since – including seven more children – but at the ripe old age of 44, enough water has passed under the bridge for Walters to have some perspective on his youth. Not that all that living appears to have left a mark: when we meet in London, he’s the picture of health, his face unwrinkled, eyes twinkling, hair cut in a crisp lineup.Back in the early 2000s, he fit a certain stereotype of Black British youth as Asher D, the rapper from deprived and supposedly crime-ridden Peckham, who rolled with the street-tough So Solid Crew, got into beefs with east London rivals such as Dizzee Rascal, was demonised by the tabloids andcalled a “boasting macho idiot rapper” by the then culture minister Kim Howells.So Solid Crew were trailblazing in terms of British hip-hop, but Walters’ view of those times is far from rose-tinted. “Everything other than the music, it was bad, it was negative,” he says. “The music was very British, but if you looked at our style, our clothes, the jewellery, the cars, that was all the Americanised stuff that we wanted to bring into it.” That also included guns – even if, in Walters’ case, the firearm was a modified air pistol.Asher D was never really him, he says. “Behind the scenes, in all honesty, I was questioning if I was doing the right thing. Because a lot of our success was underpinned with street stuff: you can’t go to that area because you might get shot; you can’t do this because that person has had beef with this person; and it was, like, all this politics.”He’d got in with the wrong crowd, he suggests, “and it took me down the road of just not giving a shit any more … but the realisation came to me when that door was shut in the prison cell. And I was like: ‘Hold on. How the f– did I get here?’”View image in fullscreen‘I wanted it to feel, look and sound the way it felt, looked and sounded to me’ … Walters on the set of Animol.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/SkyWe’re talking about his prison days because Walters is now revisiting them, from the other side of the door. He has just directed his first film, Animol, which is set in a young offender institution. It is by no means autobiographical (it was written by Nick Love, of Football Factory fame), but he says that a lot of it is based on his own experience and memories of being locked up. “I wanted it to feel, look and sound the way it felt, looked and sounded to me.”This is a genre that comes with certain expectations: brutality, bullying, staff-inmate relations, internal hierarchies. Animol meets many of them.The tension winds up from the first scene, when the story’s 15-year-old protagonist, Troy (Tut Nyuot), is coerced into smuggling in a phone. But the film also defies those expectations in surprising ways, not least with a queer romantic element that’s sensitively and sensuously handled. In that sense, it’s as muchMoonlightas Scum – “slightly elevated,” as Walters puts it. “I didn’t want it to feel grey and gloomy like the other prison-genre films.”Like Walters in his youth, these young men are playing roles, Animol suggests, concealing their authentic selves in order to navigate a landscape of fear, shame, trauma and codes of masculinity that has really changed very little over the years. “Every character in there, no matter how bad they are, no matter how manipulative or violent even at times, all of their actions are born from fear,” he says. “The idea a lot of people grow up with, like I did, of masculinity: being hard, never backing down, stoic, keep your emotions to yourself and never cry in front of other people. I was brought up with those rules and those regulations.”View image in fullscreenMarginalised … Tut Nyuot as Troy in Animol.Photograph: Anthony Dickenson/SkyTroubled young men, masculinity, fathers and sons – one way or another, these have become recurring themes in Walters’ career. There’s a continuity, I suggest, between Animol and his recent role in the highly acclaimed Netflix drama Adolescence. He anchored the second episode as the investigating detective visiting the perpetrator’s school, seeking answers. The technical aspect alone was a ballet dance – Walters had to hit multiple marks as the one-take episode roved around a chaotic secondary school – but on top of that, he delivered a soulful, understated performance as a father struggling to connect with his teenage son.It’s not a link he would make himself, Walters says, “but the theme, I guess, that runs through it is uncovering a marginalised group of people. And in the UK one of the biggest marginalised groups is kids.” And especially young men. “Over the years we’ve been pushed into repression and keeping your mouth shut, not questioning things and not having conversations with your friends and your peers about how you feel about life … Men just don’t do that. I think women find that a lot easier. That’s why we find we have a lot higher suicide rates, especially in young men in the UK.”View image in fullscreenFathers and sons … Amari Jayden Bacchus as Adam Bascombe and  Walters as DI Bascombe in Adolescence.Photograph: Ben Blackall/NetflixWalters’ own struggle through this territory would make for a movie in itself. He was mainly raised by his mother, Pamela, who worked in local government. She enrolled him at the Sylvia Young Theatre School aged seven (as a child actor, he performed in the stage version of Oliver!, had a role in Grange Hill and studied ballet and tap).His father was mostly absent, Walters says. “He’d turn up one Sunday and then you wouldn’t see him for four months. And then he’d try and take me out, and then not take me somewhere and get drunk instead, and then I’d have to come home by myself.” He died in 2005, by which time they had made their peace. “He wanted to be a dad; he just didn’t have the tools and the resources. And he didn’t have the best start in his own life.” Born in the UK to Jamaican parents, Walters’ father was put in care, and was in and out of borstal, then prison, his whole life.So when that prison door slammed on Walters in 2002, he felt as if he was repeating the cycle. Except he was a celebrity, so all the other inmates knew who he was. When he arrived that first night, “all hell broke loose”. For hours, people shouted insults, and threatened to kill him in the morning.“It wasn’t a pleasant experience at all,” he says. “I was tried, I was tested, it was pressure, there was loads of fear. But I had no choice. It’s an experience I had to go through, and actually it was one of the best things that happened to me.”How so? “It pushed me to the thoughts I needed to have: who do I want to be? What do I want from life? And then, looking around me and seeing my circle of friends and entrusted loved ones, do they reflect that? And the answer was a big resounding no.”He was in effect starting again. “When I came out of prison, I didn’t know what I was going to do with my life, and a lot of doors were shut.” His music career had ground to a halt; he didn’t have an acting agent; he was not allowed to travel to the US owing to his conviction. Fortunately, the British film-maker Saul Dibb had written a role with him in mind: Bullet Boy, the story of a young ex-con returning to a very familiar set of troubles: guns, local rivalries, council estate life.View image in fullscreenBreakthrough role … Walters, 21, in Bullet Boy.Photograph: AccuSoftThe film, and Walters’ performance, werewidely praisedand his acting career hit its stride: shows such as MTV’s stoner sitcom Top Buzzer; a part in 50 Cent’s biopic Get Rich or Die Tryin’; the adaptation of Andrea Levy’s immigrant drama Small Island. Then in 2011 came the role that pushed him into the mainstream: as Dushane in Channel 4’s Top Boy, chief drug dealer on his Hackney estate, whose quest for bigger and better things takes him on what becomes an epic journey.As with So Solid Crew,Top Boywas accused of glamorising crime and violence, but Walters disagrees. The show went deeper in terms of character, morality and complexity, he argues. Many of the storylines and characters were based on real people and events. “It came from the source, so it felt real and rich,” Walters says. “Our whole thing was, we wanted the drug dealers to like it. If the drug dealers call us and go, ‘Bro, that’s the first time I’ve seen myself portrayed properly,’ then the rest should fall in place.”View image in fullscreenAs Dushane in Top Boy.Photograph: Chris Harris/NetflixIt wasn’t just the drug dealers; Top Boy became a global hit – and people still identify him with the role. “A lot of the time, if I walk down the street, my name’s Dushane. I spend a lot of my time having to tell people that stop me: I’m a 44-year-old man. I’m not even a ‘boy’ any more. I’ve got eight kids, three grandkids, I’m paying a mortgage! Like, I’m really not in that life.”After Top Boy, his next act was something of a breakthrough, albeit a tainted one from today’s perspective. Bulletproof was a buddy cop series that unprecedentedly featured two Black leads: Walters and Noel Clarke. The two of them spent years trying to get the series made, pitching it as a British Bad Boys, and being told it could only work if one of the characters was white. When it came out on Sky in 2018, the show was a success, running for three seasons, but it was cancelled after allegations against Clarke came to light in April 2021.At the time, Walters put out a statement saying his thoughts were with the women who had made the allegations. He and Clarke have not spoken since, he says. “But I don’t want to hate on anyone. Everyone has got their own journey and everyone has their own story to tell, and I think when they are ready to tell it, they will tell it.”View image in fullscreen‘It’s no coincidence that my life’s changed, like, amazingly.’Photograph: Jamie Salmons/The GuardianWalters had been going through his own struggles around that time. He had been an alcoholic and a drug user – predominantly cocaine – for about 15 years, and things had come to a head a few months before, in November 2020.“Maybe in the first year, alcohol and substances were great,” he says. “They helped me perform, they helped me be more lively at parties and network with people that I was shit-scared to talk to before.”Does he mean performing on set? “Performing on set I was freer, maybe wilder – who knows how I looked at that point? I felt I was doing a good job and giving people what they wanted, but the truth is, very, very quickly it stopped working, and started to hold me back.”The breaking point came during lockdown, after an argument with his wife about his drinking and drug use. He had been married to Danielle, the mother of his four youngest children, since 2013 (his eldest child is now 27, his youngest 10).He immediately sought help. “The next morning, my wife dropped me at rehab and I was there for four weeks, came out and I’ve never drunk or drugged since and it’s coming up to six years in November. So, very thankful for that. Sad it took me so long to get there, and there’s a lot of amends to make with family and kids and friends, but one of the best things I’ve ever done.” He also moved out of London in 2021, and now lives on the Kent coast. “In the last six years, it’s no coincidence that my life’s changed, like, amazingly. The truth is, nothing started working for me until I was clean and sober.”View image in fullscreenWalters and Stephen Graham at Netflix’s Golden Globe afterparty in January.Photograph: Gonzalo Marroquin/Getty Images for NetflixThat includes his sensitive turn in Adolescence, and his new career as a director, which began with a short film in 2021, Boys, then episodes on multicultural school drama Ackley Bridge and underrated Victorian crime series A Thousand Blows. The latter came thanks to his old friend Stephen Graham, who starred and co-produced the series – they’ve been mates since the 2004 sitcom Top Buzzer. After that, Graham cast him in Adolescence. Graham now plays the welfare officer in Animol. He gives the young inmates a stirring talk about shame that ends the film on a cathartic, hopeful note.“This is a tender, tactile sort of film where you’re seeing men hold each other – even the ones that are not gay, they’re embracing each other,” Walters says. “There’s love, and I’m like that with my friends. I kiss my friends on the cheek, my stepdad will give me a kiss, I still kiss Mum, I’ll kiss my kids. I wanted to show that on screen, like how boys are with each other, even in the worst environments, even when they’re going through the worst things.”The theme resonates with Walters, of course, but this is also him challenging those codes of masculinity and male relationships that shaped his own life, and his father’s, and many others besides. “I realised that vulnerability is part of a man’s DNA as well,” he says. He’s breaking the cycle.Animol is out on 30 October in the UKDo you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
