title: ‘Vicarious wish-fulfillment’: why That Thing You Do! is my feelgood movie | Tom Hanks | The Guardian
description: The latest in our ongoing series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films is a journey back to the 90s for Tom Hanks’ heartfelt 60s-set music comedy
Author: Stephen Snart
Headline: The latest in our ongoing series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films is a journey back to the 90s for Tom Hanks’ heartfelt 60s-set music comedy
Content: The cast of That Thing You Do!.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyView image in fullscreenThe cast of That Thing You Do!.Photograph: Photo 12/AlamyMy feelgood movieTom Hanks‘Vicarious wish-fulfillment’: why That Thing You Do! is my feelgood movieThe latest in our ongoing series of writers explaining their most rewatched comfort films is a journey back to the 90s for Tom Hanks’ heartfelt 60s-set music comedyStephen SnartMon 26 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on Google“How did we get here?” That’s the question Steve Zahn’s character in That Thing You Do! asks his bandmate with bemusement right before they perform on live television.It’s a moment I have thought of many times over the past 30 years. Sometimes, it’s been a moment I’ve aspired to, and sometimes it’s a moment I’ve felt myself. When the band hears their song on the radio for the first time, it’s one of the most ebullient moments I’ve ever seen on film. There is a euphoria that is recognizable for anyone who has ever felt the joy of a creative accomplishment – and isn’t that all of us, in one way or another? That’s what makes That Thing You Do! my feelgood movie.‘A beautiful dismantling of cynicism’: why Galaxy Quest is my feelgood movieRead moreIn 1996,Tom Hankswas on top of Hollywood. He had back-to-back best actor Oscar wins, and two of 1995’s highest-grossing films with Toy Story and Apollo 13. I presume he could have done anything he wanted. I will be forever grateful that he chose to write, direct and co-star in this modest, gentle ode to 1960s pop music. It’s a movie of such warmth that any scene viewed at any time will instantly make me happier.The fictional pop band at the center of the film is named the Wonders. Taking inspiration from the Beatles, they initially spell their name as the Oneders, but are forced to change when they repeatedly get introduced as the “oh-need-ers”. The band soar to fame when Guy Patterson (Tom Everett Scott) sits in as drummer and spontaneously ups the tempo of their song, That Thing You Do!. The song quickly garners the attention of local restaurateurs, promoters and, soon enough, a record producer named Mr White (Hanks).The song drives the plot and is also the film’s superpower. Written by the late Adam Schlesinger of Fountains of Wayne, That Thing You Do! plays constantly throughout the movie and you’re always happy to hear it.The film itself resembles the fast beat and breezy melody of its title track as it zips through its 108-minute running time. Their record climbs the charts and opportunities present themselves at a dizzying speed that suggests their success will never let up. But creative tensions, unhappy relationships and professional callings get in the way, threatening to end their run as quickly as it started. And, indeed, they do.I think that’s what makes this film so special. It offers vicarious wish-fulfillment but doesn’t shy away from sobering reality. There isn’t the blissfully happy ending that I’d instinctually consider necessary for a feelgood movie. Instead, wistfulness takes the lead and you’re more likely to feel a tiny lump in your throat than a tap in your toe. When things fall apart, it’s an undeniable sting, but it’s not a mortal wound the way it is in most cautionary tales of show business. There’s a big beating heart in this movie that shares clear-eyed wisdom in a way that is funny, cheerful and encouraging.In a recent interview, Matthew Rhys said that the advice he received from Hanks was “this too shall pass.” This was given as a reminder for both the bad days and the good days. That same sense of humility pulses through That Thing You Do!.There is also a sense of kindness throughout. There are no real villains here. Jimmy, the brooding talent, could be the villain, but he has a point with his self-righteousness. There’s also the superficial Tina (Charlize Theron) who is uninterested but never cruel. Or the comically hard-nosed dad (Holmes Osborne). Even the grotesque Sol Siler (Alex Rocco), who couldn’t care less about the music, still gets credit for making things possible as the head of the record label. They all have a purpose and identity. They receive a little ribbing, but also grace.The feelgood vibes are also fueled by the charming camaraderie of the band, the effervescence of Jimmy’s girlfriend Faye (Liv Tyler) and Hanks himself, who could have played this over-the-top or completely straight but instead delivers both laughter and poignancy while never overshadowing the cast.Hanks seemed so old to me when I saw this at 11. Now, I think he looks so young. He was around 40 at the time he made this, which is roughly my current age. The ending used to sting me more than it does now. I used to think: “If only this character had done that, the band could have stayed together.” But now I watch it, and it’s as if Hanks is quietly saying: “Between fame and happiness, choose happiness.”Mr Hanks, I hope you’ve found both. This is my way of saying thank you for giving us this cinematic gift. May this “onederful” film bring joy to many more generations.That Thing You Do! is available on Pluto in the US, to rent digitally in the UK and to watch on Disney+ in AustraliaExplore more on these topicsTom HanksMy feelgood movieComedy filmsDrama filmsComedyCharlize TheronfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Never After Dark review – ghostbuster-for-hire meets her match in Japanese exorcism horror | Movies | The Guardian
description: Shogun’s Moeka Hoshi stars as a travelling caster-out of ghosts who confronts a wounded and recalcitrant spirit in this inventive chiller
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: Shogun’s Moeka Hoshi stars as a travelling caster-out of ghosts who confronts a wounded and recalcitrant spirit in this inventive chiller
Content: Spontaneity and intelligence … a scene from Never After Dark.Photograph: Blue Finch Film ReleasingView image in fullscreenSpontaneity and intelligence … a scene from Never After Dark.Photograph: Blue Finch Film ReleasingMoviesReviewNever After Dark review – ghostbuster-for-hire meets her match in Japanese exorcism horrorShogun’s Moeka Hoshi stars as a travelling caster-out of ghosts who confronts a wounded and recalcitrant spirit in this inventive chillerLeslie FelperinMon 26 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 09.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleIf you watched this Japanese-language ghost-story horror thriller cold, you might be a little surprised that the credits reveal that the director is one Dave Boyle – and not someone fromJapan, so steeped is it in Japanese lore and culture. It turns out that Boyle has been interested in Japan for a long time, and even wrote, directed and starred in the 2006 feature film Big Dreams Little Tokyo, about an American sharing a flat with an aspiring sumo wrestler.More recently, Boyle was a key director-producer for the Netflix series House of Ninjas, and Never After Dark seems to have evolved as a spun-off side hustle between Boyle and Ninjas star Kento Kaku, who produced it and takes a supporting role.That all goes a little way to explain how this ends up feeling like a larky, low-stakes, one-for-funsies exercise – inventive and full of charm even if the scares are sort-of predictable.Shogun’s Moeka Hoshi stars as Airi, a young woman who looks like a hipster with her torn jeans and raggedy haircut and who travels the country in her Volvo as an itinerant ghostbuster for hire. The ghost of Airi’s dead older sister Miku (Kurumi Inagaki) is always by her side but is only visible in mirrors (as per folklore), and is available to give advice about imminent danger and vibes in the spirit world.Airi’s latest gig is to exorcise a spirit haunting what used to be a hotel in the sticks. New proprietor Teiko (Tae Kimura) has been hearing bumps in the night and getting creepy phone calls that are either from spirits or perverts, or possibly both. Teiko’s son Gunji (Kaku) is less convinced there’s a supernatural explanation but he takes a shine to Airi all the same, especially when it is revealed that they share a taste for niche music.Soon Airi works out that the apparition wandering the corridors and scrabbling at the wainscoting is a man with a gruesomely smashed jaw (Mutsuo Yoshioka), and she can interact with him on the astral plane via a ritual involving a candle, burnt offerings of her own hair (thus the shaggy hairstyle), and aphenakistoscope, a 19th-century persistence-of-vision toy, which in this case depicts a spirit rising from a body. But getting the smashed-mouth spirit out of the house proves to be anything but the run-of-the-mill exorcism Airi expected.Boyle and his collaborators deploy charmingly old-school physical effects, the sort of thing actual phenakistoscope users might have been impressed by in films by the likes ofGeorges Méliès. It’s mostly a matter of camera angles capturing faces in mirrors and reflections, wire work and well choreographed use of body doubles. The old school vibe makes this particularly endearing, even if the characterisation isn’t especially complex or nuanced, but Hoshi brings a spontaneity and intelligence to the lead role that is consistently winning.Never After Dark is on digital platforms from 2 NovemberExplore more on these topicsFilmHorror filmsJapanAsia PacificreviewsShareReuse this content

title: All About the Money review – confusion and compelling weirdness of wealthy leftwing heir  | Documentary films | The Guardian
description: This profile of James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, who set up a commune in rural Massachusetts and is fighting extradition from Spain, is a brave attempt to package a complex character and story
Author: Leslie Felperin
Headline: This profile of James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, who set up a commune in rural Massachusetts and is fighting extradition from Spain, is a brave attempt to package a complex character and story
Content: A confused soul … Fergie in All About the Money.Photograph: Publicity imageView image in fullscreenA confused soul … Fergie in All About the Money.Photograph: Publicity imageDocumentary filmsReviewAll About the Money review – confusion and compelling weirdness of wealthy leftwing heirThis profile of James ‘Fergie’ Chambers, who set up a commune in rural Massachusetts and is fighting extradition from Spain, is a brave attempt to package a complex character and storyLeslie FelperinMon 26 Oct 2026 05.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 05.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleFor a film that dispenses a lot of backstory information via intertitles, you are left with a lot of questions when the credits finally roll. For example, how in the world did Irish film-maker Sinéad O’Shea gain access to her main subject: James Cox Chambers, AKA “Fergie”, the American heir to a multimillion-dollar fortune – whom we first meet as the founding member and bankroller of a communist community of less than a dozen people in Alford, a town in rural Massachusetts. A scion of the wealthy Cox family, a liberal clan who have backed leftist causes in the past, Fergie wants to take things even further politically and is willing to use his own hefty inheritance (about $250m) to support his fellow communards’ commitment to learning, self-sustaining farm work and running a jujitsu studio and gym that won’t accept members of the police as members.But when the group decide to protest at Elbit Systems, the Israeli-owned arms manufacturer, its actions slide into “criminal mischief and criminal trespassing”, according to reports. Several Alford members are arrested, including one Paige Belanger; O’Shea’s film cuts back and forth between interviews with Belanger and other communards and Chambers, who has scarpered to Tunisia. Although he pays for Belanger’s defence and covers other costs arising from the action, considerable rancour rises between Fergie, Paige and other former Alford community members, that O’Shea perhaps wisely doesn’t let the film get too bogged down with trying to parse.Nevertheless, O’Shea’s admirable attempt to not take sides leaves a muddle of sorts at the centre of the story, making it unclear who or what is the real subject of the film. We are left with a messy tangle of historical fact, colourful personalities and dramatic biographies that could have made a longer film. But any way you slice it, Fergie –whose extradition to the US from Spain is being sought over his alleged support for Hamas– comes across as a compellingly weird character, a confused soul who covers himself in tattoos, discourse and delusions to hide a considerable amount of pain stemming from a traumatic adolescence. Sure, it would be easy to sneer at him and say poor little rich boy, but there’s something about his struggle for authenticity that feels timely and significant in these complex times.All About the Money is in UK and Irish cinemas from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsDocumentary filmsIsraelPalestineMiddle East and north AfricareviewsShareReuse this content

title: Ever Since I Knew Myself review – confronting the scars of childhood | Movies | The Guardian
description: Maka Gogaladze’s debut feature looks at generational differences in the context of Georgia’s education system and emphasis on collectivism
Author: Phuong Le
Headline: Maka Gogaladze’s debut feature looks at generational differences in the context of Georgia’s education system and emphasis on collectivism
Content: Disciplined atmosphere … Ever Since I Knew Myself.Photograph: True StoryView image in fullscreenDisciplined atmosphere … Ever Since I Knew Myself.Photograph: True StoryMoviesReviewEver Since I Knew Myself review – confronting the scars of childhoodMaka Gogaladze’s debut feature looks at generational differences in the context of Georgia’s education system and emphasis on collectivismPhuong LeMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe scars imprinted on impressionable young minds can never fully fade away. Aiming her lens at a rocky beach thrashed by crashing waves, Maka Gogaladze opens her intimate film with a painful anecdote from her adolescent years. Through on-screen texts against a stormy sky, the Georgian film-maker recalls the time she dumped all of her poems into the garbage. The impulsive decision was a gesture of rebellion against her domineering mother; Gogaladze had wanted her to feel guilty.This debut feature would appear, at first glance, to be another act of revolt. Putting her mother in front of the camera, Gogaladze asks probing, at times blunt, questions about the strict education thrust on her in childhood. Together, they talk about piano lessons that ended in tears, and tough academic exams that continued to haunt the director well into her adulthood. Their contrasting personalities are fascinatingly revealed across these conversations in all their tension, yet these sequences also represent a moving effort to reach across generational differences.Gogaladze widens the frame to include a series of observational vignettes shot at various children’s classes in Georgia. The subjects vary – history lessons are sandwiched between ballet and dance sessions – yet the disciplined atmosphere remains the same. Even during art class, teachers leave little room for individual expression or debate. Obedience, rather than dialogue, is the order of the day.At times, the transition between Gogaladze’s personal story and these external sections feels jarring, requiring extra layers of contextual information. Still, it shows that the film is interested in more than just education. For a nation that has undergone invasion numerous times, it is perhaps understandable that Georgia would place such an emphasis on collectivism. Under pressure to uphold a homogenous national identity, however, childlike wonder and innocence is in danger of being lost permanently.Ever Since I Knew Myself is on True Story from 30 OctoberExplore more on these topicsFilmDocumentary filmsGeorgiaFamily filmsParents and parentingFamilyEuropereviewsShareReuse this content

title: The Pianist review – Władysław Szpilman’s Holocaust memoir retold with his own music | Musicals | The Guardian
description: This adaptation is perhaps too smooth but is well-staged and performed, and draws strong feeling from the pianist’s compositions
Author: Arifa Akbar
Headline: This adaptation is perhaps too smooth but is well-staged and performed, and draws strong feeling from the pianist’s compositions
Content: Chamber piece … Daniel Krikler as the Polish pianist Władysław Szpilman and Mischa Jardine as Janina in The Pianist.Photograph: Richard SouthgateView image in fullscreenChamber piece … Daniel Krikler as the Polish pianist Władysław Szpilman and Mischa Jardine as Janina in The Pianist.Photograph: Richard SouthgateMusicalsReviewThe Pianist review – Władysław Szpilman’s Holocaust memoir retold with his own musicPark theatre, LondonThis adaptation is perhaps too smooth but is well-staged and performed, and draws strong feeling from the pianist’s compositionsArifa AkbarMon 26 Oct 2026 01.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThe idea of turning the survival story of the Polish pianist Władysław Szpilman into a musical might, on paper, seem distasteful given the stark subject matter of the Holocaust. There is risk of triteness, too, in the light ofRoman Polanski’s acclaimed film, starring Adrien Brody,based on Szpilman’s celebrated memoir.But those who are acquainted with both those retellings of Szpilman’s second world war experiences will still find something new and affecting here. The form of the musical becomes meaningful through its use of Szpilman’s own compositions. Thom Southerland, who has adapted Szpilman’s book and directs, creates an atmospheric chamber piece, with actors playing instruments, including a piano that twirls on and off stage.View image in fullscreenOut of body experience … Malcolm Forbes-Peckham as Szpilman’s wartime self with Krikler, and Oliver Grant as Hosenfeld.Photograph: Richard SouthgateSzpilman (Daniel Krikler, elegantly otherworldly) is narrating his own story, seeing not just the ghosts of his family drift back to life but also himself (played by Malcolm Forbes-Peckham, the show’s musical director). This wartime self is always before the piano, playing Chopin (Nocturne in C-sharp minor) and Szpilman’s compositions, as Krikler’s haunted version watches on. It is a good way to portray out of body experience; he is a man removed from himself, judging himself, too.Not all the songs suit the subject matter; there is a warm, nostalgic 1930s glow to some numbers that show Warsaw just before and after its surrender, when Szpilman is working for Polish radio. Music accompanies the story in a way that verges on sentimental.View image in fullscreenAn exceptionally musical family … Krikler with Szpilman’s mother, played by Rosalind Ford.Photograph: Richard SouthgateThe piece is too smooth, the savagery of the world outside Szpilman’s own seen only in glimmers. But that is also the point, especially in the first part when we see the exceptionally musical family to which he belonged, from Szpilman’s father (TJ Holmes), who uses his cello to escape reality, to his quietly determined mother (Rosalind Ford) and brood of siblings. The actors are accomplished musicians and strong in their roles.Family of man who inspired The Pianist film win defamation appealRead moreSzpilman’s arguments with his brother Henryk (Nitai Levi) too emphatically hash out the question of an individual’s responsibilities in wartime: whether to resist and protest, as Henryk would have it, or to stay together and just survive, as Władysław does for the main. The place of music is also tacitly explored, though again this could be more penetrating.The production is good at drawing out class distinctions and the family’s privilege at this point, as well as Szpilman’s survivor’s guilt. It shows effectively the slide into totalitarianism, with denials and disbelief, even as the family’s world narrows. The scene when Szpilman separates from them, just as they arrive at Auschwitz, is terrible, the back wall of Andrzej Goulding’s set design suddenly resembling a cattle truck. There are other chillling moments: when he sees a boy bludgeoned to death; when the person who has been hiding him orders him to leave his home.The pace just slackens too much in the second half when Szpilman is alone and in hiding. The musical interludes seem protracted, perhaps because Szpilman’s music is being honoured in fullness. It is still a handsomely orchestrated production, and moving, too, when finally Krikler sits down to play the piano himself in Out of the Darkness. A survivor, finally inhabiting his music.AtPark theatre, London, until 28 NovemberExplore more on these topicsMusicalsTheatrereviewsShareReuse this content

title: Mac DeMarco review – glowing melodies and shirtless antics at Carnegie Hall | Mac DeMarco | The Guardian
description: After winning over gen Z, the cult indie rocker makes the historic venue swoon with introspective anthems and a Michael Jackson cover
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: After winning over gen Z, the cult indie rocker makes the historic venue swoon with introspective anthems and a Michael Jackson cover
Content: Mac DeMarco performs at Carnegie Hall.Photograph: Adela LoconteView image in fullscreenMac DeMarco performs at Carnegie Hall.Photograph: Adela LoconteMac DeMarcoReviewMac DeMarco review – glowing melodies and shirtless antics at Carnegie HallCarnegie Hall, New YorkAfter winning over gen Z, the cult indie rocker makes the historic venue swoon with introspective anthems and a Michael Jackson coverLarry FitzmauriceMon 26 Oct 2026 12.27 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 15.30 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleMore than 68 years afterLeonard Bernstein’s first-ever Young People’s Concert, Carnegie Hall was yet again overrun with youthful energy on Sunday night. The occasion was the first of two sold-out performances from gap-toothed indie-pop scionMac DeMarco, whose adoringly parasocial cross-genre fanbase has been one of the few in 2010s indie to continue an increasingly aged-down trajectory. There was many a parental chaperone next to their beaming teens, while a group of bright-eyed and bushy-tailed post-adolescents sitting behind me – having travelled all the way from Wisconsin for the occasion – audibly Googled: “Where to find Mac DeMarco after the concert” and quizzed each other on whether they’d lay a smooch onThe 1975’s devilish frontman Matty Healy if given a chance.Super Graphic Spectacular review – Chappell Roan dazzles at her gloriously gay mini-festivalRead more“I can’t believe how fancy this place is for Mac,” one of them marveled – and it has indeed been a strange trajectory for DeMarco, who emerged from the shores of Vancouver in the early 2010s resembling a party-hardy modern-day Pigpen and with an aural suitcase stuffed with lovely guitar-warbles, stained with nicotine and carrying the faint stink of cheap brew. His early live sets were equally prone to Limp Bizkit covers and spontaneous audience makeout sessions; the 2014 docu-shortPepperoni Playboywas replete with scenes of new-indie-money dirtbag opulence, as DeMarco and his ragtag group drank champagne out of lobster shells and went cliff-diving amid a nonstop tour schedule.But as with many aspects of popular culture, Covid represented a turning point for DeMarco’s career. Afforded with his first real sense of downtime in nine years, he sobered up (yes, cigs included) and receded from the public spotlight for several years, allowing his back catalogue to resonatevirallyand otherwise before returning to proper songcraft with last year’s fine-feathered Guitar. DeMarco’s 2020s output has often taken a prolific and largely subdued turn; his 2023 compilation One Wayne G ran nearly nine hours long, while this year saw the official release offourlargely instrumental albums that radiated a mature, monastic beauty.View image in fullscreenMac DeMarco performs at Carnegie Hall on Sunday.Photograph: Adela LoconteDeMarco has, undoubtedly and somewhat improbably, grown up – and in the moments before he and his band took Carnegie’s tony and iconic stage, it was certainly fair game to question whether he’d clean himself up further for such a serious-seeming venue. Fear not: DeMarco and co’s two-and-a-half-hour set was a spring-loaded outing for indie’s reigning court jester. There were thrills, spills and shirtless reveries in the form of a surprisingly radiant cover of Michael Jackson’s Human Nature (which fellow joking-not-joking provocateur-of-the-moment Nathan Fielderjoined him on stagefor in Los Angeles just several weeks ago). Mac may have settled down in regards to his personal life, but he’s more than happy – knowingly so, even – to continue playing the giddy fool, and the audience eats it up in kind.Ironically, this current tour, an exhaustive and career-spanning showcase that even prompted its star to mock-apologize two-thirds of the way through, makes a very serious case for DeMarco as one of the 21st century’s most impressive and deeply felt pop songwriters. Aside from the ruminative melancholy that runs through even his most energetic tunes, the glowy guitar-and-keys fantasias contained within his catalog remain unmatched despite the legion of imitators, and Carnegie Hall proved the perfect venue for driving home his textural genius. The fat globs of melody that open Passing Out Pieces, from 2014’s breakthroughSalad Days, were practically hair-raising in their pronounced nature; a slowed-down take on the smoke-’em-if-you-got-’em tribute Ode to Viceroy (its tempo set to match the set’s more mellow midsection) was richer than a slice of tres leches with ice-cream on top.With a collection of tunes like DeMarco’s, extended goofs and acrobatic stage antics are rendered unnecessary; nevertheless, during a beefed-up take on One Wayne G’s straight-and-simple love song I Like Her, the man of the hour reassembled a mic stand to function as a track-and-field hurdle, unsuccessfully clearing it and crashing to the ground. Several songs later, he stalked the back of Carnegie’s cavernous stage like an apex predator before returning to his mic-stand foe and, to much applause, clearing the jump with ease.Cyndi Lauper on fun, fashion and freedom of expression: ‘We have braces on our brains’Read moreHis stage banter was frequently delivered in a voice resembling late Hollywood spook-meister Vincent Price, and at one point he gave the microphone to an audience member to ask them how comfortable the seats were. (More comfortable than Radio City Music Hall, in case you were wondering.) Several songs – including the title track of his twilit 2017 masterpieceThis Old Dog– were dedicated to his own canine pal, the improbably named Buck Naked DeMarco; later in the set, DeMarco rhapsodized on visions of “a trough filled with chopped cheese meat” and, strikingly, engaged in some quasi-Oedipal reflection mirroring the plight his millennial cohort perpetually faces: “I wish to be a small crying baby, to crawl back into the mother … to be born, again.”There persists the question as to whether DeMarco’s unabashed onstage silliness has kept him at arm’s length from being taken seriously by more discerning music listeners. But, for now, his fans are still making their voices heard when it comes to what they expect from him, in a very literal sense. “Do a flip!” a male concertgoer in the orchestra seats hollered during a quiet moment; “Do you think I’mableto do a flip?” DeMarco seriously asked, before performing a perfect cartwheel to a rapturous reception. “I want to be your pig,” he gamely grunted after catching his breath. Fair enough.Explore more on these topicsMac DeMarcoPop and rockNew YorkfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Igor Levit: Resistance album review – essential listening in a time of bullies and despots | Classical music | The Guardian
description: The German pianist performs these works by Beethoven and Schoenberg – linked by Napoleon – with his characteristic exquisite touch, in interpretations full of poetry
Author: Clive Paget
Headline: The German pianist performs these works by Beethoven and Schoenberg – linked by Napoleon – with his characteristic exquisite touch, in interpretations full of poetry
Content: Never afraid to stick his head above the parapet: Igor Levit performs at the Southbank Centre in April 2025.View image in fullscreenNever afraid to stick his head above the parapet: Igor Levit performs at the Southbank Centre in April 2025.Classical musicReviewIgor Levit: Resistance album review – essential listening in a time of bullies and despotsLevit/Kammerakademie Potsdam/Manacorda/Lyssewski(No Silence/Sony)The German pianist performs these works by Beethoven and Schoenberg – linked by Napoleon – with his characteristic exquisite touch, in interpretations full of poetryClive PagetMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 03.02 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleResistance is one of the inaugural offerings on Igor Levit’s own label,No Silence Records, released in collaboration with Sony Classical. Never afraid to stick his head above the parapet, the German pianist has chosen two works exploring ideas of human resilience in the face of political power, with Liszt’s transcription of Beethoven’s Symphony No 3, the Eroica, rubbing shoulders with Schoenberg’s Ode to Napoleon. The link, of course, is the French general whose self-proclamation as Emperor caused a disgusted Beethoven to scratch the forrmer’s name from the front page of what was to have been his Buonaparte Symphony.View image in fullscreenIgor Levit: Resistance album cover.Levit rightly sees Liszt’s piano realisation as a masterwork in and of itself and his dramatic interpretation is full of poetry, often surprisingly gentle, and with breathtaking pianissimos. When required, there’s no shortage of firepower, but at its heart is the long, drawn-out funeral march, an aching lament for the passing of a great soul. It’s here that Levit, whose finely balanced touch is exquisite, gets to the beating heart of the matter.The Ode to Napoleon, Schoenberg’s thinly veiled condemnation of Hitler, features a commanding Levit alongside Kammerakademie Potsdam under Antonello Manacorda. Byron’s sardonic text is delivered in lacerating English by German actor Dörte Lyssewski. In a time of bullies and despots, this is essential listening.Allow content provided by a third party?This article includes content hosted onembed.music.apple.com. title: ‘Meet my new après buddies!’: a joyous group skiing trip in Les Deux Alpes, France | Skiing holidays | The Guardian
description: One large ski chalet in the French Alps and 17 strangers. An organised trip for solo travellers is a leap into the unknown
Author: Guardian staff reporter
Headline: One large ski chalet in the French Alps and 17 strangers. An organised trip for solo travellers is a leap into the unknown
Content: Some of the chalet group.Photograph: Andrew DayView image in fullscreenSome of the chalet group.Photograph: Andrew DaySkiing holidays‘Meet my new après buddies!’: a joyous group skiing trip in Les Deux Alpes, FranceOne large ski chalet in the French Alps and 17 strangers. An organised trip for solo travellers is a leap into the unknownAndrew DayMon 26 Oct 2026 03.00 EDTLast modified on Mon 26 Oct 2026 06.15 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleEveryone had their reasons for joining the trip. Louisa from south London was putting her life back together after a split from her partner; first-timer Tim was strapping on ski boots following years of hesitation; and Lexi from Bristol had a classic case of the non-skiing boyfriend.I was there because I needed a ski gang. None of my friends ski, and my brother was out of action with an injury. Not only that, I needed a good night’s sleep. I love my two-year-old son dearly, but I have somehow spawned an insomniac – still waking four times a night. Weary from bedtime battles, Holly, my partner, bluntly pointed out we could both benefit from “a temporary break from family life”. In other words: separate holidays.Holly arranged a walking trip with friends; I opted for a week’s skiing in the French ski resort of Les Deux Alpes withFriendship Travel, a specialist operator in solo travel for more than 20 years. They find a chalet, fill it with solo skiers, provide travel, most meals and group ski lessons – that’s the basic service.View image in fullscreenThe chalet.Photograph: Andrew DayWe were staying in a comfortable, largeish chalet just back from the resort’s mile-long drag. Entering a group holiday with strangers is a leap into the unknown. I was greeted by Sam and Mike, our (thankfully) low-key hosts, shown to my private room (you can save by bunking up with a same sex stranger), then introduced to my fellow holidaymakers. It turned out that there were 17 of us – nine women, eight men – and we were whisked into the lounge for a briefing and welcome drink. The atmosphere was upbeat and easy, and we gathered round one large table for an excellent three-course dinner.double quotation markWhat was once viewed with hesitation is now celebrated, and solo holidays have become one of the fastest-growing segments in the industryMost Friendship Travel guests are aged between 35 and 65, and our group was at the top end of that range. There was Vivienne, a retired nurse from Cumbria who had just lost her partner, and Adriana, a “silver splitter” relishing retirement. For a few – myself included – it was the first such holiday, but many were inveterate solo travellers, with Ivyon, a former production operator from Bridgend, clocking up more than 90 trips.The first morning, we set off to our ski lockers at the bottom of the slopes (tip: I booked my equipment hire in advance, saving €40). The group naturally fragmented, allowing small cliques to form – people relaxed as they started to identify potential après buddies.I skied with Elaine, Clemmie, James and our guide, Luke, in the “level 4 advanced” group (we were asked to rate our ability beforehand). The backbone of Les Deux Alpes, the new Jandri 3S cable car, whisked us up to an altitude of 3,200 metres in 17 minutes – instead of the previous 40. Above broken clouds, we paused to admire the astonishing jagged peaks of theÉcrins national park.View image in fullscreenAndrew, Luke, James, Elaine and Clemmie.Photograph: Andrew DayWe blasted down a mixture of broad blue and red runs, plus some not overly challenging blacks. Although none of us had met before, we quickly settled into a rhythm, looking out for one another as the snow fell softly. There’s safety in numbers, especially on the off-piste sections. “I’d never have tried that alone,” said Clemmie.double quotation markAt times, group etiquette could be a minefield: is it rude to always sit in the same seat at breakfast?Afternoons brought more skiing, followed by hands-in-the-air après atSkandal– reopened in 2025 following an extension – with a DJ on a packed terrace. Around sundown, the chalet WhatsApp group would start to ping. “Polar Bear Pub, anyone?” would be a typical message, often sent by Mícheál from Armagh, a dependable partner for a pint.skip past newsletter promotionFree newsletter |Twice a weekSign up toThe TravellerGet travel inspiration, featured trips and local tips for your next break, as well as the latest deals from Guardian HolidaysEnter your emailSign upafter newsletter promotionSolo travel has undergone a perception shift in recent decades, according to Colum McLornan, who founded Friendship Travel in 1999. “Travelling alone was often seen as unconventional, and for many it carried a stigma. But travellers are increasingly seeking independence, flexibility and personal growth. What was once viewed with hesitation is now celebrated, and solo holidays have become one of the fastest-growing segments in the industry,” he said.View image in fullscreenClemmie, Elaine and Andrew hit the slopes.Photograph: Andrew DayAt times, group etiquette could be a minefield: nobody likes waiting for latecomers (me); is it rude to always sit in the same seat at breakfast? (probably); is it OK to peel away from the group and ski by oneself? (up to a point); will I look like a skinflint if I buy my own wine? (absolutely, but life’s too short for plonk).Honourable mention to Steve, a jolly retired doctor from north London. I enjoyed his vivid stories of cruising the Yangtze River, and skiing with his father in Austria during the late 1950s. Despite our age gap, we struck up a bond that lasted all week. Naturally, not all guests are interesting and fun. One seemingly endless dinner conversation about printer cartridges had me dreaming of Netflix in my room.Then, suddenly, I found myself hugging my ski gang goodbye, bound for the train. Would I go solo again? Yes. Our hosts were helpful without being intrusive, the skiing superb (especially the high-altitude stuff on Glacier de Mont-de-Lans) and I met people I will stay in touch with. Best of all, I finally got some sleep.The trip was provided byFriendship Travel. A seven-night packagewith a private room in a shared chalet, daily breakfast and afternoon tea, dinner with wine on five evenings, and six days of group ski lessons inLes Deux Alpes, costs from £1,820pp. Return rail travel from London to Grenoble was provided byEurostarExplore more on these topicsSkiing holidaysFrance holidaysGroup tripsEurope holidaysAlps holidaysfeaturesShareReuse this content

title: Georgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for crab and spring onion fried rice | Food | The Guardian
description: So good that I make this comfort blanket once a week
Author: Georgina Hayden
Headline: So good that I make this comfort blanket once a week
Content: Georgina Hayden’s crab and spring onion fried rice.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and Prop Styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex JorgeView image in fullscreenGeorgina Hayden’s crab and spring onion fried rice.Photograph: Yuki Sugiura/The Guardian. Food and Prop Styling: Aya Nishimura. Food styling assistant: Alex JorgeQuick and easyFoodGeorgina Hayden’s quick and easy recipe for crab and spring onion fried riceBatch-cook a load of rice, cool it, then whip up this comforting shellfish fried riceGeorgina HaydenMon 26 Oct 2026 09.00 EDTSharePrefer the Guardian on GoogleThis gently seasoned rice has become such a comfort blanket that I now make it at least once a week at home. That’s quite surprising, really, given that I’m guilty of drowning most of my food in chilli crisp oil, but this rice is so delicate yet flavourful that it’s just the gentle hug I need. The key is to cook the aromatics slowly and quietly in the oil, to soften and infuse, but not colour too quickly. Cook the jasmine rice in advance, if you like – it fries better once it has been cooked and cooled. Alternatively, packs of pre-cooked microwave rice work brilliantly.Crab and spring onion fried ricePrep10 minCook15 minServes44 tbsp neutral oil4 garlic cloves, peeled and finely sliced30g ginger, peeled and cut into thin matchsticks1bunch spring onions, trimmed and cut into 1cm slices500g cooked jasmine rice¼ tsp white pepper2 tbsp fish sauce1½ tbsp soy sauceSea salt2 large eggs, whisked150g white crab meatPut the oil in a wok or large frying pan and add the garlic, ginger and spring onions. Pop on to a low heat and leave for eight to 10 minutes – you want to infuse the oil slowly, so the spring onions turn tender and the garlic and ginger are lightly golden. Turn up the heat to medium-high, add the cooked rice and fry for a minute. Stir in the white pepper, fish sauce and soy sauce, and fry for two minutes, so it’s all combined and the rice is piping hot.Season the whisked eggs and pour over the top of the rice. Give them a minute to start setting, then drag the eggs through the rice – you don’t want clumps of egg, rather a ripple of it throughout the dish. Fork through the crab meat, cook for a further minute, then take off the heat. Check the seasoning, and add more salt, soy or fish sauce as you wish. Serve straight away.The Guardian aims to publish recipes for sustainable seafood.
